11548-mcclure-s-magazine-december-1895:
McClure's Magazine for December 1895 opens with Ida M. Tarbell's life of Abraham Lincoln, second in the series, covering Indiana, removal to Illinois, and Lincoln starting out at twenty-one. A flatboat trip to New Orleans, work as a grocery clerk in New Salem, and his first vote follow.

Tarbell stresses a father with no settled purpose, a pioneer community of makeshifts, and a boy's determination to make something of himself and to learn. Later pieces in the number turn to fiction, with a girl on a ship's deck urging a sick man to walk. The Lincoln serial anchors the issue.
15887-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
The American Missionary for March 1895, volume forty-nine, number three, published by the American Missionary Association at Bible House, New York, at fifty cents a year. Field notes open the number, with the question, Are they grateful? Pioneer missionaries in Africa and among Indians, both illustrated, follow. Secretary Beard reports a southern journey.

Tillotson at Austin, Texas, illustrated, shows the school work, while deaths of Dr. Taylor and the Reverend C. C. Painter mark losses. Southern field notes, a schoolboy's composition, and women's state organisations fill the rest, with receipts at the end. The issue gives mission work in 1895 as its friends saw it: schools, churches, and faithful service.
18001-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
April 1895 brought volume forty-nine, number four, of The American Missionary, the monthly of the American Missionary Association in New York. The issue cost fifty cents a year, and it spoke to friends of the Association's schools and missions across the South and West.

Its pages note the death of Frederick Douglass, the prosperity of the South, and work at Tougaloo University in Mississippi and the Lincoln Memorial schools. Notes from Indian and Chinese missions, and a bureau of woman's work, fill out the issue. It is a useful window on mission work in the 1890s, told by its own earnest editors.
19903-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
The American Missionary for May 1895 is volume 49, number 5. Its front matter lists auditors like Peter McCarter of Bible House, New York. The executive committee includes William Hayes Ward and Charles L. Lyman. District secretaries cover Congregational House in Boston and La Salle Street, Chicago. The American Missionary Association ran this monthly for its supporters. Names and offices fill these administrative pages.

Such lists map a national benevolent machine. The Association's schools served freedpeople across the South. Its magazine reported fields from Dakota to China. May 1895 catches the organization mid-stream, fully staffed. Researchers trace personnel through pages like these. The issue is a brick in a large archive.
22810-midnight-in-beauchamp-row-1895:
A bag stuffed with bank notes sits at the center of Midnight in Beauchamp Row, a short mystery tale dated 1895. Ned brings the money home, and his wife begs him not to leave her alone with it for the night. Their maid Tennie has gone off for a holiday, so the house stands empty except for the couple and the cash.

Fear does most of the work in the telling. Every sound in the dark house raises the stakes, and the wife's dread turns an ordinary evening into a vigil. Readers get a compact crime story built on suspense rather than gore, the kind of tale that filled magazines of the period. It rewards anyone who likes a tight plot, a house at night, and money that invites trouble.
23629-the-riddle-of-the-rocks-1895:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this 1895 story among the Great Smoky Mountains, where two great tilted blocks of sandstone stand alone on a treeless bald. To Roger Purdee, a mountain man raised on Bible stories and local lore, they can only be the stone tables of the Law. Moses flung them down in anger, and left them where they fell on a Tennessee peak.

The tale follows Purdee's fixed belief and the people around him who humor, doubt, or share it, all rendered in the speech and slow rhythms of mountain life. It is less a puzzle to be solved than a portrait of faith, place, and the way an isolated community reads its own landscape as scripture.
23630-the-phantoms-of-the-foot-bridge-18:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this eighteen ninety five ghost tale at a little foot bridge across a narrow gorge. It is two hewn logs with a cedar pole handrail, spanning dark, rocky depths where a swift mountain stream runs strong. Flimsy to the eye, it serves well enough for ordinary use, and certainly for the imponderable travellers said to frequent it.

Roxby warns his companion that few folk come this way now, except to ford the creek below. Haunts and unlikely creatures have been seen crossing the foot bridge, which bears a name for being tolerably unlucky. His listener, with his own reasons to recoil from death, draws back. Craddock builds dread from gorge, stream, and talk, making a fine mountain ghost tale where a bridge joins the living and the dead.
23631-the-moonshiners-at-hoho-hebee-fall:
Charles Egbert Craddock placed this 1895 story at a little schoolhouse in Holly Cove, high on a ridge above the Great Smoky Mountains. The school's site frames the whole tale. Endless blue ranges rise around it, a river gorge lies below, and seasons paint the landscape in turn, from spring's tentative green to winter's sepia tones.

Against that backdrop, mountain families, a schoolteacher, and the illicit stills of the title cross paths, with dialogue written in the region's own speech. Readers meet folk learning their letters in fits and starts, proud parents, and neighbors who know each other's business, in a story that values place and voice as much as plot.
23632-way-down-in-lonesome-cove-1895:
Charles Egbert Craddock set this eighteen ninety five cove tale on one memorable night in Lonesome Cove, where the county ranger faces a crisis in his life. Time is reckoned by sun and routine in the primitive household, and it is late. An old crone nods over knitting in the chimney corner, small children sleep crosswise in a trundle bed, and hickory logs burn asunder.

The ranger covers embers with ashes to keep fire till morning. His wife, faded and grown early old, brings a stone jar of yeast to the hearth lest it take a chill. Craddock writes the cove with rich dialect and close domestic detail, as a night's small acts carry a man's fate. Readers who love mountain fiction will enjoy the tale's quiet tension, where a hearth, a jar, and a late hour hold a life's turning point.
23633-his-day-in-court-1895:
Charles Egbert Craddock opened this 1895 story on a hard Smoky Mountain winter giving way to spring. Snow still lies on the treeless domes, and a tallow candle flickers in a log cabin window. Inside, a gruff voice scolds Steve, and the cabin stands in unusual disarray, signs that something out of the ordinary is afoot for its household.

The title gives the shape of the tale: a mountain man must answer for himself before the law, and the story follows his household's worry, talk, and preparation for that day. Told in Craddock's rich mountain dialect and landscape prose, it is a short, vivid slice of Appalachian life at the mercy of courts and weather alike.
26794-the-american-missionary-volume-49-:
February 1895 brought volume 49, number 2 of the American Missionary Association's monthly, printed at Bible House in New York and sold at fifty cents a year. Its contents list opens with a roster of mission field workers and a report on Howard University at McIntosh, Georgia. It continues with a financial statement for Lincoln Memorial Day and portraits of Lewis Tappan and the Honorable William Jackson. A long list of field workers fills the middle of the issue, with receipts closing it on page 80.

Reports inside cover the S'Kokomish mission and its record among Indians, the trials of missionary life, gospel changes at Grand View, Tennessee, and gleams of sunshine in Chinese mission work. The issue also prints the Association's officers, from president Merrill E. Gates down through its district secretaries in Boston, Chicago, and Cleveland.
31698-a-history-of-nineteenth-century-li:
George Saintsbury's History of Nineteenth Century Literature, covering 1780 to 1895, was published by the Macmillan Company at New York and London in 1906, with copyright in 1896. Saintsbury was professor of rhetoric and English literature at the University of Edinburgh, and his history runs in twelve chapters and more. It treats the literature of a long century, from the late eighteenth century into the eighteen nineties.

The book surveys poets, novelists, and critics in order, and it weighs movements and reputations with a critic's judgment. Saintsbury's history remains a readable guide to the century's writing, written by a scholar who knew the field at first hand.
32943-harper-s-round-table-april-30-1895:
This weekly issue of Harper's Round Table, dated April 30, 1895, gathers stories, history, and pastimes aimed at young readers of the day. Its lead piece, by Theodore Roosevelt, retells the Battle of New Orleans, following the British force from its landing in the Mississippi Delta to its defeat before the city. The account stresses bold leadership, hard fighting, and the pride of a young republic standing its ground.

Around that centerpiece the issue offers the usual mix of a boys' magazine of the period: tales, sketches, puzzles, and notes on sport and the outdoors. Read now, it doubles as a window on what editors thought American youth should admire and enjoy in 1895, from heroic history to clean adventure, all sold for five cents a copy.
32957-harper-s-round-table-may-7-1895:
The May 7, 1895 number of Harper's Round Table leads with Theodore Roosevelt's account of Anthony Wayne at Stony Point. Roosevelt presents Wayne as one of the hardest fighters of the Revolution, second as a general only to Washington and perhaps Greene. Roosevelt retells the daring night attack that earned him the name Mad Anthony. The piece aims to fix Wayne in young readers' minds as a model of courage.

The rest of the weekly keeps the magazine's usual pace, with stories, notes, and amusements for boys and girls. Taken whole, the issue shows how a leading magazine of the 1890s taught history: not through dry dates, but through heroes, battles, and vivid praise. It remains a lively sample of what American children were given to read each week for five cents.
32961-harper-s-round-table-may-14-1895:
Harper's Round Table for May 14, 1895 puts naval history first, with Theodore Roosevelt on the fight at Hampton Roads. Roosevelt argues that the Civil War sea battles mark the break between old and new naval war, ending two and a half centuries in which wooden sailing ships fought broadside to broadside. The clash of ironclads at Hampton Roads, in his telling, changed what a warship was and how wars at sea would be fought.

Beside that history lesson the weekly offers its usual stories and features for young readers, keeping instruction inside entertainment. The issue is a good example of Roosevelt's early popular history: clear, opinionated, and eager to show readers why a single battle mattered. It also preserves the look and voice of a boys' magazine at the end of the nineteenth century.
32970-harper-s-round-table-may-21-1895:
The May 21, 1895 issue of Harper's Round Table opens with Theodore Roosevelt on the death of Stonewall Jackson. Roosevelt sets Jackson's end against the wider horror of a war that set brother against brother, yet argues that both sides left the nation richer in memories of courage. His portrait stresses Jackson's valor and the grief his loss brought, even to those who fought against his cause.

The rest of the number carries the magazine's usual mix of stories and pastimes for young readers, balancing a somber history lesson with lighter fare. Read as a whole, the issue shows a boys' weekly trying to teach national memory without hiding the war's cost. It is a vivid, opinionated sample of how the Civil War was presented to children a generation after it ended.
32976-harper-s-round-table-may-28-1895:
The May 28, 1895 Harper's Round Table leads with Theodore Roosevelt on the charge at Gettysburg. Roosevelt opens at the peak of Confederate fortune after Chancellorsville, follows Lee's army north into Pennsylvania in June 1863. Roosevelt recounts how hopes of invasion broke on July 4, when Gettysburg was lost and Vicksburg fell in the west. He sets some seventy thousand Confederates against about ninety thousand Union men, both sides seasoned veterans.

The rest of the weekly mixes stories and amusements for young readers around that sober centerpiece. Roosevelt's history is direct and partisan in the manner of his Heroes of America series, praising valor while marking a turning point. The issue as a whole shows a children's magazine teaching the Civil War through its most famous battle, in language meant to stir as well as inform.
32999-harper-s-round-table-june-4-1895:
Harper's Round Table for June 4, 1895 leads with Theodore Roosevelt's Flag-Bearer, a piece on Civil War courage measured in loss. Roosevelt notes that no war since Napoleon had fought so obstinately and bloodily. He adds that praise for the Guards at Inkerman, the Light Brigade, and German troops at Mars-la-Tour and Gravelotte was well deserved. Yet over one hundred and twenty regiments from both armies each took heavier losses in one battle than any English regiment suffered at Inkerman or elsewhere in the Crimea.

The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers, keeping history beside entertainment as the magazine always did. Roosevelt's argument is characteristic: valor proved by endurance and by the price paid. The issue stands as a vivid example of how a boys' magazine of the 1890s taught the Civil War, through regiments, flags, and the men who carried them forward.
33010-harper-s-round-table-june-11-1895:
Harper's Round Table for June 11, 1895 opens with Saved by a Carcass, a whaleman's yarn by W. J. Henderson. On the forecastle deck, Farmer Joe stretches in the shade, sets his pipe going, and asks Handsome what happened after he got back to his own ship. Handsome, glad to return to the Ellen Burgee, begins a tale of whaling voyages and a narrow escape.

The yarn's title hints at the strange rescue at its heart, and Henderson tells it in the talk of sailors, with smoke, sea, and shipboard humor. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that centerpiece. The issue is a good sample of a boys' magazine using a sailor's voice to teach adventure, and it preserves the flavor of whaling life as older sailors told it.
33025-harper-s-round-table-june-18-1895:
Harper's Round Table for June 18, 1895 carries a chapter of Kirk Munroe's Snow-Shoes and Sledges, in which Nel-te qualifies as a branch pilot. The sledge party, disappointed of their guide, must push on trusting their own judgment, loading several hundred pounds of moose meat on a sledge and freezing it that evening. Dogs fed their fill grow disinclined to travel next day, while the party's latest addition sobs himself to sleep on Phil's bearskin.

The chapter gives young readers the cold, hard detail of northern travel: meat, dogs, sledges, and the judgment needed when a guide fails. Around it the weekly offers its usual stories and features. The issue is a good sample of a boys' magazine teaching adventure through a serial, where each week's chapter left readers eager for the next stage of the journey.
33037-harper-s-round-table-june-25-1895:
Harper's Round Table for June 25, 1895 opens a serial, Oakleigh, by Ellen Douglas Deland. Its first chapter describes a large white house with green blinds. It stands well back from the broad highway between Brenton and Pelham, at the end of a long shady drive winding through trees with glimpses of meadows beyond. The road forks where the trees end and circles a flatiron-shaped lawn the family calls the heater-piece. Tall white columns uphold the piazza roof and vines soften its ends.

The house on high ground, solid and substantial, sets a story of family life, neighbors, and young people growing up in a country town. Deland writes with a clear eye for place and for the small social rules that shape a household. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features around that opening, in the magazine's usual mix for young readers in the summer of 1895.
33046-harper-s-round-table-july-2-1895:
Harper's Round Table for July 2, 1895 leads with A Misplaced Fourth, by James Barnes, set in Middleton, Ohio, in the early summer of a Civil War year. The town's male population seems to consist of old men and boys, with a few young men in blue coats with brass buttons. Most of them had arms in slings, and one tall twenty-year-old, once the village's fastest runner, moved on crutches with one trouser leg empty and pinned at the knee. Three boys on a fence set the scene.

Barnes's story uses a village Fourth to show war's mark on home life. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that sober opening. The issue is a vivid sample of a boys' magazine mixing holiday fun with the costs of war, in language young readers of 1895 could grasp.
33054-harper-s-round-table-july-9-1895:
Harper's Round Table for July 9, 1895 leads with The Raleigh Reds, by Juliana Conover, a story of boys at drill. A sergeant drills his company, then scolds Billy Atkins, a fat little chap of twelve nearly used up by heat and effort. Billy begs to be let off that afternoon, promising the company will learn to drill in double-quick time, if only they can be in good shape for tomorrow.

The other panting recruits agree at once, and the sergeant faces a small mutiny of heat and youth. Conover's tale is light and comic, catching the earnest play of boys who take soldiering seriously and tire quickly. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that drill-ground scene. The issue is a cheerful sample of a boys' magazine in midsummer, full of games, heat, and good humor.
33070-harper-s-round-table-july-16-1895:
Harper's Round Table for July 16, 1895 leads with How Jack Lockett Won His Spurs, a Revolutionary War story founded on fact by G. T. Ferris. It opens on a cold January day with fourteen-year-old Jack chopping the night's firewood, his young appetite sharp for supper. A white sail skims shoreward through the dusk over dreary bay waters. The stalwart lad, fearless and hard at work, is about to be drawn into the war around him.

The rest of the weekly carries stories and features for young readers, in the magazine's usual mix of adventure and instruction. Ferris's tale uses a real boy's courage to teach history, showing how a chore on a winter evening could lead to a soldier's honor. The issue is a lively sample of the boys' magazine in the summer of 1895, five cents a week for heroes and pastimes.
33071-harper-s-round-table-july-23-1895:
Harper's Round Table for July 23, 1895 leads with Corporal Fred, a story of the riots by Captain Charles King. It opens on a warm June evening, with a family taking air on the back porch. The porch held father and mother, two slender girls, two stalwart elder sons, and a romping nine-year-old, the tribe's little Benjamin. Father reads, mother chats, and the elder sons talk in low tones of the strike of switchmen in the freight yards a block away.

Five railway companies roll trains through the thronging yards, and King's story uses that strike to bring a soldier's tale into a family home. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that tense opening. The issue shows a boys' magazine engaging with labor unrest and public order, in a story written by an officer who knew both army and home life.
33078-harper-s-round-table-july-30-1895:
Harper's Round Table for July 30, 1895 leads with Joe's Scheme, by J. Sanford Barnes Jr. The sharp crackling of gravel and a horse's hoofs up the driveway to the Thompsons' house tell Joe that Ned, always prompt for appointments, has arrived. Joe drops his book and runs to the door as a neat little buckboard pulls up. Greetings exchanged, the boys spin off to the stable, where Jerry the coachman promises the little roan Tot full measure of care.

Barnes's story follows two boys and a scheme hatched on a summer day, with horses, a buckboard, and a household's routines as its stage. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that boyish opening. The issue is a cheerful sample of a boys' magazine in midsummer 1895, where friendship, promptness, and a plan for the afternoon were adventure enough.
33092-harper-s-round-table-august-6-1895:
Harper's Round Table for August 6, 1895 leads with Great Men's Sons: The Son of Alexander the Great, by Elbridge S. Brooks. It opens in Babylon on a bright day of glory and glitter. Armies of East and West marched, sailed, and maneuvered in honor of one small boy. They numbered twenty thousand epigonoi or sons of the king in line, with horse-archers, foot-archers, slingers, spearmen, war-elephants, war-chariots, and the king's navy. The boy sat under a canopy on the palace portico, laughing as spears were tossed and shields clashed.

The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers, as the magazine always did. Brooks's piece uses pageantry to teach ancient history, letting a child reader see Alexander's world through a child's eyes. The issue is a bright sample of a boys' magazine in the summer of 1895, mixing spectacle, story, and instruction for five cents.
33104-harper-s-round-table-august-13-189:
Harper's Round Table for August 13, 1895 leads with The Story of Noel Duval, by Francis Sterne Palmer. The summer of 1814 was troubled for people in northern New York, as English troops massed just across the Canadian border and rumors of invasion spread. Farmers were hastily drilled into militia train-bands, women were anxious and frightened, and boys shared the excitement and drilled too. On a warm July evening four persons sat in the lattice-covered portico of a cottage near the border.

Most striking among them stood Madam Marston, an elderly woman, tall and upright. Palmer's story uses that household to bring the War of 1812 home to young readers, through a border village waiting for war. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features around that historical opening, in the magazine's usual mix.
33115-harper-s-round-table-august-20-189:
Harper's Round Table for August 20, 1895 leads with Braddy's Brother, by Juliana Conover, a baseball story set at the end of the ninth inning. The score stands eight to seven in Princeton's favor. Harvard has only one man out and the bases full, and freshmen cannot keep their seats while Bradfield, class of 1898, twists the ball. In the grand stand a boy stands quivering, eyes glued to the pitcher's box.

The Harvard coach urges his men on as the umpire's count rises and falls, one strike, two balls, two strikes, three balls, raising and dashing Princeton hopes in turn. Conover captures a college game at its tensest moment, where a brother's fate may hang on a pitch. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that sporting climax, in the magazine's usual summer mix.
33116-harper-s-round-table-august-27-189:
Harper's Round Table for August 27, 1895 carries a later chapter of Ellen Douglas Deland's Oakleigh, centered on Tony Bronson. Tony's father had grown rich through a questionable trade pursued by dubious means. The fortune would not bear investigation. Tony knew nothing of that past, yet he had taken on a mean temper and a resolve to bend every event to his own gain.

His family sent him young to St. Asaph's School, hoping daily contact with gentlemen's sons would turn him into a gentleman too. He has acquired only the outward veneering: courteous manners, carefully chosen language, and wit enough to adapt to his companions, without the instincts of a true gentleman. Deland uses him as a foil for Oakleigh's steadier young people. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features around that sharp character study.
33126-harper-s-round-table-september-3-1:
Harper's Round Table for September 3, 1895 leads with A Fight in the Fog, by Yates Stirling Jr., ensign in the United States Navy. All hands to muster rings from the boatswain's mates of the U.S.S. Kearsarge. The crew tumbles aft to the quarter-deck, a fine-looking set of bluejackets, the cream of the navy and the naval reserve. The new Kearsarge cruises off Great Britain to intercept an enemy cruiser, and every man aboard is wild to meet her.

The lookout has just reported smoke when the fog closes in, and Stirling's sea story builds from that moment of waiting to action in the mist. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that naval centerpiece. The issue is a rousing sample of a boys' magazine in the autumn of 1895, eager for the sea, the navy, and a fair fight in the fog.
33135-harper-s-round-table-september-10-:
Harper's Round Table for September 10, 1895 leads with How Reddy Gained His Commission, by Captain Charles A. Curtis, part one. Guard-mounting is over at a frontier post. The commanding officer works in the adjutant's office with the post-adjutant. Nearby sat the post's acting sergeant-major alongside a soldier clerk, putting together the twice-weekly mail for the office across the neighboring river. Outside, a boy musician lounges as office orderly, apparently oblivious to the grandeur around him.

To the south, seventy miles away across an undulating plain, stand the twin Spanish Peaks, and to the west the Cuerno Verde range steps down to the plain. Curtis, writing from army life, uses that post and that boy to begin a story of how a young musician earns a commission. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers, in the magazine's usual mix of adventure and instruction.
33136-harper-s-round-table-september-17-:
Harper's Round Table for September 17, 1895 leads with A Cargo of Burning Coal, by an old shipmaster. Readers may think coal a dirty but innocent cargo, the writer warns. No shipmaster fails to dread a long voyage with it, since many fine vessels have been lost when coal took fire through spontaneous combustion. The greatest care is therefore taken in carrying it, with hatches opened whenever weather permits so gases in the hold can escape.

Regular coal carriers fit ventilators in different parts of the deck, turning huge funnels to catch wind and drive circulation through the ship, keeping holds pure and wholesome. The piece teaches young readers a real sea danger and the seamanship that met it. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features around that practical lesson, in the magazine's usual mix of adventure and useful knowledge for boys and girls.
33140-harper-s-round-table-september-24-:
Harper's Round Table for September 24, 1895 leads with An Own Relation, by Sophie Swett. A country-week girl comes up the lane with her head in the air, watched by Gideon from the crotch of an old sweet-apple tree. Gideon drops down at her feet, mindful of Aunt Esther's charge to be kind. The girl, tall for fourteen, demands to know if this is Sweet Apple Hill and if they are Trueworthys.

Her letter from the Country-week Committee names her Grazella Hickins, aged fourteen, and she wears a wide sash as she looks critically at Gideon. Swett's story uses a city child's country week to explore kindness, pride, and family welcome. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers, in the magazine's usual mix for the autumn of 1895.
33147-harper-s-round-table-october-1-189:
Harper's Round Table for October 1, 1895 leads with Sea Rangers, by Kirk Munroe, author of Road Rangers, the Mate series, Fur-Seal's Tooth, and Snow-Shoes and Sledges. Its first chapter, Earning Their Bicycles, opens as Will Rogers asks Hal Bacon if he realizes the Ready Rangers will have been in existence a whole year on the thirtieth. Hal, a lieutenant, agrees they ought to celebrate, and Will plans to talk it over at that night's meeting, with suggestions from the Berks boys who are also Rangers.

The chapter follows schoolboys planning a celebration for a club born on Decoration Day. Munroe's serial gives young readers a club, a goal, and the work to earn it, in this case bicycles. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features around that boyish opening, in the magazine's usual autumn mix.
33158-harper-s-round-table-october-8-189:
Harper's Round Table for October 8, 1895 leads with The Coppertown Star Route, by W. G. Van Tassel Sutphen. It is a story of a new bicycle called the Happy Thought, already known to readers of The Longmeadow Toll-Gate. Though fitted with pedals for emergencies, its real motive power came from naphtha fed drop by drop through cylinders on a modified hot-air principle. It works directly on the rear wheel. Oil mixed with air and exploded by a spark, with a hand lever giving one to thirty miles an hour.

The power could be shut down at once by closing the oil valve or cutting the current. Sutphen's tale mixes boy adventure with a touch of science fiction, as a motor bicycle carries its riders into trouble and triumph. The rest of the weekly offers stories and features for young readers around that mechanical marvel.
33161-harper-s-round-table-october-22-18:
Harper's Round Table for October 22, 1895 carries a later chapter of Kirk Munroe's Sea Rangers, Left on a Desolate Island. Damage to the sloop Millgirl is so serious that Captain Crotty at once sees the need for prompt action to save his vessel. He shouts to the Rangers to bring bedding, provisions, and everything movable up from the hold beyond reach of in-rushing waters. Grounding offshore, the crew lowers sails and prepares to transfer passengers to land.

The disaster ends a canoe race that caused it, and leaves the Rangers stranded where their resourcefulness will be tested. Munroe's serial gives young readers seamanship, teamwork, and island adventure in weekly chapters. The rest of the number offers stories and features around that shipwreck opening, in the magazine's usual mix for the autumn of 1895.
33169-harper-s-round-table-october-15-18:
Harper's Round Table for October 15, 1895, is a weekly paper for young readers, priced at five cents and filled with stories, pictures, and short features. Its lead tale, by W. J. Henderson, imagines a future war in June 1927 between Venezuela and England, fought far from home in a harsh climate. The tale weighs how a small state might hold out when a great power underrates both its foes and the land itself.

Around that tale, the issue offers the mix its readers knew well: adventure, sport, puzzles, and notes on the world, all in short, lively pieces. The number shows how a boys' and girls' weekly of the 1890s joined fun with learning.
33181-harper-s-round-table-october-29-18:
Harper's Round Table for October 29, 1895, is a weekly paper for young readers, priced at five cents and marked volume sixteen, number 835. Its lead tale, a Halloween story by Hezekiah Butterworth, tells of Obed, a New England boy who saw a sight that filled his neighbors with wonder and fear. The tale is told in the warm, fireside voice of old farmhouse talk.

Around it, the issue keeps the paper's usual mix of stories, notes, and pictures for boys and girls. The number captures a moment in American youth reading, when a weekly could blend a ghostly holiday tale with sport, science, and news of the world. It remains a lively window on what young readers enjoyed in the autumn of 1895.
4867-history-of-the-united-netherlands-1:
France formally declares war on Spain in 1595, and John Lothrop Motley follows a year of sieges, deaths, and betrayals. Archduke Ernest dies after a year of government. Fuentes becomes governor general. The Duke of Arschot's disaffection ends with his death.

Fuentes besieges Le Catelet and Dourlens. At Dourlens the garrison and citizens are put to the sword. The fort of Ham, sold to Spain by De Gomeron, is retaken by Bouillon, and its seller is put to death. Verdugo, La Motte, and Charles Mansfeld all die in the fighting. Motley also covers marriage feasts amid the bloodshed, capturing a war that spared neither ceremony nor civilian.
7257-reflections-and-comments-1865-1895:
Edwin Lawrence Godkin gathers reflections and comments from 1865 to 1895, dedicating the book to Charles Eliot Norton, to whom the founding of The Nation was largely due. His contents run from peace, culture, and war through the comparative morality of nations, the comic-paper question, Froude as lecturer, Horace Greeley, and the morals and manners of the kitchen.

John Stuart Mill, panics, circumstantial evidence, Tyndall and the theologians, the church and science, universities in politics, the South after the war, and chromo-civilization follow in a critic's wide sweep. Godkin writes as an editor who watched America change for thirty years and judged it without flattery. The essays keep a cool, civilised sting.
9916-spalding-s-baseball-guide-and-offic:
Spalding's Base Ball Guide for 1895 served as the official book of the professional leagues, published by the sporting goods house of A. G. Spalding. It collected the records, rules, and club information that players, managers, and fans needed for the new season.

Readers find league standings, batting and fielding figures, and notes on the game as it was played in the 1890s, alongside advertisements for bats, balls, and bicycles. The guide is a time capsule of early professional baseball, when the modern game was still taking its shape and its heroes were becoming household names.
a-compilation-of-the-messages-and-papers: James Madison of Virginia, Princeton graduate of 1771, fills this first volume part compiled by James Daniel Richardson. Madison entered the Virginia assembly in 1776 and served on its executive council before national office. The volume prints his messages and papers as president. Richardson's compilation preserves the formal record of Madison's presidency. Students of early America will find the record clear, full, and easy to use.
a-residence-in-france-during-the-years-1: Charlotte Biggs carries her letters from France into 1795 in this fourth part, writing from Amiens in January of that year. She argues that the French republican government was founded on despotism and injustice, strong to destroy and weak to protect, deserted when it ceases to plunder or oppress. The reforms and reactions of a weary republic appear here through the eyes of an English lady watching weakness and anarchy attend every deviation.
a-terrible-temptation-a-story-of-to-day-: Charles Reade opens this story of today in a large London house's morning room, in Portman Square. A gentleman in the prime of life, sunburned and bright-eyed, leans on the mantelpiece making himself agreeable to a young lady playing at work. His eyes dwell on her with loving admiration while she leans over her work with a modest, demure air. Miss Arabella Bruce, with red hair and a pale neck, suspects she is being admired.
aksakov-animisme-et-spiritisme-1895:
Alexander Aksakov sorts strange feats in two great heaps in Animisme et spiritisme, in French from 1895. Aksakov was a man of state in Russia and a chief of the field in Europe. Some feats, he says, come from the seer's own hid self: that heap is animism. The rest need the dead at work: that heap is spiritism, his true faith.

Tests and famed cases fill two fat tomes in proof. His split gave the field words it still uses each day. The book, in French, is its great sort. Few works shaped its terms so much.
arxiv-2509-00295:
Fangqing Tang, Xing Xiao, and Lixiang Chen explain a petal pattern in spatiotemporal light modes in 2025 through an SU(2) symmetry. Spatiotemporal Laguerre-Gaussian modes are light pulses structured in both space and time. As they travel through free space, their far-field intensity forms a multi-petal pattern like that of tilted Hermite-Gaussian modes.

The team shows the modes carry an SU(2) symmetry, a math structure that lets them build a Poincaré sphere for the pulse family. Formulas give the mode form for any radial and angular indices in uniform dispersive media. Propagation acts as a unitary rotation driven by a conserved quantity, with the angle set by an intermodal phase. That phase depends on pulse ellipticity and the medium's dispersion.
arxiv-2509-00995:
Brett Hungar, writing alone, compares two diagram languages in higher category theory. Anchored planar algebras generalize Vaughan Jones' planar algebras. They have seen use in analysis and in field theory. They carry a natural 3D graphical calculus. Tricategories carry a similar calculus of their own.

Hungar shows these algebras live in a particular tricategory. That single fact has several consequences. More general tools can now be applied to them. The types of diagrams they can interpret also expand. The result bridges two ways of drawing higher structures. Results proved in one setting can transfer to the other. It clarifies where these algebras sit in the broader theory.
arxiv-2509-01195:
Baryons are particles made of three quarks, and rare weak decays between them test the standard model of particle physics. A. Amiri, P. Eslami, K. Azizi, and R. Jafariseyedabad study a semileptonic decay where a bottom baryon turns into a charmed baryon, plus a lepton and its antineutrino. Both baryons carry spin three halves.

The team uses QCD sum rules, a method that links quark-level theory to observed particles through correlation functions. They include effects up to mass dimension six and find stable ranges for their working parameters. From the sum rules they extract form factors, functions that encode the decay's shape, and fit how they vary. Those fits yield decay widths for all lepton channels, giving benchmarks for future experiments.
arxiv-2509-01395:
Language models solve math word problems well, yet they falter at spotting where a student's worked solution first goes wrong. KV Aditya Srivatsa, Kaushal Kumar Maurya, and Ekaterina Kochmar test that meta-reasoning skill on two data sets of step-by-step solutions with marked errors. Even leading models struggled to locate the first error step.

Allowing the models to peek at the reference solution did not fix the problem. To help, the team proposes generating an intermediate corrected version of the student's own solution, one that stays close to the student's path. That closer alignment improved the models' ability to find the first wrong step. The findings matter for tutoring systems, where useful feedback depends on naming the exact step where reasoning broke, not just the final answer.
arxiv-2509-01795:
Irene Shivaei leads twenty-five co-authors in charting how dust dims starlight in galaxies across cosmic time. The dimming curve in violet and visible light reveals grain traits and how grains sit among stars. Their sample holds thousands of galaxies with known distances from Webb surveys. Flexible dust models fit each galaxy light pattern under those distance checks.

The curve slope shifts strongly with how much dust a galaxy holds, growing flatter as dust grows. At fixed dust amount, curves also grow flatter toward earlier times. The most distant galaxies show curves flatter than a classic local curve, hinting at less violet dimming than expected. Simulations tie the shift to large grains born in supernova blasts with little later reworking.
arxiv-2509-02295:
Sapir Esther Yiflach, Yuval Atzmon, and Gal Chechik authored a 2025 computer vision paper about why text-to-image generators misplace objects in a scene. A system may put a dog on the wrong side of a teddy bear, and stranger requests fail even more often.

Their Learn-to-Steer method avoids hand-written rules for fixing images. Instead, a small classifier learns to read spatial relations, such as left of or above, from attention maps inside the generator. That classifier then guides image creation as a learned score. Training used extra examples with wrong relation words, so the classifier could not cheat by reading text traces. Reported accuracy rose sharply on two generators, and the gains held when several relations appeared together.
arxiv-2509-02395:
Christo Kurisummoottil Thomas, Omar Hashash, Kimia Ehsani, and Walid Saad present a 2025 wireless networks paper arguing that future 6G systems should track carbon cost, not just energy use. Older green designs cut power without measuring the emissions that power causes.

The authors propose a metric based on emissions per bit of data delivered. It links energy, computing, and communication choices to that footprint. Allocating those resources becomes a multi-objective problem, solved with multi-objective reinforcement learning that balances emissions, energy, and delay. The learned policy reaches a Pareto trade-off, where no goal improves without hurting another. Simulations cut average emissions per bit by roughly a quarter against methods that ignore carbon directly.
arxiv-2509-02495:
Krzysztof Mierzewski wrote a 2025 solo paper on stable belief revision. It studies how a rational agent should form all-or-nothing beliefs from graded credences. The stability rule accepts a claim only when its credence stays high under new data.

Mierzewski proves a representation theorem. It characterises exactly which revision operators fit that rule. The proof gives a selection function semantics for the logic that results. Two side results concern comparative probability. One jointly represents strict and non-strict likelihood orders. One axiomises ratio comparisons, such as an event being at least k times likelier than another. Uses in voting games and revealed preference theory are sketched. The logic is non-monotonic, so new data can withdraw old beliefs.
arxiv-2509-02695:
Dhayaa Anbajagane and Hayden Lee present a 2025 cosmology paper hunting traces of inflation, the early burst of cosmic expansion, inside today's clumpy universe. Inflation can leave non-Gaussian patterns, including oscillations and scale-dependent features, in the initial density field.

The authors analyse over thirty template patterns, including ones used on cosmic microwave background data. Simulations carry those patterns into the deeply nonlinear late-time density field. Forecasts use gravitational lensing from the Rubin Observatory's ten-year survey. Lensing sensitivity rivals the microwave background for many models and beats it when features sit at small scales. Some templates produce non-monotonic effects across mass and length scales. Simulated resonance signals appear consistently in both the power spectrum and the three-point pattern, with nearly independent limits.
arxiv-2509-03095:
Clément Hervé and 3 co-authors borrowed features from a general 3D generation model in 2025 to study brain aneurysms. An aneurysm is a dangerous bulge in a blood vessel wall. Doctors need to spot, outline, and model these bulges, yet labeled three-dimensional medical data is scarce.

Their source model, TRELLIS, learned shape features from vast non-medical 3D collections. Swapping those features in for standard surface descriptors improved three tasks at once. The team classified aneurysm against healthy vessels, segmented bulges on vessel meshes, and predicted changing blood flow with a graph network. Scores rose across the board, and flow simulation error fell by a stated fraction. The work hints that general shape knowledge can transfer into specialized medicine.
arxiv-2509-03395:
Emma Wallace, Christian Iliadis, and Sumner Starrfield predicted in 2025 what the next eruption of T Coronae Borealis will throw off. This symbiotic recurrent nova, a white dwarf stealing gas from a companion star, is expected to erupt within the next two years. Earlier simulations predicted its element yields for two possible white dwarf types. They did not, however, account for uncertainty in nuclear reaction rates.

The authors ran detailed Monte Carlo calculations of element building, using an updated 2025 set of reaction rates and their stated uncertainties. Both candidate models robustly produce the characteristic carbon, nitrogen, and oxygen isotopes. Differences grow for heavier elements. Sulfur differs by a factor of about thirty between models, with little rate sensitivity, making it the cleanest test of which type erupts. Only nine reactions dominate the key uncertainties.
arxiv-2509-03795:
Hanieh Mousavi and two co-authors work on estimating disturbed airflow around an airfoil from sparse pressure sensors, with stated uncertainty, in a 2025 research paper. During severe gust encounters, vortices interact with the gust and change aerodynamic forces abruptly. Operators need the full flow state from only a handful of surface measurements.

Their framework runs a sequential estimator called an ensemble Kalman filter inside a low-dimensional latent space. That space comes from a physics-augmented autoencoder trained on simulations of airfoil-gust encounters in two dimensions. The forecast step follows calm baseline dynamics, so the measurement step must catch each gust's deviation from sparse pressure data. Working in the latent space keeps updates fast, and decoding returns a physically readable flow. Analysis of the filter's correction directions shows which sensors matter most during a gust. Dropout experiments show the system tolerates sensor failures.
arxiv-2509-04095:
Achilleas Santi Seisa and four co-authors build a test setup for controlling flying robots through the cloud in a 2025 engineering paper. Sending a drone's heavy computing to remote servers can save onboard power and weight. Delays, security risks, and shared resources make that link hard to manage, though. Their framework packages both the cloud side and a simulated robot in containers, which are sealed software bundles that run anywhere.

A direct data tunnel joins the two sides during tests. Software controls then add artificial delay and jitter, meaning uneven timing, to mimic real networks. The flying-robot control case shows the setup working end to end. Other teams can reuse it to stress-test remote robot control safely.
arxiv-2509-04495:
Marcel van der Westhuizen and two co-authors map the dangers hiding in cosmology models where dark matter and dark energy trade energy in a 2025 research paper. Such interacting models promise relief for several cosmic puzzles, including mismatched expansion measurements. The study compares one general linear interaction with four special cases, using dynamical system analysis. Exact analytical solutions are derived for both energy densities, the effective behavior of each component, and a rebuilt dark energy equation of state.

New conditions keep densities positive and well-defined through cosmic history and help avoid a future big rip, where expansion tears everything apart. Energy flowing from dark matter to dark energy inevitably creates negative densities, the authors show, while the reverse direction avoids those pathologies.
arxiv-2509-04595:
Generalised geometry, a framework that extends plain geometry for supergravity, is recast through Cartan geometry by Falk Hassler, lead author with two co-authors, in a 2025 physics paper. Cartan geometry builds curvature and torsion from a model Lie algebra. Here that idea is widened using a differential graded Lie algebra.

The authors set out levels of generalised connections. For each level they work out the linearised torsion and curvature tensors, plus the higher curvatures that the tensor hierarchy needs. The result is a clear, step-by-step way to build curvature and torsion tensors in generic generalised geometries.
arxiv-2509-05195:
Critical behaviour at fixed magnetisation needs tools that track momentum as well as overall spreads. Félix Rose, lead author with two co-authors, extend a functional renormalisation group framework for that purpose in a 2025 physics paper. Their focus is the constraint effective action for the Ising universality class.

They derive exact flow equations. They solve them at second order in a derivative expansion. Numerical solutions in two and three dimensions give universal rate functions. They also give momentum-dependent correlation functions for the constrained system. Benchmarks against Monte Carlo simulations agree well in three dimensions. In two dimensions, the lowest-order version fails. The higher order is essential there, a limitation they document.
arxiv-2509-05295:
When does a variational quantum algorithm actually find the best answer? Marco Wiedmann and five co-authors develop a theory for that question in a 2025 quantum computing paper centred on the variational quantum eigensolver, used to find a molecule's lowest energy state.

Their criterion has two parts, stated in the language of quantum control landscapes. If the circuit can move in every local direction in a bounded way, and gradient descent stops, then almost every starting point leads to a ground state. Similar results hold on smaller closed subgroups, with tests for when the optimum found there is a true ground state. Examples and regularisation methods round out the account.
arxiv-2509-05595:
Simplifying huge three-dimensional meshes without letting surfaces cross themselves is achieved on graphics hardware by Seonghun Oh and six co-authors in a 2025 computer graphics paper. Lower triangle counts speed rendering and editing, but ordinary simplification creates self-intersections that break printing and simulation.

Their approach has three parts: parallel re-meshing into clean, watertight form, parallel simplification with a no-intersection guarantee, and a safe projection step that restores sharp features lost earlier. On one high-end graphics card it cut a two-million-face mesh to twenty thousand triangles in seconds. Tests on a standard dataset showed strong shape preservation. Speed and safety together widen where low-poly models can be used.
arxiv-2509-05795:
Epidemic spread modeled with quantum rules is the subject of a 2025 paper by Sayan Manna and two co-authors. In their setup, each infected site on a square grid releases a quantum walker, a particle whose motion follows quantum interference rather than plain chance. The walker can infect healthy sites it visits during a fixed lifetime.

Simulations sweep infection chance and walker lifetime to compute the basic reproduction number, the average count of new cases per case. At low infection chance the quantum model matches classical random-walk results. At higher values, fast ballistic motion and interference push spread well beyond the classical range, with uneven spatial patterns. The authors compare these ranges with historical outbreaks and present the model as a flexible toy for fast, heavy-tailed spread.
arxiv-2509-05995:
Students' mixed feelings about using language models in a software course are documented in a 2025 study led by Sharon Guardado with four co-authors. The course is requirements engineering, where students learn to elicit and document what a system must do. Surveys gathered one hundred seventy-nine students across two courses at two universities, with the tools woven into individual assignments in one and a team Agile project in the other.

Students said the models improved their grasp of concepts, especially elicitation and documentation. Concerns ran alongside: academic integrity, overreliance, and the awkwardness of folding generated text into coursework. Individual-assignment students felt they benefited more than team-project students. The authors recommend context-aware integration and propose research on balancing AI help with critical thinking and collaboration.
arxiv-2509-06195:
Search systems should rank the same documents for the same question asked in any language. Jinrui Yang and two co-authors measure how far multilingual retrieval is from that fairness ideal in a 2025 paper. They test traditional retrievers and a neural ranker built on multilingual encoders, assuming translations of one query deserve equivalent rankings.

The analysis exposes intrinsic language biases across methods, with notable disparities. To fight them, the authors introduce LaKDA, a new training loss designed to reduce language bias in neural multilingual retrieval. Their experiments show the loss improves fairness, and they frame language bias as a structural property of current technology rather than a data accident.
arxiv-2509-06695:
Planets that drift outward while their birth disk is being blown away are simulated by Beibei Liu and four co-authors in a 2025 planetary science paper. Starlight in X-rays evaporates gas from a young disk, carving a central cavity that expands outward. A planet near the cavity edge feels unusual forces.

Two-dimensional fluid simulations cover several planet masses and disk properties. Planets up to about Neptune's mass receive a strong outward push along the cavity edge and keep migrating out, a pattern earlier named rebound migration. The effect works best at moderate evaporation rates. Saturn-mass planets only move inward, since gas in their orbital zone is too depleted to push back. Jupiter-mass planets move modestly outward by making the leftover disk eccentric. The simulations confirm rebound migration as a real outcome of disk clearing.
arxiv-2509-06795:
Fine-tuning that quietly erodes a language model's refusal to help with harmful requests is countered by Yanrui Du and eight co-authors in a 2025 AI safety paper. Instruction fine-tuning boosts abilities but can weaken safety. Research inside these models has located a refusal direction, a pattern in hidden states that governs refusal behavior.

The authors find that this direction drifts during fine-tuning, and they identify the drift as one cause of the safety loss. Their method, ProCon, adds a loss term that constrains how strongly each training example's hidden state projects onto the refusal direction. Because the drift is sharpest early in training, a warm-up stage applies strong constraints first, and broader training data strengthens the signal. Across datasets, scenarios, and models, the enhanced method cut safety risks while keeping task gains, beating strong baselines overall.
arxiv-2509-06895: A conjecture about the depth of a group's cohomology ring is shown to be equivalent to a simpler statement by James A. Schafer in a solo 2025 algebra paper. The Connor Conjecture equates the depth of the cohomology ring with the smallest dimension among its associated primes, a measure of the ring's structure. Schafer proves this equivalence. The conjecture holds exactly when some elementary abelian subgroup has a centralizer whose cohomology has the same depth. That trades a global quantity for a check on a smaller subgroup.
arxiv-2509-07095:
Fabio Castagna, Stefano Andreon, Marco Landoni, and Alberto Trombetta estimate how pressure profiles vary across galaxy clusters in a 2025 paper. Galaxy clusters vary in their pressure profiles even after rescaling. That shows why samples must be large enough to capture how the whole population varies.

The authors present a Bayesian hierarchical model. It fits individual cluster parameters and the underlying population distribution at once. It also gives estimates of the average pressure profile and the intrinsic scatter, plus exact estimates for single objects. A flexible form based on restricted cubic splines is offered, scatter is modeled accounting for outliers, and corrections for beam and transfer function are added. The model is applied to the largest non-stacked sample of single cluster radial profiles, a complete sample of fifty-five clusters extracted from survey maps.
arxiv-2509-08095:
A mobile robot that cannot dodge obstacles cannot work outside the lab. Lamiaa H. Zain trains neural networks for that skill in a 2025 research paper written alone. Three convolutional networks were built end to end. They take synchronized color and depth images from an Intel RealSense camera and output steering commands directly.

Offline tests favored the model called NetConEmb, with the lowest angular error. A lighter model, NetEmb, used about a quarter fewer parameters and converged faster, with accuracy close behind. In live navigation, NetConEmb succeeded in every trial, in both familiar and new environments. The lighter models managed only the familiar setting. The results show what real-time sensor fusion costs and buys for small robots that must react without a human at the controls.
arxiv-2509-08395:
Searching sparse vectors for the best inner-product match gets a faster index from Ruoxuan Li and 9 co-authors in a 2025 information retrieval paper. Sparse maximum inner product search powers multi-path retrieval inside retrieval-augmented generation systems, which feed language models with fetched documents. Existing inverted-index and graph methods lose speed in production to redundant distance computations and scattered memory access.

Their index, SINDI, removes redundant inner product work and lays data out so modern processor vector instructions can engage despite the compressed sparse format. Retrieval latency sits inside every generated answer, so index efficiency decides whether augmented systems respond in a blink or a pause users can feel.
arxiv-2509-08895:
A. Floris and 15 co-authors compare polarization across tidal disruption events in a 2025 paper. A tidal disruption occurs when a star is torn apart by a supermassive black hole, causing a bright flare. One event, AT2020mot, showed the highest optical polarization yet recorded.

New polarization measures for thirteen events are combined with light curves from ground and space observatories. Physical properties are derived with fitting tools and compared across the sample. AT2020mot matches others on temperature, brightness, and rise time, but its polarization is exceptionally high. Its gas column also looks elevated. The authors say shock or reprocessing models alone struggle to explain it.
arxiv-2509-08995:
Sichen Zhu and 4 co-authors secure financial language models with differential private fine-tuning in a 2025 paper. Finance firms use large models on sensitive data, increasingly on edge devices. Privacy breaches there carry high cost, yet performance must stay strong.

Their DPFinLLM combines a strong differential privacy mechanism, which limits what training data can leak, with a streamlined model design. It is built for on-device financial use. Tests on several sets of financial sentiment data show scores close to those of fully fine-tuned models, even when privacy limits are strict. The authors present it as a practical path for safe, efficient finance models on local hardware.
arxiv-2509-09295:
Kansei Ushiyama proposes an accelerated FISTA algorithm for composite strongly convex problems in a 2025 paper. Composite problems minimize a smooth function plus a possibly nonsmooth one. FISTA is a standard accelerated forward backward splitting method for that form.

The new method improves the leading constant in the linear convergence rate by a square root of two factor. It also beats the best previously known rate for this problem class. Analysis stays valid even if one component is weakly convex, as long as their sum remains convex. The algorithm comes from discretizing a continuous time model of an optimal method called ITEM. Optimization theory gains a faster provable method.
arxiv-2509-09595:
Animated avatars can lip-sync a script, but making one perform a role with intent over minutes is a different problem. Yikang Ding and 13 co-authors present Kling-Avatar in a 2025 research paper. Earlier systems followed low-level acoustic and visual cues without modeling what an instruction means. Narrative coherence and expressiveness suffered as a result.

Kling-Avatar works in two stages. A multimodal language model acts as director, producing a blueprint video that fixes motion, emotion, and story beats. A second stage then renders sub-clips in parallel, guided by blueprint keyframes, and stitches them into long video. The team built a benchmark of several hundred curated samples across diverse instructions. Their system led on lip synchronization, expressiveness, controllability, identity preservation, and generalization. Long, photorealistic avatar performance suits livestreaming and vlogging, where a digital presenter must hold character for an audience.
arxiv-2509-09995:
Fei Xiong and 4 co-authors aim a team of language model agents at high-frequency trading in a 2025 finance paper. Earlier multi-agent trading systems reason over news and fundamentals for slow, strategic bets. High-frequency desks live elsewhere: decisions must land in tiny windows, driven by compact structured signals such as indicator readings, chart shapes, and short trends, with risk checked constantly.

QuantHarness splits the job among four specialists covering indicators, patterns, trends, and risk, each armed with its own tools and structured reasoning routine. Trials spanned nine instruments, from Bitcoin to Nasdaq futures, and the authors present the system as the first of its kind shaped for this speed class. The design bets that narrow, fast agents beat one broad thinker when the clock dominates.
arxiv-2509-10095:
Abdulrahman Allam and 3 co-authors fine-tune language models for Arabic medical text in this 2025 paper. Hospital systems need tools that can answer patients in Arabic, a language most medical AI handles poorly, especially when patients write informally and mix dialects. The team gathered a data set of real patient complaints and doctor replies from social media and cleaned it for training.

They fine-tuned several generative models, including Mistral and LLaMA variants and a medium GPT-2. The fine-tuned Mistral model scored best on overlap with reference answers, ahead of the others on precision, recall, and combined score. Checks by reading samples backed the numbers. The authors present the system as a scalable aid for hospitals serving Arabic-speaking patients.
arxiv-2509-10195:
R. Montalà and 6 co-authors apply deep reinforcement learning to a separated wing flow in this 2025 paper. At a high angle of attack, air peels off a three-dimensional NACA0012 wing and performance drops. Active flow control can push the air back down, but choosing the right actions in real time is hard for fixed rules.

Their learning agent reads live flow data and picks control actions to raise aerodynamic performance, guided by a reward built for that goal. The setup links a graphics-card flow solver with a learning library through a fast in-memory database, which speeds training. Working at a modest Reynolds number, the study shows a learning controller can find effective actions on its own in a fully three-dimensional separated flow.
arxiv-2509-10895:
Fabian Bäumer and three co-authors hunt for flaws in a security patch in this 2025 paper. The patch was meant to fix the Terrapin attack on SSH. SSH secures remote access to servers everywhere. Terrapin exploited optional messages during key exchange. The industry answered with strict key exchange, which forbids them. The authors test whether implementations actually obey. Black-box state learning extracts each server's hidden handshake state machine.

Earlier work learned only partial machines. The full one seemed infeasible to learn. This team learns the complete handshake machine, with strict mode enabled. Ten implementations were tested. Thirty-three machines were learned. Seven implementations violated the specification. Two flaws were critical. In Tectia's proprietary server, a rogue session attack was possible. In Erlang's official SSH implementation, unauthenticated remote code execution was possible. Security extensions need the same scrutiny as the protocols they patch.
arxiv-2509-11195:
Shoki Koyanagi and 2 co-authors release software for simulating open quantum systems in magnetic settings in this 2025 paper. When a quantum system touches its environment strongly, simple approximations fail, and exact methods that track the bath's memory are needed. Their package adds gauge fields to a hierarchical equations of motion solver, the standard tool for such non-Markovian problems.

The code keeps gauge invariance and rotational symmetry exact, which matters for effects like the Aharonov-Bohm effect, where a field a particle never touches still shifts its behavior. Demo programs compute correlation functions for ring-shaped geometries. The authors present the package as a way to resolve fine interference effects in dissipative quantum transport.
arxiv-2509-11495:
Cheongho Han and twenty-nine co-authors dissect three stubborn microlensing events. This 2025 astronomy paper covers the 2024 campaigns of OGLE and KMTNet. In microlensing, a foreground system magnifies a background star's light. Three events had light curves that defied standard models.

Neither standard model fit all the bumps. One used a binary lens with a single source. The other used a single lens with two sources. Each caught the main feature only. Four-body modeling fit all three events at last. In each, the lens is a binary and the source is a binary too. Color and brightness mark the source pairs as G- and K-type main-sequence stars. Two lenses look like low-mass star pairs in the Galactic bulge. The third looks like two stellar remnants in the disk.
arxiv-2509-11595:
Sabin Huda and four co-authors generate fake money laundering for research use. This 2025 financial crime paper starts from a data famine. Real transaction records cannot be shared. Synthetic sets rarely line up with real rules.

Their framework is AMLNet. It pairs two coordinated units. A rule-aware generator made over a million synthetic transactions. A small share of them are laundering. The set spans placement, layering, and integration phases. Tricks like structuring are included. An ensemble detector then hunts the laundering in the stream. It scored strongly on internal tests. It adapted to an outside synthetic set as well. The dataset is public, with realism checks on several axes.
arxiv-2509-11695:
Daniel Herzinger and three co-authors design quantum-safe sign-in for virtual private networks. This 2025 computer security paper treats IPsec authentication. A post-quantum draft standard exists. It passes over stateful hash-based signatures. Those give small signatures and long-trusted security. Their one-time state is delicate to manage.

The design here is time-based. A certificate authority uses the XMSS hash-based scheme. It issues leaf certificates with about four hours of life. Those rest on classical cryptography. A big quantum computer should need far longer to break them. The window stays safe. Clock honesty strategies are added. Wrong time can be spotted, its damage limited, and recovery made quick. An OpenBSD build shows the design light on bandwidth and compute.
arxiv-2509-11795:
V. Pomjakushin and five co-authors test whether a topological material's magnetism is purely local. This 2025 condensed matter paper treats CeAlGe. It is a candidate topological semimetal. A non-collinear, multi-wavevector magnetic phase lives in it. The team measured magnetic Bragg peaks at low and high momentum transfer in one setup.

A model built only from localized cerium moments fit the full pattern well. It differs from an earlier structure based on high-momentum data alone. Even the delicate zeroth-order satellites were reproduced. A share from itinerant electrons could not be ruled out fully. Nothing in the data demands one, though. The refined structure winds in nontrivial patterns. Spin textures carry half-integer charges. The material's topological Hall effect gains a natural source.
arxiv-2509-11995:
Convex composite optimization, minimizing a smooth part plus a stubborn nonsmooth part, underlies much of machine learning and signal processing. Zhanwang Deng and three co-authors introduce SSNCVX in 2025, a primal-dual semismooth Newton framework meant to cover that whole class in one design.

Through augmented Lagrangian duality, the problem becomes a saddle point whose optimality conditions form a semismooth system of equations. The nonsmoothness is handled inside the method, so no bespoke reformulation or extra variables are needed for each new model. Adding linear, quadratic, or shift terms means touching only a simple interface. A single loop updates primal and dual variables together by Newton steps, and benchmark tests report better robustness and speed than leading solvers.
arxiv-2509-12495:
A wooden puzzle can be a laboratory for how minds get unstuck. Gülce Kardeş and two co-authors analyze the Soma cube in 2025, a classic three-dimensional puzzle, and map its computational difficulty onto the strategies people use to solve it.

Difficulty is measured by the branching factor of the search tree, how many moves fan out at each step. The authors then layer in one strategy at a time: chunking pieces in advance, ordering moves by promise, scaffolding the search order, and pruning dead ends. Each layer cuts the effective complexity, supporting a view of intelligence as a stock of tricks that recruit the physical artifact itself.
arxiv-2509-12895:
Christian L. Hines, Samuel Spillard, and Daniel P. Martin prove an equivalence between two study methods in a 2025 paper. TimeCluster is a visual analytics method for discovering structure in long multivariate time series. It projects overlapping windows of data into a low-dimensional space where clusters can be seen.

When principal component study is the chosen reduction method, the authors show TimeCluster is mathematically equivalent to classical subspace identification of linear dynamical systems. Forming the sliding-window matrix yields a Hankel matrix, and applying principal component study to it recovers the same directions as subspace identification. Tests on man-made and real dynamical signals confirmed that the two embeddings coincide. The result connects a visualization tool to well-known system theory.
arxiv-2509-12995:
Yue Zhou, Xinan He and five co-authors show in 2025 that a plain head on a fresh vision base beats craft detectors for wild fake images. Craft tools shine on neat tests but miss many fakes in the wild, with high miss rates.

Trained on the same data, the plain head lifts wild scores by more than twenty points. Probes show fresh vision and tongue models link fake images to forgery words. Older models lack that link. Scores crash on fresh scraped data past the base cut-off. True tests thus need data free of all past training touch.
arxiv-2509-13295:
Sungwon In and 4 co-authors present ICoN in a 2025 paper on data work inside virtual reality. More and more, analysts want to take their code notebooks, such as Jupyter, into a fully immersive space. Most such tools still use windows, icons, menus, and a pointer, which feel clumsy for deep data work. Moving with the body feels more natural, but body-based tools tend to stand alone.

That split forces analysts to jump from one tool to a wholly distinct one mid-task. ICoN joins both in one immersive space, so a user can slide from notebook work to hands-on data play and back. In the authors' tests, the joined setup made those shifts faster and more smooth, a hint of how fluid data work in VR could feel.
arxiv-2509-14095:
Gaëtan Regaud and Martin Zimmermann settle the complexity of an expressive specification logic in a 2025 theoretical computer science paper. Generalized HyperLTL with stuttering and contexts can state asynchronous hyperproperties. Those are requirements about how several executions of a system relate when they run at different speeds. The synchronous original logic cannot express them at all.

For satisfiability, the richer logic turns out no harder than plain HyperLTL. Both are complete for the same very high complexity class. Model checking tells a different story. There it is equivalent to truth in second-order arithmetic. That is vastly harder than the decidable model checking of ordinary HyperLTL. The lower bounds hold even when only stuttering or only contexts are allowed. Each feature alone carries the cost.
arxiv-2509-14195:
Shalima Binta Manir and Tim Oates test a theory of mental maps in a 2025 cognitive machine learning paper. Animals and people navigate well partly because their minds hold structured internal models. Those models mirror the outside world. A standing hypothesis credits second-order learning with building those mental representations. Second-order learning means mechanisms that adapt the learning process itself. Direct empirical evidence was thin.

Their hierarchical system pairs two networks. A graph convolutional network learns directly over the maze's structure to predict good navigation paths. A small controller network retunes the first network's parameters when a structurally new maze appears. Second-order learning paid off most when the system formed an internal map matching the environment's shape. Performance and generalization on unseen mazes improved markedly, supporting the theory.
arxiv-2509-14295:
Fanqi Kong and nine co-authors present Aegis in 2025, a system for making and labelling errors in multi agent AI setups. Teams of language model agents can solve hard tasks, yet their failures are hard to trace. Hand labelled error data are scarce and costly.

Aegis uses a language model manipulator to inject realistic, context aware errors into runs that first succeeded. That process built a data set of several thousand trajectories, each labelled with the faulty agent and error type. The set spans varied agent layouts and task domains. Models can then be trained to attribute errors, meaning to name which agent went wrong and how. Better attribution is a step toward agent teams that can be debugged rather than merely rerun.
arxiv-2509-14595:
Keane Maverick Irawan, writing alone in 2025, classifies two colourings of a prime cycle that avoid a monochromatic four term arithmetic progression. Colour each residue class red or blue so no four evenly spaced same colour terms appear, for any allowed step. Existence depends delicately on the prime.

Such a colouring exists exactly for the smallest primes five, seven and eleven, Irawan proves. Where solutions exist, they are enumerated up to symmetry and a global colour swap, with minimal period equal to the prime. Nonexistence for larger primes mixes computer verified unsatisfiability certificates up to a large bound with a van der Waerden corollary beyond it. The same pipeline certifies an exact cyclic van der Waerden number, closing a concrete extremal problem.
arxiv-2509-14695:
Huihui An, Ju Tan, and Zaili Yan study a special class of Lie algebras in a 2025 mathematics paper. A Lie algebra is a set with a bracket operation used across algebra and geometry. Their focus is algebras carrying a cyclic metric, a symmetric pairing that obeys a cyclic condition. Such metrics show up in non-associative algebras and in spaces with curved geometry.

The authors first give conditions under which an algebra of this kind splits into a direct product of simpler parts. They then introduce cyclic quadruples to track how the semisimple and radical parts interact. Using a double extension method, they fully describe the cases over real and complex numbers that are neither semisimple nor solvable.
arxiv-2509-14795:
Timo Kuosmanen and Xun Zhou challenge how governments measure their own productivity in a 2025 economics paper. Total factor productivity compares outputs with inputs, but public services often lack clear output prices. The authors show that common ways of filling that gap can produce paradoxical results.

When output is valued at cost, measured productivity can fall even after genuine improvements in technology or efficiency. The same trouble appears when outputs are combined with cost-share weights. With distorted prices, the measure can move for pricing reasons alone, with no real change underneath. Examples from the United Kingdom and Finland show the problem inside widely used official statistics. The authors argue for valuation methods grounded in economic theory instead of cost-based totals.
arxiv-2509-14995:
Van Chien Le and four co-authors trace why long runs of a time-stepping method for the PMCHWT problem blow up late, in a 2025 paper. The method solves a standard problem for waves that scatter off objects made of dielectric stuff. In long runs the answer can grow without bound at late times, for reasons that were not well pinned down.

Their study pins the cause on the static, curl-free null space of the time-domain electric field operator. The failure mode is not the same as the known one for the plain electric field problem. Here, small errors in numeric integrals matter much more. The shape and smoothness of the object's surface also shape the spectrum. Knowing the cause points the way to fixes.
arxiv-2509-15295:
Stefano Antonini and three co-authors take on a puzzle about black holes and entropy. Entropy here counts how much two parts of a system are linked. In a two sided black hole with much matter inside, some sums gave a negative value. Real entropy can never be negative, so the math had to be missing something.

The team show that adding all the rare, non standard paths in the gravity sum fixes the sign. They check the fix with a twin model based on random tables of numbers. In the hard range, new stable points of that model keep the value positive. They also restate the puzzle with random networks, a toy model of space. The work guards a core rule of quantum theory.
arxiv-2509-15495:
Patrick Draper, Luis Hidalgo, and Anton Ilderton set up quantum simulations of strong field physics. When a photon hits an intense light wave, its spin can flip. That flip is a one loop effect, a faint process that simpler tree level work skips. Simulating it brings new problems, such as large errors from cutting off the math.

The team work in a basis of momentum states, which suits reading off results. They derive exact fix terms that cancel the cutoff errors at one loop. They then build quantum circuits for the process and run noiseless tests on classical machines to gauge the error from step sizes. They close with cost estimates for real quantum hardware.
arxiv-2509-15595:
Kaniz Fatema, Vaibhav Thakur, and Emad Mohammed outline the prostate in a new kind of scan. Micro ultrasound gives sharp images that may aid cancer spotting and guided care. The edge of the prostate capsule, though, is often fuzzy in these images. Past tools often fail on such fuzzy edges, so a tailored fix was needed.

Their fix is a training loss that shifts its focus as training runs. It weighs hard and easy regions by how hard each is and by how much human labels vary there. A standard loss of the same family serves as the base. The adaptive form stretches the hard regions found where expert and non expert labels disagree. This helps the model trace the true edge.
arxiv-2509-15695:
Zhaoyang Li leads a team that tests vision models on objects in odd places. Big vision and language models caption and answer well, yet they miss plain objects in atypical scenes. They also claim objects that are not there. The team frame this flaw through doubt: odd context makes recognition harder.

Their frame, ORIC, builds odd object and context pairs in two ways. One uses a language model to find hard objects that are present. The other uses an image text model to mine likely objects that are absent. Applied to a known photo set, it yields a test set and training data.
