Their framework HaDola selects data and labels automatically in four stages, bootstrapping from a seed of 5 percent of the data to identify harmful samples and prioritize informative ones. On the VQAv2 and VizWiz benchmarks it matched or beat state-of-the-art baselines with less training data, arguing that using uncertainty beats simply scaling dataset size.
arxiv-2510-11495:
The standard recipe for reasoning models is to pretrain on next-token prediction, then fine-tune with reinforcement learning, and somehow the second stage unlocks abilities the first could not reach. Nikolaos Tsilivis, Eran Malach, Karen Ullrich, and Julia Kempe explain that mechanism theoretically in this 2025 arXiv machine learning paper. Their laboratory is a mixture of short and long chain-of-thought sequences for one task: predicting the parity of a string of bits, a notoriously hard problem.

When long demonstrations are rare, pure next-token prediction needs extreme statistical or computational resources to generalize, while reinforcement learning after pretraining succeeds. Reinforcement learning succeeds by exploiting longer test-time responses. The authors prove autoregressive linear models trained this way learn parity efficiently, provided the share of long demonstrations is not exponentially small in the input size. They confirm the same effect post-training Llama models on math reasoning benchmarks.
arxiv-2510-11595:
AI policy is being written in a fog: research pours out faster than anyone can verify it, and weak reproducibility standards let noise drown out signal. Israel Mason-Williams and Gabryel Mason-Williams argue that fixing reproducibility is a governance issue, not just a scientific one, in this 2025 arXiv paper. A low signal-to-noise information environment favors regulatory capture and leaves policymakers deeply uncertain about which risks deserve priority.

The authors evaluate AI's reproducibility problem through the lens of replication crises in other sciences and propose importing the remedies that helped there. Preregistration would discipline claims, larger statistical power would steady results, and publishing negative results would correct the record. They maintain that AI governance must stay reactive given the technology's societal stakes, but insist reproducibility protocols belong in the core governance arsenal. Policymakers, they argue, should demand higher standards from AI research.
arxiv-2510-11695:
Language model agents are being handed trading accounts, but nearly all evaluations are backtests or short demos on a single market. Lingfei Qian and a large team of co-authors build Agent Market Arena, the first live, lifelong benchmark for trading agents, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The arena runs continuously on verified trading data and expert-checked news, across both cryptocurrency and stock markets, so agent designs compete under identical conditions.

Four agents compete, from a single-agent InvestorAgent baseline through TradeAgent and HedgeFundAgent with contrasting risk styles to DeepFundAgent, which reasons with memory. Each is powered in turn by five model backbones, including GPT-4o, GPT-4.1, two Claude models, and Gemini-2.0-flash. The live experiments produced a clear pattern: agent frameworks behaved in markedly distinct ways, from aggressive risk-taking to conservative decision-making, while the choice of model backbone contributed less to outcome variation.
arxiv-2510-11895:
Maryam Aliakbarpour and three colleagues tighten the theory of local differential privacy when users demand different protection levels. In local differential privacy, each person scrambles their own data before sharing it. Real deployments mix cautious and relaxed users, a heterogeneous setting. Most analyses promise accuracy only on average. Their 2025 arXiv paper insists on guarantees that hold with high probability on any single run.

For mean estimation in one and several dimensions, the authors derive finite-sample error bounds in the Euclidean norm. The bounds hold with probability at least one minus a chosen failure chance. Matching minimax lower bounds show no method can do fundamentally better; their guarantees are optimal up to constant factors. They also design an algorithm for learning whole distributions under the strictest-coordinate distance, again with high-probability guarantees under mixed privacy demands. The results give designers of privacy mechanisms principled guidance for real, uneven populations.
arxiv-2510-11995:
Gökhan Kara and six colleagues compare two ways of sensing infrared light with the same quantum dot film. Colloidal lead sulfide quantum dots make cheap, printable light sensors. A simple photoconductor is easy to build but large and slow; a hybrid phototransistor on graphene is tiny and uses trap sites to sense very dim light. Their 2025 arXiv paper fabricates both devices with an identical treated film, so the comparison is fair.

On paper the devices post comparable detectivity. In practice, at low light the photoconductor's current is too small to read comfortably. The authors also showcase a surprise in the temperature behavior. Warming activates photocurrent dynamics that produce a negative photoconductivity effect. That effect simultaneously raises the photocurrent and the bandwidth, pushing operating speeds up to one hundred kilohertz. Match the device to the light level, not the brochure metric.
arxiv-2510-12095:
Wenxu Zhou and seven colleagues build a warehouse of imaginary rooms for AI interior designers. Language-model-driven 3D scene generation needs diverse, high-quality training layouts, which barely existed. Their 2025 arXiv paper presents IL3D, a large-scale indoor layout dataset built for exactly that purpose.

The collection holds twenty-seven thousand eight hundred sixteen layouts spanning eighteen common room types, plus a library of twenty-nine thousand two hundred fifteen high-fidelity 3D object assets.  The team establishes benchmarks for language-model scene generation and finds that fine-tuning on IL3D improves generalization, beating fine-tuning on rival datasets. Layouts export flexibly as point clouds, bounding boxes, multiview images, depth and normal maps, and semantic masks, adapting to many visual tasks. Beyond decoration, the authors pitch IL3D at embodied intelligence, giving simulated agents rich homes to perceive. Dataset and code are public.
arxiv-2510-12295:
Amadio's lecture notes present the operational approach to programming language semantics, posted on arXiv in 2025. Operational semantics defines what a program means by describing its steps of computation. Amadio argues this approach needs only moderate mathematics yet scales to many language features. It also supports portable code generators and proofs about compilers.

The notes collect material taught over several years to master students in courses on semantics, foundations, compilation, and concurrency. They begin with a tiny imperative language, then treat term rewriting systems, where ending and confluence are put on solid ground. The lambda calculus follows, with closures and the contextual sameness of programs, and simulation as a practical reasoning tool. Later chapters add richer type systems, then concurrency. The notes favor simple cases and self contained proofs, aiming to show links among systems that look unrelated at first sight.
arxiv-2510-12495:
Regály, Fröhlich, and Kiss test whether standard tidal theory can explain the odd spin and orbit of the dwarf planet Quaoar and its moon Weywot, in a 2025 arXiv paper. Weywot follows a nearly circular orbit far out from Quaoar, which hosts a compact ring system. Yet Quaoar is flattened and rotates slowly, a mix conventional tidal evolution struggles to reconcile with Weywot's low mass.

They ran the system's evolution over Solar System history under two tidal formalisms. With the nominal Weywot mass, both reproduce Weywot's observed orbital distance across wide initial conditions, with eccentricity damped and today's torques negligible. Quaoar's spin, however, barely changes and misses the observed slow rotation. A match demands a satellite five to ten times more massive than occultation estimates allow. They conclude that non tidal effects, such as a largely primordial spin or an ancient giant impact, must have shaped Quaoar's rotation.
arxiv-2510-12695:
Sahoo and a large team measure how readily selenium and cerium nuclei capture neutrons, rates needed to model how stars forge heavy elements, in a 2025 arXiv nuclear physics paper. The slow neutron capture process, the s-process, builds many elements heavier than iron inside aging stars. Its predicted element abundances depend on Maxwellian averaged capture cross sections, which are hard to measure for short lived products.

The experiments ran at the SARAF accelerator facility in Israel, where a high power proton beam strikes a liquid lithium target. The setup yields an intense beam of neutrons with energies mimicking stellar interiors, strong enough to activate samples whose decay products vanish quickly. The team irradiated natural selenium and natural cerium samples in this beam and measured the resulting radioactivity with gamma ray spectrometry. The measurements supply the stellar reaction rates that s-process network calculations consume.
arxiv-2510-12895:
Epstein-Martin, Stone, and Becker study mean motion resonances in disks around active galactic nuclei in this 2025 arXiv paper. A resonance occurs when two orbiting bodies' periods form a simple ratio, and bodies migrating through a gas disk tend to fall into such lockstep. The authors ask when stellar-mass black holes embedded in these disks stay resonant, against disruption from relativistic precession, turbulence, and stirring by stars.

They derived simple analytic criteria for pairs being driven out of resonance and mapped stability across plausible disk models. Around the most massive central black holes, first-order resonances were generically unstable, while around smaller ones stable resonances always appeared, with an in-between regime depending on disk and orbiter properties. The implication is that mergers in heavy systems proceed largely without resonant chains, reshaping expected gravitational-wave pathways.
arxiv-2510-12995:
He and co-authors bring continuous speech representations into multimodal language models in this 2025 arXiv paper. Text-to-speech usually relies on discrete tokens, chopped codes for sound, which discard fine acoustic detail because speech is inherently continuous. The authors instead let the model generate speech frame by frame in a continuous space.

Their design adds a diffusion head, a module that builds speech representations by gradually removing noise. It keeps the original language model head to manage other tasks and to mark where speech starts and ends. Masked training counters the model's tendency to drift when feeding on its own outputs. A second training stage freezes the language model so the diffusion head learns from a fixed input distribution. On a standard test set the system reached leading autoregressive quality, and two-stage training cut its word error rate nearly in half relative to one-stage training.
arxiv-2510-13695:
Elliott and Niu extend a recent classification of Villadsen's exotic C*-algebras to a broader family. Their 2025 arXiv paper, the second in a series, studies algebras built from a self-reproducing seed space. The first paper classified the tensor-product style family with help from the Cuntz semigroup. This one tackles the analogue built on approximately finite-dimensional algebras instead.

Simple K-theory and traces cannot tell these algebras apart, so finer invariants must step in. The authors replace a single comparison number with a whole comparison radius function. That function varies over the space of traces and captures subtler distinctions. Their theorem says two such algebras match exactly when their semigroup data and radius functions agree. The work also makes progress on telling apart algebras built from different seed spaces. That question decides how much the seed geometry shapes the final algebra.
arxiv-2510-13795:
Zhang and a large team argue that fully open multimodal models lag mainly because their fine-tuning data is poor, then fix it. Their 2025 arXiv paper introduces the Bee suite, built around a dataset called Honey-Data-15M. Existing open datasets carry heavy noise and almost no hard reasoning examples. Chain-of-thought data, which teaches stepwise reasoning, is especially scarce.

Honey-Data-15M holds about fifteen million question-answer pairs after multi-stage cleaning. A dual-level enrichment adds both short and long reasoning chains to the data. The curation pipeline, HoneyPipe, and its DataStudio framework are released openly. Training an eight-billion-parameter model, Bee-8B, on the corpus validates the approach. Bee-8B sets a new best mark among fully open models. It even rivals or beats some semi-open competitors like InternVL3.5-8B on benchmarks. Ablations credit each cleaning stage with real gains.
arxiv-2510-13895:
Dolfin and Leonida review the kinetic theory of active particles as math for crowds of living agents that choose. Their 2025 arXiv essay spans social dynamics and behavioural economics. Classic kinetic theory tracks passive particles that merely collide. Living beings plan, breed, compete, and mutate, breaking the classic rules.

The scheme gives each agent a drive level and a spread over strategies. Meetings between agents can help them grow or do them harm, and they reshape the group's state. From those meeting rules, sets of equations describing collective motion are derived. Flocks, crowds, cell groups, and market actors all fit the same mould. The authors stress the differences: strategies vary across members and evolve over time. Studying the meetings themselves, they argue, yields new math as a by-product. The essay weighs this route against Fokker-Planck and other tools for collective motion.
arxiv-2510-14095:
Awni Altabaa and co-authors study how transformers can generalize systematically to problems unlike their training data, a weakness that limits the reasoning of modern language models, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Their testbed is modular arithmetic on computational graphs, styled after grade-school math word problems, where compositional rules must be recombined.

They introduce and study four mechanisms. One is input-adaptive recurrence, letting the model iterate a number of steps matched to the problem. Another is algorithmic supervision, training signals that teach the procedure itself. A third anchors latent states through a discrete bottleneck, forcing internal states into a tidy code. The fourth is an explicit error-correction mechanism. These yield scalable latent-space reasoning with robust generalization. An interpretability analysis, tracing what the internal components compute, shows how the mechanisms combine to produce the out-of-distribution behavior. It offers design lessons beyond the arithmetic testbed.
arxiv-2510-14895:
Cowtan, He, Williamson, and Yoder ask, in a 2025 arXiv paper, how to make a key fault-tolerant quantum operation fast instead of merely compact. Code surgery manipulates quantum information in low-density parity-check codes. Recent work shrank its space cost, but generic surgery still needs syndrome measurement rounds growing with the code's distance, so time overhead stayed high.

The authors give conditions under which surgery runs in constant time, independent of code size. Fast surgery, they show, requires an auxiliary structure described by a hypergraph rather than an ordinary graph. Their scheme, block reading, performs transversal surgery across code blocks at once. For quantum locally testable codes they find schemes with intermediate time overhead, between constant and linear. They prove a circuit equivalence between homomorphic measurement and hypergraph surgery, and bound the time cost of logical measurement. Speed, they conclude, hinges on connectivity, not on single-shot memory.
arxiv-2510-15395:
Rubi Hudson tackles a core worry in AI safety: a system that resists being retrained because its current goal rewards self-preservation. This solo 2025 arXiv paper defines corrigibility formally. A corrigible goal never pushes an agent to dodge updates or shutdown, so training can fix mistakes and absorb changing human preferences.

Hudson then gives a transformation that rebuilds any fixable goal into a corrigible version without losing performance. The trick makes the agent predict its reward in the world where it blocks updates, and pay itself that same predicted reward when it accepts updates instead, removing the motive to resist. Variants extend the property to agents the first agent creates, and block deliberate goal tampering. Two gridworld experiments show such goals can be learned and do produce the intended, update-friendly behavior. The paper claims the first specification of goals that are both corrigible and competitive.
arxiv-2510-15995:
Luigi Foscari, Emanuele Guidotti, Nicolò Cesa-Bianchi, Tatjana Chavdarova, and Alfio Ferrara show how two learning market agents can settle into charging too much without ever agreeing to do so. Their repeated game pairs a market maker, who controls liquidity, with a market taker, who picks trade quantities. Prices move through trade impact plus outside shocks.

Overpricing is measured against a path with the same shocks but no price impact. The five authors characterise which strategy pairs can sustain overpricing within cash and inventory limits, and give a sufficient condition for decentralised learning to reach that region in finite time. Projected stochastic gradient ascent meets the condition. Splitting the game into competitive and collaborative parts explains why: when total inventory is positive, overpricing pays both sides jointly, for short-sighted and far-sighted goals alike.
arxiv-2510-16195:
Anjali Nambrath reports three measurements of energy-energy correlators, a new way to probe the inner spray of particle jets. A correlator tracks how energy inside a jet is shared between pairs of particles at each angle. The data come from the ALICE detector at CERN's Large Hadron Collider.

The first measurement, in proton-proton collisions, cleanly separates the angles ruled by strong-force theory from those ruled by messy particle formation. The second sorts jets born from heavy quarks, tagged by a rebuilt D0 meson, to show how quark type shapes the spray. The third, a first in proton-lead collisions, shows how a cold atomic nucleus alters jet growth. Together they sharpen tests of how quarks turn into the particles detectors see.
arxiv-2510-16695:
Iman Deznabi, Peeyush Kumar, and Madalina Fiterau propose a forecasting model for places with little or no past data, a task called zero-shot forecasting. Their model splits a signal into parts that change at different speeds. Slow parts draw on wide spatial context, while fast parts rely on nearby local detail.

Applied to microclimate forecasting, the method retrieves past data in a way that respects these different scales. The authors report it beat standard forecasters, numerical weather models, and recent foundation time series models. On the ERA5 data set it cut error well below both the HRRR weather model and the Chronos model. The design aims to transfer to new sites with minimal history.
arxiv-2510-17995:
Abhigya Verma and three co-authors synthesize training records for software agents without any human labelers. Agents need data that link a user's goal to tool details, well-formed calls, and proof that the calls ran. Gathering that from people is slow, costly, and hard to scale, so the team generates it with language models alone.

Their FABRIC frame splits the job into small pipelines that emit whole records: task, tools, policy sketch, chat, and run traces. Strict rules keep each record machine-readable and aligned across its parts. Builders of agent systems get a recipe for practice data that can be checked, not just read.
arxiv-2510-18295:
Shouvik Sadhukhan and C S Narayanamurthy study turbulence-hit laser beams in a 2025 optics paper. Turbulence in air bends and scrambles light beams used for free-space communication. The authors track how the beam's brightness pattern changes from frame to frame.

They model brightness with Gaussian mixture models, meaning blends of bell-shaped curves fitted to the data. A geometric distance then measures how each frame's pattern drifts from earlier frames. Tests covered clean air, turbulence alone, and turbulence with one or two plastic compensator slabs. Distances shrank with compensation, suggesting the slabs partly restore the beam's statistical coherence.
arxiv-2510-18495:
M. A. Burlak and his eight co-authors examine DF Tau, a young pair of stars still feeding from a surrounding disk of gas and dust. The team analyzed a light curve, a record of the system's brightness, stretching across roughly one hundred twenty-five years. They conclude that the long brightness changes track changes in how fast material falls from the disk onto the main star, a process called accretion.

The researchers also sharpened the numbers describing the pair's orbit, which let them line up the brightness record with the changing distance between the two stars. Any link between brightness and orbital motion they found conflicts with what theory predicts, and similar mismatches appear in other young binary systems. They further located the source of polarized light very close to the star and found its changes did not follow the orbital cycle.
arxiv-2510-18795:
Xiaoxing Hu and his eight co-authors fix a known weakness of CLIP. CLIP links images and text. Its text encoder takes at most seventy-seven tokens. Long descriptions get cut off. Fine detail is lost. Languages beyond English are poorly served. A large language model embedder could replace that encoder. In principle, the swap helps a lot. But the two spaces were trained apart. Forcing them together can damage learned alignment.

Their framework, ProCLIP, aligns the pieces step by step. The pace follows a curriculum. First, CLIP's text knowledge is distilled into the new embedder. That builds a bridge to the image encoder. Next, contrastive training completes the alignment. A self-distillation guardrail protects the old knowledge. The goal is a model that reads long, multilingual text. It should keep CLIP's original strengths as well.
arxiv-2510-19095:
Alain Couvreur and Rakhi Pratihar give a recursive decoding method for binary rank Reed-Muller codes, a newer family of error-correcting codes defined over group algebras. Rank metric codes protect data when errors are measured by rank, and decoding them efficiently is the key step toward practical use.

Borrowing the recursive Plotkin construction that decodes classical binary Reed-Muller codes, the authors split the problem into smaller pieces step by step. For a specific subclass, their method beats the running time of the best recent decoder. Faster decoding widens where rank metric codes can serve, from network coding to post-quantum cryptography proposals.
arxiv-2510-19395:
Frank Corapi and seven co-authors study how electrical resistance saturates in metals made of ultracold fermions moving on an optical lattice. Watching transport directly, they measure both parts of the resistivity in a strongly interacting metallic regime built from atoms trapped by light.

As interactions grow, the rate at which current dissipates stops rising and settles at a value independent of interaction strength. A dissipation model using a renormalized two-body scattering matrix captures that plateau quantitatively. The work gives a clear microscopic account of bounded resistivity in low-density metals, a phenomenon long seen in real materials without a clean explanation.
arxiv-2510-19495:
Kevin Huang and eleven co-authors show how messy, non-expert robot data can strengthen imitation learning instead of being thrown away. Imitation learning trains robots from expert demonstrations, but expert data is costly and covers few situations. Play data, partial attempts, and rollouts from weak policies are cheaper and broader, yet standard imitation methods cannot use them well.

The authors argue that offline reinforcement learning, with the right design choices, can unlock that data. Simple changes that widen the range of actions the policy considers let the combined method recover from mistakes and generalize better. In manipulation tasks, adding non-expert data widened the set of starting conditions the robots could handle, using even partial or flawed demonstrations.
arxiv-2510-19795:
Jhionathan de Lima and Cristiano Francisco Woellner characterize hexa-graphyne, a flat carbon allotrope built from distorted hexagonal and rectangular rings mixing two carbon bonding types. First-principles calculations confirm the material is stable energetically, dynamically, and thermally up to at least one thousand kelvin. Its band structure makes it a semimetal.

Mechanically the sheet is far softer than graphene, with a Young's modulus about thirteen times lower and a Poisson's ratio nearly four times higher. Optically it absorbs ultraviolet strongly, reflects infrared well, and stays largely transparent in visible light, a rare combination. Ribbons cut from the sheet behave differently depending on edge shape and width, pointing to possible nanoelectronic and optoelectronic uses.
arxiv-2510-20095:
Ziheng Zhang and eleven co-authors test whether descriptive captions can improve biological foundation models beyond simple species labels. Images and captions can each reveal different traits of a species, so training with both should stress real diagnostic features and weaken false correlations. The hard part is getting faithful, specimen-specific captions at large scale.

The team generates synthetic captions with multimodal large language models, guided by visual information drawn from Wikipedia and by taxon-specific format examples to reduce invented detail. Training with those captions produces BioCAP, a model that performs strongly on species classification and on matching text with images. The work shows captions carry useful signal that labels alone miss.
arxiv-2510-20195:
John Nijim and three co-authors analyze the performance of Hadamard Transform Spectral Imaging, a multiplexing method that recovers spectra through multi-slit masks. The method suits faint light work where noise that does not depend on the signal dominates. Decoding multiplies the encoded spectral images by the inverse of the Hadamard matrix, which separates spectra that overlapped in the target.

Compared with direct single-slit scanning, the method raises the average signal-to-noise ratio when signal-independent noise such as detector read noise is present. When only photon noise matters, it gives no average gain or loss. Emission lines benefit under both noise types, and the advantage grows as read noise rises relative to shot noise.
arxiv-2510-20495:
Panagiotis Giannakopoulos and four co-authors set out a way to build and grade app speed gauges for edge sites by rote. True speed calls are key for task plans and stock use at the edge. But apps share nodes, and nodes clash in type, so speed is hard to call. Their way picks the gauge that wins on both truth and call speed.

Gauges train on past logs of the checks most tied to app speed. They are graded on more than one host in live mixed states. Truth tops near 90 in 100, while calls take less than one part in a hundred of trip time. Their test case is electron microscopy work, with strict live needs and mixed stock wants.
arxiv-2510-20595:
Yunyi Shen and Alexander Gagliano build a diffusion autoencoder with Perceivers for star data that come as long, lopsided, mixed sets. Self-taught nets are most tried on even sets like stills or clips. Star data break that mold. Their net splits mixed reads to tokens, packs them with a Perceiver coder, and rebuilds them with a Perceiver-IO diffusion decoder.

A mate base net, a masked autoencoder in the same Perceiver frame, sets a strong bar. On both light-curve and spectra star sets, the diffusion net posts less rebuild miss, more split latent codes, and more fine grain kept than the base net and a VAE. The frame aims at fields with lopsided, mixed streams.
arxiv-2510-20695:
Galina Weinstein, writing alone, closes a three part history of how experiments pressed Albert Einstein toward special relativity between eighteen ninety five and mid nineteen oh five. Rather than a sudden leap, the theory appears as an answer forced by a pile of stubborn results.

Weinstein traces star light bending tests, prism trials, partial drag accounts, water filled telescope ideas, and water tube flow results, plus null ether drift tests and a magnet coil puzzle. Rival ether theories tried to absorb each result with strained fixes, and Einstein even tried an emission view before flow data broke it. Seen this way, the nineteen oh five work resolves a linked web of anomalies at once.
arxiv-2510-20995:
Ignacio Boero leads two co-authors on AL-CoLe, an augmented Lagrangian method for learning under constraints such as fairness limits. Lagrangian duality is popular for constrained learning despite non convex models, but plain duality leaves a gap that augmented forms can narrow with small changes.

Strong duality results are established under mild conditions, dual ascent is proved to converge to feasible optimal primal solutions, and PAC style generalization guarantees are supplied. Tests on fairness constrained classification show the method working in practice. The package gives constrained learning a firmer theoretical base than heuristic penalty tuning usually offers.
arxiv-2510-21095:
James Tian, working alone, studies the stability of maximum entropy inference for finite dimensional quantum states under linear moment constraints. Given measured averages of a few observables, many states fit, and the maximum entropy rule picks the Gibbs state that matches while staying maximally unbiased.

Tian proves that convergence of moments and entropy forces convergence of the states themselves in trace norm, with explicit quantitative bounds tying data and entropy errors to state distance. Stability also holds under a class of noise maps. Such guarantees tell experimenters how much trust a reconstructed quantum state deserves.
arxiv-2510-21395:
Hermine Landt and forty-three co-authors report near-infrared watching of hot dust around Mrk 817. That galaxy hosts an active black hole at its center. The work sits inside a large multi-wavelength campaign. The campaign found the galaxy's soft X-ray glow heavily blocked. That raised questions about the dust around the core.

The team collected 157 spectra a few days apart. The usual echo in brightness shows no clear dust response. Yet the echo in dust temperature gives a ring radius near ninety light-days. That matches older results from clearer times. The inner edge of the dust seems set by something other than melting. It looks like a standing wall of carbon-rich grains. Farther out, hot dust stretches across hundreds of light-years. It ties to a rotating disk of ionized gas in the host galaxy's central bulge. A burst of star formation likely warms it.
arxiv-2510-21595:
Diederik van Engelenburg and three co-authors give a shorter proof of a classic estimate in percolation. Percolation studies how connections spread through a random medium. For spread-out percolation in more than six dimensions, they bound the one-arm probability up to constant factors. That is the chance that a cluster reaches far in one direction.

Matching estimates were first proved by Kozma and Nachmias for the whole space. Chatterjee and Hanson proved them for a half space, with longer arguments. The new proof sharpens an entropic technique from Dewan and Muirhead. It feeds that technique a precise estimate of a well-chosen correlation length. Two researchers close to the team obtained that estimate recently. The work sits beside a companion study of the same exponent. That study covers percolation models tied to the high-dimensional Ising model.
arxiv-2510-22095:
Yankai Chen leads a nine-author position paper arguing that brain-computer interfaces should grow into partnerships. Interfaces that read brain signals already let people with severe neurological impairments communicate and control devices. They transfer information slowly and demand long, person-specific calibration, which has kept them from spreading.

Pairing the interface with a large language model changes the job from decoding commands to understanding intentions and cognitive states. The authors say the field should name and design for that shift: brain-agent collaboration, where the system acts as an active partner rather than a passive signal processor. The paper weighs the technical hurdles and the ethical stakes of putting an agent that close to a person's thoughts. Calls for trustworthiness to be designed in from the start.
arxiv-2510-22195:
Akinori Nishino and Naomichi Hatano solve how two electrons live and leak away inside an open double quantum dot. Quantum dots are artificial atoms wired to outside leads. States inside are resonant: they linger, then escape. Spin is included. So is the Coulomb repulsion between the two electrons.

The pair derives an effective Hamiltonian for the two-dot subspace. Its non-Hermitian character comes from the infinite leads outside. Diagonalizing it reveals four types of two-body resonant states. The starting point is two electrons of opposite spin, one parked per dot. The time-dependent Schrödinger equation is then solved in closed form. The states stay normalizable because their growth is confined to a region expanding at the electron velocity. Survival and hopping probabilities are read off from the exact solution.
arxiv-2510-22295:
Quoc Anh Nguyen, Bernard Cheng, and Kelvin Soh give Vietnamese songs the transcription dataset they have been missing. Automatic lyrics transcription is hard anywhere, but Vietnamese adds a tonal language, where pitch changes word meaning, plus strong dialect variation, and with no dedicated corpus the task had barely been attempted.

The team curated VietLyrics, six hundred forty-seven hours of songs with lyrics aligned line by line and metadata attached, and released it publicly with their models. Off-the-shelf speech recognizers stumbled badly on the material, making frequent errors and hallucinating words during instrumental stretches. Fine-tuning the Whisper family on the new data beat existing multilingual lyrics systems, including the specialized LyricWhiz. The authors pitch the resource as a foundation for Vietnamese music computing and a template for other low-resource singing traditions.
arxiv-2510-22395:
Federica Gamba leads fourteen co-authors in building CAP, a data set for spotting false scientific statements made up by language models. Scientific writing is a risky place for such errors, since terms, statistics, and context can shift meaning. CAP works across nine languages, five widely resourced and four with fewer resources.

The set holds nine hundred curated scientific questions and more than seven thousand answers from sixteen public models. Each answer carries labels for factual error and for fluency problems, plus token and score data. The release aims to support hallucination detection and fairer multilingual testing.
arxiv-2510-22495:
Commercial speech recognition systems may not hear all speakers equally well. Michael Scott, Siyu Liang, Alicia Wassink, and Gina-Anne Levow test that concern in a 2025 paper, using recordings of Pacific Northwest English from speakers of four ethnic backgrounds.

Scott and co-authors measure errors in four major commercial systems and link them to eleven speech features. A new phonetic error rate ties mistakes to specific sound patterns rather than word choice. Vowel quality differences show the strongest link to unequal errors, with the largest effects for African American speakers. The findings point to training data that better covers dialect sound variation.
arxiv-2510-22695:
Ivan Nasonov and Gaiane Panina wrote a 2025 math paper. It deals with normals to convex polytopes. A polytope is a flat sided shape. A normal is a line that leaves a face point at a right angle. The paper works in higher dimensions, above three.

The pair prove a clear claim. Each generic simple polytope has a point with many normals. The count meets at least the conjectured bound. That bound is two times the dimension, plus four. The result is the flat sided twin of a known problem. That older problem deals with smooth convex bodies. So a long open question is settled for the flat case.
arxiv-2510-22795:
Editing audio with plain words has lagged behind audio creation. Michael Ungersbock leads a team with five co-authors. In 2025 they introduce SAO-Instruct. It edits audio clips from any free form instruction. Older tools need a full description of the result. Others allow only fixed edit types.

The model builds on Stable Audio Open. Training data are triplets of input, instruction, and output. Those triplets come from prompt tools and manual edits. Some training data are synthetic. Still, the model handles real wild clips well. It also handles unseen instructions. Listening tests favor it over rival editing methods. Code and weights are released.
arxiv-2510-23195:
Samson Seifu Bekele and four co-authors present a method to model smooth surfaces from very sparse measured data. They solve a discrete biharmonic equation over a domain, using inner point data as a load and inner curve data as boundary values. Building those boundary values is ill-posed, so they suggest a special regularization.

The construction targets problems with very few measurements, where standard fitting fails. Their application is in soil science, where field data is costly and patchy. A stable way to draw smooth soil surfaces from sparse samples would aid land and crop decisions.
arxiv-2510-23395:
Evy Beijen and five co-authors detect religious language inside climate discourse from secular and religious nongovernmental organizations. Religious terms and frames persist even in ostensibly secular debates about the environment. The authors ask how explicit and implicit religious language appears in climate texts.

They pair a rule-based model, built on a hierarchical tree of religious terms from ecotheology literature, with large language models in a zero-shot setting. The data set holds more than eight hundred eighty thousand sentences. Comparing the two approaches shows what each catches, informing studies of how values language shapes climate advocacy.
arxiv-2510-23495:
Chenyang Ma, Kai Lu, Ruta Desai, Xavier Puig, Andrew Markham, and Niki Trigoni introduce COOPERA, a framework for continual, open-ended human-robot assistance. Helpful robots must model individual traits, habits, and activities over time, yet most assistants handle only predefined tasks in structured settings with no human model to learn from.

In COOPERA, simulated humans driven by psychological traits and long-term intentions interact with robots in complex environments, giving continuous feedback. The framework, for the first time, enables robots to learn assistance that adapts as people change. It provides a test bed for truly personal home robots.
arxiv-2510-23595:
Yixing Chen and seven co-authors propose Multi-Agent Evolve, a way for language models to improve their reasoning without human-made training sets. Reinforcement learning works well for such models, but it leans on curated data and checkable rewards, which limits how far it scales. Self-play methods drop the human data yet usually need a grounded environment, like a code interpreter, to judge results.

Their design splits one model into three roles that train together: a Proposer that invents questions, a Solver that answers them, and a Judge that grades both. Reinforcement learning tunes all three as they co-evolve, across math, reasoning, and general knowledge questions. On a three-billion-parameter Qwen model, the method lifted benchmark scores by about four and a half percent on average. The authors offer it as a data-efficient path to stronger general reasoning.
arxiv-2510-23695:
Tae Hyun Jung and three co-authors set new limits on heavy QCD axions using Big Bang nucleosynthesis. That process forged the lightest elements in the first minutes of the universe. The measured amount of helium-4 pins down the neutron-to-proton ratio back then precisely. A heavy axion, motivated by the strong CP problem, would decay mostly into hadrons and disturb that ratio if it lived long enough.

The authors compute how axion decays shift the ratio and derive upper bounds on axion lifetimes. The tightest bound is a few hundredths of a second, for masses above three hundred million electronvolts. These bounds beat even projected limits from the cosmic microwave background. They stay robust against uncertainties in cross sections, decay branching fractions, and the starting axion abundance. The calculation also adds scattering by energetic kaons and secondary hadrons for the first time, useful for any hadronic injection study.
arxiv-2510-23795:
Akash Kharita and four co-authors compare machine learning methods for telling seismic sources apart in the Pacific Northwest: earthquakes, explosions, surface events, and noise. Networks keep densifying and signals overlap, so four-way sorting matters for real monitoring. Earlier studies mostly tried binary tasks and rarely pitted classic feature-based learning against deep learning fairly.

The team used about two hundred thousand three-component waveforms from over seventy thousand events. Random forests ran on three feature sets, while convolutional networks took raw time series or spectrograms. Spectrogram networks won, topping ninety-two percent accuracy both inside the region and on outside data, against eighty-nine percent for the best forest. One winning network is tiny — about seventy thousand parameters — and scans a full day of data in roughly nine seconds on ordinary hardware. It ships inside the SeisBench toolkit with released checkpoints, ready for real-time operations.
arxiv-2510-23895:
Hoora Sobhani and a co-author model how self-driving software fuses sensor data, and how that fusion should be scheduled. Autonomous driving stacks are drawn as directed acyclic graphs of tasks with data flowing between them. Standard scheduling treats fusion tasks as if they all trigger the same way, which misses the variety in real systems and can cost reaction time.

The framework distinguishes three fusion patterns: timer-triggered, wait-for-all, and immediate fusion. An integer linear programming approach then optimizes several timing metrics at once: reaction time, time disparity, age of information, and response time. It outputs deterministic schedules that run directly on real platforms. Tests span real driving case studies, a Raspberry Pi build, and randomly generated graphs. The authors report broad coverage of fusion patterns beyond earlier work, with substantial performance gains where comparisons apply.
arxiv-2510-24095:
Vedant Gupta and four co-authors present DEPS, a method that learns reusable skills from expert demonstrations. Instead of copying single actions, the system learns skills that take parameters, so one skill can be tuned for many objects or goals. A higher level policy picks which skill to use and what values to give it at each step.

The method learns the skills and the picker together, using tools that keep the skills distinct, long lasting, and meaningful. On the LIBERO and MetaWorld test suites, DEPS beat both multitask and other skill learning methods on new tasks. It also found skills a person can read clearly, such as grasping an object in a set way.
arxiv-2510-24295:
Mădălina Zgreabăn and two co-authors propose MERGE, a test of whether reasoning models generalize or merely memorize benchmark patterns. Many benchmarks are now saturated, and new reasoning datasets are costly to build by hand and error prone to generate automatically. Their approach instead creates minimal variants of existing natural language inference examples.

Masked language models generate high quality variants by replacing small expressions, with safeguards to keep the changes valid and non adversarial. Models are then checked for robust reasoning on these near copies of known items. The test aims to expose brittle models that fail when surface wording shifts slightly while the logic stays the same.
arxiv-2510-24395:
Iwan Morton-Blake and nine co-authors study how to configure large underwater neutrino telescopes for the best sensitivity to point sources of all neutrino flavors. Detectors like IceCube and KM3NeT have found a diffuse astrophysical flux, shifting the field toward detailed source studies. Next generation arrays need larger volumes, sharper angular resolution, and full flavor coverage.

Taking the proposed TRIDENT array in the South China Sea as a case study, the team compares detector configurations against the baseline design. They weigh track like events, mainly from muon neutrinos, which give precise directions, against other event types. The results inform design choices for future underwater telescopes.
arxiv-2510-24495:
Yuzhi Yang leads a team of seven authors on wireless receivers. Modern wireless systems split signals across many tones at once. That scheme, OFDM, needs a sharp guess of the channel state. The channel is the path the signal takes through air and walls. Poor channel guesses cap the speed of the whole system.

Diffusion models, AI tools that build data by removing noise, may help. The team recast channel guessing as a generative AI task. A rough first guess can then be refined step by step. The paper maps how diffusion fits transceiver design as a whole. It sketches paths toward AI-native receivers for sixth-generation networks. A proof-of-concept case shows gains from tuning diffusion for receivers. The survey aims to guide both wireless and AI researchers.
arxiv-2510-25195:
Shuochuan Li, Zan Wang, Xiaoning Du, Zhuo Wu, Jiuqiao Yu, and Junjie Chen build KUMIC, a frame that writes code notes with more than one aim at once. One plain note can not serve all: coders want the how laid bare, while users want plain use steps. Chat models can write such notes, but strain to tie aims, code, and notes right from few demos.

KUMIC uses step thought to make full use of what the model knows in context. It builds the ties among aim, code, and note in a clear chain before it writes. That chain lets each note match its own aim, not a blurred mean. Tests check the frame next to past top ways.
arxiv-2510-25395:
Joshua Vedral, Nathaniel Morgan, Dmitri Kuzmin, and Jacob Moore present a hydrodynamics method. Their 2025 paper presents a Lagrangian discontinuous Galerkin scheme. It solves multi-part hyperbolic systems in fluids. Form preservation is a central goal here. They adapt Zalesak flux-corrected transport for quality. A positivity-preserving scheme mixes with higher-order discretization.

Flux limiting correction factors derive from certain volume. Those factors apply to all answer parts. Mesh cell volumes evolve using geometric conservation law. Limiting those fluxes equals moving mesh with limited velocities. A slope limiter suppresses spurious oscillations locally. It also preserves bounds on answer values. Nodal velocities come from a multidirectional Riemann solver. That maintains momentum and total energy conservation locally. Linear elements and second-order time integration ensure consistency. Standard test problems showed stability and shock capture. Results showed superb results on those tests.
arxiv-2510-25495:
A Giarnetti and D Meloni review reinforcement learning for particle physics. Their 2025 short review discusses the flavor problem. That problem concerns fermion masses and mixing patterns. Classic methods extend the Standard Model with symmetries. The landscape of possible models is vast, however.

Systematic exploration of that landscape is infeasible manually. Reinforcement learning can navigate model spaces quickly, they note. Recent works construct models reproducing observed observables. Quark and lepton data are the targets there. Learning methods rediscover models already proposed in literature. They also uncover new phenomenologically acceptable answers. That dual result validates the method strongly. Automated search may accelerate flavor model building. Particle physicists face many candidate symmetries and charges. Reinforcement learning agents can test combinations rapidly. The review summarizes recent uses and their promise. It is brief, aimed at scholars entering the area.
arxiv-2510-25595:
Run Peng led seven co-authors studying agent collaboration. Ziqiao Ma, Amy Pang, and Sikai Li helped. Zhang Xi-Jia, Yingzhuo Yu, and Cristian-Paul Bara joined. Joyce Chai closes the eight-author team. Their 2025 paper studies contact under information asymmetry. Language model agents often plan actions toward goals. Collaboration abilities between agents remain poorly explored.

Agents differ in knowledge and skills. They must work jointly. The authors extend Einstein Puzzles into a tabletop game. Two language agents reason, communicate, and act jointly. Spatial and relational constraints must be satisfied. A fine-tuning plus verifier approach equips agents. Various contact strategies and verification signals are tested. Aligned contact proves critically major for collaboration. Information-seeking and providing capabilities both help agents. Agents without contact still reached high results surprisingly. Further study revealed weak rule understanding. Human evaluators trusted those silent agents less. Environment verifiers enhanced rule comprehension and task completion.
arxiv-2510-25795:
J. A. Vera wrote a 2025 mathematics paper about special points in flat systems described by polynomials. These systems are Hamiltonian systems, meaning an energy-like quantity stays fixed as motion unfolds. The paper focuses on isochronous centers, points where nearby loops all take the same time.

Vera revisits earlier work by Braun, Llibre, and Mereu on the simplest such centers in degrees five and seven. He shows one family, built in a triangular pattern, gives these centers in every odd degree from three onward. A second family, based on a quadratic shear, shows up only for some degrees, starting at seven. That pattern explains why the second family seems to appear and vanish in turns. For degree nine, he argues, the second family cannot appear at all.
arxiv-2510-26195:
Armin Ilg, working alone, presents the IDEA detector concept for the electron positron stage of the Future Circular Collider. A detector for such a collider must track grains of matter, measure their energy levels, and identify muons with high exactness to exploit the clean crashes. IDEA combines several parts: a vertex detector based on pixel sensors, a very light drift chamber, a silicon wrapper, and a high sharpness crystal electric and magnetic heat meter with dual readout.

Ilg describes the physics needs behind each subsystem and the technical solutions chosen, including a super conducting solenoid made with high temperature superconductor and a dual readout fibre heat meter. Three layers of muon chambers sit in the magnet return yoke. Ongoing research, test beam results, and expected benchmark performance are also reported.
arxiv-2510-26295:
Ya-Xin Xiang, Weibin Li, Zhengyang Bai, and Yu-Qiang Ma propose a quantum version of predator prey cycles in an array of Rydberg atoms. Predator prey cycles are self ordered population cycles, but testing their mechanism in real living systems is hard because tiny scale settings cannot be controlled. Rydberg atoms, atoms excited to large orbits, offer a tunable stand in where interactions can be dialed.

Through mean field analysis and large scale sim runs of the open system, Xiang and the team show stable cycles of Rydberg excited states on millionth of a second time scales. Nonperturbative quantum phase lock drives self started breaking of time shift symmetry, giving globally in sync cycles under short range interactions. Even when quantum jumps break sync the array, locally in sync cycles persist.
arxiv-2510-26495:
Linzhuang Sun, with eight co-authors, builds a harder test for turning plain questions into database queries. Text-to-SQL systems write SQL, the standard query language, from a user's words. Most tests use one-shot questions, but real users in finance or business refine their asks step by step as results come back.

Sun and the team create DySQL-Bench, with about one thousand seventy-two tasks across thirteen domains drawn from two known databases. Tasks are made by an automatic two-stage pipeline, then filtered and checked by experts, and human review found the data fully correct. Their test setup mimics a live chat among a fake user, the model, and a working database. Even GPT-4o scored only about fifty-eight percent overall, and far less on a strict repeat measure, which shows the gap left to close.
arxiv-2510-26895:
Minjeong Song, Hyukjoon Kwon, and Valerio Scarani ask when undoing a noisy quantum channel can be done with the same tabletop resources as the channel itself. Channels that describe open quantum dynamics cannot be reversed fully, but the Petz recovery map gives a systematic partial recovery tied to a reference state. Normally its implementation looks very different from the channel's.

Song and her two co-authors study tabletop reversibility, where the recovery is realisable with similar resources. For the exact case, they show time-sensitive control of an ancilla system is needed. For the approximate case, they give conditions that drop that requirement. They also derive conditions for Lindbladian dynamics under a random-time collision model. The results clarify when recovery is cost-free in practice.
arxiv-2510-26995:
Elliot Epstein, John Winnicki, Thanawat Sornwanee, and Rajat Dwaraknath test how well large language models judge their own uncertainty. The models answer Fermi questions, meaning rough estimate questions with a true numeric answer, and give intervals that should contain that answer. A new benchmark, FermiEval, scores both how often intervals hit and how narrow they stay.

Intervals labeled as ninety-nine percent sure hold the truth only about sixty-five percent of the time on average. A fix borrowed from conformal prediction, a method that widens intervals using past errors, restores true coverage and sharply improves scores. The team also proposes a perception-tunnel account, where the models act as if the tails of their own belief spread do not exist.
arxiv-2511-00095:
Jiaming Liu, Dingwei Fan, and Junyong Zhao present SpinalSAM-R1, a vision-language two-way system for splitting spine anatomy in computed tomography scans. Spinal splitting guides finding and treatment, but low contrast and complex spinal edges make it hard. The Segment Anything Model promises general splitting yet needs heavy tagging and adapts poorly to spinal CT on its own.

Their multimodal system fits language contact with the splitting backbone to beat those limits. Medical imaging readers get a focused offshoot of a general foundation model. Interactive, language-guided splitting could let doctors steer drawing of back bones and nearby structures with less manual drawing.
arxiv-2511-00895:
Hansjorg Albrecher, Filip Lindskog, and Herve Zumbach extend a standard insurance valuation method. Cost of capital valuation prices liabilities by charging for the buffer capital an insurer must hold, and regulators rely on it. The usual version assumes that buffer sits in riskless one year bonds.

The authors ask what changes when the buffer is invested in risky assets, such as a mix of stocks and bonds. They make precise how the split of the buffer between policyholders and investors shifts as the investments get riskier. They highlight the role of limited liability when insurance risks are heavy tailed. General theorems are paired with explicit results in specific stochastic models and with numerical work that underlines the main effects.
arxiv-2511-00995:
Tianming Wu and Dixin Tang present PathFinder, an indexing framework for filtered nearest neighbor search. The task is to find the items most similar to a query among only those whose attributes pass a filter. Filters in real applications combine several attributes with and and or conditions, which breaks indexes tuned for a single attribute.

Borrowing from relational database design, PathFinder lets users build attribute specific indexes and then uses a cost based optimizer to combine them for complex filters. New pieces include a metric balancing speed against accuracy, a two phase plan for mixed filters, and a way to borrow one attribute's index for another. On four real data sets it beat the best baseline by up to nearly ten times in throughput at high recall.
arxiv-2511-01195:
Yu Sang and Hai-Nan Lin use fast radio bursts, brief and still mysterious flashes of radio waves, to probe the galaxies the bursts come from. A burst's signal is smeared by electrons along its path, and the part of that dispersion measure contributed by the host galaxy carries information about the burst's local environment.

Analyzing one hundred seventeen well localized bursts, they find the host contribution follows a log normal distribution. It correlates moderately with the host's redshift, so more distant bursts tend to sit in denser host environments by this measure. No significant links appear with stellar mass, star formation rate, or galaxy age. The authors argue the host dispersion is a useful diagnostic for burst origins, and call for deeper multi wavelength follow up of host galaxies.
arxiv-2511-01795:
Gabriel Nobis and seven colleagues build generative models with memory. Standard diffusion models are driven by Brownian motion, which has no memory: each step forgets the last. Real processes, from protein motion to natural imagery, show long-range correlations, roughness, and anomalous diffusion that Brownian drivers cannot reproduce.

Fractional Diffusion Bridge Models swap in a Markovian approximation of fractional Brownian motion, keeping the process tractable while preserving its non-Markovian character. The authors prove a coupling-preserving bridge exists in this setting. They apply it to predicting future states from paired data. They also extend the setup to the Schrödinger bridge problem for unpaired translation, with a principled loss. On protein conformation prediction it lowered positional error, and on unpaired image translation it beat Brownian baselines on image quality scores.
arxiv-2511-01995:
The CMS Collaboration measures how often top quark pairs are produced together with a photon at the Large Hadron Collider. The analysis uses proton-proton collisions at 13 TeV, recorded by the CMS detector. The integrated luminosity is 138 inverse femtobarns. It selects events with two leptons and a photon. It measures the process inclusively and differentially, across lepton, photon, top quark, and pair kinematics.

The fiducial cross section came out at 137 femtobarns, for events with a hard, isolated photon. It came out at 56 femtobarns when the photon must come from the production stage itself. Both agree with the theoretical predictions, of 126 and 57 femtobarns respectively. The ratio to ordinary top pair production measured about 0.0133 in the data, matching the Standard Model's expectation near 0.0127 in the same units, and the study adds particle- and parton-level differential spectra plus the top quark charge asymmetry.
arxiv-2511-02295:
Shumpei Oguchi, Kenji Ishida, Atsutoshi Ikeda, Yoshiteru Maeno, and Shunsaku Kitagawa squeeze a superconducting crystal to see how its electronic state responds. The material, CaSb2, combines calcium and antimony and is known as a line nodal superconductor, meaning its energy gap vanishes along lines rather than at single points. Resistance measurements under pressure reveal how its transition temperature behaves as the lattice is squeezed.

Pressure was applied up to 4.2 gigapascals, and the transition temperature peaked at 3.1 gigapascals, where the room-temperature resistance also showed a subtle kink. A Bloch-Grüneisen analysis of how resistance varies with temperature, however, indicated that the electronic state beneath does not change notably across that peak pressure. The short report leaves its superconductivity looking robust against the compression, with the anomaly in resistance not matched by a deeper electronic change.
arxiv-2511-02695:
Some theories add a hidden dark sector of matter with its own strong force and its own photon. The Heavy Photon Search experiment hunted for signs of that sector at a fixed target hit by an electron beam. A 2025 paper from the HPS Collaboration reports the first search for displaced decays of dark vector mesons made in that setup.

The team used data from the 2016 engineering run and looked for electron pairs born away from the target, with masses from 39 to 179 million electron volts in energy units. No signal rose above the normal background from quantum electrodynamics. The null result still counts: it narrows where such dark mesons could hide and guides later runs of the experiment.
arxiv-2511-02795:
Mayank Jobanputra and nine colleagues test a basic skill in large language models: subtraction. Addition and multiplication get most of the attention in math benchmarks, but subtraction differs because order matters and answers can go negative. Their 2025 study runs eight pretrained models from four families on both operations and compares the scores.

Subtraction accuracy lagged addition by a wide margin. Errors clustered where the second number was larger, so the true answer was negative. There the models often gave the right size but dropped the minus sign. Probing showed the models did encode the sign inside, yet failed to print it. Few-shot examples helped a little. Instruction tuning nearly fixed the sign problem, suggesting the weakness is real but recoverable.
arxiv-2511-02895:
Gian Maria Campedelli argues that criminology must start studying machines as possible actors in crime, not only as tools. Autonomous AI agents already work across industries and online spaces, and machine-to-machine dealings are set to grow. His 2025 essay draws on Actor-Network Theory and an older call for a sociology of machines, both newly relevant as generative agents spread.

Campedelli proposes a two-part taxonomy of the channels through which agent interactions could yield deviant or unlawful outcomes. He then poses four questions: whether machines will just mimic humans, whether human crime theory can explain agent behavior, which crimes shift first, and how policing must change. The piece urges criminologists to join debates on AI safety and governance early.
arxiv-2511-02995:
Tarcisio Deda, William Wolf, Scott Dawson, and Brener Ramos build neural observers that reconstruct a full fluid flow from a few noisy sensors. Flow control needs the current state in real time, yet sensors are sparse and imperfect. Their 2025 framework generalizes the classic Luenberger observer: each part of the estimation loop is a neural network, blending probe readings with a learned surrogate model of the flow.

Three test systems show the range. A chaotic wave equation and a cylinder wake were both tracked well enough to close the control loop with a neural controller, even with noisy or slow sensors. A real turbulent boundary layer data set came last: fusing poor sensor data with an imperfect model beat both pure reconstruction methods and plain model forecasts.
arxiv-2511-03195:
Ting-Wen Lan, J Xavier Prochaska, and a large Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument team map the gas that surrounds distant emission-line galaxies. Using about seven thousand galaxy and quasar pairs, they trace cool and warm gas through the light it absorbs. The galaxies sit at a time when the universe was much younger than today.

Gas cover and strength both grow with galaxy mass, yet look alike once distances are scaled to each halo size. Warm gas reaches farther out than cool gas, and the two phases move in ways that are not tightly linked. Near the center, iron looks richer while the warm phase looks weaker. The team argues the phases sit in different places, and the halo gas holds mass much like the gas inside galaxies.
arxiv-2511-03295:
Mauro Cettolo and co-authors run the first broad study of scoring speech translation with help from the source audio itself. Usual scoring compares a translation only with reference texts, which wastes clues in the original speech. Text translation scoring gained from reading the source, yet speech systems rarely have a clean transcript ready.

Two workarounds are tried: reading machine transcripts of the audio, and building text stand-ins by other means. Both feed neural scoring tools that then judge translation quality. The authors check how close those scores sit to human judgment under real-world limits. Their findings guide builders who must rate speech translation where no transcript exists, a common case in live and low-resource settings.
arxiv-2511-03395: Stefan Franssen contributes a short discussion of a target work on model uncertainty and missing data from an objective Bayesian stance. Writing from a frequentist viewpoint, Franssen weighs how the proposed methods behave under repeated sampling ideas. The note is brief by design, as discussion pieces reply to a main article rather than stand alone. Its value lies in placing two statistical philosophies side by side on the same practical problems: choosing among models when data have gaps. Readers gain a counterpoint stressing long-run performance alongside prior-based reasoning.
arxiv-2511-03795:
Kobe Marshall-Stevens, Gongping Niu, and Davide Parise establish generic regularity for isoperimetric regions in closed manifolds of dimension eight. Such regions enclose a set volume with least boundary area, and their boundaries can develop sharp points that complicate geometry, in higher dimensions.

For a generic choice of smooth metric and enclosed volume, every such region has a smooth, clean boundary, the team prove. The same conclusion holds when volume is fixed first and the metric is then chosen in general. Dimension eight is a threshold case in regularity theory, so showing that bad behaviour is non-generic there settles a real borderline question.
arxiv-2511-04295:
Masood Aryapoor, writing alone, extends a key lemma behind the Amitsur-Small theorem into the skew setting of noncommutative algebra. Catalog evidence left punctuation in the title; the arXiv record gives the extensions title used here. Amitsur-Small type results control how polynomial identities behave under field extensions, a basic question for ring theory.

A notion of Amitsur-Small extensions is introduced to carry that lemma beyond its commutative comfort zone. Within that framework, a skew version of the Amitsur-Small theorem itself is established. The abstract is brief and states the construction and theorem plainly, so the contribution is best understood as a structural generalization: familiar identity theory now works where variables no longer commute freely.
arxiv-2511-04895:
Oem Trivedi and his co-author propose Solar System searches for primordial black holes. These early-universe black holes could account for dark matter in some mass ranges. Cosmological and astrophysical probes already limit parts of that range.

Local precision opens two fresh windows, they argue. Asteroid to dwarf-planet mass objects could leave dipolar timing signatures in pulsar timing arrays. Planetary-mass ones could spark detectable accretion flares when meeting Kuiper Belt bodies. Together the two channels use the Solar System's unmatched coverage. A local detection would tie the dark matter question to the neighborhood we know best.
arxiv-2511-04995:
Amol Harsh and co-authors build an AI tool to coach engineering students in public speaking. Schools offer talks and short courses, but they cannot give each student long, personal feedback on both speech and body signs.

Their system joins speech study, computer vision, and mood sensing in one model. It scores pitch, loudness, pace, and tone, plus face signs, gestures, and stance. The aim is steady, tailored feedback at scale, so students can drill a key job skill that lectures alone rarely build in a safe, repeat setting on campus.
arxiv-2511-05095:
Fuyang Liu and co-authors present a two-level learning method to restore photos spoiled by bad weather. Rain, fog, and snow blur real scenes, and models trained on fake damage often fail on the mixed harm found in the wild.

First they built HFLS-Weather, a physics-based data set that mimics many weather harms with high fidelity, to give training a strong cold start. Then local models for each weather type are tuned by reward, while a global controller picks and blends them. The aim is clear images with no need for paired clean shots.
arxiv-2511-05495:
Tejas Pawar and co-authors present IMDMR, a memory system that helps conversational AI stay coherent over long chats. Most systems search memory on one axis alone, which loses context and makes replies drift or repeat.

IMDMR searches six axes at once: meaning, entity, category, intent, context, and time. A query is split and routed across those axes to pull the best past turns. The design aims at replies that feel personal and on track across long talks. Such memory is a key gap between chat demos and tools people can rely on daily.
arxiv-2511-06295:
Vamshika Sutar, Mahek Maheshwari, and Archak Mittal build a low-cost vision system to guide forklifts in warehouses. Automating material handling needs perception that is robust yet cheap enough to retrofit onto ordinary machines. Their framework uses a single standard camera to find pallets and the holes a forklift's forks must enter.

Two recent YOLO detector versions were tuned with automated hyperparameter search and spatial cleanup steps. A mapping module then turns raw detections into spatial layouts that pair each pallet with its holes for action. On a custom dataset enriched with real warehouse photos, one model led on raw detection accuracy while the tuned other model gave better precision and steadier training.
arxiv-2511-06395:
Hung Nguyen and Jeongseok Ha study how a drone can help a satellite talk secretly to a ground user. A passive warden watches for any transmission, so the satellite link must stay hidden. The helper drone serves its own ground network while also jamming friendly noise that covers the satellite's signal.

The authors derive a lower bound on the warden's average detection error, which defines how covert the link must be. They then jointly tune the drone's three-dimensional position, the power split, and the satellite's transmit power to maximize the covert rate. Block coordinate descent with successive convex approximation solves the hard non-convex problem, and simulations confirm the bound is tight.
arxiv-2511-06595:
Yanmin Mu and Dehua Wang prove that solutions of the relativistic Vlasov-Poisson system last for all time inside a two-dimensional convex region. The system tracks a plasma or stellar distribution pushed by its own electric field, with relativity shaping the motion. Particles bounce off the boundary by specular reflection, like light off a mirror, in the setup studied.

Two boundary rules for the electric potential are covered, Neumann and zero Dirichlet conditions. The proof builds custom velocity estimates near the wall and leans on geometry: arc length parametrization plus the Frenet-Serret formulas describe how the distribution behaves at the boundary. Those tools close the argument for general starting data.
arxiv-2511-06695: Takuma Aihara gives examples of tilting-discrete symmetric algebras, a class in representation theory where the tilting complexes of an algebra form a well-behaved, discrete set. One strand asks which algebras have tilting-discrete trivial extensions. Aihara supplies a counter example to the conjecture that every tau-tilting finite symmetric algebra must be tilting-discrete. The paper also discusses tilting-disconnectedness for symmetric algebras and adds new examples of algebras with that property, refining the map of how these tilting behaviors can and cannot combine.
arxiv-2511-06795:
Neil D Lawrence introduces the inaccessible game, an information-theoretic model of a dynamical system built from four axioms. The first three axioms are known results that define information loss within the system. The fourth is new: an information isolation axiom stating that the system is cut off from observation, making it observer-independent.

Under that isolation axiom, the total marginal entropy of the system stays constant rather than growing or shrinking. Lawrence then studies maximum entropy production inside the game and shows the dynamics take a structure resembling the GENERIC system of nonequilibrium physics. That structure combines a reversible part and an irreversible part, mirroring how physicists describe systems that mix mechanics with dissipation.
arxiv-2511-06895:
Viktor Veselý, Aleksandar Todorov, and Matthia Sabatelli look for double descent in deep reinforcement learning. Double descent is the paradox where making a model bigger first hurts, then improves, generalization. It is well documented in supervised learning but largely unexplored in reinforcement learning, where the data stream keeps changing as the agent learns.

Working with actor-critic agents of varying capacity, the authors report preliminary evidence of a clear epoch-wise double descent curve. They track policy entropy, a measure of the policy's uncertainty, and find its sustained drop coincides with entering the second descent. That pattern suggests overparameterization acts as an implicit regularizer, steering policies toward flatter, more robust solutions, which could inform how practitioners size and train agents.
arxiv-2511-07095:
Meghyn Bienvenu and Quentin Manière analyze the computational cost of answering questions over inconsistent knowledge bases written in description logics. Under cost-based semantics, each interpretation is charged for the weighted axioms and assertions it violates, and certain or possible answers are read off from interpretations of optimal or bounded cost. Earlier work covered only logics between two modest classes, leaving prominent DL-Lite dialects unexamined.

Extending the analysis to logics with inverse roles and role inclusions, the authors sharpen several lower bounds and pin down the precise complexity of certain answers under optimal cost. No nontrivial upper bound was known there before. Surprisingly, for one DL-Lite family with a fixed cost bound, instance-query certain answers and conjunctive-query possible answers admit first-order rewriting, the lowest possible data complexity, against the intractability found elsewhere.
arxiv-2511-07295:
Tianrui Song, Wen-Shuo Chao, and Hao Liu fix a confusion that undermines recommender system training. Implicit feedback data contains noise from misclicks and position bias, and older methods spot noisy samples by their high loss and drop or down-weight them. The trouble is that hard samples, the informative borderline cases that teach the most about preferences, show the same high-loss pattern, so denoising throws away gold with the dross.

Their system, LLMHNI, brings in large language models as referees. Semantic relevance from model embeddings guides negative sampling toward hard negatives while filtering false ones. Inferred logical relevance joins the interaction graph to flag hard versus noisy cases, with contrastive alignment across edge-dropped graph views to suppress hallucinated links. Tests show notable gains in both denoising and recommendation quality.
arxiv-2511-07395:
Fair division asks how to share goods so everyone feels treated equally. Hadi Hosseini and co-authors study equitability, where each person values their own bundle the same as others value theirs. They focus on a relaxed version that allows a gap of at most one item.

Even that relaxed goal can fail when values are not monotone, so the authors assume everyone agrees on the sign of the whole bundle value. Under that condition they prove such allocations exist for two agents and give an efficient method to find them. For larger groups they extend existence and fast computation to wider value types.
arxiv-2511-07495:
Ken Nagai builds a bridge between counting numbers and continuous spectra. Bernoulli numbers and zeta values arise from discrete sums, while Fredholm determinants describe operators on continuous spaces. Selector kernels based on trigonometric functions link the two worlds.

Euler-Maclaurin corrections become spectral traces of compact operators in the new framework. Determinants then slide between finite projectors and the sine kernel known from random matrix theory. In the continuum limit the determinant turns into a Painlevé tau function. Bernoulli and zeta constants together govern local and global behavior. Analysts gain one language for problems that once lived apart.
arxiv-2511-07595:
Özay Ezerceli and co-authors build a search engine brain tuned for Turkish. Retrieval models turn text into vectors so questions can find matching passages. Their TurkEmbed model already handled inference and similarity tasks, but search ranking needed special training.

Fine-tuning on a Turkish version of the MS MARCO dataset, with nested Matryoshka vectors and a ranking loss using many negatives, sharpens retrieval. On a Turkish science fact benchmark the model beats a Turkish ColBERT system by a wide margin on key metrics. Better Turkish retrieval supports question answering and document search for millions of speakers underserved by English-first tools.
arxiv-2511-07895:
Ha-Na Jo, Jung-Sun Lee, and Eunyeong Ko decode intent from brain waves when speech itself is distorted. Dysarthria weakens speech motor control, causing frequent misarticulation and low clarity of speech. Brain-computer help for this group remains scarce despite clear need.

EEG recordings from a participant with dysarthria during a Korean speech task were labeled by whether each attempt came out correctly. Misarticulated trials showed higher frontal-central slow activity and lower temporal gamma. A soft multitask learning framework builds on those signatures to decode intention robustly. Even single-case foundations matter for tailoring communication aids to individual speakers.
arxiv-2511-08295:
Loren Kohnfelder and Adam Shostack argue that technology companies should publish their threat models instead of keeping them internal. Threat modeling guides secure software design, and a public version can tell customers and partners what security thinking stands behind a product. Early adopters already provide precedents, and regulators increasingly push in this direction.

Internal models usually need redaction and review before disclosure, and the authors give guidance for that process and for later updates. Publishing, they contend, lets providers show their work, helps customers evaluate claims up and down the supply chain, and could easily become normal practice because many fine models already exist.
arxiv-2511-08495:
