Hongjian Zhou and co-authors review the experimental history of the J psi phi mass spectrum, a hunting ground for exotic hadron structures since 2009. The CDF experiment first reported the X(4140) structure, and later searches in related channels claimed ten structures in one decay system. LHCb amplitude analyses and diffractive studies form the backbone of the modern picture, alongside theoretical interpretations of the claimed states.

A triplet of states with the same quantum numbers and wide mass spacing appears to form a radially excited family, with X(4140) as its first member. Its measured width still disagrees between experiments, and the review discusses possible reasons. Parallels with the double J psi system close the discussion.
arxiv-2511-08595:
Joongho Kim and three co-authors speed up Tree-of-Thought reasoning, a method where a language model explores many branching solution paths. The search wastes effort because separate branches often repeat the same idea in different words, a redundancy the authors call semantic overlap.

Their method, Semantic Similarity-Based Dynamic Pruning, watches the search as it runs, groups steps that mean nearly the same thing, and prunes the duplicates in real time. On the GSM8K and MATH500 benchmarks it runs up to two point three times faster than strong tree-search baselines. Accuracy stays within about five percent of the best baseline while the number of explored nodes falls by eighty-five to ninety percent. Code is public.
arxiv-2511-08895:
Zhiqiang Miao and Huan Yang describe a new resonance that can grab a compact-star binary and hold it in lockstep. If one star in the pair is slightly squashed, carrying a finite ellipticity, a spin-orbit resonance can engage so the star's spin evolves together with the orbit instead of drifting freely.

The chance of locking grows with the square root of the ellipticity, and both the locking and its later breaking stamp a characteristic phase pattern onto the gravitational waveform. That pattern opens a fresh observational channel for measuring how squashed compact objects are, including exotic ones. Magnetars, whose huge internal fields can supply the squash, might place the signal in the ground-based low-frequency band, though their merger rates are uncertain. A search of all neutron star binaries in the catalog so far found no positive event.
arxiv-2511-08995:
Isshin Arai and Tomoaki Itano set hard limits on what any method can reconstruct about a physical system from observations, using the symmetry structure of the data itself. They define a reconstruction dimension, the maximum number of recoverable components. They show it is fixed sector by sector by the group representations carried by the observation spaces and the maps between them.

The working example is fluid mechanics: recovering the local velocity-gradient tensor, the full record of stretching and rotation in a flow, from the orientations of particles suspended in it. An equivariant neural network built for three-dimensional rotations finds exactly the reconstructable subspaces the representation theory predicts. Whether the bound is fully saturated then depends on the physics and the geometry of the data. The authors note this gives practitioners a principled ceiling before they start fitting.
arxiv-2511-09395:
Olcay Coskun and Alp Eden study a seven-dimensional algebra. It builds on a product written down by Hüseyin Tevfik Pasha, known as Vidinli, in 1882. Lifting his three-dimensional product to seven dimensions through the octonionic cross product gives an algebra that is unital, simple, and non-associative. Its symmetry group is the unitary group U(3).

The multiplication splits neatly into a simple Jordan algebra and a Heisenberg Lie algebra. The main result grades the cross product by the group of three binary signs. The whole multiplication table then follows from three explicit rules. That grading ties the algebra to the Fano plane, whose lines mark out its special subalgebras, a duality the authors make precise.
arxiv-2511-09695:
David Minkwan Kim and thirteen co-authors report progress on a construction robot for overhead jobs. A human supervises while it handles tasks like ceiling drilling. The platform rolls on a mobile base with a two-stage lift. It carries a two-armed torso, a custom drilling end effector, and depth cameras. Overhead work is tiring and hazardous, making shared autonomy attractive.

Limited visibility in dynamic sites is handled with online three-dimensional reconstruction by Gaussian splatting, extended to model moving objects. A neural configuration-space barrier method keeps planning and control safe around those obstacles. Feasibility studies show the hardware drilling, bolting, and anchoring, and the software supporting safe teleoperation in a changing environment. The system remains under active development.
arxiv-2511-09795:
Daniel W. Collison and Archil Kobakhidze add comments to a long-running debate in quantum field theory about gauge dependence. The effective potential, a central tool for studying vacuum behavior, can appear to depend on the gauge-fixing choice, which would make physical conclusions ambiguous. The authors stress an extra condition on the gauge-fixing function that is needed before claiming independence at an extremum.

They advocate the Vilkovisky-DeWitt construction of the effective action and potential as the cleaner alternative, and show its independence from the gauge-fixing parameter. As a further check, they present a high-temperature generalization of that construction for the Abelian-Higgs model. The note aims to firm up how such potentials should be computed and interpreted.
arxiv-2511-09895:
Xiaoda Wang and six co-authors present SE-Diff, a diffusion model that generates electrocardiogram signals from clinical text. Heart disease is a leading cause of death, ECGs are its most common non-invasive check, and large well-labeled ECG collections are scarce for cost and privacy reasons. Earlier text-to-ECG diffusion models ignored both the physiology of the heartbeat and the experience-based knowledge clinicians use.

SE-Diff embeds a light differential-equation simulator of cardiac activity into the diffusion process through a beat decoder and consistency constraints, favoring realistic waveforms. A language-model-powered retrieval strategy adds clinical experience as further guidance. On real-world datasets it beat baselines on signal fidelity and on how well signals matched their text, and the added knowledge also helped downstream ECG classification.
arxiv-2511-10195:
Hefan Li, Masashi Chiba, Xiang-Xiang Xue, and Gang Zhao date when the Milky Way swallowed six substructures now seen in its stellar halo near the Sun. Using precise Gaia astrometry, they estimate accretion times from orbital frequencies in the radial and azimuthal directions for substructures identified in their earlier studies. Monte Carlo sampling sets the uncertainties, and random halo samples establish significance.

One substructure gave consistent, highly significant dates from both directions, landing near five and a half billion years ago. Two others dated to roughly seven billion and two billion years ago. Comparing potentials, the authors suggest the more massive Milky Way model may overestimate the central bulge mass, and they look to future Gaia and telescope data for sharper dates.
arxiv-2511-10795:
Juan Límaco and Luis P. Yapu prove a controllability result for a free boundary heat equation. In this model, heat spreads through a region whose boundary itself moves, governed by a Stefan condition, as in melting ice. Their data are radially symmetric and the setting is three-dimensional.

The authors show the system is locally null controllable, meaning a suitable control can steer it to zero. Their strategy reduces the problem to a one-dimensional formulation, adapts a Carleman inequality to that setting, and then closes the argument with the Schauder fixed-point theorem. They note this is, to their knowledge, the first controllability result for this Stefan boundary problem in more than one spatial dimension.
arxiv-2511-11095:
Dillon Chen, Till Hofmann, and their colleagues introduce a simple method for generalised planning, the task of writing one program that solves a whole family of like planning problems. Hand-writing such a program is hard, and search-based tools can be slow to build one. Their method learns the program from solved examples instead of searching blindly.

For each training problem, they compute a best plan for each goal fact in turn and run goal regression, which works backward from the goal through the plan. The outputs lift into first-order rules that form the shared plan. Tests show gains in build cost, coverage, and plan quality over leading planners.
arxiv-2511-11795:
Grégoire Pierra, Alberto Colombo, and Simone Mastrogiovanni reconstruct the expansion history of the universe without assuming a specific cosmological model, using gravitational wave dark sirens plus baryon acoustic oscillation data from DESI. The fourth gravitational wave catalog holds over two hundred compact binary candidates whose masses carry redshift information.

One hundred thirty-seven dark sirens are modeled with a non-parametric autoregressive description of the Hubble parameter. Earlier siren work assumed a flat standard cosmology to bound the Hubble constant; freeing the shape of the expansion history is the advance here. Independent, model-light expansion measurements are precious checks on tensions in modern cosmology.
arxiv-2511-12595:
Shenxing Zhang studies the lengths of closed saddle connections on translation surfaces of large genus, flat surfaces built from polygons whose geometry encodes deep dynamics. A stratum of such surfaces, equipped with its natural Masur-Veech measure, becomes a probability space, so one can ask how a random surface behaves as the genus grows.

Zhang counts the closed saddle connections whose lengths fall in a window that shrinks like one over the square root of the genus. He proves that, as genus tends to infinity, the count converges in distribution to a Poisson random variable. The result answers a question posed by Masur, Rafi and Randecker about this large-genus regime.
arxiv-2511-12695:
Minghui Chen and five co-authors study how to personalize federated learning models without wrecking what they learned globally. In federated learning, many clients train one shared model on their own data, which keeps data local but means each client's data looks different. A common fix is to fine-tune the shared model on each client at the end, yet that often overfits skewed local data or fails when domains shift between clients.

The authors adapt a centralized recipe, linear probing followed by full fine-tuning, to the federated setting. Probing first trains only the last layer, which protects learned features, and full tuning follows. Across seven datasets and six personalization variants, this order balanced personalization and generalization best. They name the failure it prevents federated feature distortion, explain when the recipe wins, and give conditions that practitioners can check before deploying it.
arxiv-2511-12795:
Boshu Lei, Wen Jiang, and Kostas Daniilidis present ActiveGrasp, a robot grasping system that chooses its own viewpoints. Picking objects out of dense clutter is hard, and earlier active methods gathered extra views before planning a grasp but estimated the value of a new view poorly. They either ignored the full distribution of possible grasps or flattened it. ActiveGrasp solves both parts together.

An energy-based model generates grasp poses and is calibrated so its energy levels match real success rates, making the predicted distribution trustworthy. The next viewpoint is then chosen by the information that distribution says a new look would add, steering the robot toward reachable parts of the target. In simulated and real robot trials, the system grasped cluttered objects within limited view budgets better than leading methods. Its simulation environment is offered as a reproducible platform for active grasping research.
arxiv-2511-13095:
Chuyuan Li and Giuseppe Carenini assemble BeDiscovER, a benchmark suite for testing whether language models understand discourse, the structure that ties sentences into an argument. The suite compiles five public discourse tasks spanning the lexicon, single and multiple sentences, and whole documents, fifty-two datasets in all. It covers well-studied problems like discourse parsing and temporal relation extraction, newer challenges such as disambiguating discourse particles like the word just, and a shared task on multilingual discourse relation parsing.

The authors evaluate open models including the Qwen3 series and DeepSeek-R1, plus the frontier model GPT-5-mini. The pattern is uneven: models handle the arithmetic side of temporal reasoning well but struggle with full-document reasoning and with subtle phenomena such as recognizing rhetorical relations. As reasoning models are marketed on exactly these longer-range skills, a discourse-specific yardstick shows where the claims outrun the capability.
arxiv-2511-13495:
Han-Yao Liu and 3 co-authors study how a hot quark-gluon medium reshapes charge patterns inside jets in lead-lead collisions. They use charge-weighted energy-energy correlators, which weigh energy flow by the charges of the particles that carry it. Collisions run at five point zero two tera-electronvolts, with central lead events compared against proton runs.

Opposite-charge pairs dominate the signal in both settings, as charge conservation predicts. In the medium, small-angle opposite-charge links grew stronger while large-angle links weakened, with the same pattern for quark and gluon jets. Splitting the signal into pair counts and energy weights traced the change to stronger energy weighting of close opposite-charge pairs.
arxiv-2511-13595:
Sebastiano Mengozzi and 5 co-authors solve nonlinear output regulation equations with a physics-informed neural network. Output regulation asks a system to track a reference or reject a disturbance made by an outside exosystem. Perfect control rests on a zero-error surface and a feedforward input, jointly fixed by regulator rules that form partial differential equations with an algebraic constraint.

Their network learns both objects by shrinking the residuals under boundary and range conditions, with no precomputed paths or labeled data needed. The learned map runs in real time and generalizes across exosystem settings and starting points. A test that syncs a helicopter's vertical motion with a swaying platform kept high accuracy under varied settings.
arxiv-2511-13695:
Changjie Chen studies the rational homology of the Deligne-Mumford compactification of the moduli space of stable curves through Morse theory. The compactification adds boundary curves so families of curves have limits, and its homology records the space's shape. Chen uses a family of Morse functions built from systole-type quantities on the curves.

Two traits carry the argument: an index gap in the Morse data and additivity of the index under gluing maps. With them, low-degree homology is shown to live entirely on the boundary, matching Harer's classic dimension result from a geometric angle. Across all genera and marking counts, each degree's classes are generated by finitely many elements under a simple attaching move.
arxiv-2511-13895:
Angelos Alexopoulos and Nikolaos Demiris develop a sturdier Bayesian method for estimating cause and effect from data gathered over time. Many current methods lean on structural guesses, such as factor models, to handle hidden confounding, and wrong guesses bias the answer. The authors instead target effects specific to each time point and unit directly.

Their framework uses generalised Bayesian inference, which can register and correct for model misfit while keeping results interpretable. A scoring rule that rewards both point and interval accuracy picks the learning rate that controls the correction. Simulations and real-data tests show better calibration, sharper intervals, and more robust effect estimates than standard practice.
arxiv-2511-14495:
Jiaming Zhang and four co-authors present ComGAN, a method to rebuild incomplete radio maps for indoor localization. Fingerprint methods locate a device by matching signal strength patterns to a surveyed map. Surveys often miss many points, which hurts accuracy. The team aim to infer the missing signal values at those points.

Their framework adds a feature learning subnetwork to a conditional generative adversarial network. An optimization step then merges several prediction sets to refine the result. Tests show errors close to those from fully measured data. Training on rebuilt plus measured data gives localization nearly as good as training on complete surveys alone.
arxiv-2511-14795:
R Vilela Mendes asks what happens to spacetime physics if our four-dimensional world is a slice of a larger space whose coordinates come from the quaternions, a four-part number system. When the larger manifold's symmetry group acts, how much of its symmetry does the embedded spacetime inherit? Mendes studies that inheritance for the quaternionic Poincaré group, the symmetry group of the larger space, and finds a striking absence: its linear representations contain no spinors.

Spinors appear only once they are implemented through vector bundles over the quotient spaces of the symmetry groups, and new quantum numbers emerge in the process. Mendes closes with a brief discussion of a possible relation to the structures of the standard model of particle physics. The paper is a mathematical exploration of where matter-like behaviour could come from in a quaternionic setting.
arxiv-2511-15195:
Jatin Kumar and three co-authors show that particle deformability stabilizes hexatic order and blocks crystallization in two dimensions. Normal two dimensional systems can pass from liquid to hexatic to solid phases. Deformable particles behave differently under compression or cooling. Runs reveal a continuous liquid to hexatic shift but no hexatic to solid shift, even at zero temperature.

Solid like arrangements do not have lower energy than hexatic ones in this system. Higher entropy then favors the hexatic phase at low temperature. Strain is absorbed by particle shape change, suppressing the dislocations needed for a solid. The mechanism links microscopic softness to macroscopic phase behavior. Relevance spans microgels and epithelial tissues.
arxiv-2511-15495:
Taehyoung Kim, Seohwa Hwang, and Junyong Park tackle false discovery control when many hypotheses are tested at once and extra covariate information is available. The false discovery rate is the expected share of wrong discoveries among all discoveries. Most methods start from p-values computed as if background factors did not matter, which wastes useful information.

Their framework assumes the main variable is symmetric under the null case, given the covariates, with no fixed formula for its shape. That yields covariate-aware p-values straight from raw data. A neural network then learns a rejection threshold that adapts to covariates while keeping false discoveries controlled. Simulations beat rival methods in power, and real examples use blood pressure and air pollution data.
arxiv-2511-15595:
Christoph Aistleitner, Lorenz Fruehwirth, and Joscha Prochno study sums built from widely spaced frequencies, called lacunary sums, which often behave like sums of independent random variables. With cosine waves, such sums obey the central limit theorem and a related law that tracks their largest swings. Replacing cosine by a general repeating function makes the behavior far more delicate, and number theory enters through equations linking the frequencies.

Earlier work by the same authors showed the swing law needs a stricter number condition than the central limit theorem. Here they prove a sharp cutoff: below a stated Diophantine condition the tail chances of the sum look Gaussian, and above it they can turn erratic.
arxiv-2511-15895:
Ivan Chulo and Ananya Joshi decompose theory of mind in language models by probing how emotion processing mediates belief reasoning. Steering activations is known to improve model performance on theory of mind tasks. What changes inside the model was unclear. The authors compare steered and baseline activations with linear probes trained on dozens of cognitive actions.

Steering lifts belief task accuracy substantially in their tests. Gains are mediated by stronger emotion perception and emotion valuing activations. Analytical actions like questioning and convergent thinking are suppressed at the same time. The pattern suggests successful belief reasoning in models runs through emotional understanding, not analytic deliberation. That finding reframes how theory of mind should be built and evaluated in language systems.
arxiv-2511-16095:
Manfred Einsiedler, Dmitry Kleinbock, and Anurag Rao study points with bounded orbits on homogeneous spaces, quotients of a real Lie group by a lattice. A one-parameter subgroup acts on the space in a mixing way, and points whose forward orbit stays in a compact set form a dense set of full Hausdorff dimension. The authors ask how those special points relate to each other through orbit closures.

They prove the set is indecomposable: for any bounded-orbit point, uncountably many others have orbit closures containing it, densely across the whole set. When a neutral subgroup has dimension one, they also construct many points whose orbit closure is compact and has dimension arbitrarily close to that of the full space.
arxiv-2511-16195:
Jörn Tebbe, Andreas Besginow, and Markus Lange-Hegermann turn a physics-informed Gaussian process into a predictive controller with guaranteed constraint satisfaction. Model predictive control is the leading paradigm for safety-critical tasks. It repeatedly optimizes future actions under constraints. Casting control as probabilistic inference needs constraints inside the model. A recent Gaussian method modeled state constraints with a Gaussian likelihood but gave no open-loop guarantees.

An added Hamiltonian Monte Carlo step produces safe rollouts of the open-loop dynamics. That approximates a distribution with full mass in the safe area. Formal guarantees follow, while the process ODE structure stays on a grid. Quadratic costs are optimized in closed form, and a Matérn kernel is added to the model.
arxiv-2511-16395:
Kangwei Xu, Grace Li Zhang, Ulf Schlichtmann, and Bing Li present CorrectHDL, an agentic framework that uses language models to write hardware description language code. The framework guards against the models' habit of inventing wrong logic. The check comes from high-level synthesis, a trusted tool flow that turns C code into circuits.

Given a C or C++ program as the specification, a model drafts the HDL design, and syntax errors are repaired with retrieval-augmented generation. The design's simulated behavior is then compared against the high-level synthesis reference, and mismatches drive correction rounds until the functions agree. The finished circuits beat conventional synthesis output on area and power, approaching hand-engineered quality, while functional correctness is enforced by the reference at every step.
arxiv-2511-16495:
Ullas Bhat, Chrysa Avdellidou, Marco Delbo, and Thomas Dyer search the asteroid main belt for families of dark, spectrally red asteroids, using visible reflectance spectra from Gaia Data Release 3. Such primitive bodies may hold hydrated and organic-rich material, and their family membership reveals their collisional history.

Averaging spectra over C- and X-complex families in the central and outer belt, the team found eight families with redder slopes than their classifications suggest. Four listed as C-complex and four as X-complex could fit better as T- or D-type families, and some may feed the near-Earth population, explaining an observed excess of such asteroids there. Principal component analysis hints the reclassification is real, but near-infrared observations are needed to confirm it.
arxiv-2511-16895:
Paul-Édouard Blanchard, Alexander McDonald, and Philippe St-Jean report an optical sensor whose response grows far faster than usual as the device gets larger. The trick is one-way light flow, which breaks a basic symmetry that normally caps sensor gains. They build the device inside a fibre loop, using tones to shape the light that circles within it.

Two linked chains of tones, with up to seventy tones in each, stand in for a lattice known from theory. A small added tone that couples the chains can then be picked out with a signal strength that grows by multiplication with size, not by simple addition. The team presents the result as a new path for very fine sensing, with possible uses at a distance.
arxiv-2511-17195:
Tin Nwe Aye and Linus Carlsson analyze an epidemic model for a disease that becomes endemic, settling into a population rather than dying out. Their model tracks susceptible, latent, infectious, and recovered groups, with twists for temporary immunity and distinct treated or protected classes. Delays matter in such models, since latency and waning immunity are spread over time rather than fixed.

The authors define the delays two ways at once: smooth integral kernels for gradual effects and Dirac and Radon measures for sharp, discrete lags. They then study convergence, showing the continuous model can be approximated by a discrete-lag version. Numerical results add a practical bonus: the approximating model's solutions compute considerably faster than the exact ones. The work helps modelers choose delay structures that stay both faithful and tractable.
arxiv-2511-17495:
Spyridon Lentas classifies how a family of symmetry groups can act analytically on manifolds of a matching dimension. The groups are the special orthogonal groups of indefinite signature, with both parameters at least three. The manifolds are closed and connected, of dimension one less than the sum of the parameters. Classifying such actions means listing, up to covering, every way the group can move points of the manifold while respecting both the group structure and analyticity.

Lentas constructs explicit actions on products of spheres and on a homogeneous space built from a maximal parabolic subgroup, adapting Uchida's earlier construction on a single sphere. The main theorem then shows every analytic action of this kind is covered by one of the constructed examples. As the Roman numeral in the title signals, this is the first part of a classification program.
arxiv-2511-17595:
Markus D. Solbach and John K. Tsotsos test how far modern reinforcement learning gets on a three-dimensional task that looks trivial: telling whether two objects are the same or different. State-of-the-art methods, including PPO and imitation approaches like behavioral cloning, were applied directly to this same-different visuospatial problem and struggled to learn good strategies. The task exposes a gap between benchmark success in constrained games and flexible behavior in less structured domains.

The breakthrough came from curriculum learning, teaching the agent through a staged lesson plan rather than the full task at once. Crucially, the successful curriculum was designed from the findings of a real human experiment on the same kind of task, borrowing the order in which people master the problem's pieces. The study suggests that human-informed teaching sequences can unlock learning where raw algorithms stall.
arxiv-2511-17895:
Ziye Zhang, Bin Pan, and Zhenwei Shi present a neural operator for spectral super resolution, rebuilding a detailed hyperspectral image, with many narrow color bands, from a coarse multispectral one. Such images support remote sensing, but data driven methods that treat spectra as plain lists can predict physically unrealistic curves.

Their method works in three stages, expanding, reconstructing, and refining the image, while enforcing consistency with a radiative prior from physics. A projection step, proved optimal by a decomposition argument, handles the first and last stages. Experiments support the approach for both discrete and continuous versions of the task.
arxiv-2511-17995:
Vyacheslav Futorny and Santanu Tantubay study Whittaker modules for a Lie superalgebra of vector fields, an advanced algebraic structure that mixes usual and odd directions. Whittaker modules are singled out by the action of certain special vectors, and classifying their simple building blocks is a central task.

For modules whose Whittaker vector spaces are finite dimensional, they prove that blocks of a related category match finite dimensional modules over a smaller subalgebra. Using a covering technique they then describe the simple modules when a key parameter is non singular. The results organize a complex representation category into a simpler one.
arxiv-2511-18095:
A. Leviatan analyzes intertwined quantum phase transitions in odd mass niobium isotopes, where an atomic nucleus changes shape as protons or neutrons are added. The study uses an interacting boson fermion model with configuration mixing, which treats the odd particle coupled to a core of paired nucleons.

The quantum analysis finds two transitions superimposed: a gradual shape evolution inside one configuration and an abrupt crossing between normal and intruder configurations. A classical analysis then shows what that means for the odd particle's motion in the deformed field of the neighboring even zirconium cores. Together the views clarify how competing structures reshape these nuclei.
arxiv-2511-18195:
Kyle W Fruhling and six co-authors study the magnetocaloric effect in a family of neodymium compounds, where a magnetic material heats or cools as a field is applied or removed. The compounds pair neodymium with iron, cobalt, or nickel on a kagome lattice, a woven pattern of triangles. And the choice of metal tunes the ordering temperature, the width of the transition, and the magnetic moment. That tunability makes the family a good test bed for magnetic cooling.

The team measures the effect with standard metrics and builds three-way phase diagrams over the metal mix. From those maps they engineer one composition meant to maximise the effect. The family shows a notable entropy change across a very wide span, from near ten to six hundred and fifty kelvin, with some mixes performing over hundreds of degrees.
arxiv-2511-18695:
Changcai Li, Wenwei Lin, Zuoxun Hou, and four co-authors test whether surround view fisheye cameras can support end to end three dimensional object detection. Such cameras give a car a full ring of wide angle views. Detectors built for ordinary pinhole cameras lose accuracy on fisheye images because the geometry differs.

They adapt two mainstream frameworks, one based on a bird's eye view and one based on learned queries, using spherical spatial representations that fit fisheye geometry. They also release a synthetic data set made with a driving simulator, with both camera types. Their fisheye aware modeling improves accuracy notably over baselines on that data.
arxiv-2511-18995:
Yunxiang Wang, Lixin Yan, and Hong-Wei Zhang bound how wave solutions can grow on Damek-Ricci spaces, a family of curved harmonic spaces. The wave equation there is driven by a distinguished Laplacian tied to the space's left invariant shape. Growth bounds in norm, with sharp smoothness demands on the start data, were conjectured by Müller, Thiele, and Vallarino.

The team prove bounds whose time growth rates match the gap between the chosen norm index and the energy norm. The smoothness exponents on both start terms hit their critical values, so no slack remains. The result settles the conjecture in full generality. Sharp growth control anchors later work on waves in such curved settings.
arxiv-2511-19295:
Samapan Bhadury and four co-authors check four formulations of perfect spin hydrodynamics, a theory of fluids whose particles carry spin one-half. The versions differ in treating spin as classical or quantum, and in using Boltzmann or Fermi-Dirac statistics. A sound fluid theory must be causal, stable, and consistent with thermodynamics.

The team shows all four versions fit the rules of a divergence-type theory. Using exact distribution functions rather than approximations, they prove the theory is nonlinearly causal and stable in each case. That exact treatment gives the results a nonperturbative character, meaning they do not rely on small-parameter expansions.
arxiv-2511-19395:
Endre Takacs and eighteen co-authors settle a puzzle about nuclear sizes in rare-earth elements. Along chains with fixed neutron count, odd-proton nuclei usually look more compact than their even neighbors, except lutetium, whose listed radius seemed oddly large. Charge radii encode nuclear shape and pairing, so the anomaly mattered.

Using extreme-ultraviolet spectroscopy of highly charged ions, backed by precise atomic calculations, the team measures the lutetium-yttrium radius difference in a new way. Combined with older muonic and optical data, the result removes the anomaly and restores strong odd-even staggering. The effect is far larger than expected, challenging current nuclear theory.
arxiv-2511-19495:
Shivansh Chhawri, Rahul Mahadik, and Suparna Rooj test whether the order of compression steps changes how well a large language model survives shrinking. Distillation, structured pruning, and low-bit quantization each squeeze a model, but their combined effects were unclear. The test bed is the Qwen2.5 model at three billion parameters.

Pipelines are scored on perplexity, judged quality, clarity, prompt fit, and compression ratio. Quantization alone compresses most, while pruning costs moderate quality. Order matters a great deal: pruning, then distillation, then quantization gives the best balance, shrinking the model by more than three and a half times while keeping instruction following strong.
arxiv-2511-19695:
Josep Martí and Pedro Luis Luque-Escamilla revisit the odd geometry of the microquasar V4641 Sagittarii, a black hole feeding on a massive star. Its radio jets seemed to run nearly across its extended gamma-ray glow, hinting at strong bending or diffusion. New observations suggest that reading was wrong.

The authors report evidence that the radio jet and the very high-energy gamma rays share one axis, pointing to a single tightly collimated outflow as their common source. Local particle acceleration up to hundreds of TeV then becomes plausible, and the system stands out as a candidate PeVatron, a natural accelerator reaching peta-electronvolt energies, inside our galaxy.
arxiv-2511-19995:
Jiyeon Han, Ali Mahdavi-Amiri, Hao Zhang, and Haedong Jeong build CREward, a reward model that scores creativity by type rather than as one lump. Creativity is complex, and a single number flattens it. Their model splits it along three axes drawn from how images form: geometry, material, and texture.

The team first ran a human study to capture how people judge creativity on each axis across varied images. Large vision-language models matched human judgments well, so labels from those models were used to train CREward at scale. The model serves three uses: scoring creative images, explaining the scores, and gathering creative samples to inspire human designers or to guide generation through low-rank adaptation.
arxiv-2511-20195:
Itaba and Minaki complete a dimension formula for a family of noncommutative algebras. Their 2025 paper computes Hochschild cohomology of Beilinson algebras. The algebras come from graded down-up algebras with weights. Those down-up algebras are cubic AS-regular of dimension three. Weights are coprime integers n and m here.

Earlier work covered the cases where n equals one. Belmans handled the smallest case, both weights one. Itaba and Ueyama covered n one with larger m. The new formula handles all weights at least two. Dimensions of each cohomology group are given explicitly. A striking byproduct follows for m bigger than n. The derived category of the associated noncommutative scheme differs fundamentally. It matches no smooth projective surface's derived category. The ring structure is also determined fully. Yoneda products on cohomology are described for all weights. Noncommutative geometry gains complete invariants for this family.
arxiv-2511-20395:
Schoppema and colleagues hunt environmental clues behind a shellfish poison. Their 2025 paper studies tetrodotoxin in bivalve mollusks. The toxin, famous from pufferfish, appeared in European waters in 2012. Contaminated shellfish threaten food safety and cause economic losses. Early prediction would help the industry and regulators. Prior work blamed shallow habitats and warm water.

The team built an explainable deep learning model for prediction. Its setting was the Dutch Zeeland estuary. Inputs were weather and water measurements over time. The output was simply whether contamination was present. Sunrise time, sunset time, and global radiation mattered most. Water temperature and chloride concentration also contributed strongly. Day length and total sun hours thus drive contamination risk. The explainable outputs make the model trustworthy for authorities. It offers a practical tool against marine toxin risks.
arxiv-2511-20495:
Bodart, Ron-George, and Yadin finish a sorting of groups by their geometric edge. Their 2025 note studies Cayley graphs of groups built from finite generator sets. Busemann functions measure distance relative to a fixed basepoint. Closing their set adds points at infinity, forming an edge. How many such points a group has reflects its large-scale shape.

The theorem: finitely many Busemann points forces the group to be virtually cyclic. Such groups are nearly just the integers in disguise. Combined with earlier work, this completes the full sorting. Every group with a finite such edge is now classified. A new notion called annihilators drives the proof. The edge stays fixed under the group's own action. Metric-functionals were proposed as analogues of linear functionals for spaces. Support came from the Israel Science Foundation. Finite edges turn out to be extremely restrictive.
arxiv-2511-20595:
Laguë and colleagues read galaxy feedback's fingerprint in the microwave sky's motion signal. Their 2025 paper builds the first fully data-driven emulator of matter clustering. Star formation and black holes blow gas around, reshaping small-scale structure. That baryonic feedback muddies cosmological inferences from lensing. Fitting formulas exist, but their knobs are not observable.

The kinetic Sunyaev-Zeldovich effect traces free electrons around halos. Its power spectrum shape correlates with feedback's suppression pattern. A neural network learns that mapping from simulations. Training used the FLAMINGO suite spanning many feedback recipes. The emulator rebuilds the matter power spectrum to sub-percent accuracy. That holds for scales up to five and redshifts 0.2 to 1.25 in their tests. Unseen feedback models and cosmologies stay near percent-level too. A forecast pairs Simons Observatory maps with DESI galaxies. Feedback and new physics can finally be told apart.
arxiv-2511-20795:
Souradeep Dutta and colleagues report in 2025 a small rebuild of KRISP, a Facebook AI model that answers questions about images by consulting a structured knowledge graph. The original was built for industrial-scale training and is heavy and bound to a large backbone. The team's lightweight reproduction keeps the concept, neural embeddings grounded by explicit knowledge, slashing parameters for edge devices like phones and AR-VR headsets.

Their model freezes CLIP encoders for vision and text, projects the 512-dimensional features, and queries a local ConceptNet graph using question keywords and recognised image concepts. On the DAQUAR dataset and a synthetic proof-of-concept set, the replica reached about 75 percent of the original's performance. The rebuild also exposed design flaws, hidden assumptions, and practical pitfalls the original paper never discussed, documented through ablations. Confined to the graph's domain, the model refuses to hallucinate outside it.
arxiv-2511-20895:
Kimia Ahmadi and Wouter A. Serdijn improve in 2025 the circuit logic that squeezes maximum power from small solar cells. Their target is a head-mounted optical power receiver for freely moving rodents in neuroscience experiments, where light levels swing fast. Classic perturb-and-observe tracking wobbles around the peak. Their algorithm adds adaptive gradient descent: the step size scales with the power-voltage slope, cutting tracking time and steady-state oscillation. An optional start-up routine hunts the global peak under partial shading.

Simulations and measured rodent-derived light data show tracking efficiency of 99.94 percent under standard test conditions and 99.21 percent on experimental data. Temperature profiles stayed above 99.6 percent, and the shading routine added up to 7.8 percent under partial shading. A gate-level complexity analysis and a combined figure of merit place the method ahead of 35 rival perturb-and-observe algorithms.
arxiv-2511-21295:
Wenbo Fan and Weihua Gu propose a new kind of shared transit in 2025, built from small electric vehicles that team up and split apart. Earlier modular bus ideas needed vehicles to couple while moving and passengers to transfer mid-ride, technology far from ready. Fly-by transit instead pairs cheap trailer modules, which run solo feeder trips to each rider's door, with high-performance leader modules that haul coupled trailers in fast platoons along trunk lines.

Fan and Gu couple trailers only while stationary at hubs, then release the tail trailer on the move so the convoy never stops for drop-offs. A stylized corridor model optimizes the design and compares it with buses and ride-hailing taxis. Fly-by transit cut travel times versus buses and operating costs versus taxis. Its economies of scale beat both rivals, saving more than 13 percent in generalized system costs.
arxiv-2511-21395:
Qixun Wang and seven coauthors teach a multimodal AI to think in pictures it never has to draw, in 2025. Models that reason with images usually fetch or generate real pictures mid-thought, chained to external tools. Their framework, Monet, instead lets the model reason inside its latent visual space, producing continuous internal embeddings that act as visual thoughts, a style of abstract picturing closer to human imagination.

Wang and his coauthors train Monet with a three-stage distillation pipeline on Monet-SFT-125K, a new dataset of 125,000 interleaved text-and-image reasoning traces covering real photos, charts, text reading, and geometry. They also introduce VLPO, a reinforcement learning rule that grades the latent visual thoughts directly, after finding the standard GRPO rule mostly sharpens text reasoning instead. The resulting Monet-7B improves across perception and reasoning benchmarks and generalizes strongly to abstract visual puzzles outside its training mix.
arxiv-2511-21495:
Saurabh Gupta, Dmitry Bykov, Tracy Northup, and Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero work out how to chill a levitated nanoparticle using ions as a refrigerator, in 2025. Both objects float in the same dual-frequency Paul trap, an electric cage, and they interact through their Coulomb repulsion. The ions can be laser-cooled directly, a trick called Doppler cooling, while the nanoparticle cannot, so the team asks whether the cold ions can sympathetically drain the particle's motion through their coupling.

Gupta and his coauthors derive the system's quantum master equation and compute the cooling in detail. A single continuously cooled ion should bring the nanoparticle below 1 kelvin, even with the trap's micromotion jitter and no feedback control. Adding ions helps in direct proportion: the cooling rate grows linearly with ion count. With the shared motion of 12 ions, the forecast drops to tenths of a millikelvin, deep into the quantum regime experimentalists want.
arxiv-2511-21595:
Mauro Bernardi, Antonio Canale, and Marco Stefanucci fill a measurement gap for adaptive regression methods, in a 2025 statistics paper. Effective degrees of freedom say how much information a fitted model really uses, guiding model choice and error estimates. The classic Lasso penalty has a neat formula, but its adaptive descendants, which set penalty weights from a first-pass fit, had no equivalent theory despite wide use.

Bernardi and his coauthors derive the first unbiased estimator of the Adaptive Lasso's effective degrees of freedom, and the Adaptive Group Lasso's. Within Stein's unbiased risk estimation framework, they cover designs with independent or correlated predictors. The formulas contain inflation terms driven by the penalty size, the signs of fitted coefficients, and the least-squares estimates themselves. Tests on synthetic and real data show the payoff: sharper model choice and unbiased error estimates, putting adaptive methods on their parent's footing.
arxiv-2511-21695:
Ruchira Dhar and thirteen coauthors argue that how AI models are scored deserves its own standard card, in 2025. Models now release rapidly and openly, yet test reports remain scattered and uneven. Surveying recent work, the team identifies three persistent failures. Results cannot be reproduced, reports defeat non-specialists, and write-ups are too weak for emerging governance rules.

Their proposal, Evaluation Disclosure Cards or EvalCards, puts testing at the center, where Model Cards and BenchmarkCards leave it peripheral. The format prizes brevity: cards should take little effort to write or to read, and resist gaming. Uniform cards would make test details visible and consistent across releases. Researchers gain firmer ground for cumulative work, adopters a basis for informed choices, and regulators the transparency governance frameworks demand. The paper treats the card itself as research infrastructure.
arxiv-2511-22095:
Bommarito, a researcher, releases Binary-30K, a dataset built to fix an infrastructure gap in deep learning for binary analysis and malware detection. Existing datasets cover a single platform, demand specialized tooling, or ship only hand-engineered features that modern neural networks cannot use. Unlike those predecessors, Binary-30K instead spans Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android across more than 15 CPU architectures, including exotic chips targeted by Internet-of-Things botnets, with material from 2012 to 2025.

The release holds 29,793 binaries with a realistic 26.93 percent malware share, chosen by platform-first stratified sampling. Plus pre-computed byte-level BPE tokenization with a 65,536-token vocabulary so sequence models like transformers can start immediately. Distributed through Hugging Face with official train, validation, and test splits at about 11 GiB compressed. It targets cross-platform transfer learning, architecture-invariant detection, longitudinal malware studies, and classroom use on ordinary student hardware.
arxiv-2511-22295:
Fedorov, Dmytrenko, Akhmetov, and colleagues map how fast the Milky Way rotates, using almost nothing but Gaia data. From the Gaia DR3 catalogue they take 4,547,980 red-giant-branch stars with spatial velocities and solve the Jeans equation in cylindrical coordinates to build the circular velocity curve out to 20 kiloparsecs. They correct for systematics and check whether the curve changes with galactic azimuth rather than assuming perfect symmetry.

At the Sun's position the circular velocity comes out at 229.63 kilometers per second, with an uncertainty of only 0.30, agreeing with many earlier estimates. The curve declines gently at about 2.29 kilometers per second for each kiloparsec between 6 and 20 kiloparsecs. Dips near 13 and 18 kiloparsecs persist under other distance estimates. Azimuthal variations up to about 20 kilometers per second caution against one global curve.
arxiv-2511-22895:
Hsiung and Chen make the maths of laboratory black holes computable. Experiments like AnaBHEL, using an accelerating plasma mirror as a flying mirror, aim to detect analog Hawking radiation, the particle creation a moving mirror induces in the quantum vacuum. Predicting the spectrum means evaluating Bogoliubov integrals over the whole trajectory, but realistic trajectories from particle-in-cell simulations make them analytically intractable and numerically brutal.

Their Inertial Replacement Method replaces the trajectory's inertial head and tail with analytic extensions, so numerics concentrate on the finite accelerating segment. They derive perturbative error bounds for perfect and imperfect mirrors, validate against solvable trajectories, and apply the method to the numerical AnaBHEL trajectory. The spectrum is determined almost entirely by the finite accelerating region, with negligible sensitivity to the far past and future. So even if acceleration stops, the Hawking-like spectrum and its entanglement structure survive essentially unchanged.
arxiv-2511-23195:
Hoàng and colleagues chip away at a long-open problem in graph theory, whether graphs avoiding both four independent vertices and a four-cycle can always be coloured efficiently. They study the narrower class that also avoids the six-vertex path. They prove a structural theorem about the members that still contain a six-cycle, the case that had resisted the methods used for sibling classes in full.

Any such graph, they show, has bounded clique-width, a measure of how simply a graph can be assembled from small pieces. And bounded clique-width makes colouring solvable in polynomial time with known algorithms. The result therefore yields a polynomial-time colouring algorithm for the whole (4K1, C4, P6)-free class. The authors note that their new technique for bounding clique-width is of independent interest beyond this one forbidden-subgraph problem for other researchers.
arxiv-2511-23395:
Yan and colleagues explain why a chain of strongly interacting Rydberg atoms under local dephasing can get stuck in long-lived metastable states instead of relaxing normally. The mechanism is Hilbert space fragmentation, where dynamical constraints split the system's state space into disconnected pieces that cannot reach each other. The team shows the fragmentation here is captured by a dephasing version of the well-known PXP model in experiments.

The fragmented pieces are built from multiple degenerate zero modes that form block-diagonal subspaces of maximally mixed states. Each piece is labeled by conserved quantities defined through a consecutive double excitation addressing operator the authors introduce. Most strikingly, the number of fragments grows exponentially with chain length following a modified Fibonacci sequence, multiplying by roughly 1.75 with each added atom asymptotically, which makes the effect increasingly rich in larger quantum arrays for control.
arxiv-2512-00695:
Manoj Belavadi and Kathie Cameron wrote a 2025 graph theory paper on Kempe changes. A graph coloring assigns colors to points so that linked points differ. Pick two colors, and the points using them split into connected groups called Kempe chains. A Kempe swap flips the two colors inside one chain.

Swaps turn one valid coloring into another, so they map out how colorings connect. Belavadi and Cameron study graphs that avoid a fixed pattern graph, known as H-free graphs. Knowing when swaps can move between all colorings helps solve counting and sampling problems. It also bears on puzzles and timetables, where colorings model the choices.
arxiv-2512-01195:
Tao Luo, Yu Ning, and Xiande Zhang study the quantum chromatic number of certain graphs in a 2025 math paper. The chromatic number of a graph is the fewest colors needed so adjacent vertices differ. In the quantum version, players use entangled states to color cooperatively, sometimes with fewer colors than any classical method allows.

Few graph families have known quantum chromatic numbers. Orthogonality graphs are a notable exception, fully determined already. The authors study subgraphs of those graphs, and the distance-two Hamming graph, where words differing in few positions connect. Pinning down exact values shows where quantum strategies truly help.
arxiv-2512-01295:
Mihai Christodorescu and co-authors set out the safety needs for AI agents. Agents are programs that plan and act on their own. They use tools, read files, and send messages. A safe model alone does not make a safe full system.

The authors look at the whole system, not just the model. They list short-term and long-term research tasks for agent safety and privacy. Each task asks how an agent can be tricked, leak data, or cause harm. Their plan gives builders a shared map for tests, guards, and design rules that cover real use.
arxiv-2512-01495:
Joanne Lin and co-authors tackle video segmentation in dark clips. The task marks each object in each frame. Low light brings noise, blur, and low contrast. Both humans and machines find it hard. Large labeled sets for dark video are scarce too.

Fake dark clips made by past pipelines miss how real dark video degrades over time. The team's method, ELVIS, aims to lift low-light clips for better segmentation. Clearer input helps the model track objects through dark frames. Gains would aid night driving, security, and wildlife film work. The method is tested on real dark footage, not just bright clips dimmed by hand, which makes its scores harder to game.
arxiv-2512-01795:
Torrecilla Pinero and co-authors quantify risk in Voronoi service area models. Voronoi maps assign each place to its nearest service point. Straight-line distance drives that assignment. Rules like waste proximity principles rest on such maps in law.

In rough terrain or sparse infrastructure, straight lines mislead. True travel can be far longer than the map suggests. The team measures the misallocation risk that follows. Safer maps would assign services by real routes, which matters for equity in rural regions. Road-network distance is the natural fix the study points to, since travel time, not raw meters, decides who can reach a service.
arxiv-2512-01895:
Moving a facial expression from one face to another is easy within photos of real people and much harder across styles, say from a photograph to a cartoon. Avirup Dey and Vinay Namboodiri present StyleYourSmile in 2025, a method for retargeting faces across such domains without paired training examples in each style.

The hard part is keeping identity, expression, and style separate, so one can change without dragging the others along. Earlier methods often failed to generalize across domains, or needed slow test-time tuning and carefully built multi-style datasets. A method that skips those demands would make stylized animation and avatar tools far easier to build.
arxiv-2512-02095:
The Milky Way's small satellite galaxies are fossils of galaxy formation, but reading them requires separating chance variation from the physics of gas and stars. Jonah Rose and a large collaboration analyze in 2025 over a thousand simulated Milky Way-mass galaxies from the DREAMS Project.

The simulations use the TNG galaxy-formation model inside a standard cosmology, varying both the physics of ordinary matter and the cosmological settings. With so many hosts, each with its own environment and history, the team can disentangle halo-to-halo variance from the effects of baryonic feedback. The satellite populations that result give observers a sharper baseline for judging the real Milky Way.
arxiv-2512-02295:
Some spots on the Sun spout jets time and time again, like geysers. Each blast frees magnetic force stored low in the Sun's air. Aabha Monga and four co-authors probe in 2025 what drives these jets. They home in on how flows of magnetic flux meet and clash.

Flux that rises and flux that cancels out are known to feed jet birth. But what reloads one spot for blast after blast is still not clear. The team tracks how flux fields clash and build stress anew. The work feeds the broad study of how the Sun's magnetism drives blasts that can reach Earth.
arxiv-2512-02495:
Ali Mohammad-Djafari, Ning Chu, and Li Wang tackle inverse problems, where hidden causes must be inferred from indirect, noisy data. Such problems turn up across science and engineering, from medical scans to earth sensing. They are often ill posed, meaning small noise can cause large swings in the answer.

Classic fixes include regularization, which adds prior rules, and Bayesian inference, which tracks uncertainty openly. The authors combine Bayesian thinking with physics informed neural networks, which respect known physical laws. Their test case is infrared image processing, where cleaner inference could sharpen heat based pictures used in inspection and diagnosis. In plain terms, the method lets the data speak but keeps wild guesses in check.
arxiv-2512-02695:
Md Faysal Hossain and Sean B. Andersson track single tiny particles in real time as they move inside cells. Feedback driven tracking measures light from a labeled particle and steers the instrument to follow it. Watching one particle in its native setting reveals motion that snapshots cannot show.

Their double helix based method shapes the light so position can be read quickly and well. Fast, accurate estimates feed the control loop that keeps the particle centered. Better tracking opens longer, clearer views of transport and binding inside living cells, key processes in health and disease. Long clean tracks beat short bright ones when the goal is to watch a cell at work over time.
arxiv-2512-02795:
Marcus Kessel argues that code generating AI should learn from watching software run, not just reading it. Today's models train on static artifacts: source code, comments, and specifications. They rarely see recorded behavior, so they can absorb buggy or mislabeled code as if it were truth.

Deep facts about a program cannot be decided in general, so observed runs are the practical ground truth. Kessel proposes observation lakehouses: living, interactive archives of software behavior. Feeding models real execution traces could teach them what code does, not just what it looks like, cutting confident errors. Runs leave a trail that reads can check, and that trail is the part most code tools throw out too soon.
arxiv-2512-03195:
Matching job ads to skill lists is slow work by hand. Stylianos Saroglou and co-authors test language models for that task in this 2025 work. They link job vacancy texts to two European frameworks for skills and qualifications.

One framework, ESCO, lists skills, competences, and occupations. The other, EQF, sets levels for qualifications. The authors compare two methods from past work, sentence linking and entity linking. Better linking could help job seekers find fitting roles. It could also help schools see which skills employers want most. Public job services could use such links to guide training funds toward real demand.
arxiv-2512-03395:
Ratios of partition functions can reveal phase transitions. Satoshi Morita and Naoki Kawashima compute such ratios with tensor renormalization in this 2025 work. At criticality, theory predicts universal values for these dimensionless ratios.

Those values come from conformal field theory through partition functions on a torus. Tensor methods let the authors compute the ratios in practice. Matching theory and computation is a strong check on both. The approach helps study critical phenomena in magnets and other many-body systems. Universal ratios give sharp targets, because their values do not depend on material details, only on the transition class.
arxiv-2512-03895:
Two fashionable ideas in machine learning, spiking networks and quantum circuits, are usually trained separately because spikes do not differentiate smoothly. Luu Trong Nhan and colleagues merge them into one trainable system in a 2025 neural computation preprint. Their SQDR-CNN, a spiking-quantum convolutional network using data re-uploading, trains a spiking encoder and a quantum circuit together in one backpropagation framework.

Earlier hybrid designs leaned on pre-trained spiking encoders and trimmed datasets. The new architecture needs neither shortcut and still converges to reasonable performance. They test design choices around quantum data re-uploading, training algorithms, and initialisation, including under noisy simulated quantum conditions. The model reached most of the accuracy of leading spiking baselines while using a tiny fraction of the parameters. The team hopes the integration opens fresh directions for learnable systems that mix neuromorphic and quantum parts.
arxiv-2512-04095:
Keeping a modern power grid stable as inverter-based renewables flood in requires fast, accurate security control, and the underlying equations are slow to solve. Amin Masoumi and Mert Korkali test a quantum-flavoured remedy in a 2025 systems preprint. Their framework embeds quantum computing elements inside a deep reinforcement learning controller for dynamic security control of the grid.

Model-free reinforcement learning already performs reliably here. It learns control policies without solving the full differential-algebraic system each time. The authors organise a hybrid version drawing on near-term, noisy quantum hardware concepts. They assess its dependability on the standard IEEE 39-bus test network. Results, they report, show promising applications alongside shortcomings they name openly. The paper is framed as groundwork: an organised framework and an honest evaluation, pointing at what to fix before quantum-embedded control can be trusted with a real grid.
arxiv-2512-04195:
Stars forge heavy elements slowly, one captured neutron at a time, and laboratory beams try to mimic that stellar furnace. Sarah Agus-Bina's 2025 master's thesis in experimental nuclear physics examines one candidate mimic: firing protons at oxygen-18 to release neutrons via fluorine-18. Earlier work showed its neutron spectrum near threshold closely resembles the thermal flux inside asymptotic giant branch stars.

The thesis repeats that experiment at PTB and builds a computational tool, OxyGen. The tool predicts the neutron energy spectrum and angular distribution for a planned liquid-water oxygen target at the SARAF facility. Those predictions feed into Geant4 transport simulations, which the author compares against the experimental results. The verdict is reassuring: OxyGen forecasts the spectrum reliably. Future SARAF experiments can therefore be planned and analysed with it at different proton energies.
arxiv-2512-04495:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing develop a general method to steer open quantum systems whose energy can leak or grow. Such systems are called non-Hermitian, and past control work copied tricks from closed systems by staring at energy spectra. That focus left time behavior and scale hard to handle. Their 2025 arXiv paper builds control in the Heisenberg picture instead, where operators carry the motion.

The method works for any number of bosonic modes under a Hamiltonian that changes with time. It rests on moving frames defined by helper operators mixed from the lab-frame ones. A gauge potential, born from the twist between frames, steers the dynamics. This view reaches far past states with a few excitations. It also stays workable as mode counts grow. The theory could guide control of light and sound modes in leaky quantum devices, where loss is a fact of life.
arxiv-2512-04695:
Jinglue Xu, Qi Sun, Peter Schwendeman, and co-authors present TRINITY, a small coordinator model that directs larger language models as a team. Merging model weights fails when architectures differ or APIs stay closed. A coordinator sidesteps both walls by delegating in words. Their 2025 arXiv paper trains a compact coordinator, well under a billion parameters, plus a tiny routing head, using an evolutionary strategy rather than gradient training.

Across several turns, the coordinator hands each query step to a chosen model in one of three roles: Thinker, Worker, or Verifier. Complex skill stays inside the big models; the coordinator only learns whom to ask and when. Tests across coding, math, reasoning, and domain knowledge show the team beating single models and prior routing methods. The approach also carried over to new model pools, a hint that cheap coordination can scale with the model market.
arxiv-2512-04895:
M. Zeeshan, Saud Satti, and co-authors present Chameleon, an attack framework that hides hostile instructions inside images where only machines can read them. Vision-language models now drive document processing and automated decisions. To save compute, their pipelines shrink incoming images by default. That innocent scaling step opens a hole: text invisible at full size can sharpen into clear instructions after downscaling. Their 2025 arXiv paper shows how adaptive agents can exploit the gap.

Older attacks are static, painted once for one pipeline. Chameleon instead adapts its hidden prompts to the workflow it faces, in the spirit of agentic systems themselves. The planted instructions wake only after the model's own preprocessing, slipping past human review of the original image. The work warns builders of multimodal systems to audit every resize and crop as a security surface, not a mere efficiency step.
arxiv-2512-04995:
Markus Meinert takes a fresh computational look at ruthenium dioxide, a metal oxide caught in an argument about magnetism. In perfect bulk form the material shows no magnetism, yet a popular calculation method predicts a special magnetic state called altermagnetism, and strained or doped thin films give mixed signals. Which answer is right depends heavily on the tools used to compute it.

Meinert reruns the calculations with a more advanced method that tracks extra detail about how electrons move and bunch up. The newer method strengthens the push toward magnetism but still finds the undisturbed material nonmagnetic at its measured size. Stretching the crystal, removing some electrons, or straining it along one axis, though, tips it into the magnetic state. The study sets cautious thresholds for how much distortion or doping that takes.
arxiv-2512-05595:
Tommaso Polonelli and five co-authors built a radar system that watches lab rodents without touching them. Checking heart and breathing rates in mice and rats usually means implants or wires, or picking the animals up. Their 2025 paper puts a low power radar beside the home cage. Working at sixty gigahertz, it reads tiny body motions from the echoes that bounce back.

The team tuned where the sensor sits and built a processing chain. It picks the right range slice, reads phase shifts, and pulls out breathing rates. In tests with two rodents, rates came out accurate to about two breaths per minute. The radar also tracks where each animal is and how it moves, sensing shifts as small as a few centimeters, even in group housing. Nothing is attached and no one handles the animals, so the setup promises calmer subjects and cleaner data, around the clock.
arxiv-2512-05695:
Chunyu Wang and Brian Tom write on learning the best sequence of treatments for a patient over time, known as a dynamic treatment regime. Precision medicine wants rules that say which treatment to give at each decision point, based on the patient's history. Clinicians prefer rules built from simple, readable models. But a simple model can miss the true pattern, and a late error feeds back into earlier estimates.

Their 2025 paper focuses on picking the model for the contrast functions that compare treatments. Because a model's rank can flip with sample size, they judge candidates by performance at the sample size actually in hand, not by far-off limits. They use a counterfactual cross-validation score, and add a new way to estimate its variance. Knowing the uncertainty lets researchers test whether a preferred simple structure is really supported. The result is model selection that admits its own doubt.
arxiv-2512-05995:
Ali Dasdan's working paper argues that two famous frustrations are the same failure. Productivity has risen roughly eightfold since Keynes predicted the fifteen hour week in 1930, yet people still work about twice those hours. AI development also races ahead despite stark warnings from its own leading researchers. Dasdan shows both are coordination failures with one game theoretic skeleton: rational choices producing worse outcomes together. Five conditions define such tragedies, from defection paying more to blocked enforcement.

The framework is validated on canonical cases, then sharpened with a Tragedy Index built from condition intensities. Governing transformative AI scores orders of magnitude harder than climate change or nuclear weapons. Applied to labor, firms cannot convert productivity gains into worker welfare under competition. The drone war in Ukraine appears as field evidence. Dasdan stops at naming the problem.
arxiv-2512-06295:
Angelina Mendoza Tavera, Adrian Escobar Ruiz, and Robin Sagar compare three ways of picturing a quantum state as it shifts from one well to two. Their test case is a special oscillator whose energy curve can be solved in part by hand, making it a clean lab. As a knob turns, its single dip splits into two dips, and a particle can tunnel between them.

The team draws each picture for the lowest states with high care: the Wigner view, a smoothed Husimi view, and a plain size only view of the first. Measures of spread and shared detail show a clear ranking. Only the Wigner view caught the wave like clash effects as the wells split, with a wavy pattern in its spread measures. The others saw only the split itself. The work gives a yardstick for picking the right picture when quantum states change shape.
arxiv-2512-06595:
Joe Shymanski presents ChargingBoul, an automated negotiator that nearly won its class at an international contest. Software agents that haggle over price and terms serve online markets, resource sharing, and machine to machine deals, where no human has time to bargain. In the twenty twenty two Automated Negotiating Agents Competition, ChargingBoul placed second on individual gain by an exceptionally narrow margin.

Its design is deliberately light. The agent sorts opponents into types by how their bids move, then tunes its own bidding to match. Early on it holds firm; late in the talks it shifts to a concession policy that trades a little gain for a higher chance of closing a deal. The study reviews its contest record and later uses of the agent in other research. ChargingBoul held up across many rival styles, and the author points to richer opponent modeling as the next step.
arxiv-2512-06695:
Haipeng Cao, Kaining Zhang, Dacheng Tao, and Zhaofeng Su unblock a quantum generative model that stalled as it grew. The quantum denoising diffusion model learns to build quantum states by reversing a noising process, and it has shown promise on correlated noise, many body phases, and topological data. The authors prove, and confirm in experiments, that a barren plateau appears as the system grows: the training signal flattens to nothing, so learning stops.

Their analysis pins the plateau on a cause distinct from the known ones for quantum circuits. They then redesign the architecture so the signal survives, restoring trainability in the settings tested. A conditional version of the fixed model can also generate ground states matched to given Hamiltonian parameters, widening its use for preparing complex quantum states. The work speaks to the wider problem of keeping quantum learning trainable at scale.
arxiv-2512-07395:
Alessandro Letti and co-authors keep fully powered machines safe while they move through space in the mathematically natural language of their motion. Their systems are mechanical and fully actuated, able to command every direction of movement, and their poses live on a Lie group, the smooth space of positions and orientations. Safety is enforced by zeroing control barrier functions, fences in the mathematics that the controller is forbidden to cross.

Two new families of such fences are introduced and proven sound. The first enforces kinematic constraints, the machinery behind obstacle avoidance. The second caps kinetic energy along chosen directions of translation and rotation. The relevant limit when a machine must touch its surroundings gently, as in safe physical interaction with people or fragile cargo. Computer simulations put the fences to work in two scenarios: slipping through a narrow slit, and landing safely.
arxiv-2512-07695:
Natalie Allen and twenty-six co-authors wrote this 2025 astronomy paper on a nearby planetary system. TRAPPIST-1 hosts several small rocky planets, and one, planet e, sits at a temperate distance. Finding air on such a world is a flagship goal for exoplanet science.

The James Webb Space Telescope watches planet e cross its star. Starspots and other surface features contaminate those transit readings badly.  The team's program uses a clever partner: airless planet b. Its close transits trace the star's face without any atmosphere in the way. Those passes should let the team correct planet e's spectrum without a star model. Simulations say the planned set of close transits can reveal an Earth-like air. Early observations are reported here. Strong flares can spoil the trick by changing the star. The cleanest visit shows the correction working as hoped.
arxiv-2512-07795:
Nearchos Potamitis, Vansh Ramani, Har Ashish Arora, Dhairya Kuchhal, Lars Klein, and Akhil Arora wrote this 2025 machine learning paper. Leaderboards for reasoning models report one score per system. Run the same system again, and the score, and the cost, can shift meaningfully.

That wobble is not mere noise to be averaged away. The top strategy beats its nearest rival in only about three runs out of four.  Their benchmark, ReasonBENCH, records many repeated trials for each contender. Ten strategies, a dozen models, and six tasks enter the design. Quality and cost are treated as distributions, not point values. A two-part taxonomy sorts the variance into global and run-level noise. Architecture, they find, predicts a strategy's stability profile. Most score variance traces to benchmark, system, and item structure. Cheap methods resist joint cost-quality failure; expensive ones stay exposed.
arxiv-2512-08095:
Miguel Alcubierre, Juan Barranco, Argelia Bernal, and colleagues, relativists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about clouds of scalar field gathered around black holes. These self gravitating clouds resemble atoms, with the black hole as nucleus. Earlier work built such gravitational atoms mainly without angular momentum structure.

The team presents new solutions of the Einstein Klein Gordon equations that include an angular momentum number. They call them noble gravitational atoms, by analogy with noble atoms and their closed electron shells. In the right limit, the solutions approach the known boson star family, differing only very near the horizon. For higher angular momentum, the density peaks can sit far from the hole, and the usual spike at the horizon may vanish or dip. Some of these objects could be as large as galaxies, as dilute as dark matter, and as long lived as the universe.
arxiv-2512-08295:
Neil Beri, John Palastro, Qian Qian, and colleagues, plasma physicists, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about photon acceleration in a plasma wakefield. When a drive beam crosses a plasma, a laser pulse riding its wake can shift to much higher frequency, promising intense short wavelength light. Tailoring the plasma density keeps the pulse in step with the wake.

The team studies how photons move in phase space near that matching condition. A photon kinetic model, checked against full particle in cell simulations, supports a linear theory of the dynamics. The theory yields scaling laws for the witness pulse and a self similar solution for the photon pattern. One striking prediction says the pulse can be compressed without any lower bound on its duration. If borne out, photon acceleration could become a source of sub femtosecond, short wavelength radiation for probing ultrafast matter.
arxiv-2512-08495:
Michael Ling and Yang Yang, researchers in space dynamics, posted a study on arXiv in December 2025 about sorting low Earth orbit debris. When a satellite breaks up, its fragments form a family, and reconnecting those families supports space sustainability and awareness. Machine learning on proper elements, the stable fingerprints of an orbit, is a key tool, but models trained on old debris pictures may age badly.

The team builds a pipeline on synthetic breakups from a standard model, flown through a high fidelity simulation. They extract proper elements in three coordinate sets, widening the fingerprints a classifier can use. Neural networks then judge whether two fragments share a parent. One subtle trap surfaced: standard quaternion features lose orbital size data during normalization, wrecking accuracy until an augmented set restored it. With the joint feature sets, the best model clearly beat the single set baseline, sharpening automated debris genealogy.
arxiv-2512-08595:
Rohan Sarkar, a probabilist, posted a research paper on arXiv in December 2025. He studies spectral heat content, a quantity that watches a random process wander inside a region and measures how much of it stays put. Its behavior at very small times encodes the geometry of the boundary.

Sarkar gives a new technique for deriving those small time asymptotics for a broad class of processes at once: any translation invariant, isotropic process whose far jumps are negligible. One proof thereby recovers several known results for Levy processes and Gaussian processes. It also yields new results for stable Levy processes whose clock is warped by a self similar process, linked to equations nonlocal in space and time. One method thus simplifies a scattered literature.
arxiv-2512-08695:
Rashmi Kamran and coauthors review a recent telecom standard that updates the design of next generation networks. Those networks underpin most wired and wireless packet based systems, including advanced mobile networks. A core design goal was to keep user services separate from the transport layer that carries them, so services would not depend on one transport technology.

In practice, that split was applied to outside services but not to internal ones such as mobility and authentication. Internal services stayed tied to transport control, forcing each transport to support them on its own and causing duplication. The new recommendation extends the split to internal services as well. The review explains the evolved design and why it is more modular and scalable, including as a template for future sixth generation networks.
arxiv-2512-09095:
Xinyue Pan, Yuhao Chen, Jiangpeng He, and Fengqing Zhu tackle a surprising failure in food image generation. A prompt such as egg noodle can yield an image with eggs and noodles as separate items, which is wrong. Such compound categories are common in real food data sets and form a large share of standard benchmarks.

The errors come from two sources. Text encoders lack knowledge tied to multi noun food categories, and models misread how the nouns relate, leading to wrong layouts. Their method, FoCULR, adds food domain knowledge and introduces core concepts early in the generation process.
