Emotion regulation is hardest exactly when it is most needed, and current tools lean on reflection or words, which may fail in intense moments.  Preeti Vyas and five co-authors test another pathway: touch, through CHORA, a zoomorphic robot with looped biomimetic breathing and heartbeat behaviors.

In a mixed-methods lab study with thirty participants, haptically experienced animacy supported emotion regulation, with physiological, self-report, and questionnaire evidence converging.  The work builds on a prior theory of comforting haptic co-regulation.  Designers of wellbeing technology get evidence that a breathing, beating companion can calm through touch alone, opening a nonverbal route to regulation.
arxiv-2602-07495:
Decoding what the brain sees from neural signals is limited when models capture only high-level meaning and miss pixel-level detail.  Jiawen Zheng and six co-authors propose a brain-image match strategy using several pre-trained visual encoders with other inductive biases to capture hierarchical, multi-scale representations.

A contrastive objective aligns brain signals with those visual embeddings. A Fusion Prior learned on large-scale visual data stabilizes the mapping before brain features are matched to it.  Brain experts and AI teams get a decoding approach that respects both semantics and fine visual detail, clarifying how much visual information brain signals truly carry.
arxiv-2602-07695:
E-commerce demand forecasting breaks during flash sales, holiday campaigns, and policy shocks, when demand shifts abruptly.  Congcong Hu and six co-authors present EventCast, a hybrid method that folds future event knowledge into time-series prediction without asking a language model to forecast numbers.

Instead, the language model reads unstructured business data on campaigns, holidays. Seller incentives and converts it into interpretable textual summaries, using world knowledge for cultural nuance and novel event combinations, which then inform the forecaster.  Retail operations teams get forecasts that anticipate events rather than reacting to them, a crucial edge during high-impact periods.
arxiv-2602-07795:
When a light field drives the classic Jaynes-Cummings system of an atom coupled to a photon mode, the system can pass through a photon-blockade breakdown transition. Ken Chen and six co-authors look past that transition itself to the geometry of the quantum states involved, a side that had received little attention.

They treat the drive's amplitude and phase as control knobs and compute the quantum metric and Berry curvature for each eigenstate. Both quantities diverge near the critical point, and the divergence is far stronger for bright states than for the single dark state. Because circuit quantum electrodynamics setups realize this driven model, the predictions can be tested in the lab, linking geometric quantum theory to experiment.
arxiv-2602-08095:
In 1927, Artin and Schreier characterized real closed fields by their Galois group having order two. That result inspired a p-adic analogue: a field is p-adically closed exactly when its absolute Galois group matches that of the p-adic numbers. Leo Gitin and two co-authors give a new proof of that theorem, originally solved in 1995.

Using modern valued-field methods from the last twenty-five years, they build an elementary, self-contained argument centered on a Galois characterization of henselianity, avoiding Galois cohomology entirely. The paper also connects to recent work on perfectoid fields and model-theoretic transfer. Field arithmeticians and model theorists gain a cleaner, more accessible route to a landmark characterization.
arxiv-2602-08495:
Future transport systems may use one millimeter-wave radio both to sense the road and to talk to vehicles, switching between the two jobs in time slices. Akanksha Sneh and Shobha Sundar Ram study how radar settings shape the communication payoff in city environments. Their arXiv paper models the radar's scan first, then the beams that serve the users it finds.

Duty cycle and beamwidth turn out to be critical choices: they govern how well targets are detected among clutter scatterers and how much throughput remains for data. A stochastic-geometry framework links radar metrics to network throughput across varied target and clutter conditions. Monte Carlo simulations validate the analysis. Readers get design guidance for sharing spectrum between sensing and service.
arxiv-2602-08695:
Training data is noisy, yet models are expected to work on clean inputs, and whether transformers manage that leap is unclear. Evan Peters and four co-authors study noise-robust learning in transformers versus LSTMs. Their arXiv paper tests sparse parity, majority functions, and random juntas under feature noise.

Transformers succeed on sparse parity and majority tasks where LSTMs fail even at modest noise. But they typically fail on random juntas, especially when the optimal noise-robust solution is simpler than the target function. The authors argue that a bias toward simple functions traps transformers, then show an extra loss term penalizing high sensitivity lets them escape. Readers get a nuanced verdict: transformers are strong but not uniformly robust to feature noise.
arxiv-2602-08995:
Computer-use agents that click and type on your behalf sometimes drift off-task, through outside manipulation or their own faulty reasoning. Yuting Ning and seven co-authors define and study misaligned-action detection for the first time, covering both external attacks like indirect prompt injection and internal slips. They build MisActBench, a benchmark of realistic trajectories with human action-level alignment labels.

Their guardrail, DeAction, checks each action before it runs and corrects it through structured feedback. It beats all baselines by over fifteen F-one points on the benchmark. In live tests it cuts attack success by over ninety percent while preserving or improving task success in benign settings, at moderate latency cost.
arxiv-2602-09095:
Future electron-positron colliders could spot heavy neutrinos that travel measurably before decaying. B. Fuks and three co-authors survey displaced signals of heavy Majorana neutrino birth at the proposed FCC-ee, in the Left-Right symmetric model. Channels span W and heavy W-R mediation, scalar mixing, and gauge and scalar boson fusion, tied to how they gain mass.

Signatures feature possibly multiple displaced ones, sometimes with prompt activity and forward leptons. Production rates and spreads let analysts tell channels apart and estimate yields, while a dedicated vertexing algorithm reconstructs decay positions and momenta. Realistic reaches strongly surpass LHC projections, probing left-right breaking scales deep into the multi-TeV regime.
arxiv-2602-09195:
Diego H. Correa and three co-authors derive an integrable reflection matrix for excitations scattering off a boundary that carries its own degree of freedom, while preserving a residual SU(1|2) symmetry. That symmetry alone does not fix the matrix, so the authors invoke the boundary remnant of Yangian symmetry to obtain a set of integrable solutions.

A concrete realization appears in insertions on the half-BPS Wilson loop in ABJM theory. There, the boundary degree of freedom shows up as a bound state tied to poles in the reflection matrix's dressing phase. Comparisons with the boundary bound-state bootstrap agree, and the Wilson-loop example allows perturbative checks. The work extends integrability methods to boundary problems with internal states.
arxiv-2602-09395:
Sharpness-aware minimization favors flat minima that generalize well, but its extra perturbation step doubles compute cost, a bottleneck for fine-tuning. Yifei Cheng and seven co-authors propose SL-SAM, a 2026 method that sparsifies the approach at the layer level. Each iteration samples a subset of layers by gradient norm to join the perturbation and update steps, framing layer choice as a multi-armed bandit problem.

The paper backs the method with a convergence analysis, then tests fine-tuning across several tasks. Performance matches leading baselines, including a top rank on language-model fine-tuning. Crucially, backpropagation activates only a fraction of the parameters that standard sharpness-aware minimization always uses. The savings grow with model size, making the method most valuable exactly where fine-tuning costs most.
arxiv-2602-09495:
Photonic quantum technology needs ways to prepare chosen quantum states from simple inputs using linear optics and photon detection to herald success. Lacking strong single-photon nonlinearities, photonic preparation cannot borrow the deterministic gate approach of other platforms, and deciding whether a target state is reachable can be cast as a polynomial feasibility problem. Deepesh Singh and four co-authors apply an algebraic geometry algorithm to settle such questions definitively.

Their tool, the Nullstellensatz Linear Algebra algorithm, proves infeasibility when a preparation task has no solution, yielding rigorous no-go results. The paper uses it to validate and set lower bounds on physical resource needs for several ubiquitous optical states and gates. The work thus turns state-generation questions from open searches into decidable claims, mapping what linear optics with heralding can and cannot build.
arxiv-2602-09595:
Moving treatment effects from a random trial to a target group assumes maybe-result spreads stay the same after sorting by seen traits. Amir Asiaee and three co-authors note that unseen effect traits, spread differently in trial and target, break that carry-over rule. Their 2026 paper builds a response plan bounding how far conclusions can move when carry-over fails.

A scalar knob caps the odds ratio between target and trial result curves, with unity giving standard carry-over. For each knob value, the paper derives sharp bounds on the target average treatment effect, the tightest interval sure to contain the true effect under all fitting processes. Optimal odds ratios show a simple cutoff shape, yielding a greedy algorithm that sorts trial outcomes and moves mass in near-linear time. Sims show stated coverage, tighter intervals than worst-case bounds, and informative results across realistic carry-over breaks.
arxiv-2602-09895:
Heat usually spreads through a material the way ink spreads in water, steadily outward. A 2026 paper by Angelo Russomanno looks at a chain of Josephson junctions, a standard superconducting circuit element, joined at one end to a heat bath through a resistor. He works in the classical regime, where the energy cost of charging each junction far outweighs the Josephson coupling energy. The question is how heat moves along such a clean, orderly chain.

The answer is far slower than diffusion. Heat creeps forward at a logarithmic pace, so both a defined thermalization length and the total energy grow only slowly with time. That sluggish pattern recalls localized quantum systems, yet here it appears in a clean classical model with glassy behavior. Russomanno argues the effect may help non-ergodic behavior survive when ergodic patches intrude in the charge-quantized regime.
arxiv-2602-10195:
Sequence models usually rely on linear steps that hide structure, but shape itself can carry the links. A 2026 paper by Truong Minh Huy and Edward Hirst introduces Versor, a sequence design using conformal geometric algebra instead of usual linear steps. States embed in a shape space and evolve via rotor moves, showing 3D matching links by design without added shape coding.

Versor beats rivals, graph networks, and shape rivals on chaotic N-body motion, topological puzzles, and standard mixed-media tests. It uses two hundred times fewer weights than rivals, splits focus clearly into nearness and angle parts, and transfers zero-shot across scales where vision models collapse. Custom kernels run over a hundred times faster, cutting per-step latency to about a thousandth of a second.
arxiv-2602-10495:
Tianxiang Dai and Jonathan Fan analyze the spatial conduct of a core neural-graphics method in a 2026 paper. Multi-resolution hash encoding powers instant neural graphics primitives, yet its spatial traits have been chosen by heuristic rather than understood. Hyperparameters get tuned by trial because no real picture guides them.

The authors portray the encoding through its point spread function, the analogue of a system's Green's function. They derive a closed-form approximation for the collision-free case, revealing grid-induced anisotropy and a logarithmic spatial profile. The idealized bandwidth, they show, is set by the average resolution. The analysis turns a bag of tricks into a measurable instrument with known resolution and fidelity.
arxiv-2602-10795:
Michaela Borzechowski and four co-authors give two new proofs of a biased ham-sandwich theorem in a 2026 paper. The classic theorem says one hyperplane can at once bisect any collection of point sets in matching size. The biased version asks for cuts that take a prescribed fraction, not a half, from each set.

The first proof is fully combinatorial, linking the biased theorem to unique sink orientations of grids. The second uses point-hyperplane duality and the Poincare-Miranda theorem, generalizing the result to and beyond oriented matroids. Along the way the authors present rainbow arrangements. They transfer colored pseudo-hyperplane arrangements, and their realizability problem is complete for the existential theory of the reals.
arxiv-2602-10895:
Chen-Wei Wang and collaborators report a second fast-radio-burst-associated magnetar X-ray burst in a 2026 paper. Fast radio bursts are millisecond radio pulses mostly from cosmological distances, and the association of one burst with a magnetar X-ray burst advanced grasp greatly. But a single event left open whether the association was genuine or coincidental.

The team reports a bright magnetar X-ray burst from SGR J1935+2154 detected by GECAM in October 2022. It is associated with a fast radio burst seen by CHIME and the Green Bank Telescope. Detailed time and spectral analysis shows a bright, typical burst lasting roughly a quarter of a second. A second association strengthens the magnetar origin of at least some fast radio bursts.
arxiv-2602-10995:
When a language model writes, whose words is it echoing? Amelie Wührl and three co-authors argue that creators now have little say over how their text is used, while users may quote sources without knowing it. Their paper builds a human-centred frame for tracing model output back to input data.

Rather than one fixed rule, the frame lets each use case, such as writing help or fact-checking, set its own aims and tests through stated settings. Creators, users, and go-betweens like publishers and platforms then negotiate those terms. The authors present this as a bridge between technical attribution methods and policy work. It also links to the economics of creator pay, aiming for a data economy that can last.
arxiv-2602-11095:
Cells make and destroy molecules at random, yet reactions still find their targets. Gabriel Mercado-Vásquez and Denis Boyer study particles that are built and broken down at steady rates while wandering by diffusion. They borrow tools from resetting theory to work out first-passage traits.

When build and breakdown rates match, mean reaction time can be tuned to a minimum, with a clear criterion for when tuning helps. Counting build costs gives a best build rate instead. In bounded spaces, fast enough building beats a lone non-decaying particle, above a universal threshold. Brownian examples on a line and in an interval show the results in concrete form.
arxiv-2602-11395:
Steering diffusion models to unseen terms usually needs retraining or costly gradients. Qingsong Wang and two co-authors present Noise-Aligned RFM Steering, a recipe that steers without gradient guidance at inference. Two offline signals combine: noise matching from principal component statistics of target examples, and trait-machine signal steering from labelled forward signals.

Noise matching gives coarse control at high noise, while the learned direction is reused across middle and late steps through light signal edits. Tests on image benchmarks show better target scores than gradient-based post-hoc guidance, better image quality scores on class-guidance tasks, and large speedups. Code is released for controllable making without retraining.
arxiv-2602-11495:
Jailbreaks leave traces inside models, not just in prompts. Sri Durga Sai Sowmya Kadali and Evangelos E. Papalexakis analyze internal forms across several open models, finding steady latent patterns tied to harmful inputs. Layer-wise analysis spans model and state-space designs alike.

A tensor-based latent form frame captures structure in hidden signals, enabling lightweight jailbreak finding without fine-tuning or auxiliary detectors. The same signals can actively disrupt jailbreak execution at inference time: bypassing high-susceptibility layers blocks most jailbreak attempts on a modified model while preserving benign conduct almost entirely. The work suggests design-agnostic, internal defences as a complement to prompt-level guards.
arxiv-2602-11795:
Detecting language variety usually relies on prior cleanup or preset variant lists, both of which bake in assumptions about what counts as a variant. Anne-Marie Lutgen and two co-authors take an embedding-based route for Luxembourgish user comments. They train subword vectors on raw text and group related forms through combined cosine and n-gram similarity. Spelling and morphological diversity then appear as linguistic structure rather than noise.

On a large corpus of user comments the approach uncovers extensive lexical and orthographic variety matching patterns from dialectal and sociolinguistic research. Induced families capture systematic correspondences and highlight regional and stylistic differentiation. The procedure needs no strict manual annotation, yet it yields transparent clusters for quantitative and qualitative analysis. Distributional modeling thus reveals meaningful variety even in noisy, low-resource settings.
arxiv-2602-11895:
Online food delivery and related shipping hinge on assigning riders to orders, a problem close to classical matching but hardened by real-world operational constraints. Tharrmashastha SAPV and three co-authors cast the Rider-Order Assignment problem as a constrained binary optimization problem and compare standard, quantum-inspired, and gate-based quantum solvers across multiple instance sizes. Solver performance is judged on solution quality, computational runtime, and constraint meeting.

A consistent cleanup step ensures valid results across all solvers, keeping the comparison fair. The study speaks to a practical question for shipping: whether new tuning methods beat standard methods on real-world matching problems, and under what conditions. By testing across sizes and solver families with shared metrics, the authors give managers evidence about which approaches merit further investment for rider matching.
arxiv-2602-12095:
Warehouse robots usually pack bins that start empty and avoid touching anything already inside. Real containers, though, are often partly filled in awkward arrangements left by transport around the warehouse. David Russell and three co-authors tackle packing into such containers through deliberate contact.

Their approach uses a contact-based trajectory optimizer inside a model predictive controller, paired with perception that estimates object poses even when objects hide each other. A placement method then suggests physically feasible spots inside the container. By nudging previously placed items to make room, the system can place new items where collision-free strategies would fail.
arxiv-2602-12395:
Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards is now standard post-training for visual reasoning, yet it is unclear what it actually improves over supervised fine-tuning as a starting point. Xirui Li led this work with two co-authors, using a Frankenstein-style analysis that pieces models together to localise effects. End-to-end benchmark gains mix many factors, so attribution needs sharper tools.

Three tools are used: functional localisation by causal probing, update characterisation by parameter comparison, and transfer tests by model merging. Results show reinforcement learning does not uniformly sharpen visual perception. Instead, it induces a consistent inference-time shift mainly in mid-to-late layers, and those refinements are both transferable by merging and necessary, by freezing, for the gains. The reliable contribution is thus refined mid-to-late reasoning, not better seeing alone.
arxiv-2602-12695:
More than half of Korean workers now use generative AI on the job, and a survey of workers across the country asks what that time saving actually becomes. Donghyun Suh and Samil Oh find that 51.8% of workers use the tools for work, and users report cutting working time by 3.8%. Yet the link between time saved and output gained is close to zero, so the gains do not show up in standard productivity figures.

The reason, the authors argue, is that workers mostly pocket the saved time as leisure during the workday rather than producing more. That gap matters for how AI's value is counted: if official measures only track output, they may understate the benefit workers get from easier, less pressured days. The study draws on a representative survey, so its patterns speak to the wider Korean workforce.
arxiv-2602-12895:
Standard discrete element methods treat grains as rigid, but real grains deform, and that deformation matters for granular conduct. Thomas Henzel and Konstantinos Karapiperis present a deformable discrete element method built on a reduced-order description of elastic grain deformation. An energetic varying formulation extends rigid-body motion to include translation, rotation, and deformation in one unified description.

Deformation itself is realised through evolving level sets within the level set discrete element formalism, handling general shapes, topologies, and deformation modes. The system keeps the toughness, clarity, and scalability of standard discrete element methods at a similar machine cost. Comparisons with full finite-element mock runs agree excellently at particle and system scales, establishing a general, extensible tool for particulate systems.
arxiv-2602-13095:
Open quantum systems evolve under Lindblad formulas, and their long-time conduct under time-linked driving needs rigorous sorting. Hironobu Yoshida and Ryusuke Hamazaki classify long-run conduct for time-linked Gorini-Kossakowski-Sudarshan-Lindblad formulas with Hermitian jump operators. Their results cover looping time dependence: time-stand-alone, periodic, quasiperiodic, and certain random cases.

First, they give a criterion for steady-state uniqueness phrased via the algebra made by the system's operators, needed and enough when generators are analytic in time, illustrated with quantum many-body spin chains. Second, they split strong balance into Schrödinger-picture and interaction-picture forms and classify long-run motion with each. Interaction-picture balance drives time-linked steady states like tidy oscillations, while Schrödinger-picture balance governs time-stand-alone ones, unifying known mechanisms and revealing new balance-predicted motion.
arxiv-2602-13195:
Referring image cutting usually handles categorical or spatial queries like the left-most apple, missing functional and physical thinking like where to safely store a knife. Aadarsh Sahoo and Georgia Gkioxari present conversational image cutting, which maps abstract, intent-driven concepts to pixel-close masks, plus ConverSeg, a benchmark spanning intent, affordances, safety, functions, spatial relations, entities, and physical thinking.

They also present ConverSeg-Net. It fuses strong cutting priors with language grasp. An AI-powered data engine makes prompt-mask pairs without human supervision. Current language-guided cutting models prove inadequate for conversational cutting, while ConverSeg-Net trained on engine data gains greatly on ConverSeg and stays strong on current language-guided benchmarks. The work moves cutting from pointing at things toward grasp what people intend to do with them.
arxiv-2602-13295:
A coupled system links a quantum wave equation with an electric potential, posed on a bounded region in three dimensions. The twist is a critical nonlinear term, which breaks the usual compactness properties that existence proofs rely on, plus a normalization rule fixing the total mass of the solution. Handling both at once demands care.

The authors use a truncation method with genus theory to build several families of normalized solutions, then invoke concentration-compactness to get past the compactness failure. They also show the system tends to the classical Schrodinger-Poisson system as the small parameter vanishes. Li Chen leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13395:
Fault-tolerant quantum computing wants codes where the full logical Clifford group can run transversally, gate by gate across physical qubits. The Steane code achieves this for one logical qubit, but no multi-qubit analogue was known, and this paper proves why that gap is fundamental. No stabilizer code admits a fully transversal Clifford implementation on more than one logical qubit.

The result strengthens further: fold-transversal implementations fail beyond two logical qubits, and in general, running the Clifford group on k logical qubits needs at least k-fold transversal gadgets. Code-automorphism constructions fail too for multiple logical qubits, forcing more complex fault-tolerance designs for multi-qubit code blocks. Aranya Chakraborty leads the work with one co-author.
arxiv-2602-13595:
Scaling laws promise that cutting bit precision linearly improves efficiency and energy use, but this paper shows that recipe breaks for multi-hop reasoning. Reducing precision from 16-bit to 8 or 4 bits oddly raises net energy use while hurting reasoning accuracy, a phenomenon dubbed the quantization trap. Theory blames hardware casting overhead, especially the hidden latency cost of dequantization kernels that rule step-by-step reasoning chains, plus a step-by-step energy spreading failure.

A Critical Model Scale predicts when the trap dissolves or deepens with model size, batch size, and hardware setup, validated across a 120-fold size range on six GPU setups. The authors argue the smaller-is-better heuristic backfires for complex reasoning tasks. Henry Han leads the work with four co-authors.
arxiv-2602-13995:
Nicola De Nitti and two co-authors study a 2026 arXiv model of one-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics. With no magnet field, it drops to the De Gregorio model for Euler flow. The paper looks at calm near its first excited state on the torus. That widens recent work by Guo and Jiu on the De Gregorio case alone.

The authors prove the linear system is well-posed for all time. They prove the non-linear system is well-posed for short time. Then they show both linear and non-linear blow-up for a wide class of starts in a weighted Sobolev space. They trace the blow-up to a linear map shared with the De Gregorio model. Yet in one part of that space, both systems prove well-posed for all time and calm.
arxiv-2602-14295:
Edwin Chen and one co-author introduce a 2026 arXiv design pattern called Machine Learning as a Tool. Pre-trained statistical models become callable tools inside language-model agent workflows, so an orchestrating agent can invoke quantitative predictions when needed and reason about them in context. That differs from pipelines that treat inference as static preprocessing.

The validation case, PitchCraft, turns discovery-call recordings into professional proposals with machine-predicted pricing. A Research Agent gathers prospect intelligence through parallel tool calls, while a Draft Agent calls an XGBoost pricing model and drafts the proposal via structured outputs. Trained on 70 examples mixing real and human-verified synthetic data, the pricing model shows how small-data models can serve agents as live tools.
arxiv-2602-14595:
Shirin Pirouzkhah and two co-authors test a 2026 arXiv consistency problem in automated code revision tools. Such tools make rewrites from reviewer feedback, promising less hand effort, but their real-world worth hangs on handling like code variants stating the same issue steadily. The chance nature of rewrite tools can break that steadiness, yielding split rewrites for meaning-same code variants.

Nine types of meaning-keeping tweaks were designed and used on 2,032 Java methods from real GitHub projects, making over 10,000 tweaked variants. Five top transformer-based rewrite tools were tested for steadiness on those variants. Correct-rewrite power dropped by up to 45.3 percent under tweaks, showing tools that score well on old data may falter on same-meaning code, a trust gap for field use.
arxiv-2602-14695:
A persistent X-ray source found over fifty years ago turns out to sit remarkably close. Eliot C. Pattie, with five co-authors, revisits 4U 1556-60 after Gaia placed it only about 700 parsecs away. That short distance rewrites what its brightness and size can mean.

New X-ray and radio data join a fresh reading of the literature. The authors conclude it fits a candidate ultracompact neutron star binary, with a small accretion disk and a very high X-ray-to-optical ratio. Its steady luminosity near 2×10^34 erg per second matches other ultracompact systems. The radio jet stays undetected, roughly a thousand times fainter than expected.
arxiv-2602-14795:
Ivan Diliso and colleagues argue that knowledge graph datasets for refinement algorithms usually hold only ground facts, starving methods that need schema knowledge, ontological constraints, and reasoning. Their resource offers a workflow for extracting datasets that carry both schema and ground facts, ready for machine learning and reasoning services, alongside a curated suite of resulting datasets.

Handling inconsistencies during extraction keeps the suite usable rather than merely large. Evaluation can then test neurosymbolic and reasoning-heavy methods on realistic, large-scale graphs instead of on fact-only shadows. Knowledge graph research gains datasets that match the richness of their sources.
arxiv-2602-14895:
M. R. Schmidt reports the first detection of the TiO i1Pi-a1Delta system in stellar spectra, with laboratory characterisation to match. Titanium oxide shapes the atmospheres and visual spectra of M-type stars, and synthetic spectra for late M giants showed systematic discrepancies between 5810 and 5850 angstroms.

Experimental absorption cross-sections trace the mismatch to a molecular band with an R-head at 5814.8 angstroms, overlapping another TiO band, whose lower state is the a1Delta vibrational ground state and whose upper state is most likely the i1Pi ground vibrational state. An empirical band intensity follows from comparison with models. Stellar spectra gain a missing molecular fingerprint.
arxiv-2602-15195:
Puertolas and colleagues detect backdoors in LoRA adapters from weight space alone. LoRA add-ons let users fine-tune large language models cheaply, but shared ones from open hubs such as Hugging Face Hub face backdoor attacks. Current screening methods run the model on test inputs, which is too slow for screening thousands of add-ons when the trigger is unknown. The new method reads weight matrices as-is, without running the model, making it trigger-free in design.

For each attention projection, query, key, value, and output, the method extracts five spectral statistics from the low-rank update, yielding a 20-number profile per unit. A logistic regression detector trained on that profile splits benign and poisoned units across three model families: Llama, Qwen, and Gemma. On unseen test units from how-to tasks, reasoning, question-answering, code, and classification tasks, it achieves 100 percent accuracy across all three architectures.
arxiv-2602-15395:
Wang and colleagues track builder-led trading on BNB Chain. BSC's bid-split setup uses a slim plan: only approved builders join, blocks come at faster gaps, and hidden flow skips the open pool. These traits have sparked crowd worries over control, which the team backs by tracking the trading moves of top builders from April 2025 to February 2026.

Two top builders, 48Club and Blockrazor, made over 87 percent of blocks and took over 90 percent of profits. Profits gather in low-hop trading paths over cased coins and stable coins, and block building narrows to a one-player game. Beyond control, the study shows a built-in source of gap: BSC's short block gap and approved PBS shrink the open window for racing, boosting lag edges and cutting slow builders. MEV taking on BSC is not only more clustered than on Ethereum, but also more open to blocking and fair decay.
arxiv-2602-15695:
Gagné and colleagues present MOCAdb, a public census of nearby star groups, open clusters, and young substellar objects within 500 parsecs of the Sun. The MySQL base, with a Python front end, lists members for 10,259 groups and clusters, plus published measures such as spectral types, kinematics, spin periods, activity indices, and photometry. All known substellar objects are listed, with 2,943 public spectra.

The set maps between rival group definitions and updates the BANYAN Sigma membership tool, now covering 8,125 groups with better handling of mixed, linked errors and complex shapes via Gaussian mixture models. Joined with Gaia DR3, the team finds 11,535 new candidate members, mostly M dwarfs, plus a fresh census of age-calibrated exoplanets and substellar objects, including 101 candidate lone planetary-mass objects.
arxiv-2602-15995:
Fu and colleagues make OpenMP programs replayable at scale. OpenMP remains the most popular shared memory framework, yet its nondeterministic runs frustrate debugging and testing. Recording a run so it can be replayed exactly is the key tool, but scalable replay for OpenMP had stayed unsolved.

Their answer is two recording schemes based on distributed clocks and distributed epochs, which cut the thread synchronization that older methods paid on every shared memory access. Built into ReOMP and tested on representative high performance codes, the schemes run two to five times more efficiently than traditional approaches. The method also plugs into an MPI replay tool, so combined MPI plus OpenMP codes replay with only a small overhead that does not grow with MPI scale.
arxiv-2602-16095:
Cheongho Han leads a very large survey team reporting three Saturn-mass planets found by microlensing. Each planet betrayed itself through a brief positive anomaly on the wings of its light curve, recorded in high-cadence data from KMTNet, OGLE, MOA, and PRIME. The three events span recent survey years, and their anomaly shapes match perturbations from planetary companions near the peripheral caustic.

Systematic checks rule out rival accounts, including binary-source scenarios and higher mass-ratio lenses, firmly establishing a planetary origin for each signal. Combined with angular size and event timescale measures plus Galactic priors, the hosts emerge as low-mass stars, while the companions are Saturn-mass worlds orbiting beyond their hosts snowlines. The results show microlensing can find and characterize cold giants around faint stars at great distances, filling the gap between ice giants and gas giants.
arxiv-2602-16195:
Cities under natural hazards can flip fast from largely safe to largely damaged as hazard intensity rises, like a discontinuous phase shift. Sebin Oh and coauthors show that urban structural damage exhibits such phase shifts, driven by coupling between damaged buildings. Higher diversity in the building portfolio smooths the shift, but multiscale damage clustering traps the system in a volatile regime that suppresses predictable Gaussian statistics.

An effective random-field Ising model interprets the patterns, with its key parameters translated into tangible engineering factors such as hazard demand, building mix, and modeling doubt. Common simplifications can distort the inherent phase of real urban sets. Such distortions can substantially bias hazard loss figures, producing relative errors of up to half in exceedance odds under moderate earthquakes, equivalent to a several-fold gap in expected repair costs. The phase-aware description turns collective damage traits into actionable checks for urban risk planning.
arxiv-2602-16295:
Taweewat Somboonpanyakul and coauthors present a deep Chandra X-ray analysis of the galaxy cluster SPT-CL J0417-4748, at redshift near six tenths. The focus is its thermodynamic properties and apparent absence of central star formation. With a long Chandra exposure, they find large-scale X-ray morphology consistent with a dynamically relaxed, cool-core system. The intracluster medium shows central density, pseudo-entropy, and cooling time values typical of massive cool-core clusters.

Despite those conditions, no evidence of recent or ongoing star formation appears in the brightest cluster galaxy. Spectral energy distribution fitting indicates the bulk of stars formed at redshift near one and a quarter, with no significant star formation over the past three billion years. Optical spectra show no oxygen emission, and radio and infrared data indicate a lack of strong current AGN activity there.
arxiv-2602-16395:
Kurt Liffman, writing alone, studies how a magnetic field brakes a protostellar disk. A static field threads the disk perpendicular to its surface, and the field acts to slow the disk's rotation, drawing disk material inward toward the protostar. The paper derives general analytic equations for the accretion speed and the mass accretion rate.

Simplified equations follow for the disk's energy dissipation, the accretion timescale, and the disk's radial position plus surface density as a function of time. Beyond the physical insight they offer, such equations may serve as a check on computational models of protostar and protostellar disk formation. The paper is short and formula-driven, giving readers equations they can test against simulations.
arxiv-2602-16495:
Hamed Barzegar leads two coauthors on warp-drive spacetimes in general relativity. Popular claims about warp drives rest on models that the authors examine closely and sort by their limits within relativity. For each class they sum up the general formalism, while flagging errors and misunderstandings in the literature that back claims of physical warp drives.

Along the way they prove several new no-go theorems. Their analysis finds that, once relativity is applied correctly, most claims for physical warp drives must be rethought, and justifying such models is highly challenging for reasons beyond energy-condition violations. The paper thus demystifies the field, separating what the math allows from what popular accounts suggest.
arxiv-2602-16595:
Simone Costa investigates the distribution of sums of independent, identically distributed random variables taking values in Z_p. The focus is the regime of small values, which is less explored than the asymptotic case. Starting with the case of three variables, Costa proves an anticoncentration bound when the distributions are uniformly bounded and the prime is large enough relative to that bound.

When the distributions are also separated from one, the constant in the bound can be made explicit. Iterating the argument yields effective anticoncentration bounds for larger counts as well. Those estimates are nontrivial already in small and moderate regimes where asymptotic results do not apply. Probability theorists get sharp, usable bounds for a classic small-sample question.
arxiv-2602-16695:
J. Martin Smit and Fernando Santos study fairness on digital service platforms where ratings can entrench bias. Such platforms match providers with consumers in short, one-off deals between strangers. Ratings build trust by reporting past quality, yet they can also perpetuate negative bias against marginalised groups. The paper asks how to design around biased reputation while keeping providers keen to offer high quality.

An evolutionary game model traces how platforms perpetuate or counter rating-based discrimination. Focus falls on platform choices to promote highly rated providers or members of a protected group. Results show a core trade-off: promoting top-rated providers helps users but cuts demand for marginalised providers hit by biased ratings. Tuning promotion rules can shift that balance, giving platform designers evidence for fairer ranking.
arxiv-2602-16795:
Mariam Bouhmadi-López and Beñat Ibarra-Uriondo propose dark energy models in which the cosmological constant flips sign. It is negative early on and positive at low redshifts. The frame holds a generalized ladder-step path plus smooth-transition paths, giving one account of sign-changing constants. Theory and background motion are studied with cosmographic checks.

Moving to linear perturbations, the authors solve perturbation laws from the radiation era with adiabatic start values. They trace matter density contrast, gravity potential, and the f-sigma-8 observable. Scores are set beside standard Lambda-CDM and current data. Sign-changing dark energy proves viable in tests, with distinct marks on cosmic structure growth arising from the flip itself.
arxiv-2602-16895:
Alyssa Hwang and co-authors present a frame for surfacing structure in documents through AI-generated cross-modal links. Dense documents such as recipes and scientific papers scatter details across text, figures, tables, and other visuals. Specialized terminology makes it hard to locate or connect related ideas. Existing tools offer limited support for synthesizing info across media types. Complex material thus stays cognitively demanding.

The frame is instantiated in an augmented reading interface. It populates a scientific paper with clickable points on figures, interactive highlights in body text, and a persistent reference panel for consolidated details with no manual scrolling. In a controlled between-subjects study, readers using the tool scored significantly higher on a reading quiz. No evidence appeared of increased time to completion or cognitive load. Fine-grained integration thus offers a systematic way to reveal relationships within a document.
arxiv-2602-16995:
Mingrui Liu and co-authors present imaging results for three quadruply lensed quasars from the Hubble and James Webb space telescopes. The quasars sit at redshifts near two and a half, three, and one and a half. Targets are modeled with a singular isothermal ellipsoid mass profile and an elliptical Sersic profile. That rebuilds each system's geometry, with measured Einstein radii under one arcsecond.

No spectra exist for the lenses, but their redshifts are constrained to roughly one half to one and a half. The best-fit light model gives a de Vaucouleurs Sersic index near four for all three. Effective radii run about one and a half to three and a half kiloparsecs. The three lenses are early-type galaxies at intermediate to high redshift, a common type for strong lensing galaxies. Against other known quadruple lenses, these sit low in Einstein radius and high in lens redshift.
arxiv-2602-17095:
Chuiyang Meng led a three-author team fixing a subtle flaw in federated fine-tuning of large language models. Low-rank adaptation splits tuning into two small matrices. Federating it creates two headaches. Aggregating the matrices separately introduces error, and aggregating their product forces a re-split that is not unique, so updates drift. The paper proposes FLoRG, a framework built on a single low-rank matrix.

Instead of aggregating matrices, FLoRG aggregates the Gram matrix of inner products, which removes the aggregation error and trims communication. A Procrustes alignment step lines up decompositions across rounds, cutting drift and tightening the convergence bound, which the authors prove in theory. Across several fine-tuning benchmarks, FLoRG beat five strong baselines on downstream accuracy while lowering communication cost.
arxiv-2602-17295:
Minwoo James Kim led a five-author team fusing variational quantum eigensolvers with classical neural networks under rigorous guarantees. The paper builds a joined setup linking neural changes, measurement stats, and stability through three demands: self-run training, power-law resource scaling, and consistency. Its concrete form, U-VQNHE, couples a quantum circuit to a neural phase function through norm-keeping steps.

The learned change is read from records, preserves the exact bound, and admits range-independent tightness bounds for distinct finite-shot tests. The authors also map amplitude reweighting limits: sampled-support mismatch can spoil observed scaling, while exact matching can demand hugely large dynamic range in some settings. Tests on Ising and messy XYZ spin models show better energy scores over the base solver and greater toughness than reweight rivals.
arxiv-2602-17595:
Antonia Kuhn and team built a high-throughput screening platform to find polymer electrolytes for safer, higher-energy solid-state batteries. The hard trade is to balance ionic conductivity with transference number. The team searched a space of well over a million hypothetical candidates with molecular dynamics simulations.

Batch Bayesian optimization, warm-started from past literature, picked hundreds of homopolymers for testing. Several beat the benchmark polyethylene oxide system. The runs point to branched architectures and ketone groups as boosters of ion hopping in the polymer matrix. A lithium-versus-sodium comparison and an open-source framework round out a toolkit to speed the hunt for liquid, gel and multi-cation electrolytes.
arxiv-2602-17695:
Xin Yu and team introduce EXACT, a decoding-time personalization method for large language models. Personalized alignment must adapt to each user's shifting context, yet past decoding-time methods lean on implicit, hard-to-read taste encodings and rigid user profiles that ignore how tastes shift across prompts.

EXACT aligns output with limited pairwise taste feedback through a predefined set of plain attributes. An offline stage picks user-specific attribute subsets by maximizing the likelihood of preferred replies. At run time, it retrieves the most relevant attributes for each prompt and injects them into context to steer output. Theory backs the method under mild assumptions, and tests on human-annotated taste data show it beating strong baselines on taste modeling and personalized output quality.
arxiv-2602-17795:
V. Ivanov obtains best-point rules for a limited optimization problem in terms of the lower Hadamard slope. The problem carries unequal, equal and closed set constraints. The results come from applying exact penalty functions, a trick that folds constraints into the goal with penalty terms that stay exact.

Readers gain rules that mark best points under a broad constraint mix, stated through a slope notion suited to nonsmooth settings. The treatment is compact and theoretical, offering a clean route to best-point tests where old smooth slopes fall short. It suits workers in nonsmooth tuning and change-based analysis who need strict rules for limited problems.
arxiv-2602-17895:
Krishna Neupane introduces the Strategic Gap: how AI-driven timing and clutter shape investor trust today. Traditional market models assume prices reflect content alone, neglecting effects of reporting timing and cadence. The paper introduces the Autonomous Disclosure Regulator, an AI watchdog frame auditing filing clutter and filing shifts.

Analyzing nearly half a million filings, the research identifies a Strategic Gap. Companies use confusing language and unpredictable timing to slow market learning of the truth by sixty percent. Investors now spot copy-paste text well, yet remain vulnerable to strategic timing that hides decline. The frame isolates thirty-nine priority failures where dense text plus timing surprises enabled rent taking by insiders. A recursive agentic audit identifies welfare clawback of over three and a half times and strong toughness against data outages. That supports a shift toward an agentic regulatory state with auditing nodes for live review.
arxiv-2602-17995:
Kana Yamada and colleagues study dose choice in oncology phase one trials, where model-assisted designs make dose escalation adaptive yet simple to run by leaning on accumulating safety data. In practice, a trial may gain a new dose level midway, to probe safer doses or gather more efficacy data. The challenge is assigning doses well and picking the maximum tolerated dose or the optimal biological dose once that new level appears.

The authors propose a hybrid design starting with a non-informative model-assisted design, then applying an informative-prior extension only to the newly added dose at insertion time. To guard against a misspecified skeleton, they add two adaptive extensions: an online-weighting scheme that revises the skeleton as data accumulate, and a Bayesian-mixture approach that robustly combines several candidate skeletons. Simulation studies test how the proposed methods perform on dose assignment and dose selection.
arxiv-2602-18195:
Yicheng Feng and four co-authors built LERD, a system that reads Alzheimer's signals from brain wave recordings. Their 2026 paper starts from a limit of current tools. Black-box classifiers spot the disease in multi-channel EEG, but they never model the hidden timing of brain events or how channels coordinate behind their calls. LERD infers those hidden events and their links straight from the recordings, with no hand labels.

The system joins a continuous-time event finder with a random event generator, steered by a brain-inspired dynamics prior, and the team proves stability and a workable training penalty for it. On synthetic tests and two real Alzheimer's EEG groups, LERD beat strong baselines and returned rate, timing, and graph summaries that match physiology. The result is a diagnosis aid clinicians can inspect, not just a score.
arxiv-2602-18695:
Molecules and graphs are built piece by piece, and the order of those pieces matters for quality. Dhruvesh Patel, with five co-authors, presents LoFlexMDM in 2026, an insertion-based masked diffusion model that learns the build order from the data instead of following a fixed schedule.

The model generalises discrete flow matching to sequences that change length, and trains the generator and the order dynamics together under one objective. On new-molecule generation and on fragment-constrained generation, it improves sample quality over the earlier FlexMDM model. The lesson is that a learned order can raise quality without giving up a tractable training recipe, and the code is open source.
arxiv-2602-18895:
A smooth explanation is not the same as a true one, and that gap drives this test. Wenxi Geng, with three co-authors, asks in 2026 if language models can explain credit risk models after the fact. The study runs on a LendingClub dataset, setting language-model output against SHAP and coefficient-based attributions.

Three major models take part: Gemini-2.5-Flash, Claude-Sonnet-4.5, and GPT-4-turbo. With tightly controlled prompts, they reproduce reference rankings reliably, but left to explain on their own, their alignment drops sharply. The authors therefore place LLMs as narrative interfaces for credit risk governance, not as replacements for formal attribution methods. A fluent story, in short, is not a faithful account of why a model decided.
arxiv-2602-18995:
Second-harmonic generation converts light at a base frequency into light at twice that frequency. Its efficiency is measured by an effective value, and whether it can be worked out in uniaxial crystals is the subject of this work. Die Xiao, with one co-author, studies that coefficient in 2026 using the symmetry of nonlinear optical susceptibility tensors.

Calculation becomes tuning models with geometric constraints, exploiting the special nature of base frequency light. The number of variables in the maximum models is halved, to two, making calculation easier. A comparison with the C-eigenvalue of the response tensor is also given. Examples from typical crystal classes verify the correctness and broader use of the theoretical results. The work thus turns a physical yield measure into a tractable tuning problem. Light doubling can be computed. That computation is the contribution.
arxiv-2602-19295:
Robert Amevor and two co-authors compare two KRAS variants in people with non-small cell lung cancer, using real-world records rather than a clinical trial. Posted to arXiv in 2026, the paper focuses on G12C, which already has approved targeted drugs, and G12D, which does not. It draws on de-identified data from the AACR Project GENIE lung cancer set, tracking time to next treatment and overall survival.

Across 162 patients with usable treatment-timing data, the two groups looked similar overall, with median times near 29 and 32 months. Yet the pattern shifted over time: G12D fared better early on, then the gap faded. Survival also leaned toward G12D, while G12C tumors carried higher mutation burden and more STK11 and KEAP1 co-mutations. The authors call the results exploratory, needing larger cohorts before they guide treatment choices.
arxiv-2602-19395:
Rebuilding the speech envelope from scalp EEG recordings helps decode what a listener is attending to, as in neuro-steered hearing aids. Karan Thakkar and Mounya Elhilali note that current methods treat the task as static regression, reading each EEG window alone and ignoring the temporal shape of continuous speech. Their study introduces a dynamic framework that uses that shape as a predictive prior.

The model is a state-space fusion design: direct neural estimates from EEG combine with predictions from recent speech context, balanced by a learned gating mechanism. Tested on the ICASSP 2023 Stimulus Reconstruction benchmark, it beats static, EEG-only baselines by a wide margin. The work reframes envelope reconstruction as a joint neural and temporal problem, where the two information streams reinforce each other.
arxiv-2602-19495: Joon-Hwi Kim presents a twistor particle account of the Kerr black hole, giving an all-orders worldline effective action. In plain terms, the paper builds one action that captures the black hole's behavior across all orders of approximation, rather than stopping at a few terms. Readers get a concise theoretical result in twistor particle theory, where Kerr geometry is treated through particle worldlines.
arxiv-2602-19695:
People learn about online safety from many places: work training, news, friends, and family. A 2026 arXiv paper by William Seymour and Martin J. Kraemer reports an online study of people in four countries. The study asks how they find and pass on cybersecurity content at work and at home.

Workers who had taken workplace training were less inclined to share such content at home, and their attention shifted toward the workplace. They also recalled employer-shared material better than material from any other source, with recall tied to the type of content and how it reached them. The authors reflect on what this shift means, and where sharing at work and at home could be improved.
arxiv-2602-20095:
How large can twisted L-functions grow at their centre? A 2026 arXiv paper by Filippo Berta, working alone, addresses that question in the twist aspect. It concerns one fixed unitary cuspidal automorphic representation of the general linear group of rank three over a number field.

The twist runs over a sequence of prime ideals whose norms grow without bound. Each twist is given by a finite-order character whose conductor is the prime ideal in question. The paper establishes a subconvex bound for the twisted L-function at its central point, with an explicit exponent saving of up to one thirty-sixth below the convexity threshold. Readers gain a sharp quantitative estimate in the twist aspect of the subconvexity problem for rank-three automorphic forms over number fields.
arxiv-2602-20495:
Parameter identifiability matters for data-driven models of complex biology, but tools have gaps. Shun Wang and Wenrui Hao note that profile likelihood needs costly retuning, while Fisher-information tests drop the Hessian and may misjudge weakly bound ways. From a well-posedness definition, they study how estimates hold under small changes in the data with the full Hessian.

The analysis gives Hölder one-half steadiness at zero leftover error with degenerate Fisher information, and it corrects the Fisher matrix otherwise. Error size and data change size decide the order: Lipschitz below a crossover scale tied to error size, Hölder one-half above it. Local squared fits give per-value measures that allow singular Jacobians and nuisance Hessian blocks. Spectral bounds link corrections to value and forecast doubt. Tests on JAK-STAT signaling, HIV spread, and amyloid-beta buildup back the theory, which needs only local derivatives.
arxiv-2602-20695:
Andreia Chapouto and three co-authors study how smooth the solution map stays for the intermediate long wave equation on the real line. They focus on a scaled form of the equation, already known to converge to the Korteweg-de Vries equation in the shallow-water limit.

Splitting the motion into a low frequency part and a leftover part, they show the low frequency waves behave smoothly when the depth is small enough. The leftover part, by contrast, fails to be twice differentiable. They also prove shallow-water convergence of the low frequency motion to Korteweg-de Vries, explaining why the solution map gains smoothness in that limit.
arxiv-2602-20895:
The half-wave maps equation describes maps from a circle into a sphere, evolving under a nonlocal rule. Patrick Gerard and Enno Lenzmann study it in this 2026 arXiv paper. Starting from rational initial data, they build a unique, continuous flow for data in the critical energy space.

Solutions prove almost periodic in time, and for rational data they are quasi-periodic with bounds at every higher regularity level. The analysis rests on an explicit formula from a Lax pair acting on a Hardy space, plus a general stability principle for such formulas that also covers related integrable equations. Results extend to matrix-valued maps into Grassmannians, with a companion work treating the real line.
arxiv-2602-21095: Mean-field theory is a workhorse approximation, but it breaks down in ways that need diagnosis. Pok Man Lo develops theoretical diagnostics for that breakdown in this 2026 arXiv paper. The work shows how spatial structure and finite interaction ranges enter the effective description of a system. Those scales do more than decorate the theory: they qualitatively modify the renormalization-group flow. Readers get tools for recognizing when mean-field descriptions fail and for tracing how spatial detail reshapes the effective theory.
arxiv-2602-21295:
A sub-solar-mass black hole detection would open a window onto new stellar physics or primordial black holes as dark matter. Alberto Magaraggia and Nico Cappelluti examine that possibility in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their trigger is a November 2025 gravitational-wave candidate. Its chirp mass lies between a tenth and just under nine-tenths of a solar mass, with over ninety-nine percent probability that at least one component is sub-solar.

The authors test whether primordial black holes formed at the quantum chromodynamics epoch with a broad mass function could explain such a signal. They predict under one event per year for one observing run, compatible with the observed rate if the trigger is astrophysical. Their rate also matches expectations for stellar-mass binaries. If confirmed, the detection would bound the primordial fraction above four percent in their model.
arxiv-2602-21495:
Devansh Jalota and two co-authors ask how much is lost when congestion pricing uses simple static tolls instead of optimal dynamic tolls. Dynamic welfare- or revenue-optimal tolls are often impractical. Real deployments, including New York City's recent program, rely on far simpler, often static tolls.

The team analyzes the gap in two canonical frameworks: Vickrey's bottleneck model with a public transit outside option, and its city-scale extension based on the Macroscopic Fundamental Diagram. Across many practically relevant regimes, revenue-optimal static tolls capture at least two-thirds of maximum revenue and incur at most twice the minimum system cost, with stronger guarantees in the bottleneck model. Numerical results corroborate the theory: static tolls reach roughly 80 to 90 percent of dynamic optimal revenue at only 8 to 25 percent higher total system cost.
arxiv-2602-21695:
Quentin Staelens and five co-authors study quasi-one-dimensional strongly correlated materials with a chain of methods: density functional theory, downfolding, and tensor-network simulations. Downfolding yields multiband Hubbard models that balance electron hopping against local Coulomb repulsion. Solved with matrix product states, the pure one-dimensional treatment of three cuprates gave no long-range magnetic order, though experiments show ordering.

Adding links between chains through a self-consistent mean-field scheme stabilized staggered magnetization, matching experiment. For two further compounds, a ladder-based approach failed, because hopping within ladders was too small. The combined method thus captures magnetic order where the one-dimensional treatment alone cannot.
arxiv-2602-21795:
Magnetized rotating neutron stars, or pulsars, result from massive star evolution, and their wind meets supernova ejecta, the progenitor's circumstellar medium, and then the interstellar medium. A still massive star's circumstellar medium stretches along the magnetic field, and its supernova remnant briefly appears rectangular. D. M. -A. Meyer and one co-author explore how the angle between interstellar field and pulsar axis shapes the pulsar wind nebula. They use 3D MHD simulations with PLUTO and radiative transfer for non-thermal radio maps.

When polar elongations develop, they bend in opposite directions under the cavity carved by stellar wind and filled by supernova ejecta. The result is a complex mix of magnetized ejecta and pulsar wind appearing as rectangles, circles, or oblong radio shapes. The angle between rotation axis and ambient magnetization governs shaping and radio properties, though mixing in old nebulae, 50 to 80 thousand years, depends little on it.
arxiv-2602-21895:
Julien Cassaigne and three co-authors examine a two-symbol Thue-Morse-style sequence from the base-3/2 writing of whole numbers, a textbook automatic sequence in a rational-base number system. It grows by repeating morphism steps on a cycle, not one primitive substitution, so classic Perron-Frobenius tools cannot fix symbol frequencies alone. The team proves 0 and 1 each appear half the time, and the factors recur evenly and mirror each other.

Their argument links word combinatorics with harmonic analysis. The first difference sequence turns out Toeplitz, which stiffens the dynamics, while filtered frequencies carry a dyadic pattern rising to the 2-adic integers as a compact group. There, undoing a substitution acts as a linear map on Fourier coefficients, and a spectral squeeze leaves one limiting density. The findings settle several Dekking conjectures about a sibling sequence, and show harmonic analysis on compact groups joining substitution dynamics.
arxiv-2602-22095:
Quantum behavior is usually taken as fundamental, but one research line reinterprets it as the shadow of an underlying random process. Jason Doukas generalizes that stochastic-quantum correspondence, widening its lifting recipe so it reaches more quantum states without enlarging the underlying space. A compatibility rule and a Kraus dictionary link random-process kernels to valid quantum maps.

Doukas shows every finite-dimensional kernel admits a compatible lift, and that varying the kernels covers all quantum channels. He describes smooth, composable quantum dynamics through time-local Lindblad generators, and proves every rooted quantum dynamical family has a stochastic realizer on the same space. A revival of distinguishability, he shows, rules out any Markovian realizer there.
arxiv-2602-22195:
Decentralized consensus needs a scarce resource to stop attackers from minting fake identities for free, and the usual resources carry heavy costs. Dar Gilboa and two co-authors build a consensus protocol that uses geospatial position, verified with quantum computers, as its external resource. The protocol, called Quantum Proof of Position, aims for energy efficiency without the wealth concentration of stake-based systems.

Its Sybil resistance is non-rival: checking a position occupies a quantum computer only briefly, so one device can secure many chains at once with full benefit each. The resource also cannot be agglomerated, which pushes the network toward geographic decentralization. The paper offers a permissionless design whose security rests on where you are, not what you own or burn.
arxiv-2602-22495:
Reinforcement learning post-training has driven large gains in long reasoning models, but those models cost much to run. That cost motivates distillation into smaller students. Zhaoyang Zhang and eight co-authors note most distillation methods were built for supervised fine-tuning, relying on fixed teacher traces or divergence penalties.

Paired with reinforcement learning, those methods suffer distribution mismatch and objective clash. Teacher guidance may not fit the student's evolving rollouts, and the penalty can fight reward maximization. The team proposes RL-aware distillation, which imitates the teacher selectively, only when it improves the current policy update. Its core, Trust Region Ratio Distillation, swaps the divergence penalty for a PPO-style likelihood-ratio objective anchored to a teacher-old mix. That yields advantage-aware, trust-region-bounded distillation on rollouts. Across logic and math benchmarks, it beats offline distillation, standard GRPO, and KL-based teacher-student distillation.
arxiv-2602-22595:
Taozhe Li and four co-authors argue that object detectors throw away useful clues. The YOLO family and transformer-based DETR detectors focus on foreground objects and neglect background context. Yet setting often predicts content: cars belong on roads, wild animals in forests, not offices or busy streets.

Their model, Association DETR, is built to use background information rather than ignore it. The authors set it against the recent history of the field, noting YOLOv12 at about 55 points and RT-DETRv2 at about 53 points on the COCO val2017 benchmark. Association DETR reached leading results on that same benchmark, suggesting that context the field discards can sharpen detection.
arxiv-2602-22795:
Óscar Rodríguez-Villalba and three co-authors study fuzzy dark matter in one spatial dimension, where contact interactions join gravity in shaping structures. The standard cold dark matter picture explains large scales well but strains at small scales, and fuzzy dark matter offers an alternative in which local self-interactions matter further.

Simulations cover attractive and repulsive contact interactions in static and expanding backgrounds, across three scenarios: the lowest-energy stationary state, relaxation of localized states, and gravitational collapse of spread-out states. Contact forces reshape the stationary density profile and shift the onset of collapse stages, including shell crossing. Notably, relaxation never settles into the lowest-energy state in this one-dimensional model, even with self-interactions included.
arxiv-2602-22895:
Bruno Aristimunha and seven co-authors unify shape deep learning for neural reading in one Python library. Versions of SPD matrix networks for brain reading scatter across research code with ad hoc curved-space handling and clashing training setups, blocking reruns and modern workflow hookup.

SPD Learn gathers core SPD tools and neural layers, including spectral tools stable in numbers, and locks Stiefel and SPD limits via flattening-based settings. Standard backprop and tuning then run in free flat spaces while yielding curved-space-bound knobs by build. Sample versions of SPDNet-based models plus links to MOABB, Braindecode, Nilearn, and SKADA support rerun-ready testing and hands-on use.
arxiv-2602-23295:
Ayush Roy and three co-authors propose ManifoldGD, a training-free way to distill large data sets into compact ones with geometry-guided diffusion. Distillation seeks small synthetic sets that preserve a large training set's knowledge while cutting storage and compute. Recent training-free methods use diffusion priors, but guidance is limited: they denoise blind or steer toward simple mode-based prototype centroids that are often crude.

ManifoldGD instead builds instance prototype centroids through hierarchical, divisive clustering of VAE latent features, giving a multi-scale coreset capturing coarse modes and fine variation. At each denoising step, it projects the mode-alignment vector onto the local tangent space of the estimated latent manifold. That keeps generation faithful to the manifold and semantically consistent. Tests show gains over training-free and training-based rivals in FID, embedding distance, and classification accuracy. It is the first geometry-aware training-free distillation framework.
arxiv-2602-23395:
John Campbell and one co-author present meta-automatic sequences, a natural mix of two rule worlds. Nested meta-Fibonacci rules, such as the one fixing Hofstadter's Q-sequence, and the digit-based rules behind automatic lists both appeal to number theorists and pattern experts. Allouche and Shallit showed that the rate sequence of a Q-sequence variant is 2-auto, sparking the new mix.

The authors exhibit two binary meta-auto sequences, M1 and M2, whose core rules do not straight satisfy the Allouche-Shallit auto criterion. For each sequence they prove exact DFAO checks plus 4-uniform morphisms, and they also weigh the factor patterns of these two. The paper thus extends automatic sequence theory to a class of rules that mix self-linking with digit-based structure.
arxiv-2602-23495:
Yangyi Li and one co-author improve concept bottleneck models, which first map inputs to high-level meaning concepts and then combine those concepts for classification. Their clarity is attractive, but labeling concepts demands much expert labor, and language-model labels carry unmeasured uncertainty and hallucination risk.

The authors propose an uncertainty-aware method that strictly measures uncertainty in language-model concept labels with valid, distribution-free guarantees, then folds that measured uncertainty into training to reflect varying trust across concepts. Theory backs the method, and wide tests on real-world datasets confirm its desired traits. The work thus makes language-model-built concept bottlenecks both more trustworthy and more practical to adopt.
arxiv-2602-23795:
Wenwu Tang and three co-authors present GRAIL, a post-hoc fix that restores accuracy after a neural network has been compressed. The 2026 paper targets aggressive pruning and folding, where accuracy loss usually forces retraining that may be costly or impossible without labeled data.

GRAIL needs no retraining and no labels. It runs a small calibration set through the network, sums hidden activations into a Gram matrix, and uses ridge regression to rebuild the original hidden signal from the compressed one. The rebuild map folds into later weights, so inference cost stays low. Across image and language models, GRAIL beats data-free and data-aware baselines in practical compression ranges, with modest overhead and no backpropagation.
arxiv-2602-23895:
Mathias Garny and two co-authors argue that a dark radiation-matter decoupling scenario, proposed to ease the Hubble tension, predicts dark acoustic oscillations similar in scale to ordinary baryon oscillations. The 2026 paper tests that prediction using only cosmic microwave background data and supernova data calibrated independently of large-scale structure.

The analysis finds evidence for a dark oscillation signal, with a drag-horizon scale in the tens of megaparsecs and a small amplitude, both within stated confidence ranges. Those predicted properties match what would be needed to explain a recent anomaly in Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument data. The result offers an alternative to evolving dark energy and a concrete target for upcoming surveys. DESI, Euclid, and the Roman telescope can confirm or refute the dark oscillation picture.
arxiv-2602-24095:
Fabian Lenzen and Lena Weis define and analyze tropical k-means clustering for phylogenetic trees, using the asymmetric tropical distance. The 2026 paper works on the tropical torus and, in particular, on the Bergman fan of the complete graphical matroid. That fan corresponds to the space of equidistant trees with a given number of leaves.

That correspondence lets tree clustering be treated as clustering in a tropical geometric space, where distances respect the combinatorial structure of trees rather than forcing them into Euclidean coordinates. The authors define the tropical k-means algorithm on that space and analyze its behavior for equidistant phylogenetic trees. The work offers a principled clustering tool for evolutionary biology. In short, the tool groups trees by their own true geometry. The groups match the trees' past.
arxiv-2603-00195: Bhardwaj presents SkillFortify, a formal analysis and supply-chain security study of agentic AI skills, with 32 pages, five theorems with full proofs, 68 references and an open-source tool. Version 2 corrects the bibliography, where 22 entries had author lists mismatched to their cited arXiv papers, and revises three external claims against primary sources. It also flips experiment E3 to a negative finding: flow analysis adds no detections beyond pattern matching on this corpus. E1 and E2 stay unchanged, holding F1 at 96.15% on their tests.
arxiv-2603-00395: Oh and three colleagues build Aurchestra, the first tool giving fine grained live soundscape control on small hearable devices. Current controls offer only blanket noise cut or one sound focus, yet real scenes mix many sources a listener may want to tune apart. Their design shows only active sound classes and splits each class into its own stream, handling up to five overlapping targets. Users then mix per class volumes like tracks, with tests showing strong gains in target lift and interference cut.
arxiv-2603-00495: Cruz introduces AI Runtime Infrastructure, an execution time layer sitting above the model and below the application that watches, reasons about, and steps into agent behaviour while it runs. Unlike model tweaks or passive logs, the layer treats execution itself as a surface to optimise, tuning task success, speed, token use, reliability, and safety on the fly. It supports adaptive memory handling, failure spotting and recovery, and policy enforcement across long agent workflows. The paper frames runtime control as distinct from model level optimisation.
arxiv-2603-01095: Urabe and seven colleagues report a giant flare on the binary star UX Arietis, caught in X-rays and followed for twelve days with optical spectra. The hydrogen-alpha glow dims and returns with binary rotation. Part of the flux hides at one orbital phase while all of it shows at the opposite phase, placing the flaring region low and about as wide as the star. Velocity shifts put it beyond the stellar limb above a large starspot, consistent with plasma trapped in a tall magnetic loop.
arxiv-2603-01195: Dong and six colleagues select multimodal training data by visual necessity, since many instruction samples can be solved from text alone or carry misaligned supervision. VisNec scores each sample by how much its loss changes with versus without visual input. It flags vision-critical, redundant, or misaligned cases, then picks high-necessity samples within semantic clusters to preserve diversity. Training on just 15 percent of a large dataset matches full-data performance, and on a smaller set it beats full training by about 16 percent.
arxiv-2603-01795:
Robin Shing Moon Chan, Rita Sevastjanova, and Mennatallah El-Assady help users fix vague database questions through dialogue. Their 2026 work starts from a flaw: plain-language query tools often force one guess when a request could mean several things. Users phrase requests tersely, while systems guess from priors that may not match user intent.

Their tool, PleaSQLarify, treats the fix as pragmatic repair through small clarifying steps. It lays out the space of possible SQL readings and asks about the choice that splits that space best. A visual panel lets users explore options and trace how beliefs update across turns. In a study with twelve users, the tool helped people spot rival readings and settle ambiguity fast. The authors offer repair as a design rule for user control in query tools.
arxiv-2603-01895:
G. Buldgen, M. Kunitomo, A. Noels, and colleagues revise how much helium the early Sun held. Their 2026 study targets the protosolar helium mass fraction, a base input for solar and planetary models. Past values leaned on simple treatments of chemical transport inside solar models, plus shaky envelope estimates.

The team combines their own inversions of the solar envelope makeup with spectroscopic abundances and literature values. That blend yields a robust range for helium in the convective zone today. Solar models that add mixing at the base of that zone then trace back to the birth value. Mixing there cannot be neglected, they show, and lithium and beryllium loss can calibrate its strength. The revised birth interval sits slightly below prior estimates, which shifts enrichment laws built on the old value.
arxiv-2603-01995:
Oskar Riedler gives a sharp test for maps that keep a key wave rule intact, in this 2026 work. Such maps, called harmonic morphisms, send curved spaces to curved spaces and keep Laplace solutions valid. They have long been tied to least-area shapes, called minimal submanifolds, in deep ways.

Riedler shows these maps are just the ones that stretch in a weak, flat way and keep the least-area rule true in codimension two. Codimension counts how many dims a shape lacks next to the space around it. More such rules follow for shapes of other codimensions as well. One worked case then yields a new set of least-area cones of degree four. Those cones sit in high-dim space and add fresh test shapes to the field.
arxiv-2603-02095:
Guy Smorodinsky, Sveta Gimpleson, and Itay Safran prove a slow-learning result in this 2026 paper. They use the smallest useful setup: a two-neuron network and just two training cases. Gradient descent trains the network to sort the two cases correctly. It also widens the safety margin, the gap between the decision line and the cases.

That margin does grow to its best value, but at a painfully slow pace. The authors prove the pace cannot beat a rate tied to the log of time. Tests with many starting points show the same tight, slow pace each time. The proof tracks the network through each pattern of active neurons. It is the first firm lower bound of its kind for a non-linear model.
