arxiv-2605-12395: Lorandi and Belz compare controlled text generation systems on a genuinely level playing field. Rival systems have usually been judged on different data sets with different scoring methods, so rankings were hard to trust. Their approach standardises all outputs the same way and applies one shared set of methods and data sets to each system. Re-scored this way, representative systems perform very differently from their originally reported results, usually worse. The gap, they argue, shows why shared, standard evaluation matters for the field.
arxiv-2605-12495: Huang and four colleagues apply group relative policy optimisation to unified multimodal models. Their AlphaGRPO framework needs no extra cold-start stage. It unlocks two skills. First, text-to-image generation from reasoning, where the model infers hidden user intent. Second, self-reflective refinement, where it spots and fixes its own misalignments. A decompositional verifiable reward breaks each request into atomic, checkable questions. Those questions are scored by a general multimodal model. Tests show robust gains across generation benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-12695: Bychkov and Ryzhikov study averaging for ergodic multiflows on a probability space. They apply a general theorem on universal averaging for flows to means along manifolds in Euclidean space. That link shows the general theorem covers this shape case, tying abstract theory to concrete shapes. The work is brief, giving the result and its use there. The theorem does most of the work.
arxiv-2605-12795: Portnoi, Hillenbrand and Carvalho present near-infrared spectroscopic diagnostics for identifying FU Orionis stars. FUOrs are young stellar objects in extreme outburst, driven by mass inflow from their accretion disks. The team gathered near-infrared spectra of 28 known FUOrs with the Palomar Hale TripleSpec spectrograph. They measure atomic line strengths with equivalent widths and design band ratios for molecular features. Comparing FUOrs with late-type dwarfs and evolved stars, they propose spaces that distinguish FUOr disks from normal stars.
arxiv-2605-12895: Bellibatlu and four colleagues present RISED, a pre-deployment check for high-stakes AI decision-support tools, applied first to healthcare. Most such tools win clearance on a single aggregate accuracy score, which hides gaps across patient subgroups, threshold sensitivity and input reliability. RISED grades five dimensions with verdicts of pass, fail or inconclusive. Across seven cohorts spanning 35 years it exposes failures that accuracy alone misses, including severe threshold sensitivity in one survey cohort.
arxiv-2605-13095: Aremu, Zhang and Lukas argue watermarking should be judged and governed as a monitoring primitive, not just a provenance trick. They contrast inside watchers, who use detector access and entity maps for attribution, with outside watchers, who learn entity signals from labelled outputs without keys. Even zero-bit watermarking supports inside attribution under per-entity multi-key deployment. Outside identification works only in selected text and image settings, and both paths stay conditional on reliability and access.
arxiv-2605-13295: Zehle presents CANTANTE, a way to tune multi agent language systems by splitting system scores into per agent signals. Scores arrive only for the whole system, while the settings that matter live inside each agent. Contrasting runs of several joint setups on the same query yields local update signals for prompt tuning. It tops rival optimizers on average across coding, math reasoning and question answering tests, gaining nearly nineteen points on coding over the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-13395: Lilin Zhang and four colleagues study adversarial training on long-tail data, where a few classes dominate and most have few examples. Adversarial training defends networks against small input changes, but most work assumes balanced classes. The authors find two problems: class imbalance skews the training goal, and adversarial distributions shift in an unstable way. They show that perturbations can address both weakness and imbalance at once. Their RobustLT framework adjusts perturbations during training, and tests show gains in both defence and balance.
arxiv-2605-13495: P. M. Dejardin revisits Rayleigh light scattering theory in dense isotropic polar fluids. Plain equations are derived for Rayleigh ratios in side scattering, covering pure dipole-induced dipole, pure rotation and mixed cases. For pure dipole-induced dipole, the ratios are fully simple. For pure rotation, a mean field approximation holds, giving ratios through a single orientation link value found as a positive root of a square equation.
arxiv-2605-13595: Sophia Hager, Simon Zeng and Nicholas Andrews pose the problem of artificially inducing uncertainty in language models. Safety-critical uses need models that report uncertainty as meaningful probabilities. Supervised uncertainty methods need hard unseen data, scarce for models trained on vast scraped text. The authors test ways to induce artificial uncertainty on trivially easy data when no hard data exists at training time. Probes trained on artificial uncertainty beat plain probes at spotting real uncertainty, with higher calibration on hard data and minimal loss on easy data.
arxiv-2605-13795: Shibing Chen and three colleagues give a new proof of the three-dimensional symmetric Mahler inequality. It states that every origin-symmetric convex body K equal to its negative in R^3 has volume product at least 32 over 3. The new proof uses a pure shape path based on even allowed shadow systems, growing the tricks from the authors' proof of the three-dimensional non-even Mahler conjecture.
arxiv-2605-14095: Cocke, Lewis and McCulloch formalize a new kind of group map: the centralizer-respecting homomorphism. Such maps are onto maps that respect taking the centralizer of a subgroup, in an equivariant sense. The paper builds a functor from the category of these maps to the category of centralizer lattices. Closing theorems show that this category holds many interesting maps, giving the new idea genuine math content.
arxiv-2605-14195: Ahmadian, Cohen and Roghani frame stochastic matching under local bandwidth limits. Classic online matching demands immediate, final decisions, yet in spread-out systems like ride-hailing and cloud jobs, local bandwidth often binds tighter than match timing. Their two-stage local sparsification plan has new requests prune seen match sets to a strict budget of k edges before a central hub runs the global matching. That middle ground balances local information limits against global optimization gains, with a local pick plan set by a fractional solution of the expected instance.
arxiv-2605-14395: Siddiqui extends three-state overlap analysis to n-cycle overlaps, finding their exact quantum maximum over finite pure states for any cycle length from three upward. Evenly spaced qubit states along a Fubini-Study geodesic meet the bound, so the optimum is reached in dimension two. Under ideal interferometry, overlaps can be read from pairwise fringe patterns. The three-state case recovers the maximum of five quarters, and the quantum-classical gap approaches one as cycle length grows. Such violations can witness preparation contextuality in noncontextuality, given needed operational links.
arxiv-2605-15295: Gideon Popoola and John Sheppard propose a procedural fairness metric for machine learning in high-stakes decisions like loans, hiring, and recidivism forecast. Outcome metrics capture gaps in choices but not in the reasons behind them. Their Group-level Explanation Stability Disparity gauges group gaps in how stable, robust, and touchy model reasons are. Built in a multi-objective framework balancing fairness, explainability, and utility, it lifts both utility and fairness on benchmarks.
arxiv-2605-15395: Oscar Peralta settles two open questions from Bladt and Nielsen on multivariate matrix-exponential and phase-type distributions. In the matrix-exp case, the projection-defined class matches with Kulkarni algebraic class, via a state-space build theorem plus add-ons into K-form. Every proper fractional multi-way Laplace transform thus gains a finite-size Kulkarni-type representation once memoryless sign constraints drop. In the phase-type case, subset turns strict from three factors onward, with a Wishart trace distribution inside the larger class but outside the smaller one.
arxiv-2605-15495: Rafaela F. S. Penacchio and nine colleagues report a new compound, Y4Co3Ag, built by adding yttrium to the immiscible cobalt-silver pair. Its crystal structure holds one-dimensional cobalt chains inside yttrium channels, with no direct cobalt-silver neighbors. Transport, magnetic, and heat-capacity measurements show antiferromagnetic order at 14.9 kelvin with small, mobile magnetic moments and strong fluctuations, making the material a promising setting for studying itinerant magnetism in nearly one-dimensional systems.
arxiv-2605-15995: Gwenolé Quellec proposes Constrained Latent State Modeling. It is a framework for judging what a learned hidden state should keep, drop, and sort. He defines six traits: predictive sufficiency, minimality, temporal coherence, observation fit, invariance to nuisance factors, and structural limits. He separates these traits from the training goals and tests used to impose or check them. He rereads major representation groups through this lens. A synthetic benchmark then shows how distinct training goals yield distinct hidden layouts and trade-offs.
arxiv-2605-16295: Noviello, Birillo, and Migut present ANVIL, a mixed-media system that turns concept meanings into teaching videos for CS. ANVIL writes a textual analogy, builds it into a set visual screenplay, and writes working manim code to render the video, with auto repair for toughness. Teacher testing grounds quality grading, an LLM grader screens analogy drafts at scale, and screenplay match proxies video quality. Teachers in a user study rated lessons often good enough and replied warmly to felt value and ease of use.
arxiv-2605-16495: Sfaradi and thirty-one others present optical, X-ray, and radio observations of Type Ic-BL 2012ap. Previous studies suggested a weak engine-driven explosion, lacking gamma-ray bursts. Radio surveys revealed rebrightening, suggesting density enhancement or an off-axis jet. Optical spectra lack broad lines of interacting supernovae, but radio and X-ray analysis implies both scenarios. If density enhancement causes rebrightening, changed mass-loss or wind velocity explains it. If the radio component is an off-axis jet, an energetic narrow jet at 80 degrees suffices.
arxiv-2605-16995: He and Huang supply construction details for the Q/D-space framework behind sufficient order conditions for explicit Runge-Kutta methods. These are numerical schemes for differential equations. The note gives a general sufficiency theorem and worked checks of the conditions. It also gives a full order-10 scheme with its linear systems and coefficient tables, plus an analysis of how costly the construction algorithm is.
arxiv-2605-17095: Srbinovska and three colleagues turn body-camera video into visual timelines that help reviewers find key moments without watching whole recordings. Each ten-second slice gets labels for its operational setting and its motion level, with weak-evidence tags where darkness, blur, or blocking hides detail. Their best models score about seventy-nine percent on setting and eighty-eight percent on activity. Audits show the timelines speed incident review and officer training.
arxiv-2605-17195: Oparin and colleagues probe candle-flame-shaped solar flares with a three-dimensional magnetohydrodynamics model, testing how the bright cusp above a flare arcade relates to magnetic reconnection. They find the points where field topology switches need not sit at the apparent cusp tip. Apparent speeds of plasma downflows above the arcade, they also show, understate true Alfvén speeds in the inflow zone by at least a factor of two.
arxiv-2605-17295: Shaobo Wang and colleagues introduce DISA, a method that moves partition-function calibration for distribution-matching reinforcement learning out of the training loop. Proposal trajectories are drawn offline, the partition function is estimated by importance sampling, and that estimate is frozen before policy training starts. On two backbones across nine math and code benchmarks it matches or beats the coupled baseline and keeps far more strategic diversity than reward-maximizing rivals.
arxiv-2605-17495: Sipacheva proves that every infinite elementary abelian topological group contains an infinite maximally almost periodic subgroup. The result settles the existence question for this class of groups in a single theorem. It guarantees a large subgroup with strong almost-periodic traits inside any infinite member of the class. That sharpens the picture of elementary abelian topological groups, showing how much almost-periodic structure such groups must contain.
arxiv-2605-17595: Kettinger and Moles develop the S-relative Davenport constant from Skałba to tackle non-closed order elasticity. Orders in number fields have long been central, and despite non-maximal orders that are not Dedekind, class groups may determine elasticity. Although Skałba's construction aided binary quadratic forms, the invariant is the tool for non-closed order elasticity. The paper investigates elasticity of orders with prime conductor ideal, and quadratic-field orders with primary conductor. Conditions are given for an order to share elasticity with the full ring of integers.
arxiv-2605-17795: Ningkang Peng and four colleagues show high accuracy on noisy labels does not guarantee safe rejection of strange inputs. Their ACC-OOD benchmark freezes noisy-label models and tests them on near and far out-of-distribution routing. Low-confidence, misclassified in-distribution samples overlap the score regions of out-of-distribution inputs, a flaw they call uncertainty collapse. Virtual Margin Regularization, a light repair, builds fake boundary outliers on trusted batches and widens the energy margin. It partly cuts far-OOD failure without hurting closed-set accuracy.
arxiv-2605-18095: Gabriella Damas and G. D. de Moraes Neto study shortcut-error signs in coherence-keeping work quasistatistics. Usual two-point measure gives positive values but erases phase. For work defined against a reference Hamiltonian, an exact counterdiabatic shortcut pulls the final one back to a form diagonal in the initial energy basis. Endpoint quasistatistics then lose feel for starting coherence and match the two-point result. Flaws restore it: a clashing control error yields off-diagonal elements at first order, while level-only transition chances change only at second order.
arxiv-2605-18395: Sungwoo Kang presents Dynamo-K, a 2026 census-grounded simulation of Korean-language language-model behavior across four models and six Korean elections from 2017 to 2025. The study names three failure modes: progressive bias in moderate agents, collapse of third-party salience, and regional polarization collapse in party strongholds. Scenario reframing recovers 62 percent of 2017 error, and a learned reweighting adapter calibrates opposing-valence models without candidate names.
arxiv-2605-18495: Ziqi Chen and Ning Xiang study, in a 2026 paper, how cylindrical tube modes affect three-microphone tests of porous samples. Several mics around the tube rim widen the valid frequency band for impedance tests. Wide-band tests show phase jumps in the measured wave coefficient. Step-by-step Bayesian inference unwraps the coefficient and recovers values that match the measured transfer curve.
arxiv-2605-18795: Jia Wei and seven colleagues adapt low-rank fine-tuning to mixture-of-experts models, where only some experts fire per token. Their HELLoRA method attaches adapters only to the most used experts in each layer, cutting trainable weights and adapter compute while lifting scores. A stricter variant, HELLoRI, freezes one projection and sparsifies the other. Across three expert models and maths, coding, and safety tasks, HELLoRA beats strong efficient-tuning rivals.
arxiv-2605-18995: Evan Linck and Robert Mathieu measure rotation speeds of Sun-like blue stragglers in three clusters: M67, NGC 188 and NGC 6791. Rotation shows a Kraft break like field stars: hotter stragglers spin rapidly, cooler ones slowly, with a mixture in between. Binary interactions should spin up progenitors, so all these stragglers reached periods below two days, short of critical velocity, then spun down as envelopes evolved. Temperature dependence shows straggler envelopes behaving like single stars, turning convective and making magnetic fields at the same temperatures, and velocity dispersion also shapes rotation.
arxiv-2605-19095: Aaron Defazio scales schedule-free learning, a method that trains without a learning-rate schedule, up to large language models. Earlier success at this scale was limited to small models. He identifies the fixes needed for larger batches and model sizes and presents ScheduleFree+, which needs neither a learning rate nor a schedule. It outperforms warmup-stable-decay schedules. For long training runs at 1000 tokens per parameter it beats the best schedules by 31 percent. The work gives a theoretical basis for model averaging and checkpoint merging during pretraining.
arxiv-2605-19195: Samuel D'Ambrosia, Sultan Daniels, Michael DeWeese, and Anant Sahai price the energy cost of simple linear regression, a basic modeling task. Fitting models from data already eats a large share of computing energy, so physical limits on such routines matter more each year. Following Landauer, they bound the cost of exact fitting and of stochastic gradient descent on floating-point numbers. From those bounds they derive scaling rules for the best dataset size at a given error target, plus a way to bound entropy from mismatch in continuous-input routines.
arxiv-2605-19395: Wang and Ozturk explore a puzzle: xenon, a chemically inert gas, anesthetizes, and mouse tests once showed its potency shifting with nuclear spin. They link that pattern to chiral-induced spin selectivity, where spin steers charge flow in mirror-asymmetric molecules. Their kinetic model ties isotope passage through chiral tissue to receptor binding, reproducing the reported spin dependence. Unlike theories needing long-lived quantum coherence, the scheme survives warm, messy biology, and it invites tests of spin effects beyond anesthesia.
arxiv-2605-19695: Wang and Cornell tackle cross-talk in conversational separation, where microphones worn by each speaker pick up others' speech plus noise. Their cross-talk reduction task isolates the wearer's speech from close-talk mixtures, and CTRnet learns it from real pairs of close-talk and far-field mixtures. PuLSS uses estimated clean speech as pseudo-labels to train far-field separation models on real target-domain data, not simulations. On CHiME-6 the framework reaches state-of-the-art speech recognition under oracle and estimated speaker diarization.
arxiv-2605-19995: Hongji Yang and six co-workers build CogOmniControl, a video-making framework that first reasons about a creator's intent and then generates from it. A vision-language model tuned on authentic anime production data reads sparse, abstract prompts such as storyboard sketches, while a diffusion model unifies the controls and selects among candidates. Two new benchmarks from professional workflows show it surpasses existing open-source models.
arxiv-2605-20395: Ngui and four co-workers speed multi-robot motion planning by up to an order of magnitude. Planning all robots jointly avoids collisions but costs dearly in search over the joint configuration space. Their method searches a discrete workspace decomposition to coordinate robots, then refines it so planners search smaller decoupled spaces. The refinement step goes beyond prior topology-based methods that only decide when robots must be planned jointly.
arxiv-2605-20695: Noga Alon and eight colleagues present a short, human-verified digest of a recent machine-generated counterexample to the Erdos unit distance problem. The problem concerns distances among point sets in the plane, and the new example was first produced by OpenAI tools. Their version distills the argument and adds reflections on its ideas. Key ingredients trace, in retrospect, to Ellenberg-Venkatesh and others.
arxiv-2605-20795: Hangyu Lin and six colleagues diagnose what meaning lives on through the link between vision-language models and diffusion transformers in video editing. Flow-based video editors prepend vision-language models, on the view that a link can smoothly align rich multimodal reasoning with the text embedding space. The authors argue that link instead acts as a severe meaning bottleneck, harming fine-grained structural variables. A careful composition pipeline yields TRACE-Edit, a diagnostic set focused on relation-based editing, plus a protocol to separate link failures from generation errors.
arxiv-2605-20895: Melia Haase and Nicolas Nagel give precise asymptotics and exact formulas for tensor product energies of Fibonacci lattices. They consider sums involving Fibonacci numbers, with terms built from a function f and sine denominators raised to a power sigma. Such sums appear in discrepancy theory and in numerical integration methods recast as energy minimization problems. For sigma above one and a large class of functions, they show the sum behaves like C times n plus D plus an exponentially small error.
arxiv-2605-21395: Liang Wu and co-authors present a BlueSky vision for resilient and autonomous AI-native 6G networks. Emerging apps such as autonomous driving and immersive experiences demand networks that are faster and fundamentally more resilient and autonomous. The vision shifts from network for AI to AI for network, anchored by a foundation model and orchestrated via collaborative multi-agent systems. Two directions follow: a 6G foundation model as unified backbone, with task knowledge distilled into compact edge models, and agentic orchestration of network functions.
arxiv-2605-21595: Cisco Gooding, Taylor Cey, and Robert Mann propose an experiment testing superpositions of detector trajectories. They test response of a particle detector in a superposition of spots interacting with a relativistic quantum field. A beamsplitter splits a laser probe into two superposed branches, which meet a pancake-shaped Bose-Einstein cloud at two spots, then recombine. Heterodyning one output reveals the Unruh-deWitt response in the difference photocurrent power spectrum. The test uses light and a cold gas cloud.
arxiv-2605-21795: Won Joon Yun and co-authors present IRIS, a compiler for distributed quantum computers, where chips link through photonic interconnects and teleportation moves qubits and runs cross-chip CNOT gates. Non-local CNOTs run over four times slower and four times more error-prone than local ones, hurting fidelity. Existing compilers schedule CNOT blocks, without lookahead between blocks and without scheduling later blocks early. IRIS fixes this with utility-driven lookahead over multi-candidate schedules and capacity-aware early scheduling, cutting teleportations thirty-four percent and latency twofold on average.
arxiv-2605-22195: Manuel Noah Riesen and co-authors propose Reinforced Graph of Thoughts, an automated take on graph-of-thoughts prompting. Graph of Thoughts structures language model thoughts as an arbitrary graph of operations, but the graph is usually defined by hand and stays rigid. RGoT uses reinforcement learning to generate the operation graph adaptively from a human-defined set. Results show graphs can be built to match task complexity under certain constraints. The approach removes the need for deep prior knowledge of each problem solution.
arxiv-2605-22495: Rogatko scrutinises charges bound to visible and dark sectors near their magnetic poles. The system has angular momentum even though the charges are at rest. Electric charges of visible and hidden sectors held at rest outside a magnetically charged black hole are then studied. Even treated as perturbations on a spherically symmetric magnetic static black hole in dark photon theory, the system looks different at large distances. There it resembles a stationary axisymmetric magnetically charged black hole.
arxiv-2605-22795: Balasubramanian studies finite-particle drifting models, which build samples in one step. A velocity field pushes particles from noise toward data. For one conservative velocity, built from smoothed score gaps, a joint-entropy identity bounds the error terms. Keeping bandwidth effects explicit yields a rate under uniform regularity. A second analysis covers the exact Laplace kernel, despite its kink.
arxiv-2605-22895: Peña presents a new exact solution to Einstein's equations that unifies the Kerr rotating black hole with Friedmann-Lemaitre-Robertson-Walker cosmology. The metric becomes Kerr-de Sitter in the right limit and tracks cosmic expansion both inside and outside the hole. It predicts a stationary mass, with the ergosphere and event horizon contracting against the expanding cosmic rest frame. The ergosphere fades as the universe expands, with no further dark-energy interaction with the hole's spin.
arxiv-2605-22995: Nemkova, Indukuri, and Charles survey 112 works on agentic AI for social good from 2015 to 2026. They find a moral-geographic asymmetry. Fully 73 percent specify no geographic context. The gap is widest where local context matters most. Health and ecological papers specify geography 37 to 40 percent of the time. Institutional and social-policy papers do so only 13 percent of the time. Only a quarter report any real-world deployment or small test. The authors propose a minimal reporting standard for accountability.
arxiv-2605-23095: Iyaniwura, Qiu, and Peng study escape of chiral Brownian particles, spinning agents that trace round paths like swimmers. In 1D they derive closed-form limit solutions in the high-spin regime for ranges with two exit edges, or one bouncing and one exit edge. This shows how escape time scales with spin speed. In 2D they solve by number escape from a disk with one or two exit arcs. Mean first passage time can vary up and down with spin, with lowest escape at middle spin.
arxiv-2605-23195: Yerrapati, Dixit, and Shukla link character degree sums to the number of twists tied to maps of a finite group. They build tools for inner maps and the symmetric group. They give a criterion for spotting groups with complex, non-real irreducible representations and probe the structural consequences of these results.
arxiv-2605-23395: Roketlishvili and colleagues argue the real block in compositional reasoning is not combining parts but the bumpy, non-convex shape of the learned energy landscape. Their framework, convex compositional energy minimization, builds each factor from an input-convex neural network and optimizes over a tight convex relaxation of the feasible set. Since sums keep convexity, a plain projected first-order method finds the global relaxed optimum. Two-stage training lets models learned on small problems transfer to larger ones with no retraining.
arxiv-2605-23595: Pham and colleagues introduce MetaEvaluator, a cheap, model-agnostic framework for fast label-free evaluation of unseen models on unlabeled data. Current routes lean on costly labels, repeated fine-tuning, or assumptions that fail on new models. It meta-learns over a pool of reference models to gain a good starting point for judging unseen models, spreading test cost and removing per-model retraining. Tests show stable, accurate estimates at far lower cost than conventional routes, enabling scalable bench work for new models.
arxiv-2605-23695: Adamov and colleagues test threat modeling with vulnerable test applications, tackling completeness, hard to judge without an oracle. Expert models and human baselines can omit items or disagree. The authors apply threat modeling to apps with a known flaw set, measuring related flaws found. They compare ThreMoLIA, an LLM-aided tool from their team, with the Microsoft tool across AzureGoat and Vulnerable Bank, using only architecture, data flow diagrams, and descriptions. ThreMoLIA covers more flaws in both systems, showing vulnerable test apps offer a benchmark beside expert checks.
arxiv-2605-24095: Gondhalekar, Möller, and Sánchez-Sáez present a self-taught mapping of star light curves with Multi-Time Attention. The model learns time-aware latent codes from patchy, partial curves without clean-up, filling in with small bias and scatter even for sparse curves. Its space tracks peak time, change, and colour, while skipping brightness and tally, and it splits supernova and AGN samples despite AGNs ruling. It also extends to unseen classes, though it misses RR Lyrae's roughly half-day pulse, far below its two-day limit.
arxiv-2605-24195: Brodjian, Hobley, and Perona recover seafloor shape from a single imaging-sonar picture, without training data, in under 30 seconds. Forward-looking sonar measures range and angle but flattens vertical structure, so three-dimensional recovery stays ambiguous, and current bathymetry methods demand many views, costly rigs, or large training sets. Their method uses differentiable sonar ray tracing and tunes a height field until it reproduces the target image, given a known tilt. On synthetic data it beats a supervised convolutional network under distribution shift and stays close on rough terrain.
arxiv-2605-24295: Ferrando and four co-authors present PACE-GGM, a data-adaptive private method for covariance estimation. It spends its privacy budget on top entries rather than perturbing all entries. The setting assumes separate bounds per variable, so single entries can be measured with less noise. Each round selects a poorly approximated entry, measures it with the Gaussian mechanism, then rebuilds a full matrix through a maximum-entropy objective, yielding a Gaussian graphical model. Tests on datasets show steady error improvements over the Gaussian mechanism and other baselines.
arxiv-2605-24395: Yu and five co-authors propose AvAtar, active alignment for optimal transport. Alignment underlies point-cloud registration, multimodal learning, and multi-network analysis, and transport methods depend on supervision. AvAtar scores each candidate by its gradient impact on the global result, tracing gradients back to every supervision of that candidate. Differentiating through transport is hard, so the team uses the adjoint-state method to turn the computation into a system. Encoding the global result through utility functions makes AvAtar fit general problems, and tests on three tasks show effectiveness.
arxiv-2605-24495: Yifan Zhang and colleagues present Elevator-LIO, a 2026 system that keeps a robot located while riding elevators between floors. It models robot motion and elevator motion apart inside a mode-dependent Kalman filter, and spots elevator entry and exit from laser ranging data. Stops trigger zero-velocity and zero-acceleration updates that curb vertical drift. Across 20 test runs covering 79 elevator rides, 17 runs ended with height error under one centimeter.
arxiv-2605-24595: Didier Sornette shows that exact criticality need not rule out stationarity for self-exciting Hawkes point processes, despite infinite mean activity. Stationarity in law hinges on whether the infinite-past Poisson-cluster construction stays locally finite. Mean intensity does not control it. For memory and fertility tails, he proves stationarity when the fertility exponent lies between one and two and memory exceeds it. In the finite-memory, finite-variance regime, the exact local-finiteness condition fails, but direct analysis gives the sharper condition theta above gamma minus one.
arxiv-2605-24795: Siddhartha Ganguly and co-authors study stochastic density control between Gaussian-mixture endpoints. The direct bridge between mixtures lacks a closed form, so they lift the problem to path space, tagging paths with labels. The problem then splits into Gaussian component bridges with explicit formulas for drift and cost. Discarding the label yields a projected law meeting endpoint constraints, yet its entropy differs from the lifted one by a nonnegative gap. That gap blocks identifying the lifted optimizer with the direct unlabeled bridge.
arxiv-2605-25195: Shuyuan Tu and colleagues introduce Baton, a framework that plans before generating video and audio together. Current open-source diffusion models lean on coarse text embeddings and lack a shared long-horizon plan, so sound and picture drift out of coordination. Baton's VA-Planner, a multimodal language model with dual alignment towers, drafts matching video and audio plan tokens pitched at keyframe level. Those tokens steer the diffusion backbone through cross-attention. A relative positional encoding maps tokens and latents into one shared frame.
arxiv-2605-25295: Emmanuel Akame Mfoumou and David Holcman speed up work on fastest arrivals, where the first of many diffusing bodies reaches a target. Tracking every path costs too much at large counts, so the pair builds arrival-time ranks from short-time asymptotics. A recursive inverse method makes the first several arrivals without following paths, starting from instant release. A version handles time-varying release, from rapid bursts to long injection. The method also yields mean fastest arrival times for reaction networks, rare-event spotting, and activation.
arxiv-2605-25395: Chung-Yiu Yau and colleagues stabilize Nesterov-style lookahead for deep learning optimization. Standard lookahead builds on short-horizon update signals, which are noisy and can point in unstable paths. The team argues speedup should follow low-frequency trajectory trends instead, and offers EMA-Nesterov, which replaces lookahead with an exponential moving average of parameter updates. That smoothed path acts as a filter while staying adaptive through shaped weighting. The method keeps an accelerated rate on convex problems and beats prior lookahead methods on language-model pretraining.
arxiv-2605-25595: Yuanye Liu and colleagues benchmark how close AI now stands to radiologists at staging liver fibrosis. Their LiFS set, drawn from the CARE-Liver challenge, holds 610 patients across centers and scanners with full gadoxetic-enhanced MRI sequences and pathology-confirmed labels. Nine methods from 96 registered teams were scored against in-cohort radiologist references. The best AI rivals a senior radiologist and tops a junior in some settings, while typical AI nears junior level; scanner variation, label imbalance, and sequence differences remain the main barriers.
arxiv-2605-26195: Yihe Fan and six colleagues introduce CyberEvolver (2026), a cybersecurity agent framework that rewrites its own scaffold from failed runs instead of fixed human designs. A four-layer architecture splits scaffold optimization into structured parts, a diagnosis step turns noisy logs into revision signals, and beam search keeps variants alive. On CTF, vulnerability, and penetration tasks with four open language models, it lifts the seed agent's success rate by thirteen point six percent on average. It also beats six human-built agents and two self-improvement methods from other fields.
arxiv-2605-26295: Eldiane Borges dos Santos Durães and João Batista Florindo's 2026 study adapts a self-supervised brain-signal model to classify sleep stages more efficiently. They simplify mulEEG by swapping its ResNet-50 encoder for a lighter ResNet-18 backbone. Trials show cutting training data volume beats simplifying the model on cost-benefit grounds, and concatenated time-series and spectrogram features with ResNet-18 top the original model's linear evaluations. The simplified extractor plus a linear support-vector classifier yields faster, more accurate sleep staging, with promise for other biological signals.
arxiv-2605-26595: Zedian Shao, Charles Fleming, and Teodora Baluta expose a stealthy poisoning trick for language models trained on unvetted text. Older attacks plant fixed trigger phrases that filters and monitors can catch. Their Cordyceps method instead links shared facts to attacker phrases, teaching the model a hidden code for smuggling orders. Across five models it beats heuristic prompt-injection tricks by about 40 percent in relative success. It keeps up to 93 percent success after backdoor defenses and 98 percent after prompt-injection defenses.
arxiv-2605-26695: András London studies a degree-preserving Builder-Chooser game. Each round, Builder grows a graph and Chooser keeps half its edges. Starting from triangle-free graphs, he pins down an exact one-round test for forcing a triangle. He adds exact thresholds on paths, exact forcing times on cycles, and the five-cycle as the first true two-round case. He also gives a one-round test for larger cliques, a sharp result for forcing a four-clique, general lower bounds on forcing times, and a conjectured amplifier lemma.
arxiv-2605-26795: Wang and Wei probe what chain-of-thought prompting actually contributes when rationales are held fixed at probe time. Shuffling rationale sentence order barely dents accuracy, and even shuffling the words leaves performance well above the no-rationale baseline. Restoring only short-range word order recovers most of the gain, with three-word windows already capturing much of it. The benefit, they argue, comes mainly from local word co-occurrence rather than global reasoning order.
arxiv-2605-26995: Lodro and four co-authors test dual-user Wi-Fi 7 transmission over the air when one access-point transmit chain is weakened. In a shielded enclosure, one radio sends a two-user waveform while another recovers both streams. The first user's stream stays clean across the tested range, while the second user's stream degrades and then collapses in a threshold-like way. Common signaling stays readable, showing the failure is stream-local, not packet-global. Swapping the second user's coding to LDPC delays collapse by about 5 decibels.
arxiv-2605-27195: Berkane and Majumder build a test for reading epidemic curves out of published charts. Their EpiCurveBench set holds 1000 real curve images from public health sources, and their new score aligns predicted and true series while tolerating small time shifts and gaps. The best of six tested systems reaches only 52.3% on that score, and the score spreads general systems far wider than older key-value scores do. Higher scores also track smaller errors in totals, peak timing, and peak size.
arxiv-2605-27295: Madhuri Shanbhogue and colleagues introduce Gemini Embedding 2, a single model that embeds video, audio, image, and text together. Trained with large-scale contrastive learning across stages and tasks, it leads embedding benchmarks for retrieval in many forms. Its zero-shot range spans fields as different as astronomy, bioscience, fine arts, and cooking, suiting search and recommendation uses.
arxiv-2605-27395: Julia Barnett, Kimon Kieslich, Natali Helberger, and Nicholas Diakopoulos build a method for ranking AI policy options against specific harms. It blends public evaluation of policies, expert cost estimates, and language-model judgments of harm reduction. A genetic algorithm search over policy combinations shows which balances of cost, public input, and mitigation are viable, giving deliberation a concrete starting point.
arxiv-2605-27495: Nithesh Chandher Karthikeyan, Jonas Unger, and Gabriel Eilertsen train diffusion models on synthetic images and test them as classifiers. Images made from DINOv2, DINOv3, and CLIP features beat class-prompted images by about 11 points on ImageNet100. Growing the synthetic set further beats a model trained on real data, and the generated images also improve standard data augmentation.
arxiv-2605-27595: Partho Ghose, Al Bashir, Prem Raj, and Azlan Zahid study hallucinations in multimodal models for agricultural imaging. In image-to-text tasks, zero-shot accuracy runs only 63 to 75 percent, while few-shot prompting lifts it to about 87 percent, though false detections and missed infections persist. In text-to-image generation, relaxed prompts yield up to 91 percent biologically inconsistent scenes, exposing deep reliability gaps.
arxiv-2605-27895: Ben Whewell, Nathan Gibson, and Ajeeta Khatiwada use reinforcement learning to choose energy groupings for neutron transport calculations, a task where accuracy hinges on grid design. Their agent starts from a fine grid and drops boundaries, guided by fast surrogate models instead of full simulations. On two classic test problems its grids beat commonly used groupings.
arxiv-2605-27995: Shi and colleagues test whether AI agents can juggle several tool-using tasks at once while waiting on slow tool replies. Their AsyncTool benchmark runs varied tasks concurrently with realistic delays, scoring coordination as well as completion. Delayed feedback degraded current agents markedly, with the best coordinators winning on task switching, dependency tracking, and state upkeep.
arxiv-2605-28295: Soeun Kim and Albert No diversify reasoning-model training by varying the very first token of each rollout. Since first-token probabilities concentrate sharply yet relate weakly to final correctness, sampling first tokens uniformly from the top candidates broadens explored paths cheaply. Their REFT method improved pass rates across eight models and beat rival diversification schemes at lowest rollout cost.
arxiv-2605-28395: Kushal Ramakrishna, Mani Lokamani, and Attila Cangi test MACE potentials for iron-nickel alloys against quantum data. A model trained on their own disordered-structure set matched energies, volumes, and elastic traits more steadily than broad foundation models. It also put pure iron's transition pressure nearer to experiment than rivals did. Yet all models wrongly raised that pressure as nickel rose, showing that magnetic collapse still eludes these potentials.
arxiv-2605-28495: Cheng Chen and five colleagues propose Janus-LoRA, a low-rank adaptation method that holds stability and plasticity in balance for continual learning. Standard LoRA updates keep breaking right angles to the zone holding past knowledge, bringing back clash. A gradient fix splits the factor updates and restores right angles against a quickly guessed history zone. A split margin loss then pushes new signals away from old ones, and benchmarks show a better stability-plasticity balance with state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2605-28595: Yongqiang Liu and Alexander Suciu introduce twisted homology jump loci, refining classical characteristic varieties with twisted rank-one local systems. Their main theorem bounds Bieri-Neumann-Strebel-Renz invariants above by tropicalizations of these loci. Twisting truly strengthens the bound: for a one-relator group it fixes the invariant exactly where the untwisted bound excludes only two ways. For compact orientable 3-manifolds with toroidal or empty boundary the twisted bound stays sharp, giving back fibered faces of the Thurston norm ball and a finer Kähler obstruction.
arxiv-2605-28995: Polytimi Anna Gkotsi, Andrii Zadaianchuk, and Mohammad Mahdi Derakhshani align vision-language latents to patch-level image features for 3D asset generation. Their diffusion-based GAP3D lets a frozen generator use a vision-language model as prompt encoder while keeping spatial structure. Training mainly on general image-text pairs avoids large-scale 3D data. The method shows zero-shot skill on multimodal prompts despite text-only training, though it currently favors high-level meaning over fine detail.
arxiv-2605-29095: Subhajit Ghosh and colleagues study the connected pieces of random polynomial lemniscates. They take polynomials whose roots are drawn at random, uniformly, from the unit disc, and look at the set where the polynomial's size is below one. The paper proves that the expected number of connected components grows like the square root of the degree, and it identifies the exact constant of that growth. The result gives a precise asymptotic picture of how these random shapes break into pieces as the degree rises.
arxiv-2605-29395: Jiachun Li, David Simchi-Levi, and Will Wei Sun rank language models from sparse comparisons. Global leaderboards hide task differences, while per-task ranking alone is unstable. They model the task-by-model ability matrix as low rank, sharing information across tasks. A max-norm estimator combines a convex start with alternating refinement. Cross-fitted debiased estimators yield valid intervals, and bootstrap calibration gives rank sets and top-K tests. Tests on synthetic data and Chatbot Arena show low-rank sharing beats independent estimation, when data are sparse.
arxiv-2605-29595: Lars Sjöström and eleven colleagues observe higher-order nonlinear charge transport up to the seventh harmonic in layered magnetic topological insulator MnBi2Te4. Second- and third-order effects are well studied, but higher orders stayed out of reach, leaving finer details unseen. Odd-order parts rule while even orders stay weak, and heat and field data tie the response closely to its phases. Scaling analysis and theory name quantum metric multipoles and nonlinear Drude conductivities as the tiny origins.
arxiv-2605-29695: Kjersti Engan and six colleagues propose FHRFormer, a masked model system for fetal heart rate filling and looking ahead. About ten percent of newborns need help starting to breathe, so fetal heart rate watch matters for catching odd patterns early. Sensor shifts during motion often cause gaps, and simple filling fails to preserve spectral shape. Their masked model coder rebuilds missing signals from local time and pitch parts, robust across gap lengths. The approach can serve research data for AI risk tools and later worn devices for earlier risk alerts.
arxiv-2605-29895: Tomoya Suzuguchi and Kohei Inayoshi investigate star-envelope collisions as transients in little red dots. These compact objects, found by the Webb Telescope, show broad Balmer lines, unlike ordinary active galaxies. One explanation embeds accreting supermassive black holes in dense envelopes of compact clusters, where stars scatter onto plunging orbits striking envelopes. Red supergiant collisions about a thousand radii wide, in envelopes as massive as black holes, promise bright events. In clusters under ten parsecs, such stars can collide near a third per year per object, detectable by surveys.
arxiv-2605-30395: Matthias Keulen, Timo Giese, Kolja Joeris and Jonathan Kollmer test how three grain samples settle under low gravity. Samples are fine basalt of 1-200 μm, coarse basalt of 2-5 mm, and glass beads of 750-1000 μm. Test gravities run from 150 to 1000 mm/s². Samples take more room at lower gravity, so they pack less dense. Fine basalt shifts most, up to about a fifth, then coarse basalt to about an eighth, and glass beads least to about four percent. Packing shifts hinge on grain size, roughness, and spread.
arxiv-2605-30595: Reid and colleagues ask which shape measures best reveal how galaxy clusters assembled, using the IllustrisTNG simulations. Present-day clusters, the largest and latest-formed structures, vary widely in late assembly, which may explain scatter in their scaling relations. They compare the most and least relaxed clusters on intrinsic, projected, and stellar traits. The brightness gap between top galaxies and lopsided stellar mass picks out recent versus old accretion well, even in projection. The team urges adding structural classification to studies of completeness and scaling.
arxiv-2605-30695: Singh and colleagues ask whether primitive-aware training gives robot policies a library of sub-skills for new tasks. Training two architectures on an assembly dataset, they compare flat trajectories with segmented episodes and specific prompts. Holding out six combinations, trained models reach 78 percent of fine-tuned ceiling performance with only three demonstrations, while flat-trained models need ten for the same level. Ablating the decodable subspace cuts few-shot transfer sharply while ablating a random subspace has no effect, showing these representations are causally necessary.
arxiv-2605-30995: Bertaglia and colleagues build a traceable language-model system and dashboard for EU consultations, too large to read by hand. The system reads PDF files and forms, extracts topics, and grounds every item in an exact quote. Applied to thousands of Digital Fairness Act submissions, it gave tens of thousands of topics backed by more quotes. Beyond preset topics, it found concerns a fixed taxonomy would miss, such as age verification, payment censorship, and digital ownership. The design rests on exact grounding, traceability, and transparency.
arxiv-2605-31295: Prokopiou and colleagues steer musical traits in a symbolic music model with no new training. Their method finds latent paths for pitch and duration in the Multitrack Music Transformer. It uses a mean-difference method. Steering strength tracks trait shift closely, the tests show. Steering two traits at once tangles them, so a dual method with Gram-Schmidt pulls them apart in geometric terms. The result is separate, exact control of traits even against strong autoregressive pull, with less clash and signal loss.
arxiv-2605-31495: Oschinski and colleagues test general-purpose language models as makers of constrained crystal compositions, using Elpasolite materials as a benchmark. Finding new inorganic materials is hard because the space of possible mixes is vast and full screening is costly, while task-specific generators need tedious training data first. With an iterative prompt-and-response loop, the models recover on average 96 percent of low-energy Elpasolites in the target region, beating prior task-specific models.
arxiv-2605-31595: Kim and team present C4G, a feed-forward 4D reconstruction system built on compact Gaussian query tokens. Existing methods predict 3D Gaussians pixel-wise per frame, suffering duplicated Gaussians and view-dependent biases. Each token aggregates features from the full temporal context, decoding a 3D Gaussian whose position shifts with the target timestamp, enabling coherent motion modelling. The system also lifts features into a 4D feature field supporting point tracking, with strong novel-view synthesis, far fewer Gaussians, and no camera poses required.

arxiv-2606-04095:
Rishanth Rajendhran and colleagues present POLARIS in 2026, a training recipe that teaches small language models to write long stories without losing quality or stopping early. Small open models usually fall short of requested length, or their writing decays as the story grows.

The recipe grades drafts with a large model's structured quality rubric and anchors each training group with a human-written story as a high-scoring reference. Applied to a nine-billion-parameter model on about fourteen hundred story pairs, it produced a writer rivaling much larger open models across five benchmarks. Blind human judges preferred it over its base model and rated it even with a model three times larger. Quality held even for stories triple the training length.
arxiv-2606-04295:
Mykhailo Klymenko and colleagues build a quantum simulation tool in 2026 for ultrafast optical spectroscopy of semiconductors. Such tests reveal how a material absorbs and boosts light on femtosecond scales.

Classical tools lean on the semiconductor Bloch equations. Their tool instead runs on digital quantum computers. It works on a grid of momenta and computes absorption and gain spectra. It handles broadening, heat-driven band filling, and thin-layer effects. For gallium arsenide it matched classical results in the noiseless limit. Real hardware noise acted like extra scattering and widened the spectra. No exponential speedup is claimed at this level. But the tool extends to the many-body regime, where classical methods blow up.
arxiv-2606-04395:
Feng proposes a way to learn models of controlled systems that must stay stable when outside forces push on them, in a 2026 arXiv paper. The method joins Koopman operator theory with neural differential equations. Koopman theory lifts nonlinear motion into a form where it acts linearly. The design has three stages. It separates parts tied to the setting, keeps the learned spectrum in the stable half-plane, and adds a bounded neural correction.

Feng proves that the fibers of the system stay invariant. He also gives a clear formula for the stability gain. An error bound ties accuracy to the approximation residual. Tests covered a pendulum, a cart-pole, a unicycle task, and a Franka robot arm. The method beat neural ODE and Koopman baselines on accuracy and robustness under matched disturbances. Stability penalties train together with prediction loss. So the guarantee is built into learning, not checked afterward.
arxiv-2606-05395:
Yunhao Yang and colleagues introduce VASO in this 2026 arXiv paper, a framework that makes self-evolving robot skills formally verifiable. Foundation models have collapsed the cost of writing reusable robot skills, but not the cost of trusting them. Existing skill-evolution loops refine skills using execution feedback, unit tests, rewards, or model self-critique.

In VASO each skill is a semantic contract with two coupled interfaces. A model checker first filters inconsistent contracts, then verifies skill-induced plans against global and local temporal specifications. When verification fails, the counterexample trace is translated into a gradient that updates the contract while the foundation model stays frozen. On Clearpath Jackal ground robot and PX4 quadcopter tasks, VASO reached 97.2 percent specification compliance using fewer than one hundred optimization samples, beating execution-feedback, prompt-optimization, and fine-tuning baselines.
arxiv-2606-05495:
Zhengxiong Li, Tsung-Wei Huang, and Umit Ogras present SET in this 2026 arXiv paper, a runtime framework that squeezes more performance out of GPU pipelines. Peak GPU throughput is often lost in the gaps between kernels, through host-device synchronization delays and scheduling overheads. Even CUDA Graphs, NVIDIA's mechanism for replaying captured kernel sequences, leave compute cores and copy engines underutilized.

SET attacks the gaps with two innovations. First, a multi-stream task-parallel pipeline programming model uses event chaining, where stream events trigger follow-on work without round trips to the host. Work stealing lets idle streams take tasks from busy ones. Second, a graph-based execution flow with per-stream buffers keeps memory safe while jobs run concurrently. On representative real-world workloads, SET delivered speedups between 1.15 and 1.44 times over state-of-the-art CUDA Graph baselines, and cut scheduling overheads by 18 to 54 percent.
arxiv-2606-05595:
Jing Zeng and colleagues built two fiber lasers that pulse in lockstep in a 2026 arXiv paper. One laser uses erbium fiber and the other ytterbium fiber, so their light differs in color. Many tools need two such pulse trains timed together. Active control gear can force the match, but it adds cost and fragility. The team locks the rates with light alone, through a shared loop device.

Cross-phase modulation inside the loop mirrors ties the two pulse rates together. The whole setup keeps one polarization, which adds stability. The lasers stayed locked even when their cavity lengths differed by over sixteen millimeters. That margin is at least ten times wider than earlier reports. The timing wobble between pulses measured just thirty-one femtoseconds, a span far shorter than a trillionth of a second scaled up. Such tight locking suits pump-probe imaging and Raman sensing.
arxiv-2606-06295:
Rishal Aggarwal and co-authors introduce Flux Matching in this 2026 arXiv paper on rare event simulation. Molecules and materials sit in stable states for ages, then jump to another state in a fleeting transition. Path sampling can generate many such jump trajectories, but reading the mechanism out of that tangle is hard. Committor functions, the usual tool, break down when the system is described with lossy summary variables.

Flux Matching learns two objects straight from the trajectories. One is a current velocity field whose streamlines trace the dominant reaction pathways. The other is a scalar potential that acts as a data driven reaction coordinate, a single dial tracking progress along the jump. Both are fitted with quadratic losses, much like flow matching in generative modeling, and neither needs the underlying dynamics. The potential's level sets then guide smarter sampling, and the method reproduced rate constants on molecular systems.
arxiv-2606-06595:
Wenkai Li and co-authors confirm a black hole caught wandering in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most giant black holes sit at galaxy centers, but mergers and gravitational wave recoils can exile some. A tidal disruption flare far from a nucleus is a prime clue. AT 2023mfm was flagged as a high confidence off nuclear candidate from optical surveys. The team pointed the Very Large Array radio telescope at it for high resolution imaging.

The six gigahertz images resolved two distinct radio sources. One sits at the host galaxy's nucleus. The other is offset by zero point six five one arcseconds, about one point zero six kiloparsecs, exactly matching the optical flare position from the Zwicky Transient Facility and Pan STARRS. That coincidence confirms AT 2023mfm as a genuine off nuclear disruption. The result shows radio imaging can validate such candidates and reveal hidden black holes drifting through their galaxies.
arxiv-2606-06695:
Turning messy photo based scans into a clean wireframe model of a building is a hard vision problem. Skvrna, Purkrabek, and Neumann describe the winning entry to the S23DR 2026 challenge in this 2026 arXiv paper. The inputs are sparse structure from motion points, fitted depth maps, and labeled image regions, and the output is a labeled three dimensional graph of roof corners and edges.

Their system treats the building corners as a set of sixty four tokens and cleans up noisy guesses with a flow matching transformer, guided by a compact encoding of the whole scene. A first pass sketches the coarse shape, a second pass zooms into the hull to refine it, and a small consensus step averages several runs to calm the randomness. The entry placed first on the private leaderboard, earning a hybrid structure score that rewards both correct corners and correct edges.
arxiv-2606-06795:
Human ears do more than collect sound: feedback from the brain constantly retunes them. Hanyu Meng and co-authors copy that trick in BiEAR, presented in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their system is a binaural front end, a two eared hearing stage for machines, meant to locate several speakers at once and judge how far away each one is.

A neural controller imitates the medial olivocochlear feedback pathway, adjusting how sharply each frequency channel in a filter bank responds while listening is under way. That lets the representation shift with changing room acoustics instead of staying frozen. In tests in echo free and real rooms, with speakers and rooms the system had never met, BiEAR located sounds more accurately and held up better than standard fixed front ends. Plots of its learned settings show it spotlighting whichever frequency bands carried the useful clues at each moment.
arxiv-2606-07095:
Mixing many metals into one alloy usually scrambles its electronic order, yet some properties refuse to fade. Kushwaha and co-authors test that resilience in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their material is an entropy stabilized Heusler alloy with cobalt plus four metals sharing one site. Titanium, vanadium, chromium, and iron each take a quarter share.

The alloy crystallized in the expected cubic structure. It behaved as a soft ferromagnet with a metallic response. Its saturation magnetization matched the classic Slater-Pauling prediction closely. The star result concerns the anomalous Hall effect, a sideways voltage from magnetism. Its conductivity reached about one hundred thirty four units on the paper's scale. That rivals the largest values in the tidy parent compounds. Theory ties the effect to Berry curvature of the electron bands. Disorder, in other words, did not wash the signal out. The authors call that survival the cocktail effect.
arxiv-2606-07595:
Wang, Tang, Qian, and Zhao benchmark a privacy failure: vision-language agents copying sensitive text from images into the tools they call, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agents reading screenshots and documents may write to memory, send messages, or invoke external services, and text in an image can cross that boundary unnoticed. Their VisualLeakBench provides 500 images across interface, chat, document, form, and dashboard scenes, with a 100 image subset tested on 4 production systems under note-taking and external-handoff workflows.

At baseline, strings propagated into tool arguments in 4 fifths of personal-data cases and even more of the unsafe-text cases. A defensive system prompt cut personal-data propagation but by suppressing tool use altogether, while unsafe text still crossed in half of cases. Propagation rates depended on tool type, with search-like tools resisting personal data best. The authors localize failures at the tool boundary, framing a measurable safety target.
arxiv-2606-07795:
Chmielewski, Draghici, Olteanu, and Haozhe Zhang show that the algebra beneath a database decides how cheaply it keeps query results fresh, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Incremental view maintenance updates stored query answers as rows arrive, instead of recomputing from scratch. Their setting is K-databases, where each fact carries a weight from a commutative semiring, arithmetic with addition and multiplication but no subtraction.

The key observation is that maintenance complexity depends fundamentally on which semiring supplies the weights. The team defines a class of conjunctive queries called p-hierarchical. For those they build a data structure whose update time per insert is governed by a width measure of the query, and which lists results with constant delay. For the nicest subclass, acyclic queries, updates take constant time on average. Matching lower bounds show non-p-hierarchical queries without self-joins cannot achieve that pairing of fast updates and fast listing.
arxiv-2606-07895:
Sung-Wook Lee, Kang, and Kuo redesign how robot action models generate movement, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Vision-language-action models turn camera input and instructions into robot actions, usually token by token. That autoregressive style is slow at inference and mostly ignores the temporal structure of action trajectories, how movements unfold over time.

Their model, TBD-VLA, partitions action sequences into temporal blocks. Inside each block, a masked diffusion process generates tokens in parallel, letting them depend on each other. Across blocks, generation stays autoregressive, preserving the order of the plan. The design also enables asynchronous execution: while the robot performs one chunk, the next is prepared by temporal in-painting, filling predicted motion into gaps. In simulation and real-world manipulation, TBD-VLA significantly outperformed earlier approaches. The authors present it as a scalable route to discrete action models that are fast and temporally aware.
arxiv-2606-08295:
Tianyuan Liang and co-authors teach language models to reason about tables while explaining themselves, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Tables store much of the world's structured information. Traditional predictors perform well on them but give no readable explanations, which decision makers need. Language models can produce predictions with explanations, yet they struggle with dataset-specific patterns such as feature distributions and interactions. Fine-tuning on labels alone improves accuracy at the cost of catastrophic forgetting, the loss of earlier abilities.

Their framework, TLRD, converts label-only tabular datasets into structured rationale supervision, training text that justifies each label. A high-capacity teacher model synthesizes a rationale corpus grounded in three complementary levels of evidence, starting with instance-level features of each row. Distilling rationales at three levels is meant to transfer the patterns that make tabular data hard, anchored in checkable evidence.
arxiv-2606-08795:
Torkko introduces PairWise Image Finder, an open-source tool for researchers who study how city streets change over time, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such studies compare street-level photographs of the same place taken years apart. The catch is that two photos from one spot rarely frame the scene identically, because camera position and angle shift between visits. Coordinates alone cannot confirm the views line up, so researchers waste effort checking pairs by hand.

The tool measures alignment directly from the images. It matches visual features between the pair and reports what share matched, how far apart they sit, and how much of the scene they cover. It also compares semantic masks, outlines that label roads, buildings, and sidewalks in each photo. A demonstration with longitudinal street photos shows that viewpoint differences alone can distort change measurements.
arxiv-2606-08895:
Park and Lee pin down how fast the best decision maker improves with more data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their setting is a Bayesian decision problem with finitely many states of the world and finitely many actions. Each observation narrows down the true state, and regret measures the loss from acting without certainty. Optimal regret was known to shrink exponentially as samples accumulate, but its exact rate was open.

The authors prove that optimal regret always decays exponentially and identify its exponent. The exponent is the minimum multivariate Chernoff information, a measure of how distinguishable states are, taken over the minimal incompatible subsets. A subset is incompatible when no single action is best for every state in it. Their formula recovers the classical exponents for symmetric hypothesis testing and for hypothesis exclusion. It gives the first exact exponent for list hypothesis testing, where the answer is a shortlist.
arxiv-2606-08995:
Fonseca and colleagues dissect which interactions create spin correlations, and relativity's effect on them, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In Moller scattering, electrons collide and their spins emerge correlated, entanglement generated by collision. The authors study a process with a witness particle that watches without interacting. At tree level in quantum electrodynamics, they use nonrelativistic scattering amplitudes to find the forces responsible.

Two couplings do the work: dipole-dipole coupling of magnetic moments, and current-dipole coupling between one electron's motion and the other's moment. The evidence is the change in von Neumann entropy, a measure of entanglement, for separable and three-particle W-states. Under Lorentz boosts, Wigner rotations twist the spins. Entropy stays invariant under the boost, but coherence appears in the density matrix at large rapidities. The final spins encode the scattering, and the framework lets the authors address an electron-positron to muon process.
arxiv-2606-09095:
Raj and colleagues combine two wireless ideas, antennas that slide along a waveguide and messages split in two, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Pinching antennas radiate from elements on a shared waveguide. The elements can move to shape propagation. Rate-splitting multiple access serves many users: each message becomes a common stream everyone decodes plus a private stream, a strong anti-interference tool. The authors maximize sum-rate fairly over antenna positions and power allocation.

The joint problem is non-convex, mixing discrete positions with continuous powers. They solve it by alternating optimization: greedy placement, then successive convex approximation for power. Results show the combined system improves sum-rate, user fairness, and bit error rate over systems without rate splitting. As user density grows and channels correlate, managing interference rather than enduring it becomes decisive. The paper gives an early design for that regime.
arxiv-2606-09295:
Yang and colleagues give an endangered script its voice back, building the first text-to-speech system for Nüshu, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Nüshu is a phonetic script created and used by women in Jiangyong County, Hunan, written for the local dialect syllable by syllable. Prior computing work digitized and recognized the characters but left the sound untouched. Recordings are scarce: mostly isolated syllables, not natural sentences.

The team built NüshuVoice, a sentence-level dataset aligning Unicode Nüshu text, phonetic transcriptions, Chinese translations, and archival recordings: 1,252 utterances totaling 98.8 minutes of audio. Their model, Nüshu-PitchVITS, conditions a VITS speech synthesizer on Nüshu's five-level pitch notation, using the script's tone marks as a prosodic guide. It beat strong baselines on spectral fidelity, pitch reconstruction, and human-rated intelligibility. Sentence audio assembled from archival syllables cannot capture natural rhythm, a limit the authors state plainly.
arxiv-2606-09495:
Dan Zlotnikov, Alex Lazarovich, and Ohad Ben-Shahar build a test that isolates how much object detectors lean on context in this 2026 arXiv paper. A detector may spot a boat partly because water sits around it, not from the boat itself.

Their benchmark, ContextShift, starts from COCO 2017 images and changes context while keeping each object intact. Objects are moved within scenes, or placed on new backgrounds, both made and real. A scale based on co-occurrence statistics grades how well each new pairing fits. Across many detector designs, missed objects rose sharply, by up to about two hundred twenty-seven percent. The total count of predictions fell by as much as forty-four percent. False alarms, by contrast, barely moved. The team links the drop to fewer valid candidates forming at all. Training with context-mixing augmentation beat plain training on both clean and altered images.
arxiv-2606-09595:
Ali Tourani and his co-authors ask what a movie recommender should actually look at in this 2026 arXiv paper. Films are long works of sound and image, yet most tests feed models trailers, stills, or plain facts. Full films hold the true viewing feel but are heavy to store and scan. Trailers pack in hype. Stills are cheap but thin.

Their benchmark, Popcorn, puts these sources on one footing. It aligns full-film and trailer vectors by title and adds still-image features from modern vision models, all tied to MovieLens ratings. One config file drives assembly, fusion, splits, and scoring. Tests showed still-image models give strong, scalable item evidence. But controlled swaps proved the sources are not interchangeable. The choice of source and fusion style moved ranking accuracy, coverage, diversity, and calibration. Popcorn turns a hidden design choice into one that can be measured.
arxiv-2606-09695:
Arnaud Lazarus, Georgi Gary Rozenman, and John Bush show that plain classical waves can wear a quantum-like trait in this 2026 arXiv paper. Quantized energy, energy that comes only in set steps, is a hallmark of quantum physics. Plain wave equations in plain media give smooth spectra instead. The team asked what kind of medium could force steps out of linear waves.

Their answer is a periodic medium tuned so waves barely pass at all. A discrete set of narrow pass bands is the exception. In that regime, standing waves settle into a discrete ladder of energies and pitches. The effect looks like quantum steps, yet the math stays fully linear. No extra rules, couplings, or noise fields are bolted on. Since the trick is general, labs could build it with spring, circuit, or light waves.
arxiv-2606-09995:
Capecci and his team ask whether the tricks that make quantum annealing faster also make it harder to simulate classically, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum computing. Quantum annealing solves hard search problems by slowly changing a system toward its lowest-energy state. Standard protocols are stoquastic, a property letting classical Monte Carlo methods simulate them well. Adding a non-stoquastic catalyst, active only mid-protocol, can ease hard transitions and block Monte Carlo simulation.

The team computes entanglement entropy and stabilizer Rényi entropy, two resources whose growth makes tensor network and stabilizer methods steeply costly, along the annealing path. They test a fully connected p-spin model and a local Ising model, tracking the energy gap as well. Numerics suggest the resource scaling is at least maintained in the deeply non-stoquastic regime, and sometimes greatly enhanced. Improved quantum speed thus coincides with a presence of quantum resources.
arxiv-2606-10095:
Panda asks whether language models playing personas can stand in for human judges of charts and graphs, in a 2026 arXiv paper on chart research. His framework, Literacy-Stratified LLM Evaluation, first builds personas grounded in chart literacy tests such as VLAT, which measure how well people read charts.

The framework is benchmarked against open human data from past studies of VLAT and BeauVIS, using the same stimuli and questions as the first studies. Literacy-stratified personas are compared with published human patterns and with default, non-persona model baselines. The analysis maps where personas converge with human response patterns and where they fail in set ways, by task type and test dimension. Panda proposes limits for safe use: persona simulation suits early design exploration as a complement to hands-on studies, not a replacement for human participants.
arxiv-2606-10195:
Panigrahi and his team publish a database on over one hundred forty-nine thousand inorganic crystals in a form designed for learning from scarce data, in a 2026 arXiv paper on materials science. Their graphlet histogram forms are computed from crystal structure alone, using domain knowledge rather than learned features. Seventy-nine curves describe each crystal across atomic sites, bonded pairs, and bond-angle triplets, extracted through screened Voronoi tessellation.

The database covers the Materials Project's inorganic crystals and ships with a complete technical specification of the scheme. An Earth Mover's Distance metric lets users compare crystals in this space. An open-source codebase generates graphlet histograms for arbitrary crystal structures, including ones measured in labs, and extends the database to new crystals or target traits. Because the features encode local shape and bonding that composition-only forms discard, the resource targets data-efficient, clear crystal prediction.
arxiv-2606-10295:
Hohmeier and his team build a nearest-neighbor classifier that compares graphs directly, without first mapping them into vectors, in a 2026 arXiv paper on statistical learning theory. The Gromov-Wasserstein distance compares metric measure spaces of different sizes and shapes, making it natural for network data with different node counts. They implement k-nearest neighbors classification using both distances and ask whether it is universally consistent, meaning its error approaches the best possible as data grows.

They prove universal consistency for the Gromov-Wasserstein classifier on finite metric measure spaces with uniform measure. For the fused distance, they prove the same on structured objects with feature maps into Euclidean space, covering node-attributed graphs as well. Consistency promises are rare for graph learning methods, which are usually checked only by tests, so the proofs give users theory-backed confidence in distance-based graph sorting.
arxiv-2606-10595:
Nguyen and a team of co-authors review federated learning from the data side in this 2026 arXiv survey, published in Neurocomputing. Federated learning trains one shared model across many clients, such as hospitals or phones, without moving their private data. This review argues that data decisions drive whether training converges smoothly. It breaks the catch-all label non-IID, meaning clients' data differ, into measurable traits and ranks each trait's influence on convergence as strong, medium, or light.

It also links laboratory data-splitting practices to the real phenomena they imitate, exposing artifacts those splits create. Finally, it analyses data-related attacks and defences by their effect on convergence, making the robustness trade-off explicit. A takeaway per concern gives practitioners guidance for predictable, stable training.
arxiv-2606-11095:
Yu and six co-authors combine two rival solver families in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum impurity models. These describe a few interacting orbitals, pockets where electrons repel each other, coupled to a calm bath. They sit at the heart of correlated materials research. Hamiltonian solvers discretize the bath and stall beyond a few sites, while diagrammatic solvers, summing interaction pictures order by order, suffer sign problems and slow convergence.

The hybrid adds a small auxiliary bath to the diagram side. That shrinks what remains until low-order perturbation theory, normally too crude, becomes highly accurate and converges fast. In a simple benchmark, its precision surpassed bold-line calculations by several orders of magnitude. For a two-orbital model with a severe sign problem, it converged at three orders of magnitude lower cost than competing methods. On a difficult realistic problem, convergence toward the unknown exact answer also accelerated sharply.
arxiv-2606-11295:
Semenzato, Wandelt, Liguori, and Raccanelli propose a learnable way to extract more cosmology from galaxy surveys in a 2026 arXiv paper. The power spectrum captures only two-point statistics, missing non-Gaussian signal in the matter density. Marked statistics fold some of that signal back to the two-point level by reweighting the field with nonlinear functions, marks. Their neural marking scheme generalizes marks while keeping them interpretable.

A contrastive objective aligns the learnable marked summaries with the cosmological parameters. The mark is a translation-equivariant scalar response built from spherical-harmonic-filtered, rotation-invariant channels, readable as morphological preferences. At the tested cutoff, the neural mark tightened constraints on sigma-8 by a factor of 2.9 and on Omega-m by a factor of 1.8 versus classical marks. It also cut parameter error by a factor of 1.45 across the prior. The learned latent geometry aligned with the two parameter directions, breaking their degeneracy.
arxiv-2606-11695:
Ha-Linh Nguyen leads a seven-author team repairing mislabelled datasets in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their framework, Canola, starts from the observation that correction works better when the pattern of label noise itself is estimated. Canola learns the underlying noise distribution, summarised in a transition matrix showing how true labels flip into wrong ones, and feeds that knowledge into training a noise-aware neural network.

The aware model down-weights unreliable supervision and focuses on trustworthy patterns. Correction then proceeds cautiously: labels are refined step by step in soft form, blending model predictions with observed labels so no wrong update locks in early.
