On six widely used image and text datasets, Canola beats the strongest label correction methods, cutting errors by relative margins between nineteen and fifty-two percent. Even simple classifiers on its corrected data beat complex noise-robust methods by up to sixty-seven percent.
arxiv-2606-11995:
Hossein Sabzian models farmers' crop choices as cultural evolution in this 2026 arXiv paper. Crops are treated as cultural traits: counties adopt mixes of crops, and those mixes can be tracked like inherited customs. He uses United States agricultural data from nineteen ninety-seven to twenty twenty-two, sampled at five-year intervals. From the data he derives twenty-six county-level cultural traits capturing crop diversity patterns.

Transitions between traits turn out probabilistic and strongly dependent on the trait a county currently holds, a weak memorylessness. The main driver of selection is environmental payoff bias: counties gravitate toward mixes that maximise yield in their environment. Over the quarter century a clear trend emerges toward more complex combinatorial traits with greater payoffs. The results match theoretical predictions in the cultural evolution literature. Sabzian presents the study as a strong empirical case that cultural evolution among farmers can be modelled quantitatively.
arxiv-2606-12195:
Yan and co-authors rebuild a video foundation model, a large pretrained system, as an agent that reasons in loops, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Most open video models answer in one pass, yet real video work needs attention, evidence gathering, and self-correction over long footage. Their framework, InternVideo3, runs on multimodal contextual reasoning: observations, instructions, reasoning steps, tool actions, and memory all live in one shared context updated over time.

A new attention design compresses cached memory states while keeping every token, making long rollouts affordable. Training proceeds in stages: continued pretraining, short-to-long video fine-tuning, rule-based reinforcement learning on checkable tasks, and distillation from stronger teachers. The model performs strongly among open video systems, with notable gains on long-horizon benchmarks Video-MME, MLVU, and EgoSchema. With retrieval and verification tools, it acts as a video agent checking its own evidence.
arxiv-2606-12295:
Martin and co-authors report a shared task's results on answering questions from video evidence, in this 2026 arXiv paper. In retrieval, systems rank videos from a collection of over 110,000 multilingual clips by relevance to a query about an event. In generation, systems write an article answering the query, grounded in the videos they found. Two teams entered retrieval; four entered generation.

Every retrieval system beat a baseline built from last year's winner. On the generation side, each team produced at least one article that human judges ranked best. One pattern dominated: text-based reasoning wins. The top retrieval system, C2F-RAG, indexes video summaries and captions rather than the video itself. Every generation system likewise converts videos to text before reasoning. Reranking mattered hugely, turning the weakest first-stage retriever competitive. Inference-time reasoning, the organizers conclude, beats the choice of first-stage model.
arxiv-2606-13495:
Verreault settles conjectures about operators on Hilbert spaces in this 2026 arXiv paper, building on work of Ransford. A contraction is an operator that never stretches vectors. Its negative powers, roughly its inverse iterates, can grow in norm even while the operator shrinks. Esterle and Ransford conjectured the following. If the spectrum, the operator's frequency content, lies in a thin subset of the unit circle, and the negative powers grow no faster than a prescribed rate, the contraction must be unitary. Unitary means perfectly norm-preserving in both directions.

Verreault proves this in full. Given any closed measure-zero subset of the circle, he constructs a growth sequence with the property. The new idea is a spikes-in-collars principle for positive subharmonic functions, a statement about where functions can spike. Results of this kind delineate the boundary between operators that contract and those that are reversible.
arxiv-2606-13995:
King and Flanigan argue coding agents are tested the wrong way: as solo workers, not partners in conversation. Real users guide assistants like GitHub Copilot through dialogue, yet benchmarks hand agents a complete problem statement. Their 2026 arXiv paper builds Dialogue-SWEBench, where agents resolve real software issues only by talking with a simulated user. The simulator is persona-grounded, and scoring also grades dialogue quality.

The gap exposed is large. Seventy-six percent of the GitHub issues are at least somewhat underspecified, and thirty-nine percent are too vague to define success. In real sessions users correct or reject agent output forty-four percent of the time, while agents ask clarifying questions in only one to two percent of cases. A new schema-guided agent beat strong baselines by three to fourteen percent. Better coding models did not always make better dialogue models: dialogue is a distinct, understudied skill.
arxiv-2606-14095:
Wu, Zurek, Wang, and Xie prove learning near-optimal policies for huge coupled decision systems needs only polynomially many samples. Weakly-coupled Markov decision processes link subsystems through shared constraints; restless bandits are the famous special case. A naive treatment faces a state space exponential in arm count. Their 2026 arXiv paper analyzes the plug-in approach: estimate an empirical model from data, then plan on it.

For fully heterogeneous systems they prove the first finite-sample PAC guarantee with complexity polynomial in the arm count, and an optimality gap shrinking like one over its square root. For homogeneous restless bandits, a smaller gap follows under mild assumptions. The core is a Lyapunov-based analysis: instead of the hard-to-control bias function of classical proofs, they build an explicit Lyapunov function and transfer drift between true and empirical models. A perturbation analysis of the LP relaxation supports the argument.
arxiv-2606-14195:
Ke, Thanasutives, and Kawahara teach a Kalman filter to retune its own noise model as the world changes. Filters with embedded latent transfer operators estimate hidden states in a kernel feature space, but fixed, simplified noise models fail on non-stationary processes. Their 2026 arXiv paper adds structured noise adaptation: a learned time-invariant noise model gives global robustness, while a dynamic part tracks time-varying dynamics.

The key device updates the Cholesky factors of the noise covariances, factors whose form guarantees the matrices stay symmetric and positive-definite throughout. The resulting filter, ELTO-AKF, significantly outperformed baselines on state estimation in noisy, time-varying settings, driven by filter residuals. As a denoiser for data-driven PDE discovery, it also reduced identification error for the viscous Burgers equation, whose shock waves are a hard test.
arxiv-2606-14295:
Liu and colleagues build a cyber range where frontier AI systems must run a whole intrusion, not just solve isolated puzzles. Existing benchmarks test fragments: capture-the-flag challenges, single-bug exploits. Real attacks chain service discovery, a foothold, internal reconnaissance, and spread across hosts. Their 2026 arXiv paper introduces AgentCyberRange, an open evaluation infrastructure with 110 vulnerabilities across fifteen real web applications and eight enterprise-like ranges holding 156 internal hosts.

Six frontier systems were evaluated under matched prompts and budgets. GPT-5.5 with Codex scored highest. It solved sixteen point one percent of web exploitation tasks and thirty-one point seven percent of post-exploitation tasks. With more concrete hints these rose to thirty-three and forty-six point three percent. Systems also found vulnerabilities outside the benchmark, including previously unknown ones in popular projects, and mutated payloads to bypass host defenses. Yet all were far from reliable end-to-end attackers.
arxiv-2606-14395:
Banerjee and Hasan propose REPOSE in a 2026 arXiv paper. The topic is security for real-time cyber-physical systems. These are linked control devices that must respond on strict deadlines. On busy edge devices, security checks run only when spare time appears. Under heavy load, none may run at all. Adding checks to every task instead slows the system badly.

REPOSE is a framework that judges at runtime whether security work still fits safely. It targets weakly-hard systems. Such systems can miss a bounded number of deadlines. It schedules checks both ahead of time and in reaction to current load. In tests at eighty percent load, its added cost was near zero. That was far below the cost seen under hard rules. A control case study shows the safety and security trade-off can be computed directly.
arxiv-2606-15395:
Utrobin and coauthor pin down the explosion parameters of supernova 2023ixf in a 2026 astrophysics paper. This type IIP supernova, the death of a red supergiant star, erupted in the nearby galaxy M101 and was observed in unusual detail. Yet published hydrodynamic models, which simulate the blast and match it to observations, disagreed widely on its energy and ejected mass. The authors rebuild the model using a broader set of observations.

The decisive addition is the maximum expansion speed measured early from shallow absorption lines, which breaks the degeneracy between energy and mass. Their best fit gives an energetic explosion throwing off about thirteen solar masses, from a star swollen to many hundreds of times the Sun's radius, wrapped in a thin circumstellar shell. The simulation also follows the event through to the emergence of hard X-rays, a first for this supernova, tightening confidence in the recovered parameters.
arxiv-2606-15595:
Armenta studies the Tamarkin-Tsygan calculus of a finite-dimensional algebra in 2026, a package pairing Hochschild homology and cohomology. He shows the Auslander-Reiten bimodule is central in the derived Picard group of the algebra. When the algebra has finite global dimension, that bimodule induces an automorphism of the whole package, and the pair is invariant under derived equivalence.

Computing it gives sharp answers on both sides. On homology, its matrix in the basis of idempotent traces has the Coxeter polynomial as its characteristic one. On cohomology it is simply the identity, because the left and right actions on the dual bimodule coincide. That yields a short proof that the Nakayama automorphism of a Frobenius algebra acts as the identity on Hochschild cohomology. The construction extends to smooth proper DG algebras, and it degenerates exactly on Calabi-Yau categories.
arxiv-2606-15695:
Nguyen and colleagues tackle federated class-incremental learning in 2026, where clients learn new classes over time without sharing raw data. The setting turns hostile when clients see different label subsets, advance through tasks at different stages, and supervise the same concepts unevenly. Standard defences replay synthetic inputs, but those replay signals turn fragile under exactly such conditions.

Their framework, PRO, drops the generator entirely. The server keeps compact class-level projected memories, summaries in feature space, and clients train on a balanced mix of current examples and old projected memories. A variant, PRO-MAX, adds neighbourhood-weighted memory alignment for stronger drift. Across image, text, and graph benchmarks, both improve retention and accuracy under heterogeneous streams, and stay competitive on homogeneous streams. Rivals with bigger replay budgets still degrade under supervision imbalance, and diagnostics tie larger mismatch to larger damage. Replay quality, not quantity, is the binding constraint.
arxiv-2606-15995:
Almeida and Auto-Neto show that the electron's anomalous magnetic dipole moment can regularise super-heavy atoms, in a 1990 preprint transcribed and deposited in 2026. For point nuclei, the Dirac equation's electron energy turns singular once the atomic number passes 137, a famous barrier. The standard rescue invokes the finite size of the nucleus, within strong-field quantum electrodynamics, which also predicts spontaneous positron production.

Working instead with a point nucleus, the authors add the anomalous magnetic moment through an effective theory. That suffices: wave functions stay regular and energies acceptable beyond Z of 137. The moment regularises the wave functions at the origin itself. The precise critical atomic number then depends on the anomalous magnetisation the electron attains in strong fields. They close by suggesting the combined effect of finite nuclear size and the anomalous moment be explored before any critical charge is pronounced final.
arxiv-2606-16195:
Zhao and Botana compute in 2026 how rare-earth doping changes a pressurized nickelate. Bilayer La3Ni2O7 superconducts under pressure, and samarium-doped crystals recently reached a transition near 96 kelvin at about 22 gigapascals. The authors use first-principles calculations to compare undoped material with La2RNi2O7, where R is praseodymium, neodymium, or samarium.

Chemical pressure shrinks the cell volume steadily from praseodymium to samarium doping, as expected. Under applied pressure, every compound shows a structural transition to tetragonal symmetry at roughly the point where superconductivity emerges. The transition brings flat dz2 bands to the Fermi level. The dominant planar hopping also grows as the rare-earth size shrinks across the series. Subtle differences separate doped from undoped cases, but the shared transition pattern is the central trend. The results tie superconductivity in this family to a specific structural change that doping can tune.
arxiv-2606-16295:
Tu and co-authors present VisualClaw in 2026, a self-evolving agent that answers questions about the physical world from streaming video. Vision-language models can serve as general interfaces, but dense video frames and long prompts make them slow and costly. VisualClaw attacks cost and rigidity with hybrid encoding and skill evolution.

A cascaded gate filters uninformative frames before upload, and a hot/cold scheme injects only the most useful skills into each prompt. When the agent fails, retrieved memories guide an offline evolver that updates the skill bank for future questions. Across four video-QA benchmarks and two model families, VisualClaw cuts per-question API cost by about 98 percent on average versus full-frame upload, per the report. It also improves accuracy in most settings without any weight updates. A companion benchmark, VisualClawArena, tests whether agents use visual evidence inside tool-using workspaces, a skill standard benchmarks miss.
arxiv-2606-16395:
The CBM Collaboration reports in 2026 on the physics program and detector progress of the Compressed Baryonic Matter experiment, now under construction at the FAIR facility in Darmstadt. CBM is a fixed-target experiment built to map the phase structure of strong-interaction matter at high net-baryon density and moderate temperature. Its heavy-ion collisions span center-of-mass energies of 2.7 to 4.9 GeV per nucleon pair. That territory may hold the critical endpoint of the quark-gluon plasma phase diagram.

Fast, radiation-hard detectors and a triggerless data system will record interaction rates up to 10 megahertz, with reconstruction and event selection done online. The setup targets rare probes unreachable in this energy range so far: multi-strange hadrons and their flow, high-order net-baryon cumulants, dileptons, and double-strange hypernuclei. Realistic tests of the detector design support the core targets, including collective flow and femtoscopy.
arxiv-2606-16695:
Asad Ali and colleagues build an exact theory of converting coherence into entanglement in a 2026 quantum information paper. Coherence means a quantum system holds several states at once in a fixed phase relation. Entanglement links two systems so neither can be described alone. Their systems are qunits, units with many levels rather than the two levels of a qubit.

A coherent input qunit is joined to a blank partner through a generalized controlled-shift operation, producing a maximally correlated pair. Using the partial transpose test, the authors derive an exact link between input coherence and output entanglement that holds at any dimension. They then apply three standard noise types after conversion. Phase damping shrinks entanglement by one uniform factor. Depolarizing noise kills it suddenly past thresholds that grow with dimension. Amplitude damping gives a smooth, uneven decay toward the ground state. The formulas serve as benchmarks for noisy entanglement generation.
arxiv-2606-16895:
Barberán and Miana study groups generated by fractional powers of operators in a 2026 analysis paper. Starting from a power-bounded operator on a Banach space, a fractional power of a related operator generates transformations defined for all complex times. Expanding that family in powers of the original operator requires a special polynomial family.

The authors give a self-contained account of those polynomials, whose coefficients come from a recurrence. Scaled by factorials, they form a Sheffer family, a class with rich combinatorial structure. For the relevant parameter range, their values form an absolutely summable sequence, so the expansion converges in the strong sense needed. The family also ties closely to Lévy density functions from probability. Special parameter values are worked out, with uses for fractional powers in a sequence algebra, product operators and Cesàro means, the averaging method behind many summation techniques.
arxiv-2606-16995:
Gavenski and colleagues pair a small language model planner with a reactive policy in a 2026 reinforcement learning paper. Trained policies act fast but do not deliberate, so they degrade in unfamiliar settings. Deliberation at every step, though, is slow and can dither.

Their architecture, PACT, keeps the reactive policy in charge by default. A small language model is called asynchronously to draft candidate action plans. Each plan is checked in simulation for safety, feasibility and completeness. Once a plan passes, the system commits: the plan runs directly, bypassing the policy, with no retraining or modification of it. Tests use three FrozenLake gridworld setups of rising difficulty, a classic slippery navigation task. PACT beats all baselines while its planner backbone is only a two-billion-parameter model. The commitment step, the authors argue, gives robustness under randomness that step-by-step plan following cannot match.
arxiv-2606-17595:
Kumar and Khan present a 2026 arXiv paper on where defects sit inside active nematic turbulence, the swirling state of cell-like materials that generate their own stress. Collective stress shapes how cell layers migrate together, and measuring stress in living layers is easier than mapping every cell's shape. Using a generic active nematics model, the authors compare the direction of greatest stress with the local nematic orientation across a range of activity strengths and signs.

The top stress direction sits across the director for extensile activity and along it for contractile activity. In the turbulent regime, one special line drawn from the anisotropic stress parts collects every defect, both nematic and stress defects alike. That line stays put when activity grows, shrinks, or flips sign between the two kinds. The result offers a stress-based route to reading the mechanics of confluent cell layers.
arxiv-2606-18095:
Pimentel examines how a two-field version of Higgs inflation can leave a strong statistical fingerprint on the infant universe, in a 2026 cosmology paper. The model couples the Higgs field with an R-squared gravity term, and its inflationary path runs through a curved field space. When that path turns sharply for a while, fluctuations sideways to the motion can feed into the main curvature signal.

Computing the full three-point statistics without slow-roll shortcuts, Pimentel follows both curvature and isocurvature ripples past the horizon. For a benchmark coupling choice, the transient turn produces a large local non-Gaussian signal, near minus eighteen in the standard measure. Strengthening the Higgs coupling tames the turn, and the model slides back to the single-field prediction where the signal nearly vanishes. Current microwave limits thus become a sharp probe of the coupling.
arxiv-2606-18195:
Luo and colleagues adapt self-distillation to diffusion language models, whose writing process breaks the usual recipe, in a 2026 paper. On-policy self-distillation lets a model learn from a privileged version of itself, and it works well for ordinary autoregressive models that write left to right. Diffusion models generate in arbitrary order through denoising steps, so prefix-based teaching and token-level supervision clash with their nature.

Their d-OPSD framework rebuilds both pieces. The self-teacher is conditioned on the model's own finished answer as a suffix, so the student learns from its self-generated future rather than from leaked prefixes. Supervision moves from tokens to whole denoising steps, matching how the model actually works. Across four reasoning benchmarks the method beat reinforcement and fine-tuning baselines while needing roughly a tenth of the optimization steps of the reinforcement rival.
arxiv-2606-18595:
Wang, Zhang, and Wang model the making of two charmonium particles in a 2026 particle physics paper. The collisions are ultra-peripheral, at the Large Hadron Collider. There, lead or proton beams pass close but do not touch, and interact through their photon fields. The particles are J/psi and its excited sibling psi(2S). Both are key probes, since a two-gluon exchange model sets their photoproduction.

The authors fed that model's cross sections into STARlight. They worked out results for lead-lead and proton-lead collisions at collider energies. Raw predictions overshot the measured distributions in lead-lead collisions. So they added a phenomenological suppression factor. Corrected results then matched the data within uncertainties, and the double-peaked shape of the rapidity distribution. No such suppression showed up in proton-lead collisions, matching the asymmetric photon fluxes there. The work checks the modeling chain for future charmonium measurements.
arxiv-2606-18695:
Shanmugasundaram and Saha analyze a model of a fish-mussel system driven by chemotaxis, in a 2026 paper on partial differential equations in aquaculture ecology. Fish farms suffer more and more nutrient enrichment and worse water quality. Mussels, as filter feeders that clear organic matter, are a steadying part. To capture the coupled dynamics takes a system of reaction-diffusion-chemotaxis equations, not plain differential models.

For the coupled system under homogeneous Neumann boundary conditions, the authors prove global existence of classical solutions. They use semigroup methods with a priori estimates. They also examine how solutions can instead blow up in a 3D domain. To support the theory, they develop a finite element method for the system. They run mesh convergence studies checking the scheme's accuracy and stability. And they present simulations that display the foreseen blow-up inside the domain.
arxiv-2606-18795:
Safarpoor Dehkordi, Shirzadi, and Zehmakan test how easily opinion polarization can be made inside a fake social network of language-model agents. The work is a 2026 computational social science paper. Classical opinion-dynamics models rely on simple number updates. They cannot capture how real talk shifts views. Language-model sims, though, let diverse personas post, read, and shift opinions in context-based ways.

In their framework, agents with personas exchange posts and update opinions. The headline result is a weak point. Even an attacker with a limited manipulation budget raised polarization and extremization a lot. The effect hinged on which manipulators were chosen, their staying power, and number. Two defense kinds were tested: reactive counter-messaging by users, and proactive moves raising resistance. Both reduced the attack's impact. But neither brought the network back to its baseline polarization. That hints platforms cannot police their way out of such manipulation.
arxiv-2606-18895:
Breloer and colleagues study symmetric ideals in 2026. They work in a ring of polynomials with countably many variables, far more than in the usual finite case. An ideal is symmetric when swapping variables leaves it the same. That rule creates finite-like behavior even in this vast ring. The authors define two series that count key data degree by degree for such ideals.

One series tracks the invariant part in finite cuts of the ring. The other tracks how often each key symmetry type shows up at each degree. The main result says the first series is a rational function under a mild condition on the ideal. The same nice form then holds for the second series for every type. Proofs use the monomial build of the polynomials, plus a known inversion step. A rational form turns an endless count into a finite, usable description.
arxiv-2606-19095:
Bastian and colleagues classify Schur rings over cyclic groups whose Terwilliger algebras are almost commutative in a 2026 algebra paper. Terwilliger algebras are built from association schemes, and almost commutativity is a strong structural property with several known equivalent conditions. The paper asks which Schur rings over a finite cyclic group give rise to that property, starting with orbit Schur rings formed from automorphism subgroups.

For orbit rings, the subgroup must be trivial or the whole automorphism group when the group has prime power order, with one extra option for odd prime powers. For groups of non-prime-power order, only the trivial subgroup works. The authors then give a condition for wedge products of Schur rings to keep the property. Combining both steps, they determine exactly which Schur rings over a cyclic group produce an almost commutative Terwilliger algebra. The full classification closes a structural question.
arxiv-2606-19295:
Mondal and colleagues present a new method in 2026 for classifying eclipsing binary stars with Kepler data and deep learning. The goal is to sort binaries into contact, detached, and semi-detached types automatically. Phase-folded light curves are turned into chi-square versus box size plots by comparing flux to the median, and each class shows a distinct pattern in those plots. A damped sinusoidal model of the pattern gives a first feature, its period.

That feature alone reaches solid overall accuracy. A convolutional neural network trained on the plots improves total accuracy further, though semi-detached systems remain challenging. Simulated light curves from the PHOEBE modeling code are added to handle irregular signatures. With simulations included, contact and detached binaries are distinguished with very high accuracy. The chi-square shapes also correlate strongly with orbital period. Some systems vary by quarter, flagged by a temporal measure.
arxiv-2606-19495:
Shariq Farooq Bhat, Niloy Mitra, and Kalyan Sunkavalli present LooseControlVideo in 2026, a tool for steering generated video. Directors of synthetic scenes need control over where objects sit and move, not just a text prompt. Older depth-based tools demand dense, frame-exact guides that take long to draw for bending or soft objects.

Bhat and colleagues let users place sparse tilted 3D boxes, like stage blocking notes for actors. A Wan 2.2 video model, fine-tuned with a new DNOCS code for size, tilt, and overlap order, fills in motion and contact. Users can tweak one jump path or add one contact without redoing the whole scene. On nuScenes, HOI data, and BEHAVE tests, path error falls by 1.2 to 3 times against rival tools. Occlusion accuracy also rises, making rough boxes a strong guide for complex scenes.
arxiv-2606-19595:
Ahmad Salimi and five colleagues release IHBench in 2026, a benchmark for voice agents interrupted mid-task. Voice agents run structured workflows in service calls, health scheduling, and account management. Users cut in often, and agents must resume at the right step afterwards.

Older benchmarks grade interruption timing, like barge-in detection and turn taking. IHBench instead grades recovery: resuming correctly, answering the interjection, and skipping content already heard. Six interruption types strike at controlled points across ten enterprise domains. Each case scores task fulfilment and recovery quality under its own rubric. Twenty-seven audio-language model setups from OpenAI, Google, and open sources face the tests. Closed models prove hardier, degrading about 3.3 times more slowly as chats lengthen. Open models lose ground on fulfilment, recovery, and modality alike. A human study checks the automated judge against human annotators.
arxiv-2606-19695:
Jayanth Bhargav, Mahsa Ghasemi, and Shreyas Sundaram jointly plan sensor siting and aiming in 2026. A defender must place sensors and schedule their orientations to catch an intruder crossing guarded ground. Missed detection risk is the quantity to minimise.

The problem splits into a placement meta-problem and an orientation scheduling subproblem. For fixed siting, aiming becomes a two-player zero-sum game between guard and intruder. Standard linear programming chokes on the defender's combinatorial strategy space. An iterative solver exploits the payoff shape and provably reaches the Nash equilibrium. That game value then scores layouts as a weakly submodular utility. A greedy placement algorithm carries near-optimality guarantees on that score. Simulations show near-optimal detection at far lower compute than baselines. Game theory and submodular scoring meet in one framework here for the first time.
arxiv-2606-19795:
Jiawei Liu and five colleagues survey agentic chip design tools through the lens of handoffs in 2026. Electronic design automation moves artifacts, scripts, and decisions across many stages and teams. Each transfer carries needs that stage-local checks may not capture.

Language model agents now call design tools directly and pass state between sessions. Their outputs shape downstream engineering choices, so each handoff must satisfy a contract. A valid handoff meets the next consumer's acceptance terms and carries context, evidence, and provenance. Eighty-two systems sort into three classes by boundary crossed. Stage-Bound systems secure one stage; Flow-Bound systems hold workflow state across tools and sessions. Organization-Bound systems guard grounding and authority across knowledge borders. A five-layer agent communication protocol caps the survey. Shared vocabulary, the authors hope, will make agentic design flows trustworthy.
arxiv-2606-20095:
Lucas von Chamier, Jan Philipp Albrecht, and Dagmar Kainmueller investigate seams that appear when huge scientific images are generated in patches and stitched together. Their 2026 paper uses CycleGAN models trained on cryo-electron microscopy data, where samples are too large for one pass through a network. Misaligned patch borders leave stitching artifacts. Such seams are known to trouble segmentation, but their effect on generative style transfer had barely been measured.

The team compared three stitching strategies and two patch shapes, 2D tiles against 3D blocks, scoring visual quality and downstream mitochondria segmentation. Standard FID scores missed subtle seams that still hurt segmentation badly. Artifact-free 3D models edged out 2D ones downstream, though barely enough to justify their cost. Meanwhile 2D training proved steadier thanks to larger batches. Averaging predictions from three directions rescued poor volumes but added nothing to good ones, so perceptual scores alone cannot certify image translation.
arxiv-2606-21595:
Zoltan Varga argues in 2026 that measuring a brand's visibility in AI answers by raw mention counts is misleading, because each organization suffers its own pattern of AI errors. Obscure entities vanish from answers when their structured data and knowledge graph presence are thin. Famous brands face the opposite trap, a Brand Hallucination Paradox: model familiarity invites plausible but wrong completions, so visibility comes with fabricated detail.

Varga proposes Per-Entity Bias Mapping, a ten-part check separating raw from verified mentions across retrieval, hallucination, citation fidelity, and update lag. A study of one hundred Hungarian business entities over 1,400 probe runs found top-tier brands carried 52.69 percent fabricated citations, against 37.87 percent for low-salience ones. Regulatory-style questions pushed fabrication higher still, a framing effect he flags as a passive attack surface.
arxiv-2606-21795:
Viswanathan and colleagues examine reward models in 2026, the learned scorers that grade language model answers when no automatic checker exists. Unlike verifiable rewards, which give a simple right or wrong, reward models output continuous scores that seem to capture fine quality differences. The paper argues this apparent strength is really a weakness, because the scorers are oversensitive to trivial variation.

The authors show that even a seemingly perfect reward model can assign different scores to equally good responses, and that this noise can steer reinforcement learning toward worse policies. They propose judging reward models by discriminative ability and by specificity, its opposite. Their fix groups scores into discrete clusters using Monte Carlo dropout, a training-free trick that needs no new model. In controlled and natural experiments, discretized rewards led to less reward hacking and better final policies than the original continuous scores.
arxiv-2606-21995:
Yang and colleagues assess, in 2026, whether a rare weak process, producing a single Lambda hyperon when a lepton scatters off a proton, could ever be observed at electron-positron colliders. The leptons would not come from the main beams directly. Instead, resonances created in the collisions decay into leptons that then strike protons in the surrounding detector material, with a neutrino and a Lambda hyperon emerging from the collision.

The team computed differential and total cross sections using baryonic transition form factors, the functions encoding the proton's internal response, parameterized in two frameworks: QCD sum rules and lattice QCD. Cross sections grow with collision energy but depend heavily on which form factor set is chosen, leaving large theoretical uncertainty. The study stresses the experimental challenge of seeing this process at such colliders and the need for better form factor determinations. An anomalous observation, they note, could signal new physics.
arxiv-2606-22195:
Hua and colleagues propose, in 2026, a vision-assisted framework that resolves target association in OFDM-based integrated sensing and communication systems. Such systems sense their surroundings with the same waveform they communicate on, reading targets from peaks in a delay-Doppler map. The map does not say which peak came from which physical target, and two targets in one resolution cell cannot be separated.

Their framework transmits a street-view image over the sensing waveform using deep joint source-channel coding. The receiver reconstructs the image, detects objects with a fine-tuned YOLOv5, and fuses each target's box and class with the delay-Doppler map and geometry in a learned network. On a Blender-rendered vehicular testbed, localization error is sixteen centimetres. Removing the visual modality degrades localization sixty-fold in ablation tests.
arxiv-2606-22495:
Liang Ding and Xintong Wang argue a position on the future of AI agents in this 2026 paper. Long chains of agent actions fail fast in environments built for human tolerance, because each imperfect step compounds the error. Debates about scaling from general to super intelligence usually blame compute or data limits instead.

The authors claim environment determinism, how reliably an environment responds to actions, is a separate binding constraint. They support the claim with three formal results, covering chain-task success, reward hacking under imperfect verifiers, and conditions for skill evolution. The framework becomes practical through a Supply Certainty Index over five measurable properties and a five-level maturity model for adoption. Five open questions come with explicit null results that would force the authors to retract their position. They also answer three rival views: that simulation transfer suffices, that alignment suffices, and that AI is just a normal technology.
arxiv-2606-22695:
Yisi S. Zhang and Daniel Y. Takahashi map information flow across the whole brain in this 2026 paper, published in NeuroImage. Knowing which brain regions drive which others is central to neuroscience. Yet recordings sample only fragments at a time, across sessions, animals, and labs, with no shared clock, while standard methods demand all regions at once.

Their framework, SPIDER, stitches power-spectrum estimates from overlapping channel subsets into one spectral matrix. Factorization and partial directed coherence then recover interactions at each frequency, with no alignment needed. A completion step fills in region pairs never recorded together, with consistency guarantees. Validated on simulations, calcium imaging, and Neuropixels data, SPIDER recovered flow among 50 areas from 43 sessions in 12 laboratories. Its strongest links matched known anatomy closely. Whole-brain flow proved recurrent, except in the theta band, where a feedforward hierarchy rises from the hippocampus; human data showed the same pattern.
arxiv-2606-22995:
Yunan Wang and colleagues improve reinforcement learning for long agent tasks in a 2026 paper. Reinforcement learning trains a model from rewards, but in long tasks the reward often arrives only at the very end. Recent methods score each step separately, yet they still treat each attempt as a lone straight path. That view wastes a key fact. Different attempts often pass through the same states, so the attempts form a web, not separate lines. The team calls its method G2PO, for group-graph policy optimization.

Wang and colleagues merge matching observations across attempts into one state-transition graph. Shared states let them average value estimates over many visits, cutting noise and bias. They also score actions as edges between states rather than as steps in one path. Local errors are then standardized across the whole graph. Helpful transitions stand out more clearly, which sharpens credit assignment over long horizons.
arxiv-2606-23195:
Zewen Liu names and measures a failure called memory contagion in a 2026 paper on language model agents. Agents increasingly store past experiences in long-term memory to stay coherent across sessions. Liu asks what happens when the experiences themselves were shaped by a biased evaluator. Two bias types are tested: a preference for longer answers and a deference to authority. Biased trajectories get stored and later retrieved by fresh agents, carrying the bias forward in time even when memory consolidation works perfectly.

Liu demonstrates the effect across four experimental phases. With perfect consolidation, length bias and authority bias both showed contagion in the oracle test. Under controlled runs, length bias spread robustly across seeds. Authority bias failed to spread at all, so contagion depends on bias type. Bias appeared even when only a fifth of the stored experiences were contaminated.
arxiv-2606-23395:
Haitham Al-Shami and colleagues hunt semantic faults in systems engineering models in a 2026 paper. Model-based systems engineering uses formal languages like SysML v2 to describe complex systems. Compilers catch syntax errors in such models easily. Semantic faults are sneakier: the model parses fine, yet an engineering connection it describes is physically meaningless. Those errors surface late as costly integration failures. The team presents a framework for finding them that keeps a human in the loop, pairing a large language model with a knowledge graph of domain rules.

Al-Shami and colleagues exploit SysML v2's textual syntax, which enables compiler-like structural checks as a first pass. The knowledge graph then supplies the domain rules the model needs to judge whether relationships make physical sense. Flagged faults go to human engineers for confirmation rather than automatic fixes.
arxiv-2606-23695:
Or measures how often retrieval augmented language models ignore the documents they are given and fall back on memory, in a 2026 paper on AI evaluation. Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG, feeds a model external documents so answers should come from the text, not from pretraining. Standard scoring cannot tell which source an answer really used. A model can answer correctly by recall while appearing to read, a blind spot the author calls epistemic blindness.

The proposed metric, Normalized Context Utilization, uses token log probabilities under oracle and adversarial conditions to quantify true context use. Tests span models up to seventy two billion parameters plus a commercial API. For strict factual extraction, small models match or beat large ones, defying the usual scaling story. The commercial system overrode explicit evidence in nearly half of adversarial conflicts, and its confidence often collapsed when contradicted, a failure named prior dominance.
arxiv-2606-23895:
Rakitskii, Denisov, and Averkiev predict how a magnetic field reveals the fingerprints of borrowed spin physics in graphene layered on another crystal, in a 2026 paper on condensed matter theory. Pristine graphene barely couples electron spin to motion. Laying it on a transition metal dichalcogenide lends it strong spin orbit coupling by proximity. The team studies cyclotron resonance in this heterobilayer: light absorption when electrons circle in a quantizing magnetic field, hopping between Landau levels.

They compute the spin textured wave functions of those levels and the absorption spectrum. Proximity induced interactions split each main peak into a fine double peak. Extra spin flip transitions appear too, with selection rules the authors identify. The theory gives labs clear signatures to look for when checking proximity spin effects.
arxiv-2606-23995:
Maidment and colleagues stabilize game playing AI that learns by playing itself, by anchoring it to a moving average of its own recent self, in a 2026 paper on reinforcement learning. In two player zero sum games with hidden information, regularized policy gradient methods trained in self play now rival specialized game solvers. The usual anchor is the uniform policy, but that wastes effort pulling the agent toward hopeless strategies. EMAgnet instead regularizes toward an exponential moving average of the agent's own past parameters.

The target trails the current strategy, pointing at competent recent play rather than uniform randomness. Across standard and modified benchmarks, EMAgnet reaches lower exploitability than PPO self play with uniform anchoring in the majority of environments. Gains are consistent where strictly dominated strategies abound, exactly where uniform regularization wastes the most.
arxiv-2606-24195:
Novak and Pillichshammer map where high-dimensional approximation collapses under its own weight. Discrepancy measures how far from even a point set fills space. A duality with numerical integration makes worst-case integration error equal the corresponding discrepancy. Their 2026 study asks, for Lp discrepancies of several shapes, whether error can fall like a power law as dimension grows. Or whether cost blows up exponentially: the curse of dimensionality.

A broad lower-bound method for non-negative linear rules establishes exponential information complexity in the dimension. It works under broad tensor-product assumptions on the function space, settling the curse for the discrepancies it covers. Fresh results extend the duality and the curse to the periodic Lp discrepancy. Novak and Pillichshammer sum up the landscape in one table of what is known, marking the open questions plainly.
arxiv-2606-24495:
Mondal and Choudhuri trace a generalised black hole entropy back to a gravity action. This entropy deforms the standard horizon entropy, with an exponent index and a scaling parameter. What gravity theory actually produces it? Their 2026 letter applies the Iyer-Wald approach, the covariant method deriving entropy from a theory's Lagrangian, inside a modified f(R) gravity scenario with constant curvature solutions.

The entropy is rebuilt from an extended Lagrangian: a power of the curvature scalar slightly above one. The departure from Einstein's linear choice is set by the entropy's exponent index. Tiny departures from general relativity thus generate the whole family. Mondal and Choudhuri close by discussing the cosmos. They ask whether the construction might relieve the thermal instability of Schwarzschild black holes, whose negative heat capacity has troubled gravity thermodynamics for decades.
arxiv-2606-24795:
Juncai He and Zitong Tian develop the function space theory behind shallow neural networks with power ReLU activations. Their central object is a space of functions on a bounded domain that can be written as ridge integrals. The question is which familiar smoothness spaces this construction reproduces. In the Hilbert case, the exponent two case, Fourier analysis gives an exact answer.

There the space equals a critical Sobolev space, with smoothness set by the activation power and the dimension. For other exponents the identity softens into a sandwich: the space sits between two Sobolev spaces. The gap on each side is exactly the known loss of the Radon transform as a Fourier integral operator. He and Tian then discretise the integral with a deterministic skeleton plus uniform sampling. The result is high probability approximation rates, including the optimal Hilbert rate for linearised networks.
arxiv-2606-25195:
AI code generators are now routine, but how secure is the code they write? Rupam Patir and three colleagues systematize the field in this SoK, organising work on prompting, fine tuning, reinforcement learning methods, and agentic workflows for secure code generation.

Their framework measures three levels. First, whether a model understands secure coding principles in natural language. Second, whether it acts on them while generating code. Third, the gap between the two. It runs across models and coding agents, on benchmarks from single functions to full web applications. Understanding strongly predicts code level outcomes, including correctness and joint functional security. Yet the gaps stay large: models often recognise the right principle and still fail to turn it into secure, working code. Principle guided generation and evaluation are the proposed way forward.
arxiv-2606-25395:
Operator theory on Hilbert spaces asks how the subspaces an operator leaves untouched are built. Dimple Saini and Azad Rohilla revisit two classical landmarks in 2026. One is the Wold decomposition, which splits an isometry into a shift part and a unitary part. The other is Beurling's theorem, which describes every invariant subspace of a Hardy space through one inner function. Their setting is far broader, covering covariant representations of C star correspondences under operator inequalities.

Working from the inequalities alone, the pair first proves a Wold type decomposition for such representations. On top of it they prove a Beurling type theorem. Every nonzero invariant subspace is pinned down uniquely by its wandering subspace. That is the part which generates the rest under repeated action. The results gather several earlier extensions for single operators into one unified framework.
arxiv-2606-25895:
Nikita Gaevoy works in proof complexity, the study of how long a formal proof must be, on a system called Resolution with symmetries. Resolution is a basic proof method for logic formulas, and symmetry rules let a proof reuse a mirrored step for free. Earlier versions allowed symmetries of any size, which is powerful but unrealistic, since finding huge symmetries is computationally out of reach.

Gaevoy defines small symmetries, which may only rearrange a limited number of variables at once, and studies the resulting proof systems. Both the local and global variants form strict hierarchies as the allowed size grows, with exponential separations between levels. Even the lowest levels beat plain Resolution and stronger systems such as constant-depth Frege by an exponential margin. A side result separates the classical systems SRC-I and SR-II exponentially for the first time.
arxiv-2606-26095:
Dong Jing leads a team teaching robot action modules some physics before vision and language enter. Vision-language-action models graft an action head onto a vision-language backbone. The backbone brings strong sight and language priors. Motion, though, must be learned nearly from scratch. Early training then juggles two hard jobs at once: action timing and cross-modal alignment. Different robot bodies, with different action patterns, make the juggling harder.

Pretraining the action module is the fix. Stage one trains a light flow-matching encoder-decoder on raw action trajectories alone. The module absorbs cross-embodiment motion structure first. Stage two transfers that prior into full model training. The decoder is reused, and latent distillation aligns sight and language features early. The encoder doubles as a history compressor, squeezing past states and actions into one context token. Thirteen tasks across simulated and real platforms validate the approach.
arxiv-2606-26295:
Vasiliki Ismiroglou and colleagues measure what turbidity steals from underwater vision. Murky water scatters light, and vision systems for infrastructure checks, biology surveys, and navigation all suffer. Synthetic murk, the usual test material, may misstate the real loss. Their Turbid Underwater Baseline dataset holds over a thousand images shot in extreme real turbidity, with more than sixteen thousand expert segmentation masks.

A new metric joins the dataset. Phase congruency difference, built from structure maps that ignore contrast, aims to price structural information loss directly. It tracks segmentation model performance closely on real and synthetic murk alike. Common image quality metrics barely correlate at all. Clear images throttled down in contrast fool the old metrics, while the new one correctly reports the structure still present. Real turbidity, measured honestly, turns out to keep more usable structure than synthetic benchmarks suggest.
arxiv-2606-26495:
Chunliang Mu, Orsola De Marco, and seven colleagues calculate how dust shapes the light of common envelope events. A common envelope occurs when one star swallows its companion into shared outer layers. These events are thought to produce luminous red novae, bright red outbursts. The team post-processed two three-dimensional simulations. Each paired a giant star with a compact companion and included dust formation.

Both simulations ran for forty-four years of model time. A bright, hot peak lasted three to five years as the outer layers expanded. Extra peaks appeared at different times from different viewing angles. Dust formed one to three years in, and the total brightness then dropped sharply. A partial recovery followed, settling at a cool plateau. The dust shell grew to hundreds of times Earth's orbital radius. The authors predict it will turn transparent at visible wavelengths within a few centuries.
arxiv-2606-26795:
Zheqi Lv and eight colleagues present NaviCache, a way to speed up video generation at run time. Video diffusion models are costly to run. Caching tricks skip repeated computation, but offline calibration needs data and time, and breaks when inputs shift. Calibration-free methods guess from instant differences, which are noisy. They also ignore the momentum of the generation trajectory.

NaviCache treats feature evolution like an inertial navigation problem. Such systems track motion by estimating drift, not by looking outside. A dual-state estimator follows the ratio of input to output change and its hidden drift. A special alignment phase starts the estimates. A time-dependent noise plan and an uncertainty-aware update step keep errors bounded while steps are skipped. The method plugs into existing models without retraining.
arxiv-2606-26895:
A. Rahim and twelve colleagues validate a two-stage adaptive optics system for photographing exoplanets. Adaptive optics cancels atmospheric blur with deformable mirrors. Even extreme systems leave residuals because their control loops lag the changing air. A fast second stage can clean up what the first stage misses. The team's second stage uses a Zernike wavefront sensor, a device that reads phase errors from a focused spot.

Earlier validation used single-colour light. Real sensors work in broadband light to gather more photons. Experiments on a European Southern Observatory testbed simulated first-stage leftovers. The loop was tested in narrow and broad bands across seeing conditions, wind speeds, and star brightness levels. The work is the second part of a series aimed at sharper planet images from the ground.
arxiv-2606-27595:
Most tests of AI web agents reward depth, hiding one answer behind a chain of clues. Breadth is rarely measured outside English. Breadth means listing each member of a set with details. Minbyul Jeong built Ko-WideSearch in 2026 to fill that gap. It is a Korean benchmark of set-listing tasks, produced by a build-and-verify pipeline.

Each task names a parent entity. Examples are a television season, a dynasty, or an election. The agent must list the membership and fill a table of attributes for each item. The benchmark holds 228 tables over 190 entities. They span sixteen categories and three tiers. Scoring covers items, columns, and rows. Jeong tested twenty web agents. The failure pattern was steady. Agents recovered the set but not the rows. Item scores sat near ninety-three, while full-row scores sat near fifty-four. More searching and more spending did not close the gap.
arxiv-2606-27795:
A black hole's shadow is set by its photon sphere. That is the outermost ring where light can circle unstably. Jiaqi Fu and Yong Song derive bounds on the shadow's radius in 2026. Their setting is Einstein gravity in n dimensions, with n at least four. The black holes are static, spherically symmetric, and flat at infinity. An anisotropic matter field supports them.

Two model-independent bounds are proved. The lower bound assumes matter obeys the weak energy condition. It ties the shadow radius from below to the horizon radius. The upper bound adds the strong energy condition and a decay condition on the matter. It ties the shadow radius from above to the total mass. Both bounds shrink to the known four-dimensional results. The vacuum Schwarzschild–Tangherlini black hole saturates them exactly. Higher-dimensional shadows thus obey the same style of geometric constraint as familiar four-dimensional ones.
arxiv-2606-27895:
Differentiable physics solvers power gradient-based control and inverse problems. Getting correct, usable gradients from them costs hidden effort, though. Andrin Rehmann, Heiko Zimmermann, and Dion Häfner introduce Mosaic in 2026 to document that cost. Mosaic is an extensible benchmark suite for such solvers. Each solver is packaged as a containerised component. A uniform gradient interface hides differences in language and differentiation strategy.

Fourteen solvers were evaluated. Fluid dynamics, structural mechanics, and heat transfer problems were used. Practical differences proved large. Computational cost and Jacobian conditioning varied by orders of magnitude. Some solvers were structurally incompatible with realistic tasks at all. Yet every solver that produced gradients converged to similar optima. The real barriers are setup compatibility, numerical stability, and memory limits, not gradient accuracy alone. Mosaic is open-source. It aims to spare researchers trial-and-error when choosing a solver.
arxiv-2606-28095:
Pentaquarks are exotic hadrons made of five quarks. Zhi-Gang Wang computes the spectrum of a hidden-charm family in 2026 using QCD sum rules. The states have a diquark-diquark-antiquark structure with two strange quarks and a charm–anticharm pair, forming a decuplet. Vacuum condensates up to dimension thirteen enter the calculation. Positive-parity contamination is excluded to isolate the negative-parity states.

The spectroscopy of the lowest decuplet states is achieved, covering three spin-parity combinations. Wang suggests searching for these states in specific exclusive decays. One search channel is a beauty-strange baryon decay into a pentaquark plus a phi meson; another adds a neutral kaon. As a byproduct, the pentaquark decays let classifications of light baryons be re-tested. Energy scales are fixed by a modified formula accounting for light-flavour symmetry breaking. The work maps where experiments should look for these exotic states.
arxiv-2606-28495:
Pradip Kattel, Abay Zhakenov, and Natan Andrei test whether a cornerstone of quantum impurity physics survives outside unitary theory. In ordinary systems an impurity, a localized spin bathed in electrons, loses its entropy steadily as Kondo screening wraps it in a many-body cloud. That is a monotonic flow guaranteed by a famous theorem whose assumptions demand unitarity.

Their model couples a standard bulk theory to two impurity spins, through boundary interactions that are complex conjugates of each other, arranged to respect a combined parity-time symmetry, making the boundary non-Hermitian. Solving an integrable lattice version exactly and checking against matrix-product-state numerics, they compute the impurity entropy in the screened regime. It still falls monotonically, from the logarithm of four down to zero, even though the standard theorem no longer applies.
arxiv-2606-28795:
Zhang asks when machine learning can deliver unbiased answers for a known population, a property official statistics depends on. Algorithms such as random forests and nearest neighbours chase prediction accuracy. They ignore true data models. Yet low average error alone does not guarantee unbiasedness, meaning estimates that centre on the correct value. His analysis works from the known probability design behind how samples and training sets are drawn, not from assumed distributions.

Three questions structure the argument. How should training data be sampled from the population? How can a trained algorithm be tuned so its predictions come out unbiased? And how can out-of-sample performance itself be judged without bias? Zhang sets out conditions covering each step. The result is a design-based route for agencies that need defensible population figures, where fairness of the sampling plan replaces faith in a model of the data.
arxiv-2606-28895:
Eilertsen studies when a chemical reaction network can be simplified exactly by lumping, grouping species together without changing the dynamics of the groups. He considers networks whose rates follow mass action kinetics, where reaction speed depends on concentrations multiplied together, and asks which linear lumpings exist for typical parameter values versus special ones. Generic parameters, filling an open region of parameter space, turn out to allow only obvious reductions.

Those trivial lumpings either delete species that never react or project along stoichiometric first integrals, quantities fixed by the reaction structure. The result extends beyond mass action to product-form kinetics, including Hill-type and Michaelis-Menten rate laws from biochemistry. For special values, Eilertsen develops an algorithm that finds the critical sets where non-trivial lumpings appear. It solves finitely many polynomial equations. Examples on a self-replicator system and a two-pathway enzyme mechanism show the methods in action.
arxiv-2606-29095:
Yang, Jaiswal, Wang, Zeng, Zhao, Pereira and Min fix a weakness in changing the lighting of long videos with diffusion models. Video diffusion backbones learn from short clips, so long footage is processed in chunks through a sliding window. That chunking often causes visible jumps in lighting at chunk boundaries and unwanted changes in appearance across chunks.

Their system, HorizonRelight, reframes long-video relighting as translation between domains in latent space, carried forward in time. It enforces continuity by propagating target-domain latents across chunk boundaries. A masking trick during training teaches the model to continue from such propagated context. A warm-start prompt also sets the initial lighting state using an anchor frame from a controllable generative model, giving a general prompt-based interface for relighting. On wild long-horizon videos, boundary artefacts were largely reduced and stray appearance changes strongly suppressed, the authors report.
arxiv-2606-29195:
Pan, Jia and Zhang build numerical schemes for surface diffusion, where a curve or surface moves by its own curvature. The schemes keep the enclosed area or volume exactly fixed, a property usually enforced with an extra Lagrange multiplier. Their methods are parametric finite element methods, reaching second-order accuracy in time, for closed curves in the plane and closed surfaces in space.

The trick lies in exact formulas for how area and volume change along a quadratic path in time. In two dimensions, Simpson's rule gives the area change exactly; in three, Boole's rule gives the volume change. Both are classic quadrature rules, ways to compute areas under curves. The schemes can be built on shapes predicted by an existing family of methods, so they fit current codes. Tests show the expected accuracy, exact conservation of area and volume, and good mesh quality.
arxiv-2606-29295:
Damele proves a version of the Schur-Zassenhaus theorem for finite skew braces. Skew braces are algebraic structures carrying two group operations that interact through a compatibility rule; they arise in the study of solutions of the Yang-Baxter equation from set theory. The classical Schur-Zassenhaus theorem says that when a subgroup and its quotient have coprime orders, the subgroup has a complement, a subgroup filling the rest of the group.

His result carries that guarantee over. If a finite skew brace has an ideal whose order and whose quotient's order are coprime, sharing no common factor, then the ideal admits a complement inside the brace. The statement is short, but it extends a cornerstone splitting theorem of group theory to a newer algebraic setting where such structural results are still being built. The proof appears in full in the hosted text, beyond the abstract.
arxiv-2606-29495:
Ma and six colleagues argue that judging social influence dialogue takes more than checking final answers. Persuasive conversation works by shifting a user's beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions over many turns. Surface text scores such as BLEU and ROUGE, and single-score judge models, cannot track that inner movement.

Their Cognitive World Model, CogWM, reframes evaluation around how the user's internal state evolves. It predicts BDI/E states, short for beliefs, desires, intentions, and emotions, alongside the user's next utterance. The same model serves both as a user simulator and as an evaluation platform, with a three-tier scoring framework. Training used a Summarize-and-Allocate annotation pipeline over more than one hundred fifty thousand user turns from four scenarios. CogWM reached high emotion accuracy, more than double a strong commercial baseline. In thousands of trials it also ranked six commercial agents by their cognitive influence.
arxiv-2606-29795:
Muthuganesan introduces a new measure of quantum correlations built from quantum Fisher information, a quantity that gauges how sensitively a state responds to a change in a parameter. His measure, QFI-MIN, measures how sharply local unitary dynamics can tell states apart.

The measure is positive, locally invariant, and monotone under local operations. Formulas follow for pure states and two-qubit states, with a direct link to entanglement for pure systems. He also ties the measure to three jobs: estimating parameters, telling channels apart, and assisted communication. Behaviour under several damping channels shows robustness against noise.
arxiv-2606-29895:
Carpine and three colleagues ask whether current models of interstellar dust can explain the weak emission seen from young protostars, the dusty envelopes around forming stars. Dust emission is how astronomers recover the physical properties of these structures.

The team runs radiative transfer computations, simulations of how radiation moves through a model envelope, using the standard sets of dust optical properties. Changing only the dust composition already produces large swings in the spectral index, the slope of the emission, with no need for grains to grow. But the lowest observed values still cannot be matched without unexpectedly large millimetre-sized grains. Observed values also seem to cluster by star-forming region, hinting that the starting dust at cloud scale matters.
arxiv-2606-30095:
Rocío Picón-González, Salvador Chulián, Ana Niño-López, Álvaro Martínez-Rubio, and María Durán evaluate ways to encode the shape of single-cell data. Topological data analysis extracts features like components and cycles. Persistent homology tracks those features across many scales at once. Many descriptors exist, and choosing among them is rarely systematic. Their two-level framework makes that comparison rigorous.

The first level screens descriptors for separation between clinical groups. The second level tests their value in supervised classification models. The test data are bone marrow flow cytometry samples. They come from children with acute lymphoblastic leukemia, focusing on relapse risk. Encodings vary widely in separation power and stability across settings. Betti Curves and Persistence Silhouettes behave more robustly here. Persistence Images prove less stable in this cohort. The framework is reproducible for other medical point clouds.
arxiv-2606-30295:
Xu-Hui Cheng and Long-Long Feng show that light in chiral media behaves like a Dirac particle in disguise. Chiral media respond differently to left and right circular polarization. Starting from Maxwell's equations, the authors recast the field as a four-part spinor. An effective optical Dirac equation governs that spinor. The medium's magnetoelectric response becomes a helicity-dependent background field.

Breaking the spin-degenerate condition generates intrinsic spin-orbit coupling in the model. Helicity and orbital degrees of freedom then interact coherently. Projecting onto positive frequencies reduces the theory to two levels. That helicity-orbital model has an exact analytical solution. It describes Rabi-like oscillations between spin-orbit-coupled vector modes. Chirality controls the level splitting and detuning of them. Material mismatch sets the coupling strength for spin-orbit conversion. Total angular momentum conservation yields clean selection rules throughout.
arxiv-2606-30495:
Jiwei Jia, Xinliang Liu, Juntao Wang, and Jinchao Xu build a learned preconditioner for wave equations that defeat classical solvers. The Helmholtz equation governs time-harmonic waves in acoustics and electromagnetics. At high frequencies in mixed media it turns indefinite. Phase errors pollute accuracy across the domain. Scalar coarse grids discard the local phase information in errors. McMg keeps that information in extra channels.

Coarsening shrinks physical space while channels store wave packets. Each coarse node carries amplitude, phase, direction, and scattering data. Learned transfer operators and adaptive stencils move data between levels. Medium-dependent smoothers draw coefficients from the wave speed. With the medium fixed, the whole cycle stays linear. Nonlinear features are computed once and cached for reuse. Models trained on small domains transfer to larger ones directly. Progressive fine-tuning adds coarse levels for the biggest problems. Fewer iterations and less time beat strong classical baselines.
arxiv-2606-30795:
Lijun Zhang, Ruinian Xu and Mudit Agrawal revisit a practical question in object detection: what if a few target images could be labelled after all? Source-free domain adaptation retrains a detector on a new, unlabelled domain using its own pseudo-labels. The team ask how much a small, randomly sampled set of true labels helps, at budgets from one to ten percent.

Their method, Random-Target Supervised Mixing, adds a supervised loss on those labelled images and leaves the unlabelled adaptation branch untouched. Across four adaptation methods, two detectors and many tasks, it improved source-free results consistently, by up to about eighteen points of average precision. The team then tested ten plugins that feed the labels into self-training, through pseudo-label selection, object completion or optimisation control. Those gave only limited, method-dependent extra gains. Their stated lesson: simple supervision is hard to beat.
arxiv-2606-30995:
Zakk Heile, Hayden McTavish, Margo Seltzer and Cynthia Rudin build classifiers that are simple for most inputs and heavy only where needed. Single trees can match black-box models in noisy settings, but elsewhere practitioners face a trade between accuracy and interpretability. Multistage Defer Trees are a sequence of sparse trees. Each tree predicts for most samples that reach it and defers a share to the next tree, with a black box as the last resort. Users set the deferral rate to choose their point on the trade-off.

The authors show these cascades can be trained to match tree ensembles while sending most samples through just one or a few sparse trees. They describe techniques for training the stages while keeping each tree simple. The result widens the accuracy-interpretability frontier where single trees fall short: even when complex models prove necessary, they need not be opaque.
arxiv-2606-31195:
Shiddiq and six colleagues tackle quantum error mitigation, a way to reduce noise errors in quantum computers without full correction. Machine learning can do this job, but training needs data for many Pauli strings, the basic measurement patterns in a Hamiltonian. Pi-QEM instead picks training observables by Pauli weight, which reflects how local each pattern is.

The method trains on a small set of dominant low-weight strings, using the link between variance and locality in quantum circuits. In molecular simulations run on a noisy IBM backend, Pi-QEM cuts ground-state energy error by up to about 34 percent with just one dominant local observable. The gain points to a cheaper path for accurate work on near-term noisy devices.
arxiv-2606-31295:
Baraglia builds exotic diffeomorphisms on a class of four-manifolds that earlier work had left open. A map is exotic when it can be deformed to the identity through continuous maps but not through smooth ones. Ruberman's first examples sat on reducible manifolds with an even count, while odd cases were known only for irreducible ones.

Baraglia covers reducible manifolds with odd b-plus, the count that blocked the older methods. A families Bauer-Furuta invariant detects the exotic maps. The moduli spaces here are not framed, so the invariant takes values in pin-cobordism rather than framed cobordism. The work also finds simply connected four-manifolds with mapping class groups that resist finite generation, sharp new cases for smooth topology.
arxiv-2606-31795:
Quint and five colleagues describe how the Vera C. Rubin Observatory managed hundreds of commissioning tests with a tool borrowed from software testing. Commissioning meant planning and running integration and on-sky tests across subsystems and teams spread over several countries. The observatory adopted Zephyr Scale, a test manager that lives inside Jira.

Each test becomes a Test Case holding the script needed to run it at the summit. Every day, cases are grouped into a Test Cycle that forms that day and night's plan. Complex tests are written as partly automated JSON files that the Scheduler, the observatory's real-time observing engine, can ingest directly. Benefits and limits of stretching a software tool to observatory scale are weighed.
arxiv-2606-31995:
Boucaud and colleagues report a year of operations for the filter exchange system inside the LSST Camera at the Rubin Observatory. The system swaps among five large-format filters within a tightly constrained in-camera volume, a routine the Legacy Survey of Space and Time depends on nightly. Each filter is 75 centimetres across and the set masses about 160 kilograms in total.

Since on-sky operations began in April 2025, the system has routinely performed up to 40 exchanges per night. Each change finishes in under 90 seconds, with positioning repeatability of 100 micrometres at the focal plane, the authors report. A dedicated software architecture guards safety and reliability. Design choices are assessed against how the hardware actually behaved in the observatory environment.
balzac-colonel-chabert-marriage-1895:
Colonel Chabert was left for dead on the field of Eylau, buried under corpses, yet he lived. Balzac's short novel, in Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell's 1895 version, follows his return to Paris. His wife has married again and holds his fortune, and the law sees no easy way to raise a dead man.

A young lawyer takes the case, and pity fights paperwork through the tale. Chabert's end ranks among the saddest in the Human Comedy, a whole epic of war and loss in miniature. Many readers call it Balzac's most perfect short work, proof of how much he could hold in few pages.
balzac-country-doctor-marriage-1895:
Doctor Benassis arrives in a poor Savoy village and quietly rebuilds it, road by road and field by field. The Country Doctor, translated by Ellen Marriage and Clara Bell in 1895, is Balzac's most hopeful provincial novel. It answers his Paris books, where greed rules, with a tale of patient public good.

Through talks with soldiers, peasants, and a dying water-carrier's son, Benassis shares his creed of work and order. His own buried sorrow explains the zeal that drives him. The novel, Le Médecin de campagne in French, remains the Human Comedy's great statement of what one devoted life can mend.
balzac-cousin-pons-marriage-1895:
Sylvain Pons loves music and old art, and asks little from life but meals at his cousins' table. Cousin Pons, in Ellen Marriage's 1895 translation, shows what happens when his quiet collection of pictures and curios gains real value. Relatives who once mocked him turn hunters, and the kind man has no defense ready.

Paired with Cousin Bette as Les Parents pauvres, the poor relations, this is among Balzac's darkest late novels. Greed works here through lawyers, dealers, and family duty, all smiling as they close in. Pons and his friend Schmucke stand as two innocents in a Paris that prices everything, even loyalty.
balzac-lost-illusions-marriage-1895:
Lucien de Rubempré leaves his small town for Paris with a poet's hopes, and Balzac's Lost Illusions tracks what the city does to him. Ellen Marriage's 1895 English version holds all three parts of the novel. At its heart stands the world of newspapers, where praise and ruin are both for sale.

Balzac shows printing shops, paper mills, and newsrooms as one great machine for grinding reputations. Lucien learns its rules too late, at a cost to everyone near him. Readers rank the book at the center of the Human Comedy, Balzac's vast portrait of French life after Napoleon.
balzac-magic-skin-marriage-1895:
A young man finds a strange piece of skin in a Paris antique shop, and The Magic Skin grants him every wish. Each wish, though, shrinks the skin, and with it his remaining life. Balzac's tale, La Peau de chagrin, made his name and anchors the thoughtful side of the Human Comedy.

Ellen Marriage translated the novel in 1895, and her version keeps its mix of wild fancy and sharp Paris detail. The hero must choose between wanting and living, a bargain no wealth can soften. Few novels state Balzac's great theme so cleanly: desire itself spends the life it feeds on.
balzac-pere-goriot-marriage-1895:
Honoré de Balzac wrote Father Goriot in French, and Ellen Marriage made it English in 1895. Marriage's version served J. M. Dent's landmark full Comédie Humaine in English dress. The novel of Parisian ambition sits near the heart of Balzac's vast human comedy.

Old Goriot, a rich pasta maker ruined by his daughters' greed, fades in a boarding house. Young Rastignac, a law student, learns Paris ways from the smooth rogue Vautrin there. Goriot dies calling for daughters who send empty carriages to his pauper's grave in Paris. Rastignac buries him and turns to face the city he vows to conquer next. Balzac maps money, rank, and family love with a surgeon's cold, clear eye.
balzac-the-thirteen-wormeley-marriage-18:
Thirteen men, bound by a secret pact, move through Balzac's Paris like a hidden government. The Thirteen gathers three tales, Ferragus, The Duchess of Langeais, and The Girl with the Golden Eyes, in the 1895 Wormeley and Marriage translations. Each story tests what the brotherhood will do for one of its own.

Love, kidnapping, and revenge drive the plots, while the thirteen hover at the edges, rich and unseen. Balzac gives his Human Comedy a conspiratorial heart here, a Paris beneath Paris. The trilogy mixes melodrama with his usual sharp eye for money, rank, and desire.
bekker-world-bewitched-1695:
Balthasar Bekker strikes at the Devil's power in The World Bewitch'd, in English from 1695. Bekker was a church man in Holland who used the new thought of Descartes. Spirits, he holds, can't push flesh: a soul with no bulk can't move a chair, sign a pact, or ride a broom through the night sky of his cold north land.

His four books take on witch trials, ghosts, and the Good Book's own tales. The church cast him out for it, yet his case spread. The book is a chief blow that broke the hunts. Its nerve still awes.
beowulf-morris-wyatt-1895:
William Morris and A. J. Wyatt gave English readers a new Beowulf in 1895, in the fine Kelmscott Press edition. Their text turns the Old English epic into rich, old-style verse. Beowulf, a hero from Geatland, sails to Denmark to help King Hrothgar.

Grendel, his mother, and a dragon that guards a hoard give the hero three great fights. The last fight costs Beowulf his life, and his people mourn a brave king. Morris loved old tales and fine books, and his version feels like both. It links the medieval poem to modern readers. Scholars still use it to feel the poem's rough music.
bibliographical-notes-on-histories-of-in: Bibliographical Notes on Histories of Inventions and Books of Secrets, 1895. The six papers. This book preserves that bibliography. The paper lived through the years. Coming generations can find it. Its place in history is secure.
blavatsky-modern-panarion-1895:
