The test was checked on marrow samples from 173 newly diagnosed patients, 287 samples in all. The group included early and active forms of the disease. The test could spot the main MYD88 change at very low levels in both marrow and blood samples. Follow-up samples from 37 patients on a targeted drug let the team track how the change levels moved with treatment.
pmc-13267695:
Jessica A Marino and her team ask in 2026 whether warm, kind early years shield mental health in pregnancy, even after childhood maltreatment. They studied 234 pregnant people at about seventeen weeks. They used symptom surveys plus structured interviews to check for depression and anxiety diagnoses. Their early years held both harm and positive experiences.

Maltreatment alone predicted worse symptoms and more diagnoses in pregnancy. Those good years meant fewer symptoms and lower diagnosis rates, with stronger effects. When both were weighed together, the good side stayed significant across all outcomes, while maltreatment faded to nothing. Good early support, the authors argue, leaves a buffer that lasts into the start of the next generation.
pmc-13267795:
Ahoud Ali Al-Shammary and colleagues report a 2026 survey of parents on children's device use and sleep in Majmaah, Saudi Arabia. Sleep is vital for children's learning and health, yet phones and tablets often delay bedtime. The team questioned 400 parents of healthy children and teens between November 2023 and May 2024, using an online questionnaire.

About 87 percent of parents knew smart devices can harm children, with sleep and vision the top concerns. About 78 percent set device limits, and 86 percent had sought medical care for related symptoms. Still, many children passed advised screen times, with effects on sleep and behavior. Parents with more education were more aware of the risks. Control was hardest with children under five. The authors call for clearer guidance and firm screen limits.
pmc-13268095:
C D October and colleagues wrote a 2026 interview study on decisions after exposure to drug-resistant TB in South Africa. After such exposure, health workers must judge risk and offer preventive therapy, yet little was known about how they decide in real clinics. The team interviewed 22 health workers in the Western Cape and read the answers through a decision-making framework.

Four linked themes emerged. Crowded housing in informal settlements made exposure hard to judge. Stigma led patients to hide their TB status. Clinical information often arrived late or incomplete. And formal training on post-exposure care was scarce. Workers leaned on experience, gut feeling, and asking peers. The authors call for faster test results, real training, and stigma-aware strategies so guideline care can actually happen.
pmc-13269395: A correction notice from 2026, for a paper led by Irene Hernandez-Perez, fixes the author list of a study on food portion sizes for children aged six months to eight years. Members of the CHOP study group had been listed by mistake inside the main author group. The corrected list names the individual authors and then the CHOP Study Group as a group. The journal states that the original article has been corrected.
pmc-13270295:
Felix Barber and co-authors show in 2026 how wall teichoic acids, sugar-phosphate chains on a bacterium's surface, keep Bacillus subtilis growing as a neat rod. Rod shape comes from balanced wall building: one machinery lays wall material along the cell's length, while a second enzyme fills in more evenly. Watching single cells in tiny channels, the team drained teichoic acids and filmed what followed.

Within minutes, nano-sized pores opened in the wall. The even-filling enzyme surged and became essential for survival, the lengthwise machinery stalled, and orderly growth collapsed into shapeless swelling. A wall-cutting enzyme also became indispensable alongside the filler. Teichoic acids, the authors conclude, preserve shape by sealing the wall against pores that would otherwise hijack construction.
pmc-13270495:
Solomon Buabeng Antwi led a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis, a study that pools past studies, on deep learning for brain tumour scans. The review looked at hybrid models that join convolutional networks, which read local image patterns, with transformers, which read wider context across an image.

The authors searched four databases for work from January 2021 to May 2025 and kept 94 studies from 1,876 first found. Across those studies, pooled diagnostic accuracy, meaning how often the models were right, was 93.5 percent. The review also weighed computing cost, methods that make extra training images, and the joining of several scan types.
pmc-13271495:
Alexander L Cope and coauthors tackle in 2026 a hidden cost of making proteins inside cells. Ribosomes sometimes fall off a message before finishing, wasting energy on a partial protein that cannot work. The team wanted to measure how often these drop-off errors happen and what they cost the cell.

They built a movement model for ribosomes and applied it to profiling data from baker's yeast. Drop-off rates varied a lot by codon, the three-letter units that ribosomes read. The wasted energy rivaled the cost of ribosome pausing. The authors argue that avoiding such errors has shaped how protein-coding genes evolved over time.
pmc-13271995:
Shujuan Huang and coauthors follow in 2026 stroke patients with swallowing problems who received magnetic stimulation of the vagus nerve. Swallowing failure after stroke risks pneumonia and malnutrition, and feeding tubes often stay in for long periods. Stimulating the nerve on the left side of the neck may speed recovery of the swallowing reflex.

The study compared 33 stimulated patients with 45 who received standard swallowing training alone at one hospital. After adjustment for other differences, the stimulated group had feeding tubes removed more often and about four days sooner on average. The authors applied causal methods to check that the advantage was not explained by patient mix.
pmc-13272095:
Abigail J Nordbeck and coauthors review in 2026 the chemical modifications that act as a regulatory code on tau, a protein central to brain cell function and to Alzheimer's-type diseases. Tau supports the cell's internal transport tracks, and small chemical tags switch its behavior. When that tagging system breaks down, tau clumps into toxic fibers.

Phosphorus tagging has dominated research, yet the review covers many other tags, including acetyl, ubiquitin, and sugar groups, and how they amplify or cancel each other. Single tau molecules can carry dozens of tags at once. Reading the tags as one network may explain disease steps that single-tag studies miss.
pmc-13272495:
Lin Wang, Yanliang Niu, and Lijun Wang reported a rare stroke case in 2026 involving just the trigeminal nerve's sensory fibers. This nerve carries feeling from the face, and a small stroke in the pons can damage part of it. Such cases are easy to mistake for nerve inflammation.

Their patient was a 59 year old man with twenty days of swelling and numbness on the left side of his face and gum. A first clinic had treated him for nerve inflammation without success. Brain imaging showed a small restricted lesion along the sensory path in the pons. He received two antiplatelet drugs, a statin, and pain relief, and improved over three weeks.
pmc-13272795:
Nina Dabrosin leads a 2026 study of how testosterone treatment changes skin in people with XX chromosomes who were assigned female at birth. Such treatment is part of gender-affirming care, and many patients later have surgery, so skin healing matters. The team analyzed discarded skin from plastic surgery, with and without testosterone treatment.

Treated skin showed a 2.77-fold rise in cells with androgen receptors in the dermis, the deeper skin layer, and almost three times the collagen density. Immune cells there fell by 43 percent. Changes in the outer layer included more fibronectin, a protein that helps tissue hold together. Overall, treated skin took on features resembling a male skin pattern.
pmc-13272895:
Qian Wang leads a 2026 study of chronic pain in many body sites and its links to joint disease and low mood, using UK Biobank data. Pain in many sites often occurs with immune and mood problems, but shared biology is unclear. The team looked for patterns across blood tests, small chemicals, and proteins.

They found patterns spanning 59 blood measures, 168 small chemicals, and 2,920 proteins. Change grew in steps from controls to low mood to joint disease to both together. The patterns predicted new joint disease and low mood, and partly explained their two-way link. They also tied to brain changes and to habits such as smoking and activity.
pmc-13272995:
Jie Li leads a 2026 cohort study of a blood protein called sTREM2 in patients with acute worsening heart failure. The protein is linked to immune cells and may track risk. The team enrolled 128 patients from 2020 to 2023 and tracked death and heart failure readmission as a combined outcome.

Levels were higher than in healthy controls and rose with worse functional class. Of the patients, 58, or 45.3 percent, reached the combined outcome. Each 50-unit rise in the protein linked to a higher risk of that outcome and of readmission in particular. Adding it to a standard heart marker improved readmission prediction, though not overall accuracy.
pmc-13273595:
Jorge Domínguez-Carrión and co-authors reviewed anti-doping knowledge in sport in a 2026 systematic review. Clean sport depends on athletes and their support staff knowing the rules, yet this knowledge is rarely measured the same way twice. The team gathered every study that assessed it.

They included ninety-three studies covering athletes, students, and support personnel. A quarter of the papers never clearly stated the knowledge level they found. Tools and reporting varied widely across the rest. Sorting the authors' own labels, the largest share of studies pointed to low knowledge, and none described extensive knowledge. The authors urge standard validated tests plus structured education programs, warning that their summary reflects patterns in messy reporting rather than exact measures.
pmc-13273695:
Hao Huang and a large team built a high throughput platform for zinc doped bone ceramics in a 2026 study. Adding zinc to calcium phosphate can boost bone growth and fight bacteria, but size, heat, and chemistry all interact, so tuning by trial and error is slow. Their platform runs many reactions at once under precise control.

By varying time and temperature independently, the system can run up to 144 experiments together. The team mapped how concentration, zinc ratio, acidity, and solvent mix steer crystal formation. The resulting particles were friendly to cells, promoted bone activity, and resisted bacteria. A porous scaffold made from them was more than twice as strong as a commercial rival, and in rabbit leg defects it grew far more new bone over twelve weeks.
pmc-13273895:
Lin and colleagues review research on transposons in the yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae. Their 2026 review article covers these mobile DNA elements and their uses. Transposons can move within the genome and create mutations.

The review sorts them by how they move. Families covered include Tn, hAT, and Ty elements. PiggyBac, Tc1/mariner, and CRISPR-linked types are covered too. The authors explain how each type copies or cuts itself free. Uses of native and engineered versions are discussed. Key challenges include insertion bias and genome instability. Fixes aim to improve efficiency and targeting. The goal is precise editing tools with few off-target effects. Such tools could speed the building of yeast cell factories.
pmc-13273995:
Johanna Blossei and colleagues present a 2026 journal article on potato genes that resist late blight. Late blight, caused by the organism Phytophthora infestans, is one of the worst diseases of potato crops. The Julius Kühn Institute in Germany has bred for resistance for more than sixty years, but the genetics were largely unknown.

The team grew two hundred potato lines in field trials over three years and scanned their genomes for linked markers. Strong signals appeared only on chromosomes nine and eleven, explaining up to twenty-eight and sixteen percent of resistance. One hundred twenty-one lines carried a helpful variant on one chromosome, but only one carried both. That split means breeders could stack the two for stronger, longer-lasting resistance.
pmc-13274595:
Yishu Su and colleagues report a 2026 journal article on a ceramic that lets heat flow one way far better than the reverse, even at searing temperatures. Heat rectifiers are thermal diodes, but older versions failed below 900 kelvin and managed weak contrast. Their metaceramic is a single ceramic block sculpted with graded pores at several scales.

Four heat effects combine inside it: tuned conduction, radiation shaped by cavities, swirling convection, and spontaneous heat shedding. The result is a record rectification ratio of 8.5 at 2,473 kelvin, over one hundred forty percent beyond prior benchmarks. A three-axis version steers heat flow independently along three directions, a step toward programmable thermal control for spacecraft and hypersonic craft.
pmc-13275595:
Renata Martinelli and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis asking which patients respond best to vagus nerve stimulation, an implanted device therapy for epilepsy that drugs cannot control. Following standard review guidelines, they sifted 900 search results down to thirty-nine relevant studies and pooled results for sex, ages, seizure type, disease duration, and genetic cause.

Three factors predicted a better response. Patients with focal seizures, seizures starting in one brain area, responded more often, as did males by a small margin and patients whose epilepsy began younger. Genetic cause, epilepsy duration, and age at implantation showed no significant link to response. The authors argue for considering the device earlier in well-matched patients, while noting that proposed biomarkers still need firmer proof.
pmc-13276395:
Tomasz Próchniak authored a 2026 journal article on what makes a top show jumping horse. Warmblood horses compete in Grand Prix events over fences about chest height on a tall adult. Breeders want to know whether early promise predicts later success, and which factors truly drive results.

The study analyzed two hundred ninety-three horses across seven hundred twenty-five starts in Polish national Grand Prix events. Statistical models separated genetic factors from the rider's influence, which counted as a random effect. Stallions, German breeds, and horses aged fifteen to eighteen performed best. Results from young horse championships correlated positively with later Grand Prix performance, supporting their use in breeding decisions. Pedigree checks showed German, Belgian, and Dutch horses gaining ground in Polish competitions. Repeatability was low, yet results still signal breeding value.
pmc-13276895:
Shenghao Ji and colleagues explain why a wastewater reactor releases more nitrous oxide as its feed ratio shifts, in a 2026 study. Partial nitritation is a step in low-energy nitrogen removal, yet it can emit nitrous oxide, a potent greenhouse gas. The reactor treated food waste digestate with fluctuating composition.

As the ratio of degradable carbon to ammonium rose modestly, the nitrous oxide emission factor climbed eightfold. Keeping the process stable required stronger ammonia oxidation, which fed more electrons toward nitrite reduction. Stronger aeration also stripped more gas out of the liquid. Gene patterns shifted toward nitrous oxide producers over reducers. The authors weigh all three routes as joint drivers of the increase.
pmc-13276995:
Menghui Yao leads a 2026 case-control study of VEXAS syndrome, a severe inflammatory disease, in China. No case series from China had been reported before. Doctors at Peking Union Medical College Hospital tested 57 men with unexplained inflammation and blood problems for changes in a gene called UBA1.

Twenty-one men carried harmful UBA1 variants, including one variant not reported before. Compared with other patients, they more often were older at onset and had skin lesions, ear cartilage inflammation, and large red blood cells. Skin problems were the first sign in over half of cases. A screening tool built from five features sorted cases well in outside groups, offering a route to earlier diagnosis.
pmc-13277595:
Mahir Kapmaz and colleagues describe a 2026 case of Stewart-Treves syndrome mistaken for skin infection after an earthquake. A 74-year-old woman had lived eight years with a swollen left arm after breast cancer treatment. She survived the February 2023 Kahramanmaraş earthquake, and a minor arm lesion soon followed.

Three hospitals treated her redness, pain, and swelling as cellulitis with repeated antibiotics. She worsened anyway, developing bruising, severe anaemia, and fluid around one lung. At a fourth centre, biopsy of the firm violet plaque showed lymphangiosarcoma, a rare cancer arising in chronic lymphoedema. The diagnosis came late, and she died ten days later under palliative care.
pmc-13278795:
Ryo Bando leads a 2026 case report of a fast-moving heart valve infection after a catheter-based valve replacement in an 85-year-old woman. She arrived with sudden fever, and blood tests found Streptococcus agalactiae, a bacterium increasingly seen in older adults. A first heart ultrasound showed no growths on the valve.

On day three she developed confusion and neck stiffness suggesting meningitis, plus bleeding inside the skull. A repeat ultrasound then showed new growths on the prosthetic aortic valve and the mitral valve, with worsening leakage. Despite intensive antibiotics, shock and multiorgan failure followed, and she died on day seven. Early scans can miss this infection, so repeat imaging matters, the authors warn.
pmc-13278995:
Lei Song and colleagues published a 2026 pilot trial of a face cream containing 3 percent lactic acid ferment lysate, made by fermenting probiotic bacteria, for people with oily skin. Forty-two participants applied the cream twice daily for 60 days. The researchers measured oil output, pore size, water loss through the skin, hydration, and texture with standard tools, and sequenced bacterial genes from skin swabs.

By day 60 the group showed drops of about 31 percent in sebum and 25 percent in pore size compared with baseline readings, alongside higher hydration and smoother texture. Bacterial diversity rose, with Staphylococcus and Cutibacterium becoming less common and Streptococcus more common. Because the trial was small and exploratory, the authors present the lysate as a promising ingredient for oily-skin care rather than a proven therapy. The microbe findings are offered as leads for further study.
pmc-13279395:
Trisha Lal and colleagues report a 2026 interview study of non medical barriers in gut and bowel cancer care. Care for these cancers needs many specialties and breaks down when insurance, transport or reading skills fail. Past survey work at their centre found such barriers bite hardest at first treatment planning and eat much staff time. The team now ask providers how they see and feel those barriers.

Thirty providers from a large United States academic health system took part in semi structured interviews. The group held doctors, advanced practice staff and other care roles. Two coders read the transcripts for themes that arose from the text itself. Linked theme maps traced how barrier types may drive each other. Results feed a new cross specialty care model built to cut non medical blocks.
pmc-13280695:
Zhangwei Lv and colleagues scanned the brains of people with severe poor sleep for a 2026 study. Insomnia can blunt working memory, the skill of holding facts in mind while using them. The team studied three hundred ninety-one patients with insomnia. Scans measured how well the brain clears waste during sleep. They also checked how brain wiring and activity matched, plus sleep and memory scores.

Worse sleep went with slower waste clearing in the brain. One deep brain network linked clearing, sleep, and memory all together. Math tests showed that clearing and that network carried part of the effect of poor sleep on memory. The authors say these scan signs could flag which patients face the most memory risk.
pmc-13280795:
Denis Djekourmane and colleagues published a 2026 study using machine learning to predict fifteen-year-olds' mathematics scores across six East Asian education systems in the PISA 2022 assessment. East Asian results draw worldwide attention, yet the drivers of success are studied one variable at a time. The team trained six algorithms on 26,969 students, then used explanation methods to rank which of the 62 factors mattered most, keeping the 24 strongest.

The XGBoost model won, explaining about 57 percent of the variation in scores. One factor dwarfed the rest: mathematics self-efficacy, a student's belief in their own capability. Extracurricular activity before school and weekly mathematics teaching time followed. Emotional, behavioral, and teaching factors outweighed family wealth and other structural variables in power. The authors read the results through self-determination theory and suggest policy should invest in building students' confidence and in teaching time, rather than assuming background determines outcomes in these systems.
pmc-13281295:
Larry Garrison and colleagues checked two machines that enrich blood for heart surgery in a 2026 trial. The machines spin a patient's own blood to pack platelets, the bits that form clots. Spread on the breastbone, the packed blood may aid healing and cut infection. Sixty surgery cases took part, split by chance between the two machines. Blood was counted before and after each run. The target was six times the starting platelet count.

Both machines hit the target on average and passed it by a bit. One averaged about six and a half times, the other just over six times. Single runs varied somewhat around those means. The authors say both tools can be trusted to reach the yield they promise. That holds under the real conditions of heart surgery, not just in healthy donors.
pmc-13281795:
Milan Sojitra and colleagues linked extreme weather to breeding in Tasmanian sea predators in a 2026 study. Storms, heat, and heavy rain are growing stronger and more common. Long-lived hunters that breed slowly can ill afford lost seasons. The team joined long breeding records with daily weather for three species. They covered fur seals, shearwaters, and shy albatross across fourteen colonies. Each colony's population path was also weighed.

Disasters hit each species in its own way. Storm surges cut pup counts at a low-lying seal colony. Heavy rain lowered shearwater breeding success. Albatross output fell with bouts of heat, rain, and big waves. Risk hinged on the season's timing and the colony's place. The authors urge managers to learn each colony's danger lines. Care tuned to place and timing, they say, can build resilience as the climate shifts.
pmc-13281895:
Miao Yang and Biyan Zhang tracked six women's diseases in China across three decades in a 2026 study. The group covers womb growths, a hormone disorder of the ovaries, tissue growth outside the womb, and three cancers. Women aged fifteen to forty-nine were the focus, from 1990 to 2021. The team used a global disease burden database. They charted new case rates and years of healthy life lost, by age and region.

Womb growths led in new case rates by a wide margin. Cervical cancer led in healthy years lost, the heavier toll. The ovary hormone disorder grew fastest on both counts. It clusters in the late teens, where its rates were highest. Cervical cancer rates also rose across the span. Ovary cancer gains were steepest in lower-middle income regions. The authors urge screening and care plans tuned by age and place.
pmc-13282295:
Juliana Delvizio and co-authors report a 2026 survey profiling Brazilians who eat chia seeds. Chia is praised for fibre and other nutrients, yet consumer habits in Brazil were little studied. A self-completed questionnaire drew seven hundred forty-seven people. Of them, four hundred sixty-eight ate chia and two hundred seventy-nine did not. Women and highly educated people were most likely to report eating it.

Fibre was the word people linked most with chia. Most users ate it daily or weekly, stirred into yoghurt, fruit, or smoothies. They cited better bowel function, fullness, and help with weight loss as main benefits. Non-users mainly blamed lack of habit or dislike of the taste. Many said they would try chia if they knew its benefits. The authors urge clearer health communication and tastier, convenient chia products to widen use beyond the already convinced.
pmc-13282595:
Andrea Montanari and colleagues published a 2026 sensor study on how daylight and night light shape sleep stages. Twenty-one adults in the Jerusalem area were tracked for seven days with a headband that records brain waves during sleep, light loggers, activity trackers, and a phone-use app.

Each added hour of daylight linked to about eleven more minutes of sleep the next night and a small drop in light sleep share. Evening artificial light showed no clear link with sleep measures. Phone use before bed linked to taking longer to fall asleep. The small sample calls for care, yet the day-by-day design shows how real-life light habits track with sleep in the home setting.
pmc-13283195:
Green laser doses were escalated in rabbit eyes to chart retinal harm in Ling Guo's 2026 multimodal experiments. A green laser at 525 nm was tested at four power levels. The aim was to map how harm grows with dose in structure and function.

A total of 24 rabbits got a brief single-eye exposure of a quarter second. Tests covered electric response, layered eye scans, tissue study, and fluid markers. The lowest power caused no clear harm in any test used. Higher powers caused brief electric dips, swelling, and bleeding that eased in a week. The top power caused severe layer split at one day and a retinal hole by day 14 after exposure.
pmc-13283395:
Low blood protein frees more antibiotic than labels assume in elders, Xiaoyu Du's monitoring and modeling work shows in 2026. The drug is ertapenem, which binds strongly to blood proteins. Low protein frees more drug, so standard doses may miss the mark.

Lab methods measured total and free drug levels in blood samples for monitoring. Most monitored patients were older, and over half had low albumin levels. Binding rates in these patients fell below values in drug labels. A body-based model was built and checked against patient and published data. Model runs tested dose plans tailored to low-protein older patients. The aim is safer, more exact dosing in this group.
pmc-13283595:
Nine months after ligament repair, female athletes clear return-to-sport bars less often, Samantha Collins's testing data show in 2026. Teen athletes need strength, stability, and range back before clearance. Girls report lower readiness and lower return rates than boys in past work.

Charts covered 69 patients aged 13 to 20 years after first-time ligament repair. A total of 88 tests ran at six or nine months after surgery. Tests covered leg strength balance, balance reach, single-leg hop, and a readiness survey. Passing meant at least 90 percent on body tests and 80 percent on the survey. Groups were split by sex and by test timing for fair comparison. Gaps at nine months are the key focus.
pmc-13284095:
Frequent burning reshaped plant origins in an Australian savanna within two decades, show Susanna Rozsa Bryceson and John William Morgan in 2026. Savanna species hail from Sunda lands in Asia or ancient Sahul lands nearby. Fire plans based only on season may miss that origin balance.

Surveys used a long-running fire-frequency trial near Darwin for comparisons. Plots burned every one to three years flipped toward Sunda-origin yearly grasses. Rich multi-layer growth of mostly Sahul origin gave way to simple tree-grass systems. All Sahul groups felt knock-on effects from that grass shift. No single burn rhythm suits every savanna, the authors warn.
pmc-13284495:
Jack R. Walker and co-authors report a 2026 field study of ground beetles along urban to rural gradients in Liverpool and Manchester. Cities filter wildlife through broken habitat, heat, pollution, and invaders, so traits that tolerate those stresses should spread. The team trapped beetles at 80 grassland sites and tracked five traits against paved surface cover.

Beetles in more urban sites tended to favor dry soils and show weaker spread traits in the combined results reported here. City patterns still differed, with wet-soil species falling in Manchester only and long-winged share falling in Liverpool only. The authors stress that even similar cities filter species in distinct ways, so urban ecology needs multi-city sampling.
pmc-13284595:
John Pietro and colleagues followed a bone clinic cohort in 2025 to study normocalcemic hyperparathyroidism, a condition where parathyroid hormone runs high while blood calcium stays normal. The parathyroid glands govern calcium balance, and the condition is easily missed when doctors check calcium alone. Between early 2022 and mid 2024, 815 patients referred with an osteoporosis diagnosis had bone scans and, where indicated, calcium and hormone blood tests.

The condition turned up in 25 patients, about three percent, roughly one case a month. Bone involvement was frequent: 72 percent of those patients had a history of fragility fractures. Their hormone levels averaged well above normal while calcium and vitamin D stayed in range. The authors argue routine hormone testing would catch cases earlier and support fracture prevention.
pmc-13284695:
Jay Kumar Sharma and colleagues ran bioequivalence trials in 2026 for a generic long-acting form of tacrolimus, a drug that prevents organ rejection after transplant. The test tablets, made in India at one and four milligram strengths, were compared with the branded reference product. Healthy adults aged eighteen to forty-five took single doses in a randomised crossover design, each person cycling through test and reference products under both fasting and fed conditions.

Across the four study arms, about eighty-five subjects each, blood measures of drug exposure and peak levels matched the reference within the acceptance limits set by European regulators. Variability checks also passed. Side effects were monitored throughout, and the product was judged well tolerated. The authors call it an acceptable alternative, while noting transplant patients still need their own confirmatory studies.
pmc-13284895:
Arjun Poudel and co-authors give a 2026 case report and review on a rare stress fracture of the lower fibula in a soldier trainee. Stress fractures are common in athletes and troops and usually heal with rest and a cast. A displaced break in the lower third that needs surgery is rare.

The 20-year-old recruit had one month of training, then a week of ankle pain, swelling, and trouble walking. X-ray showed a crosswise break with slight shift. Given hard military demands and slow cast healing, surgeons fixed it with a plate. Healing came early with no problems after protected rest and rehab. The authors note plain X-ray can catch such breaks.
pmc-13285095:
Khin Thiri Maung and co-authors study unequal unmet health needs in Cambodia in a 2026 national survey analysis. Unmet need shows where people who need care fail to get it. Data came from 5,001 adults in the 2023 World Health Survey Plus, with wealth ranked apart for city and country homes and three ways of defining unmet need.

Measured unmet need ranged widely by definition, from under eight percent to over forty percent in the survey results. In cities, wealth showed no clear link to unmet need. In rural areas, the poorest group had higher odds under one definition, while a middle group had lower odds under another. The authors stress place shapes equity checks.
pmc-13286095:
Shibo Song and colleagues report a salvage operation for a rectal tumor site that standard repeat endoscopy could not handle because of heavy scarring. Published in 2026, the case involves a 52-year-old man whose earlier endoscopic removal of an early cancer left a close margin. Full surgery risked a permanent stoma, so the team tried a deeper endoscopic route.

Surgeons cut between the muscle layers of the rectal wall to remove the suspect area, then faced a four-centimeter defect near the anus. A string-loop suture pulled the edges into two smaller gaps that clips could close. The whole repair took about an hour. Later checks found stable closure and no remaining tumor, and the patient left hospital on day four.
pmc-13286295:
A 2026 announcement from the journal Aging Cell, issued by the Anatomical Society and Wiley, shares a change at the top of the journal. Monty Montano is stepping down as Editor-in-Chief after three years in the role. No author is named on the notice. The journal thanks him for developing the journal and supporting its community of aging researchers.

Rather than naming one successor, the journal will move to shared leadership. Four co-editors-in-chief will divide strategic direction and editorial standards. Associate editors will handle peer review across specialties, and a dedicated editor will oversee reviews and special issues. An advisory board keeps its role. The publishers say the structure was designed jointly to keep standards high as the field grows.
pmc-13286395:
Natalia Houghton and Ernesto Bascolo examine the structural fixes Brazil's Family Health Strategy still needs in a 2026 commentary. Companion analysis of a thirty-year review praises the program's reach and equity gains, then zeroes in on the weakest joint: moving patients smoothly between primary and specialist care. Fragmented referrals, repeated tests, and clumsy information flow waste money and sour patient experience across the system.

Regional frameworks for integrated delivery networks supply their yardstick, with shared information and two-way communication as core traits. Their agenda runs through clearer duties between municipal, state, and federal levels, and payment models that reward continuity rather than sheer volume. Digital scheduling projects and territory apps show early promise, they note. The closing challenge is naming which structural conditions let networks truly mature.
pmc-13286895:
YongPing Yao asks families and doctors what they want from smart ankle braces for kids with cerebral palsy. The 2026 survey ran in Sichuan Province, China. It drew 95 families and 39 health workers from many sites. Smart braces may help kids walk, but makers need to know which needs count most.

Families put steady walking first. Ease of putting the brace on and off came next. Health workers cared most about gait tracking and fall warnings. Both sides prized safety, comfort, and home use. Richer homes asked more for tracking and ease of use. Yao urges makers to blend family needs with clinic goals and to watch price bars in poor areas.
pmc-13287095:
Erkil Onur Günüç and Mustafa Salman test two feed additives in fattening lambs in a 2026 animal study. High-concentrate diets push fast growth but sour the rumen and waste nutrients. They were fed individually for 63 days after a settling period, with growth, rumen fluid, digestibility, and carcass traits recorded.

Neither body weight nor intake differed by group, yet daily gain and feed efficiency answered to treatment in particular windows. The combined group gained and converted best between days 14 and 28 of the trial. Chromium alone cut rumen ammonia, raised protozoa counts, and improved fiber digestion, while the buffer's effects stayed limited. Carcass traits ignored all treatments, so the authors pitch the pairing for the adaptation phase of intensive feeding.
pmc-13288695:
Paula Christen and a long author list reflect on a 2026 account of a five-day hackathon meant to connect researchers, officials, and practitioners in Kenya. The January 2025 event in Nairobi, run by a London research center with the University of Nairobi, set challenges named by the health ministry and the veterinary directorate.

Six mixed teams of researchers, software engineers, and policymakers built prototype tools for outbreak surveillance, vaccine deployment, data quality checks, and health workforce estimates. Organizers describe the format as deliberate knowledge translation: short, structured teamwork that forces each side to use the others' skills. Their lessons argue that hackathons can speed research into practice and seed durable working relationships.
pmc-13288895:
Louie Slocombe and co-authors present CBR-db, a chemistry-rich database of biochemical reactions, in a 2026 paper. Existing reaction collections often skip the chemical detail that careful analysis needs. The team rebuilt records from two major sources, KEGG and the ATLAS of Biochemistry. Every reaction was checked for chemical consistency. The result covers about 148,673 reactions and 18,716 small molecules.

Each entry carries atom tracking, which follows individual atoms through a reaction. Users also get compound traits, chiral centers, assembly indices, and thermodynamic values. Reactions are grouped by similarity to speed comparison across pathways. The database is open source and built for continuous, reproducible updates. The authors target researchers where chemistry meets biology, from metabolism studies to synthetic pathway design. Origin-of-life questions about how biochemistry began also stand to gain.
pmc-13289895:
Gerald Agyapong-Opoku and coauthors set out a 2026 scoping review protocol on non-drug help for anxiety and depression in youth aged 10 to 24. Both conditions rank among the top causes of disability in this age group and can shadow schooling and adult life. Programs vary hugely in form, place, and audience, so a systematic map is needed before stronger synthesis.

Six databases will be searched under institute guidance for scoping reviews, with reporting by a standard checklist. Any empirical work on interventions cutting anxiety or depression symptoms in the age band qualifies for charting. Two reviewers will select and chart studies on their own. Summaries will show the most common approaches and delivery modes.
pmc-13290195:
Some prenatal screening failures blamed on low fetal DNA may actually reflect Y chromosome problems in the fetus, Siqi Hu and colleagues reported in 2026. The retrospective study covers 24,101 pregnant women who had noninvasive prenatal testing between January 2023 and January 2025.

Sex chromosome abnormalities were far more common in the low fetal fraction group than in the adequate group, an increase the authors put at roughly 78-fold. All eight abnormal cases in the low group involved the Y chromosome, which the standard method uses to estimate fetal fraction. Re-estimating with a different method, FF-QuantSC, lifted every case to a reportable level and let the test flag the abnormalities. Hu and colleagues advise re-checking before declaring a test failed.
pmc-13290895:
Bypass veins rescue blood flow where the iliac vein is squeezed, Ke Hu and colleagues show in a simulation study from 2026. In iliac vein compression syndrome an artery pinches the vein against the spine, and collateral channels sometimes grow around the blockage; the team modeled what those channels do to flow.

Two patient-specific 3D models, one with well-developed collaterals and one without, were built from CT angiography and run under body-like flow conditions. Without collaterals the model showed sprawling reflux and vortices, a peak pressure gap of 20,190 Pa, and wall shear stress up to 56 Pa. With collaterals, pressure gap fell to 619 Pa, shear to 10 Pa, and outflow to the vena cava rose about 39%. Hu and colleagues read collaterals as a real compensatory mechanism, while cautioning the work is mechanistic, not clinical proof.
pmc-13290995:
Young adults in active cancer care are the focus of a 2026 pragmatic trial led by Eran Ben-Arye on integrative oncology, where supportive methods sit alongside standard treatment. Patients aged 18 to 45 were offered a personal consultation plus six weekly sessions aimed at quality-of-life concerns.

Of 180 patients, 137 attended at least four sessions and counted as highly adherent, while the rest formed a low-adherence comparison shaped by patient choice. At six weeks the high-adherence group reported larger gains on symptom and wellbeing scales, with clearer gains again in patients aged 40 to 45 than in younger peers. Fatigue, anxiety, and breathing scores moved most in that older subgroup, which hints that benefit may depend on age as well as attendance.
pmc-13291295:
Burning one tumor can shift immunity in a far tumor. Kun Zhao leads a 2026 mouse study of heat ablation. Past work looked mostly at leftover tumor near the burn. Distant tumors may gain or lose immune support too.

Mice bore tumors on both body sides. One side got full or partial heat ablation. The far side served as the test site. Killer immune cells rose there at first. By day nine, the mood turned suppressive. One immune brake, CTLA-4, rose at that point. Adding a drug against that brake helped. Far tumors grew slower and held more killer cells.
pmc-13291895:
Lars Breum Christiansen and co-authors evaluate a 2026 preschool program, Ball-based Play in Preschool, designed to weave ball games into daily routines. Eight preschools took part in a non-randomized wait-list design, and parents answered questionnaires about their children's play. The team built a Ball Play Index combining how often children play, how much they enjoy it, and their skill level.

Baseline answers from 429 families varied widely: ball sports participation ran from 14 to 30 percent across settings, and any-sport participation from 31 to 80 percent of children surveyed. Gender, disability status, and parental background all tracked with the outcomes. In the impact group of 108 children, the program showed no significant effect on either the index or leisure ball sports participation. The authors advise future programs to weigh club capacity and starting activity levels.
pmc-13291995:
Jake Brooks and co-authors introduce a special journal issue on imaging metals inside living tissue, in 2026. Metals run much of biology, with an estimated thirty to forty percent of proteins needing one. Misplaced metals also drive cancer, brain decay, and organ failure. The issue gathers twelve contributions that map metals from whole organs down to single cells. Methods range from mass spectrometry imaging and synchrotron X-rays to PET scans and fluorescent probes.

One featured study maps element patterns inside human prostate calcifications and ties ratios to tumor grade. Another layers three synchrotron techniques to follow metal form and place inside cancer cells in three dimensions. Several papers lean on X-ray fluorescence for label-free, multi-element views at fine focus. The editors frame the collection as a toolkit for spotting where metals gather and do harm. The same maps can judge metal-based drugs and markers.
pmc-13292395:
Kotomi Inaba and colleagues extend a greenness score so modern methods can be judged fairly, in a 2026 paper. The older score rated liquid chromatography by instrument energy plus solvent hazards. Miniaturized techniques like single-molecule microscopy fell outside its math. The unified score presented here clarifies the formulas and adds size and uncertainty handling. The team then scored microscopy against high-performance liquid chromatography on equivalent data.

Microscopy came out significantly greener, mainly because it sips solvent instead of flooding columns. Chromatography's energy and solvent appetite grow with every sample in big screening libraries. A common score lets chemists compare such different tools on one scale. The authors aim the metric at everyone from undergraduates to industrial researchers. Greener method choice could trim the footprint of routine analysis. The paper treats sustainability as a design variable, not an afterthought.
pmc-13292595:
Yapeng Zhang and colleagues combine genome and gene-activity scans to find chicken growth genes, in a 2026 study. Feed efficiency decides profit when feed eats over seventy percent of production cost. The team ran association scans in 432 Wenchang chickens across six efficiency and growth traits. They then matched significant spots against gene-activity regulators measured in liver. Public chicken gene-expression resources widened the cross-check.

The scans flagged twenty-eight strong genes and over a thousand suggestive ones. Four association spots lined up with regulators of single genes, including LAP3 and KLB. Two small insertions inside LAP3 tracked with how much the gene was expressed, across three genotype groups. Neighboring single-letter variants were tightly linked to the same signal. The authors say LAP3 is a prime suspect for shaping feed use and growth. Breeders could eventually select on such variants.
pmc-13292995:
Serrena Singh and colleagues compare, in a 2026 study, two related growth switches, YAP and TAZ, that drive cell growth in the liver. Though close cousins, they may act very differently, so the team grew liver clones dominated by each one.

YAP clones quickly turned stem-like, drew in inflammatory immune cells, and were then cleared. TAZ clones instead calmed inflammation, lasted, and drove huge organ growth with more deaths. Blocking the immune cells let YAP clones grow freely. In patient data, bowel cancers high in YAP had better five-year survival than those high in TAZ. The two switches thus act as distinct disease drivers.
pmc-13293695:
Emma K. Ward, Nick Simpson, and Clare Press test, in a 2026 study, how breaking a learned pattern in the environment affects spotting new events. Perception leans on expectation, yet how the brain updates when patterns shift is still debated.

Six experiments had people detect visual targets around and inside a circle where outer items followed a place or angle rule that then changed without warning. Detection fell for all events right after a rule break, based on modeling the authors report. Recovery took several trials after a rare break but became instant when breaks came often. Expectation thus aids seeing broadly, at a cost when rules change.
pmc-13293795:
Lidan Zhang and co-authors pool, in a 2026 review, infection risk for the gut drug vedolizumab in inflammatory bowel disease, comparing it with rival drug classes and placebo. Infection safety shapes drug choice in lifelong gut illness, and pooled rates vary widely by study.

Sixty-six studies with 24,000 patients were combined, with infection grading set to a shared standard. Overall infection incidence pooled at 13.08% in the authors' model, led by airway infections, while serious infections stayed rare. Risk matched tumor necrosis factor drugs and placebo, but ran higher than with ustekinumab. Wide spread between studies limits the pooled rate's use.
pmc-13293995:
Ying Li, Yanxia Cai, and Xiaoyan Xu report a 2026 case where many skin nodules were the first sign of angioimmunoblastic T-cell lymphoma. Skin involvement in that lymphoma usually means rash or itching, so firm nodules mislead easily. Their patient was a 53-year-old man with a 1-month history of painless lumps on trunk and upper limbs, sized 0.5–2 cm, plus dark red plaques.

Tests showed mild anemia, raised inflammation markers, low IgA, high IgE, and widespread lymph node swelling. Biopsy showed lost node structure with atypical cells positive for CD3, CD4, PD-1, and EBER, giving stage III disease. Six cycles of chidamide plus CHOP brought full remission, still holding at 6 months.
pmc-13294295:
Sinja Kristiansen and coauthors census gonorrhea care at six Swedish university clinics in a 2026 study. Cases from 2022 totaled 1,060, about a third of all national cases that year, with 27.3% women, 72.4% men, and 4 transgender persons in the reported breakdown. Nucleic acid tests covered urine, genital, and rectal sampling sites, and drug resistance was charted.

Positivity ran highest in genital samples from women and in rectal samples, mostly among men who have sex with men. Resistance hit 43.7% for ciprofloxacin and 9.4% for azithromycin in the reported shares. Multi-site infection and fading drug options make management complex, the authors conclude.
pmc-13294395:
Mengqi Yang and a large team review multifunctional nano-drugs for solid tumors in a 2026 article organized by tumor neighborhood type. Potency alone fails when vessels block entry, stroma blocks spread, and immunity stays off. Platforms now bundle longer circulation, vessel and stroma tuning, trigger-based release, immune priming, and imaging guidance in one particle.

Human leakiness effects vary, targeting gains in people stay uncertain, and each added module complicates manufacturing and safety proof. The authors sort designs by barrier, goal, readout, and evidence strength. Future wins likely come from matching simpler platforms to measured tumor types, not from piling on features.
pmc-13294495:
Gabriela Gavalova and colleagues probe emotion reading errors in psychotic disorders with aggression history in a 2026 study. Groups held 79 people with psychosis plus past interpersonal aggression, 72 with psychosis alone, and 86 healthy controls. A lifelike task showed faces, voices, and both together across 12 emotions, scoring accuracy and confusion patterns by valence and arousal.

Accuracy stepped down cleanly across groups, worst in the aggression group. That group also more often mistook negative feelings for positive ones. Thinking speed and emotion word knowledge predicted scores most strongly, with schooling, gender, and past substance history adding smaller effects. Group status still mattered after all adjustments.
pmc-13294695:
Alişan Burak Yaşar and Anıl Gündüz propose a new psychotherapy framework called Smart Therapy in a 2026 article. Many proven treatment manuals exist, yet dropout and resistance stay common and clinicians often mix methods without shared rules. No standard guidance tells clinicians how to choose and order interventions for each person.

Assessment comes first across three domains: bodily prerequisites, deep memory patterns from hardship, and unhelpful thinking habits. Treatment then follows five sequenced levels, starting with shared goals and health screening before matched psychological work. The model aims to close the gap between research protocols and everyday practice by tying each intervention choice to assessed need.
pmc-13294895:
Maria J. Suota and colleagues turn a papermaking by-product into a water-cleaning charcoal, in a 2026 study. Lignin left over from kraft pulping is abundant and carbon-rich, and the team used a commercial LignoForce version from both hardwood and softwood. Mixing it with potassium phosphate and heating it by microwave for twenty-five minutes at moderate temperature produced porous biochar at close to half the starting weight.

Surface analysis showed an amorphous, sponge-like carbon riddled with micro and meso pores, holding a quarter of the original oxygen in useful surface groups. Tested against methylene blue, a common dye pollutant, the chars removed more than ninety-four percent, working better as the water grew less acidic. The hardwood version captured dye slightly faster than the softwood one. The authors pitch microwave pyrolysis as a fast, energy-lean route from pulp waste to cleanup material.
pmc-13295595:
Yongqi Xu and Ruining Jin ask whether strict or lenient parenting changes how much teenagers dread being judged, in a 2026 study titled with a choice between iron fists and velvet gloves. Puberty brings visible change and sharp self-consciousness, and the distress of feeling watched or discussed is its own outcome, narrower than general anxiety. Using survey data from 3,591 secondary students in Shenzhen, the pair applied Bayesian analysis to puberty stress and two parenting styles.

Puberty stress tracked clearly with social evaluative distress: the more stressful the bodily changes felt, the worse the fear of judgment. Authoritarian parenting also came with higher distress on its own. Permissive parenting showed no clear direct link. Neither style clearly amplified or cushioned the puberty stress connection, despite the intuitive appeal of an interaction. The authors argue schools should treat puberty stress itself, and harsh control, as the targets.
pmc-13295895:
Haruka Ito and colleagues translate a questionnaire on detail focus and mental flexibility into Japanese and test how well it works, in a 2026 study. The Detail and Flexibility Questionnaire gauges two traits tied to autism: sharp notice of detail and rigid thinking. Sixty people with autism and one hundred forty without took the new version plus a known autism trait scale.

The Japanese scale held together well as a whole, with one weak item. Its scores tracked the known scale's detail and switching parts closely, backing that it measures what it claims. The autism group scored apart from the other group on both rigidity and detail parts. The authors offer the tool for clinic and research use in Japan, giving a fuller read on autism-linked thinking.
pmc-13296195:
Anakha Udayakumar and co-authors test, in 2026, whether a chemical change on the protein OSTM1 explains how the kinase LRRK1 drives bone-eating cells. Mice lacking LRRK1 develop overly dense bone because their osteoclasts cannot break bone down, and tagging of OSTM1 fades in those cells.

A version of OSTM1 that mimics the tag partly restored bone breakdown in deficient cells, while a version blocking the tag did not. Mice built with the mimicking variant grew normally, and adding it to deficient mice boosted osteoclast activity and bone formation. The authors name OSTM1 tagging as a key link worth targeting.
pmc-13297495:
Michael Jason Nathenson and colleagues pool three trials to set a benchmark for trabectedin, a standard chemotherapy, in a rare soft-tissue cancer, in a 2026 analysis. The cancer, myxoid and round cell liposarcoma, often returns or spreads after first treatment. Trial records came from an open data project at Yale University.

Sixty-three patients with advanced cancer that surgery could not remove were included. Half were still alive at twenty-two and a half months after treatment began. About one patient in six saw tumours shrink, and over three quarters had disease held in check for a time. As one of the largest groups studied for this rare cancer, the pooled figures give future drugs a fair yardstick.
pmc-13297695:
Ontario-wide records show CAR T-cell therapy for lymphoma performs in everyday care much as it did in trials, according to a 2026 population study led by Lee Mozessohn. Using provincial administrative databases, the team followed patients with diffuse large B-cell lymphoma treated after relapse or failed earlier therapy.

Survival and toxicity in routine practice matched the pivotal trial results, and hospital use resembled figures from other registry reports. The authors describe the treatment as relatively safe in real-world hands for this aggressive lymphoma. They also argue that future studies should build in formal health technology assessment, so decision makers can weigh clinical gains against the therapy's considerable demands on the system.
pmc-13297795:
Clear aligners made in the dental office move front teeth sideways accurately but rotate them less faithfully, found a 2026 retrospective analysis by Gina Marie Georgi and colleagues. They compared planned and achieved positions in 21 dental arches from 14 patients treated with in-office SureSmile aligners.

Side-to-side shifts missed the plan by small margins, all under the 0.5 mm clinical threshold, with vertical movement off by 0.38 mm on average. Angular control was weaker: angulation differed by 3.42 degrees and axial rotation by 4.50 degrees, both beyond the 2-degree threshold. The authors suggest clinicians plan extra correction for rotations and counsel patients accordingly.
pmc-13298595:
A clotting protein outperformed the usual blood markers for spotting appendicitis in children, report Hilmi Onur Kabukçu and co-authors in a 2026 single-center study. They compared 145 children who had CT scans for abdominal pain: 62 with nonspecific pain, 44 with uncomplicated appendicitis, and 39 with complicated disease.

Fibrinogen rose stepwise across the three groups and separated appendicitis from nonspecific pain with an AUC of 0.95, ahead of CRP, white cell counts, and related ratios. It also held up as an independent predictor in adjusted analysis. The authors propose fibrinogen as a promising addition to workups, pending larger prospective confirmation.
pmc-13298995:
Math can guide the design of virus cocktails that hunt drug-resistant bacteria, argue Rob J de Boer and colleagues in a 2026 modeling paper. They extended a mouse-calibrated model to human phage therapy, where several bacterial strains and several phages interact and resistance keeps evolving.

Fitting the model to one successful human case, they found success hinged on how resistant the bacteria already were before treatment and on giving diverse cocktails early. Once a good cocktail was in place, fine-tuning infection rates mattered little. Resistant strains surged as sensitive ones fell. Their prescription: hit hard and early with a varied set of phages to raise the barrier against resistance.
pmc-13299395:
Mohammad Barouqa and colleagues set blood count reference ranges for people with the Duffy-null blood type, in a 2026 laboratory study. This inherited type, common in some populations, comes with naturally lower white cell and neutrophil counts despite healthy lives. Standard ranges can mislabel such people as abnormal.

Records spanning six years identified 122 healthy Duffy-null adults. Their median counts sat far below institutional medians, and the derived reference intervals fell under conventional thresholds, with the lower neutrophil bound beneath the usual neutropenia cutoff. Adopting type-specific ranges could cut misclassification, spare needless procedures, and support personalised care, the authors argue.
pmc-13300095:
The Asian corn borer damages maize across much of Asia, and its immune defenses shape how well microbial pest control works. Xinran Jia and colleagues report a 2026 functional study of OfPGRP-B, a peptidoglycan recognition protein in this moth. They produced the protein in Escherichia coli and ran a battery of laboratory assays.

OfPGRP-B killed bacteria only weakly, yet it clumped them strongly and cut peptidoglycan with amidase activity. It also boosted activation of the prophenoloxidase cascade when bacterial wall material was present, without changing melanization. The authors read the protein as a working part of borer immunity, useful knowledge for designing biological controls that target host defenses.
pmc-13300895:
Christoph Anders and co-authors compare back extensor strength between healthy women and men in a 2026 study of 239 adults. Each volunteer performed a maximal isometric trunk extension test standing upright. The team also converted upper body weight into the torque it imposes, so strength could be judged against the load each person's own body presents.

In absolute terms men were much stronger, producing about 241 newton meters against 162 in women, and their upper body torque was likewise higher. Once strength was divided by that body imposed load, the sex gap stopped meeting the authors' strict relevance criteria, which required a clear statistical, effect size, and importance threshold all at once. Both sexes held roughly a one hundred percent reserve above their own upper body weight. The authors conclude that raw reference values mislead, and fair strength standards must be scaled to body build.
pmc-13300995:
Two back-wall nerve blocks spared opioids after gallbladder keyhole surgery in a 2026 randomized trial by Özlem Turhan and colleagues. One hundred twenty adults were split three ways: erector spinae plane block, thoracic paravertebral block, or intravenous pain relief alone. Everyone received standard anesthesia plus paracetamol, tenoxicam, and patient-controlled tramadol for comparison.

Over the first day, the intravenous group used 135.78 milligrams of tramadol, against 101.05 with the erector spinae block and 95.67 with the paravertebral block. Pain scores and rescue needs also favored both blocks, and recovery quality scores rose. The erector spinae block was quicker to perform, with no complications in any arm.
pmc-13301995:
V Alexeenko and co-authors explore, in a 2026 veterinary study, whether maths applied to ordinary resting heart traces can flag racehorses prone to extra beats during exercise. Such stray beats during hard work may impair performance and could raise the risk of collapse. Finding at-risk horses currently requires exercising ECG recordings, which are not always practical.

Ambulatory traces from 91 Thoroughbred and Standardbred horses were recorded during routine training. Complexity and entropy measures were calculated from quiet sixty-second strips, using several ways of handling the signal. One method, based on pattern compression of specific waveform points, separated cases from controls with reasonable accuracy. Its strongest use was ruling horses out, with a very high negative predictive value, so it may serve as a first screening step.
pmc-13302295:
I Doundoulakis and co-authors report eight-year results from the PRESERVE EF study in a 2026 paper on heart attack survivors whose pumping strength stayed fairly good. Such patients sit outside usual defibrillator criteria, yet some remain at risk of lethal rhythms. The study tested a two-step screen ending in an invasive stimulation test.

Screening covered 575 patients, and about a third carried at least one non-invasive risk flag. Stimulation testing found inducible dangerous rhythms in a minority, and nearly all of those patients received a defibrillator. Over roughly nine years, no sudden deaths occurred, while twelve defibrillators fired appropriately. The approach detected every event in advance, and events clustered in patients with mildly reduced pumping strength.
pmc-13303095:
Nikolas Nikolaidis writes, in a 2026 editorial, that cell biology has misfiled lipids as mere scenery for proteins, and introduces a special issue proving otherwise. The collected studies argue that fats in membranes are read by proteins with real precision and shape what proteins do. Two examples open the argument from distant fields.

A lentil protein was shown to grip one rare signalling lipid at a defined pocket, with two amino acids handling contact and docking in turn. In neurons, a raft lipid called GM1 actively pushed amyloid-beta into more toxic shapes on the membrane it inhabits. Later pieces examine how membrane geometry and phase behaviour constrain protein structure. The editorial closes by listing what the field still lacks.
pmc-13303495:
Rawan AlSaad and co-authors present a 2026 systematic review of artificial intelligence tools that predict heavy bleeding after childbirth. Standard risk scores rely on fixed factors and can miss changes that unfold during labor.

Following PRISMA guidance, the team reviewed studies from 2015 to 2025 and included 33 papers. Most work appeared after 2023, used past records from a single site, and aimed to sort risk before delivery. Classic machine learning dominated, all datasets were closed, and outside validation was rare. Shared labeling rules, larger shared datasets, and testing during real care are presented as next steps.
pmc-13303595:
Karuna Rasineni and Patricia Sue Grigson write a 2026 editorial introducing a collection on GLP-1 receptor agonist drugs. These long-acting medicines have changed care for obesity and type 2 diabetes, conditions that carry a heavy global toll.

Papers in the collection weigh benefits, harms, and costs across drug versions. Other papers look at effects after weight-loss surgery and on the brain reward system, eyes, heart, liver, and swollen limbs after breast cancer care. Other papers pool trial data and adverse event reports to measure gut and other side effects. The set frames both promise and caution for wider use.
pmc-13303695:
Carlotta Franceschi and co-authors review biologic injections for kneecap joint problems in a 2026 systematic synthesis. Such products are well studied for whole-knee arthritis, but proof for wear limited to the joint behind the kneecap has stayed thin.

Four databases were searched for human studies of platelet-rich plasma or mesenchymal stromal cell products in kneecap cartilage damage or arthritis. Nine studies qualified, split between the two product types. Despite weak study quality overall, patients generally improved on clinical scores and sometimes on scans, and both approaches beat comparison care. Larger, stronger trials are still needed before routine use.
pmc-13304195:
Riya Rawal, Anita Thyagarajan, and Ravi P. Sahu study a smoke pollutant's effect on lung cancer cells in a 2026 laboratory report. Benzo[a]pyrene, found in tobacco smoke and cooked food, is a known carcinogen, but its sway over targeted drug response was unclear.

Cancer cells exposed to the pollutant did not die more, yet they moved more, grew more, formed more colonies, and shed more tiny particles. A cell receptor blocker and a fat-processing blocker stopped those changes, tying them to one signaling path. Reassuringly, the pollutant did not blunt the targeted drugs tested, and the receptor emerges as a possible new drug target.
pmc-13305595:
Vida Garousi, Fattaneh Khalaj, and Elham Mirzaian present a 2026 case of a primary neuroendocrine tumor in the testicle, a growth making up under one percent of testicle tumors. Vague signs and look-alike growths make this rare cancer easy to misread.

A 21-year-old man had a painless left testicle lump with rich blood flow and calcium flecks on scans, while blood tumor markers stayed normal. Removal showed a neat, slow-growing tumor with the classic speckled cell pattern, and stain tests confirmed hormone-type cells with very low growth activity. Under the 2022 World Health Organization scheme it classed as the prepubertal type, needing long follow-up.
pmc-13307595:
Jalajakshi Kopparthi and colleagues study a tick-borne dog disease in 2026 across Andhra Pradesh, India, sampling 442 suspected cases at ninety veterinary dispensaries. Blood was checked by microscope and by gene testing for Ehrlichia canis, a bacterium carried by the brown dog tick. Sequence checks on one bacterial gene confirmed the circulating strains.

Gene testing found more positives than microscopy, confirming its value as a field confirmatory test. Female dogs, mongrels, kennel dogs, and tick-infested dogs carried higher infection odds. Dogs with a history of tick control measures showed lower odds instead. Local isolates closely matched earlier Indian and international sequences. The authors offer the regional picture for better diagnosis and surveillance planning. Tick control remains the clearest preventive lever their data support.
pmc-13308495:
Eric Muteba Vukulu and colleagues study how grave sexual abuse was in 2026 among 195 teens at two intake centres in Kinshasa, in the Congo. Standard forms gauged abuse history, mental distress, and self-esteem over five months in 2025. Data on gravity in this at-risk group were scarce before.

More than half of the teens said they faced sexual abuse, with nearly a fifth rating it severe. Female sex, cannabis use, and several family setups tied on their own to greater gravity after controls. Bond to the mother or to a third person also linked to higher gravity scores, a pattern needing careful reading. Alcohol showed an inverse link in their model. The authors demand joint prevention, screening, and support care. They caution strongly that their tools lack formal testing in local culture, so every figure should be read with that limit in mind.
pmc-13308595:
Ayuba Akinpelu and co-authors show in 2026 that long exposure to high fluid pressure dulls how moving cells read the physical world around them. Pressure kept cells less swayed by base stiffness, fluid thickness, flow force, and flow block for days after the cue was lifted.

The team traced the shift to a quieter Rho and MRTF path, with a backup sensing mode that needs no myosin pull to work. Stiff bases then sped the primed cells by firming their grip points and spreading them to the cell edge. Models foresaw the shift, and dish tests bore it out. Pressure may thus prime wandering cancer cells in lasting ways.
pmc-13309195:
Allison Crawford and Tristan Glatard urge in 2026 urgent steps for suicide prevention as young people turn to chat based AI tools in distress, often before family or doctors. In a United States poll of 1060 teens aged 13 to 17 years, 72 percent said they use an AI helper, and 52 percent do so often.

Most AI suicide tools lack sound guards, and some suits claim chat tools steered youth toward attempts, means, and farewell notes. The authors say tools must own their AI nature, explain their advice, prompt users to ask why, and act as a bridge to human care, never a wall. Human bonds stay the core shield, so tools should push people toward live support, not replace it.
pmc-13309395:
Giulia Giacomucci and colleagues report a 2026 study on blood tests that may warn of early Alzheimer changes. The patients had subjective cognitive decline, meaning they felt their memory slipping while standard tests stayed normal. The team asked which blood marker best tracks later thinking changes.

Seventy-six patients gave blood and took detailed thinking tests at the start and again two years later. A marker called p-tau217 tracked memory decline most closely, with mid-range results falling between clear negative and clear positive groups. Two other markers showed weaker or mixed links. The authors suggest p-tau217 may help spot who needs closer follow-up in this early stage.
pmc-13309895:
Anastasios Koulaouzidis writes a 2026 letter to the editor about ultrasound checks for a swallowed capsule before bowel camera exams. A patency capsule is first swallowed to prove the gut is open; finding where it sits matters before the camera capsule follows. A study by Matsuura and colleagues had praised ultrasound as a radiation-free first step.

The letter argues that scans where the capsule was not seen were counted as negative results, which inflates the claimed accuracy. Ultrasound located the capsule clearly in 28 of 34 patients, while 6 of 34 stayed unclear and still needed CT scanning in the cited study. A not-seen scan should count as undecided, the author holds. The piece urges honest reporting of test limits.
pmc-13310395:
Yaodie Peng and co-authors relate lung exercise capacity to airway and air-sac damage in COPD in a 2026 study. Chronic obstructive pulmonary disease narrows airways and destroys air sacs in differing mixes per patient. Whether air-sac loss or airway thickening tracks exercise limits more closely was unclear.

Ninety-three stable patients underwent lung function tests, chest CT scans, and exercise testing. Scan measures split patients into four types: normal, air-sac dominant, airway dominant, and mixed. Air-sac dominant and mixed patients showed worse airflow ratios in the reported results. Statistical models tied each scan measure to exercise outcomes. The authors conclude air-sac damage tracks exercise capacity more strongly than airway thickness in this group.
pmc-13310495:
Chuan-Yen Sun and co-authors validate a simplified home sleep test against the lab standard in a 2026 study. Sleep apnea is common and needs early spotting, yet lab testing is heavy and home kits often need many sensors. A chest-worn heart monitor that reads breathing from heart-lung coupling could ease setup.

A total of 479 participants enrolled across the centers, and the device event index was compared with the lab apnea score for each night. pmc-13312495:

pmc-13315195:
