pmc-13328495:
Qilian Xia and co-authors set out a trial of electrical acupoint stimulation for nerve pain after breast surgery in a 2026 protocol. Damage to the intercostobrachial nerve brings lasting numbness and burning pain from armpit to inner arm, plus stiff shoulders, and standard care lacks a nerve-repair routine. The planned trial runs at a traditional medicine hospital in Yunnan.

Two hundred patients will be randomized evenly to real or sham stimulation starting the first day after surgery, given every other day. The method joins acupuncture points with skin-level electric pulses and may help axons regrow and rewrap, early work hints. Pain, feeling, shoulder movement, and safety will judge whether the gentle method earns routine use.
pmc-13329495:
Hailai Hagos Tesfay and team hunted candidate genes for semen quality in Rhode Island Red chickens. Their 2026 weighted single-step genome-wide association study sized up genetic factors and mapped five semen traits key to breeding success and poultry profits. Heritability scores ran from 0.097 at the low end to 0.322 at the high end, showing low to middling heritability, and the study turned up 29 major gene loci and twelve candidate genes.

Gene loci sat on chromosomes 4 and 13 for semen volume, chromosome 4 for sperm motility, and chromosomes 2 and 6 for abnormal sperm rate. Four strong back-to-back regions shared by volume and motility, at 59.83 megabases to 61.43 megabases, explained 11.55% of variance for volume and 16.33% of variance for motility. The biggest-effect variants inside those spans hit both volume and motility, giving markers for marker-assisted selection. The team calls the findings a science base for genetic gain in chicken semen quality.
pmc-13329795:
Concepcion Padilla and a large team test whether thinking scores can flag who with mild impairment will develop dementia in a 2026 study. The group drew 349 patients from the SPIN cohort who had broad baseline testing between 2009 and 2021 and later follow-up visits. Composite scores covered several thinking domains.

Over 3 years, 37.8 percent of patients moved to dementia in the reported follow-up, while most stayed stable. Those who converted were older and scored lower across all domains at baseline. A tuned model sorted risk well, with repeat checks naming age, sex, schooling, and memory and planning scores as steady predictors. Right-call rates for ruling out and ruling in decline are detailed by the authors for clinic use.
pmc-13329895:
Vimal Ramanuj and co-authors model gas flow and transfer inside hollow fibre bundles for gas separation in a 2026 study. Such modules clean gases by letting chosen gases pass through fibre walls. The team studied bundle-scale flow, where uneven channels and direction effects shape how well gases move and separate.

Results show a trade-off between purity and recovery, the authors report. Smaller fibres give more surface area and higher purity, yet gases reach less deeply into tight bundles, which hurts overall performance. Measures such as a permeability tensor and Sherwood number capture the direction effects. The authors highlight settings where gains balance best. Better bundle design could cut losses and pressure needs in plant-scale modules.
pmc-13330695:
K Jonsson and colleagues survey hands-on skill practice among nursing students in Scandinavia in a 2026 study. Students from Denmark, Norway, and Sweden answered a questionnaire in 2023 about placements. In total, 706 students reported how often they performed core skills, from breathing and circulation care to medication tasks.

Practice rates ran low and uneven across all study years and skill areas in the reported results. Supervision was mostly at hand, yet some skills lacked enough preceptor input. Gaps spanned basic daily care as well as drug tasks. The authors warn that thin practice may weaken readiness for real wards. Placement planning needs firmer guarantees for core skills, they argue.
pmc-13330795:
Mitali Singh and team studied Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitors for Waldenström macroglobulinemia. Their 2026 single-center retrospective analysis reviewed records of patients on these inhibitors, pulling details, findings, imaging, treatment, response, adverse events, and infections. Waldenström macroglobulinemia is a clonal B-cell disorder with monoclonal IgM paraprotein, once treated with chemotherapy plus an anti-CD20 antibody, before inhibitor approval shifted treatment.

12 patients got ibrutinib and 10 acalabrutinib, with median age 64 years. MYD88 L265P showed up in 90.5% of cases and CXCR4 mutations in 13.3% of the patients treated. Anemia was the most common treatment reason at 50%. Overall response reached 81.8%, with major response at 63.7% of the patients treated. At a median 30 months, overall survival was 91% and progression-free survival 82%. Neutropenia affected 27.3% and thrombocytopenia 31.8% of the patients treated. Rates were 9.1% for bleeding, 13.6% for arrhythmias, and 81.8% for infections, of the patients treated. The team concludes these inhibitors work well but carry high side effects.
pmc-13331795:
Clark Mbou-Boutambe and colleagues surveyed rodents across 11 rural sites in Gabon for 2026 work on Trypanosoma lewisi, a rat parasite that has spread worldwide with its hosts. They screened 528 rodents with a gene test aimed at the wider Herpetosoma group.

Parasite DNA turned up at every site, in 56.6 percent of animals overall, and in the invasive black rat at rates from 21.6 to 85.7 percent across home-area sites. A few native species also tested positive, one at 100 percent in a small sample. Sequencing a long gene fragment from 21 positive samples showed all belonged to the T. lewisi subgroup known as genotype AF05b. The authors say invasive rats likely amplify these parasites in Gabon and should be watched as a possible source of human infection.
pmc-13332195:
Helma David and colleagues test a 2026 heat-sensitive gel that pairs two drugs against stubborn Candida biofilms. Drug-resistant Candida albicans, notably in recurrent vaginal yeast infection, exposes the limits of single-drug antifungal care. The team built a gel that sticks to moist linings and carries acarbose, a sugar-like diabetes drug, together with fluconazole. Alone, acarbose showed only mild antifungal action, but with fluconazole it sharply boosted killing.

The pair broke up biofilms, blocked the yeast's shape switch, and stopped regrowth after treatment in lab assays. Checkerboard and time-kill tests showed strong synergy against Candida species, including patient isolates, with a drop of over two log units in viable counts. The gel, built from poloxamer plus chitosan and HPMC polymers, released drugs over time. It offers a local, dual-drug route against biofilm infections that single drugs fail to clear.
pmc-13332795:
Xingwei You and Zhongwei Guo review brain imaging evidence on apathy in Alzheimer's disease in a 2026 review. Apathy, a loss of goal-directed drive, is the most common behavioral symptom of the disease. It burdens caregivers heavily, and it is now thought to rest on its own brain biology rather than trailing memory decline.

Across imaging studies published up to 2025, the review locates the core fault in the prefrontal and basal ganglia motivation circuit. Shrinkage and low activity in the anterior cingulate and orbitofrontal cortex track with failed reward weighing, while dorsolateral prefrontal damage fits planning problems. Network studies show a muted default mode system, and molecular scans add locus coeruleus decay, dopamine signaling faults, and amyloid plus tau buildup inside the circuit. The authors back family-based rating, since patients often cannot see their apathy, and point to dopamine and noradrenaline drugs plus magnetic brain stimulation as options.
pmc-13333095:
Bashir A Bashir and colleagues study 2026 whether routine blood-cell indices can sort dengue-related low blood-cell counts by cause and predict bleeding. Low blood-cell counts mark dengue infection, yet the causes behind different low-count patterns remain clinically underexplored. Those indices, drawn from standard blood counts, may offer a swift, accessible way to separate causes and gauge risk. The team set out to test those indices for mechanistic sorting, bleeding prediction, and a preliminary risk score.

The case-control study included 334 dengue cases and 101 controls, examining cell count, plateletcrit, immature platelet fraction, mean platelet volume, distribution width, large cell measures, and clotting parameters. Low-count cases were classified into cause-based patterns detailed in the full paper. The work gives clinicians a bedside-friendly route to bleeding risk sorting in dengue, plus a first Dengue Bleeding Risk Score for future testing.
pmc-13333295:
Rezan Bakır and colleagues built a benchmark dataset in 2026 for teaching machines to predict hydrogen output from a light-driven chemical process. Clean hydrogen from photocatalysis is promising, but conditions interact in tangled ways and are hard to model from theory alone.

At Sivas University of Science and Technology, the team ran controlled batch reactor experiments. They used a graphene-supported lanthanum ferrite catalyst and sucrose solution as the helper chemical, measuring evolved hydrogen by gas chromatography. A Box–Behnken design varied solution pH, catalyst strength, and starting hydrogen peroxide strength in a structured grid. The result is 1,370 data points, each tying one input combination to its hydrogen yield, released through Kaggle with raw and scaled versions plus heatmaps and importance charts. The authors present it as the first shared benchmark for AI models in this kind of photocatalysis.
pmc-13333395:
Shihui Li and colleagues show in a 2026 immunology study that boosting one small protein helps killer T cells endure the long grind of chronic infection. Constant antigen exposure usually exhausts CD8 T cells, and keeping a working pool of them has been an unsolved problem for therapy design.

The clue came from cancer survivors' vaccine-specific T cells that had persisted for years with high levels of NOSIP, a nitric oxide synthase interacting protein. Forcing extra NOSIP into CD8 T cells kept more of them in a less worn, CX3CR1-negative state. It blocked their slide toward a death-prone CX3CR1-high state, cutting cell death and extending persistence under chronic stimulation. In a tumor model, the boosted cells controlled cancer better than ordinary ones. They also answered more strongly to PD-L1 blockade treatment. The authors nominate NOSIP as a target for making cell therapies last.
pmc-13333695:
Daniel W. Griepp and a large team of co-authors looked back over a decade of cranial infections that needed skull surgery in a 2026 retrospective cohort study. The series covers both infections after earlier operations and spontaneous infections such as subdural empyema and brain abscess.

The team studied 43 adults treated at one high-volume neurosurgical center between 2015 and 2025. Cultures were positive in 41 cases, most often growing Cutibacterium acnes, Staphylococcus aureus, or Streptococcus intermedius. IV antibiotics ran a median of six weeks, and some patients needed repeat surgery. At a median follow-up of 11 months, about two-thirds of survivors with full data reached a good working outcome. The decade of work offers hands-on guidance on germs, treatment length, and likely recovery.
pmc-13335795:
Qing‐qing Xu and colleagues study 2026 mTORC2 tagging of GSDME-N driving Cullin4B-mediated protein-breakdown removal to suppress cell bursting and confer RT resistance in small cell lung cancer. RT resistance is a main reason for treatment failure in patients with small cell lung cancer. Finding the key process matters for preventing RT resistance in this cancer. An unbiased CRISPR screen identifies GSDME, a member of the Gasdermin family, as a key driver of RT response in small cell lung cancer.

Furthermore, mTORC2 aids RT resistance by blocking GSDME-N cell bursting. In detail, mTORC2 tags GSDME-N at serine 114, promoting gathering of the CUL4B-RBBP4 E3 ligase complex. This complex drives K48-linked tagging of GSDME-N at lysine 41, leading to its protein-breakdown removal. In patients, high mTORC2 is linked to a poor outlook in small cell lung cancer patients.
pmc-13336495:
Chang Zhang and colleagues study 2026 how METTL1-driven m7G tagging drives skin swelling in psoriasis by steadying Bdkrb1 and drawing in white cells. The role of RNA tags, notably N7-methylguanosine (m7G), in swelling conditions such as psoriasis remains not fully clear. This study shows that METTL1, an m7G tagger, is greatly raised in skin cells of human skin spots and in mouse models of the disease.

Using mice with METTL1 switched off only in skin cells, the work finds much weaker disease-like swelling. Fewer white cells enter skin, versus mice with METTL1 intact. In detail, METTL1 drives swelling by boosting Bdkrb1 message steadiness through m7G tagging. This steadiness lifts BDKRB1 protein levels, which switch on the p38 MAPK path in skin cells. That path spurs release of key CXCL signal proteins and strong white-cell movement toward skin.
pmc-13336895:
Xin Jin and colleagues uncovered an immune suppressing chain in kidney cancer in 2026 and reversed it with lipid nanoparticles. Iron overload is common in cancer and worsens renal cell carcinoma, yet its effect on tumour immunity was unclear. The team found excess iron lowers the enzyme ZDHHC12 in killer T cells, which destabilises a mitochondrial protein and triggers copper dependent cell death.

That death pathway weakens T cell attack and dulls checkpoint blockade therapy. Nanoparticles carrying the Zdhhc12 message restored protein tagging, rescued T cell function, and improved treatment response in models. The work links iron balance, T cell survival, and immunotherapy success, opening a new combination strategy for kidney cancer.
pmc-13337095:
Weitong Gao and colleagues trace lung cancer immunotherapy resistance to a missing RNA editor in a 2026 study. Tumors lacking RBM10 built a suppressive setting rich in M2 macrophages, the calm, tumor-helping type. The loss warped splicing of the sensor STING, shifting its form balance.

The shifted STING raised output of CCL7, a signal that summons macrophages through CCR2 and pushes them toward M2. Those macrophages even donated mitochondria to tumor cells, feeding the loop. Blocking CCL7 or CCR2 alongside PD-1 inhibition drove regression in RBM10-deficient tumors. The splicing-to-signal chain gives clinicians a targetable route around a common resistance pattern.
pmc-13337395:
Yuan Liu and a large team test whether psychological distress raises thyroid cancer risk in a 2026 UK Biobank cohort study. The cohort held 420,187 participants aged 39–73 years enrolled between 2006 and 2010, with distress read from hospital records, a short health questionnaire, and self-reported symptoms. Cancer outcomes came from national registries.

Distress was linked to a hazard ratio of 1.33 for thyroid cancer in the adjusted models, a modest but clear increase. Body measures and lifestyle explained part of the link: waist size carried the largest mediating share at 11.80% of the effect in the mediation analysis, joined by body mass index, blood lipids, and alcohol use. The results tie mental health to cancer risk partly through metabolic paths.
pmc-13338695:
Scott Schoninger and colleagues review adenovirus infection in people with blood cancers and stem cell transplants, in a 2026 survey. Adenovirus can range from silent DNA in blood to pneumonia, gut disease, hepatitis, bladder bleeding, heart disease, and brain disease in these patients. Quantitative PCR now finds the virus earlier, but no agreed viral load cutoff guides treatment.

Risk climbs with T-cell depletion, cord blood transplant, severe graft-versus-host disease, high-dose steroids, and slow immune recovery, and children face higher rates than adults. Death remains substantial once virus spreads through blood or organs. The review weighs diagnosis, monitoring, and treatment options, helping transplant teams balance early action against drug toxicity.
pmc-13339895:
Meshack Tweya Omwega and colleagues systematically build three-phage cocktails against drug-resistant Pseudomonas aeruginosa in a 2026 study. Single phages invite resistance, and cocktails are usually mixed by guesswork. A combinatorial method tested interactions directly on clinical isolates.

From 25 candidate phages, five with broad reach covering at least 60 percent of 51 resistant isolates were kept as reported. Ten triples were scored with a real-time growth system and an independence model. Single phages blocked 35.4 to 75.4 percent of growth as reported. Only one triple acted in synergy, reaching 84.1 percent inhibition, while half the triples clashed.
pmc-13341295:
LED lighting shapes both the nutrition and safety of microgreens, according to a 2026 review by Anushuya Guragain and coauthors. Microgreens are young seedlings packed with micronutrients, usually raised indoors where light spectrum, intensity, and day length can be tuned precisely.

Studies show these light settings shift growth, yield, and nutrient content, though results vary by species and most work covers the Brassicaceae family. Photoperiod remains barely studied. A bigger gap concerns microbes: pathogens can persist on microgreens, yet almost no research tracks their survival under LED systems during production or storage. The authors call for full food safety protocols built around LED growing.
pmc-13341595:
A protective gene shared by two inflammatory diseases is identified by Qinjin Dai and colleagues in a 2026 integrative study. Behçet's disease and inflammatory bowel disease overlap clinically, so the team combined single-cell blood data with genetic causal inference to hunt common targets.

Both diseases showed a shrunken pool of a specific helper T cell type, within which 45 signature genes emerged. Mendelian randomization singled out BTN3A2 as protective in both conditions, and its genetic signals aligned spatially with disease risk signals. Validation ran through a mouse eye inflammation model, outside datasets, and patient blood samples, strengthening the case for a shared treatment target.
pmc-13345895:
Samuel David Williamson and colleagues reviewed in 2026 prior work on animal-assisted treatment in spinal cord injury rehabilitation. Dogs and other animals are increasingly used to support walking, breathing, and well-being after injury, yet no overview had gathered the studies in one place.

Seven databases were searched systematically, with double screening and double data extraction, admitting only peer-reviewed studies of adults with spinal cord injury that tested an animal-assisted intervention in rehabilitation. The review assembles what has actually been tried, for whom, and with what measured effects. It gives therapists and researchers a baseline for deciding where animal-assisted work is promising, where evidence is thin, and what trials should test next.
pmc-13347395:
Asmaa M. Arafa and colleagues grow an endangered henbane in tissue culture to raise its drug alkaloids, in a study from 2026. Egyptian Hyoscyamus albus makes scopolamine and hyoscyamine that are hard to build in a lab. So callus and hairy root cultures were fed zinc oxide in plain and nano forms at varied doses, and extracts were profiled by gas methods.

Hairy roots beat the parent plant for scopolamine output, and culture-only tropinone appeared in the profiles in the reported scans. Plain zinc oxide led atropine gains in callus, while nano and plain forms split the lead for roots and their medium. Extracts also fought microbes and curbed their virulence traits.
pmc-13347695:
Clara Davoine, Gaël Cobraiville, Lionel Pochet, and Marianne Fillet measure drug binding on tiny membrane sacs taken from cancer cells, in a methods study published in 2026. Golgi sacs keep membrane proteins in near-native settings, yet binding there is hard to read. So capillary flow methods plus new maths were used to get direct affinity values without labels, tags, or large protein excess.

Tests centred on UGCG, a Golgi protein of cancer interest, using fairly even sacs near 150 nm across that kept native inner structure in the reported checks. Tiny sample needs and options for charged or plain compounds widen the method to many membrane targets, offering drug hunters a truer test bed than purified protein alone.
pmc-13347995:
Marwa Beleidy and colleagues tested in 2026 whether nano-sized gum arabic can strengthen glass ionomer cement, a dental material limited by modest strength, appearance, and bioactivity. Gum arabic was oxidised to add active groups, then spray-dried into nanoparticles and mixed into a commercial cement at six concentrations.

Laboratory tests measured film thickness, water uptake and solubility, tensile strength, shear bond strength, and optical and biological performance. The comprehensive in vitro design maps how dose changes each property, seeking a concentration that hardens the cement without harming handling or biocompatibility. The work points toward a natural, low-cost additive that could make everyday fillings last longer and bond better.
pmc-13348195:
Jean-Pierre Fina-Lubaki, Williams R. Phillips, and Klaus B. von Pressentin introduce a French edition of a primary care reporting checklist, in an editorial from 2026. Primary care has its own methods, patients, and system settings, so the CRISP checklist was built by global consensus to lift quality, relevance. Openness in reports across number, story, and mixed study types alike.

French spans the globe, above all in Africa, yet English rules science publishing and shuts out many French-speaking researchers from sharing work clearly. A French checklist serves authors, reviewers, editors, teachers, and planners, easing entry and helping readers judge and apply findings in Francophone care settings.
pmc-13348795:
Fernando Rodríguez-Rodríguez and co-authors used network maths in 2026 to map how physical condition, peer and parental backing, and moderate-to-vigorous activity link in Chilean schoolchildren. Active behaviour backs well-being. Yet it has fallen worldwide among children. Single-factor studies miss how pulls reinforce each other.

Among 655 children aged 8 to 16 in the ACTIBESE project, forms captured activity in and out of school, self-perceived condition, and backing from peers and parents, plus life details. Network maths showed which nodes link activity to its backing most strongly. The map helps schools and families aim at links, such as parental cheer or peer activity, that most effectively lift children's movement.
pmc-13349395:
Chen Chen, Hao Wu, and Lei Zhang link coaching style to athlete burnout. Their survey study appeared in 2026. It covers college athletes in China. Basic mental needs sit at the centre. Questionnaires came from 800 student athletes. Modelling ran in two stages. A structural model came first. A neural network check came second. Coaching was sorted into two styles. One style gives autonomy. The other style controls. Three needs were tracked throughout. They are autonomy, competence, and closeness.

Supportive coaching tied to lower burnout. Controlling coaching tied to higher burnout. All three needs carried part of each link. Competence carried the strongest share. The autonomy path ran clearer in female athletes. That path runs from supportive coaching to burnout. Coaches can cut burnout by feeding needs. Merely easing training load is not the lesson.
pmc-13349895:
Xiangqiong Wu and fellow authors proposed a lightweight detection system in 2026 for finding breast lesions in ultrasound images. Ultrasound is cheap and safe, but speckle noise, low contrast, and fuzzy lesion borders make automatic reading hard.

Built on a YOLOv13 detector, their design adds a module that gathers wide image context and another that follows horizontal and vertical structure, placed at chosen stages to keep costs low. On two datasets it reached strong detection results with only 2.50 million parameters and fast processing. Extra tests for robustness and cross-dataset use supported the design. A small, quick model like this could fit clinics without heavy computing power.
pmc-13350195:
S. Gogia and a Houston team described in 2026 how a multidisciplinary programme supports infant feeding choices for parents living with HIV across a national guideline change. Newer guidance backs shared decision making, and their centre built a team model in 2020 ahead of that shift.

Records covered 336 parents entering care between 2020 and 2025. Seventy-five considered breastfeeding, 51 took a specialist consultation, and 37 breastfed, with no transmissions recorded and most keeping the virus undetectable, for a median of 47 days. The experience shows a structured, team-based conversation can safely support parents who choose to breastfeed.
pmc-13351095:
Qilin Shu and colleagues tracked microbes and chemistry together as a traditional Chinese medicine starter ferments, in a 2026 study. The process reshapes the active parts of Hua Feng Dan, but which microbes do the work was unclear.

Sixty flavonoids shifted notably during the process, with catechin and naringin rising while many others fell. Bacteria such as Tetragenococcus and Bacillus led at different stages, and the fungus Aspergillus was also prominent. Two strains were tied to ten of the flavonoid changes. Re-running the process with those two strains raised the total flavonoid level a lot, so makers could steer quality on purpose instead of leaving it to chance.
pmc-13351395:
Atefeh Valaei and co-authors reviewed gut microbes in blood cancers in a 2026 narrative review. It covered evidence from 2022 to 2025. Gut microbes help keep immunity balanced. They support blood cell growth. They also release active compounds such as short-chain fatty acids.

When that ecosystem is disturbed, blood cancers may grow faster. These include leukaemias, lymphomas, and myeloma. Infections grow likelier, and treatment grows harder to bear. Chemotherapy, antibiotics, and stem cell transplants in turn batter the microbes. The review maps this two-way relationship mechanism by mechanism. Guarding or restoring gut microbes is emerging as a support strategy beside standard treatment.
pmc-13351695:
Ebtihal Elameen Eltyeb leads a 2026 systematic review of regenerative medicine for children with cerebral palsy. Current care mainly manages symptoms, while cell-based approaches aim to support brain repair and better function. Four databases were searched for work from 2010 to 2025, covering trials, cohort studies, and case series with at least three children.

Eighteen studies with 1,087 children were analysed, and most used products drawn from umbilical cord tissue or blood. Cord-based treatments showed moderate motor gains in selected trials. Combined cord blood with erythropoietin gave the largest motor and thinking gains in the set. Because study designs differed widely, results were combined in words rather than pooled numbers.
pmc-13351895:
Fahad Idrees Shaikh and co-authors report a 2026 case of an ancient schwannoma on the cervical sympathetic chain in the neck. Such slow, benign nerve sheath tumours develop wear-like changes over time that can look like cancer. A 53-year-old man had a painless swelling below his left ear for six months.

Scans suggested a dead lymph node in the neck, and a needle sample gave too few cells to judge. Surgeons removed the mass fully, and tissue study confirmed the ancient schwannoma diagnosis. Horner syndrome followed surgery and was managed without further procedures. The case stresses tissue proof and careful planning for nerve risks before neck surgery.
pmc-13353795:
Karen Sanchez-Tamayo and co-authors report pressure alopecia in a young child in 2026. The hair loss type follows long immobilisation and is seen mostly in adults, with few child cases known. A four-year-old patient developed a bare patch after a two-week intensive care stay.

Scope exam of the scalp showed comedone-like dots that supported the diagnosis. After two months of steroids and zinc pyrithione shampoo, signs of scarring hair loss still appeared. Lasting pressure above capillary levels starves the scalp of oxygen and can kill follicles. Early suspicion after long hospital or surgical immobilisation is vital, since most cases recover on their own but scarring can be permanent.
pmc-13354295:
Wolfgang Miesbach surveyed patient-given results in haemophilia gene care, in 2026. Three virus-based gene care have gained approval in Western countries since 2022, but commercial uptake has been slow. Standard endpoints such as bleeding rate and factor action show whether blood clotting helps, yet they miss what people themselves value most.

Drawing on papers from 2017 to 2026, the review covers outcome instruments, trial evidence, cost-value work, and story-based patient data. Regulators more and more treat patient reports as meaningful endpoints, so the review matters for approval and funding decisions. Readers learn which tests capture life with haemophilia after gene care, and where the results still fall short.
pmc-13354395:
Muhammad Farhan leads a 2026 pooled analysis of rivaroxaban plus aspirin versus aspirin alone in peripheral artery disease. Aspirin is the base drug, yet clot risk stays high in the narrowed-leg-artery disease. Trials following PRISMA guidance were pooled with random-effects models, with bias and certainty graded by standard tools.

Six trials with 90,325 participants qualified. Dual therapy cut major cardiovascular events, with a risk ratio of 0.82, plus heart attacks at 0.87 and limb ischaemia at 0.68. Heart death and major amputation did not fall clearly. Major bleeding by TIMI rules rose at 1.41, though brain and fatal bleeding stayed similar. Net benefit favours dual therapy for many patients.
pmc-13354695:
Ziyi Yang and colleagues comment on why CAR T-cell therapy often fails to hold in extramedullary multiple myeloma, in a 2026 piece. Disease outside the marrow should count as high-risk biology, not a mere variant of relapse. The key split is paraskeletal spread, which stays near bone, versus true extraosseous disease, which travels through blood and signals marrow escape.

BCMA-directed CAR T cells can shrink relapsed myeloma fast, yet patients with active extraosseous disease respond less often and progress sooner than those without it. Pooling the two forms, the authors warn, inflates how durable cell therapy looks for the patients who need help most. The comment calls for separate reporting and trials aimed at the extramedullary niche.
pmc-13354995:
A 2026 proceedings volume gathers abstracts from the International Congress on Academic Medicine, held in Ottawa from April 16 to 19. The meeting, run by the Association of Faculties of Medicine of Canada, drew more than 1,900 people. Attendees included students, residents, teachers, researchers, and patient partners from many countries.

Sessions covered health falsehoods, kindness in care, food and child health, and the health of the planet, alongside workshops and poster talks. The stated goals link research, teaching, and care with patient voices at the center. The volume lists talks in blocks and serves as the record of what was presented at the congress.
pmc-13357095:
Junjie Liu and co-authors built in 2026 a relapse prediction chart for HER2-positive breast cancer treated with trastuzumab, a targeted drug some tumors learn to resist. They mined public gene datasets and a hospital cohort, using network tools to find hub genes tied to relapse. Then they tested a two-gene chart across training and validation groups totaling several hundred patients.

Two genes, DYX1C1 and GNAI1, independently predicted relapse, and the chart scored high accuracy, near 0.89 in training and 0.83 in validation. Each gene linked to a distinct tumor trait: immune suppression for one, tissue stiffening signals for the other. High levels of both also meant poorer response to pre-surgery therapy.
pmc-13358995:
Eun-Jeong Seo and co-authors map collagen genes in scarred lungs in a 2026 study. Idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis stiffens the lungs as too much matrix builds up between air sacs. Cells called fibroblasts lay down that matrix, chiefly collagens. Two collagen types are well known culprits, but the full family had not been charted in these cells.

They read the gene activity of lung fibroblasts from 33 patients and 10 healthy controls. Fourteen of 17 collagen genes differed in the disease, and some linked to patient survival. A fuller map of which collagens switch on could reveal new targets for slowing the scarring.
pmc-13359695:
Vimal Murugesan and co-authors survey the modern treatment of melanoma in a 2026 review. This aggressive skin cancer was once nearly hopeless once it spread. Surgery still cures early disease. For advanced cases, two revolutions changed the outlook: drugs that target a common mutation and shrink tumors fast, and immune therapies that can hold the cancer off for years.

Newer options grow a patient's own tumor-attacking immune cells and return them, or use viruses that attack the tumor. The central problem now is choosing the right treatment, in the right order, for each patient. The review lays out the full spectrum so clinicians can match tools to the case at hand.
pmc-13361295:
Oliver Planz reviews how cancer drugs that block a signal enzyme affect the immune system's alarms in a 2026 paper. Toll-like receptors are sensors that spot germs and danger signals and start inflammation. One signal path they use runs through an enzyme called MEK. Drugs that block MEK were made for cancer care and are now widely used in oncology.

Growing proof shows these blockers also change how immune cells answer the alarm sensors. The effect can raise or lower inflammation depending on dose and timing. That matters for cancer patients, who face infections and may get vaccines or immune therapies. Planz weighs what this cross-talk means for treatment choices and side effects, urging care when the two fields meet.
pmc-13361395:
Lu Xing and co-authors studied what helps or blocks a bladder care method after womb surgery in a 2026 paper. Clean intermittent catheterization lets patients empty the bladder with a fresh tube each time, a skill many need after radical hysterectomy. The study took place at a women's and children's hospital in Chengdu, China. It mixed surveys with deep interviews for a full picture.

Surveys went to 156 health workers and 300 patients. Interviews added the voices of 11 staff members and 12 patients. The team sorted the helps and hurdles into levels, starting with the evidence itself. Knowing where the friction sits, in habits, staffing, or supply, tells managers what to fix first so proven care actually reaches patients.
pmc-13362395:
Afifa Aziz and colleagues wrote a 2026 review on how plant and food polysaccharides, the long sugar chains in many foods, may help heal the gut in colitis. Colitis is long-term swelling of the bowel that current drugs treat with side effects and high cost. The review pulls together lab and animal work on these food compounds as add-on care.

The authors explain that the compounds feed good gut bacteria, which then make fatty acids that fuel the gut wall. They also help seal gaps in the bowel lining and calm swelling and cell damage. The review sorts which chain shapes work best, and it presents the foods as support for standard care, not a swap for it.
pmc-13362595:
Sungki Kim and co-authors report a 2026 study on using sunlight and titanium dioxide to break down live chemical warfare agents. The tests ran in a lab certified by the global chemical weapons watchdog and covered four agents: the nerve agent GD and three blister agents. Sunlit titanium dioxide acts as a catalyst that attacks toxic compounds with reactive oxygen.

After six hours of sun, the setup destroyed between about three fifths and more than nine tenths of each agent, with the blister agent HN2 breaking down most. Chemical traces hinted at how the nitrogen mustards fall apart. The approach could yield greener cleanup methods that need no harsh chemicals, and it also informs safe handling of other toxic waste.
pmc-13363695:
Mihaela Buleandră and colleagues present a 2026 review on using electrochemical sensors to judge essential oils in food work. Plant oils serve as natural flavors and preservatives, but their strength varies, so makers need fast quality checks. The review weighs electro-sensing methods that read the oils' active, charge-responsive compounds and their antioxidant power, set against slower lab standards.

These methods stand out for being simple, cheap, and low in waste, and they suit on-site testing. The authors sort the published approaches by target compound and sensor design, flag where results disagree or methods fall short, and sketch the fixes most needed. Their aim is a shared framework so future sensor studies build on, rather than repeat, past work.
pmc-13364695:
Hyoung Choi and co-workers use linked health records from 13 care sites in 2026 to weigh harms of strong new drugs for gut swell disease, next to old care. Trial pools are hand picked, so real world risk can hide. The team matched like patients and tracked harm rates across drug groups.

Strong drug users faced more lung TB and more low mood or fear ills than non users. One drug class drove most of that risk, yet it cut bone thin risk. Herb like small drugs showed no such rise. The word is to watch strong drug users close for these harms.
pmc-13365295:
Adam Ley and co-workers build in 2026 a lab on a chip style math model of how cells reshape the fiber net that holds them. Cells pull on the net, the net shifts, and the new shape steers the cells in turn. Their open code model runs round of pull, rest, and re read.

With soft, bend back links in the net, the model shows real gains: more fibers pack near the cell, fibers point out from it, and strain stays in the net. Set nets that start lined up act in unlike ways. The tool helps labs guess how scar and heal nets evolve.
pmc-13365495:
Yun Ma and others found a micropeptide, PAMP, that suppresses lung adenocarcinoma by rewiring proline energy use, in 2026. Long non-coding RNAs can encode working micropeptides through small open reading frames, reshaping views of the supposedly non-coding genome. A forty-eight-amino-acid peptide encoded by PSMA3-AS1 emerged as a choice tumour suppressor.

PAMP was much downregulated in lung adenocarcinoma tissues and correlated with favourable prognosis. Working assays showed it inhibits cancer cell proliferation in vitro and suppresses tumour growth in vivo, acting through inhibition of PYCR1 and proline energy rewiring. Cancer teams gain a novel micropeptide way with healing power in lung adenocarcinoma.
pmc-13366095:
Nina Gubina and co-workers chart in 2026 how a water borne cancer chem builds DNA harm in mice, and where cell guards give out. The chem, found in some treated water, makes two DNA marks in the liver. One mark grows in a straight line with dose. The key harm mark stays near nil up to a set dose.

Past that dose, the harm mark and gene faults shoot up. A fix protein that clears the mark tops out at a set harm rank, shown in the counts. Fault shapes match a known human cancer mark set. Dose lines for risk work can rest on this cap.
pmc-13369795:
Emil Boros builds in 2026 a guild frame to count how water birds move energy cross eco sys, a flow not yet fully weighed. He uses bird counts from 1986 to 2017 at two salt pans in mid Europe, both world prized sites. Birds sort by feed way, home use, and stay span into import and export guilds.

Year flows swing by huge spans. Net import beats net export in each year by a clear lead, so the pans act as energy sinks through their birds. Guild mix, not bird count, sets that lead. Open water size does not call the score.
pmc-13371195:
Yeong Jun Ju and colleagues build a simple risk score for hospital readmission within 30 days in a 2026 study. Readmissions signal care quality and carry heavy costs, yet spotting high-risk patients in the general community has been hard. The team used health insurance records for adults in Suwon City, South Korea, from 2016 to 2019, selecting predictors with machine learning and turning them into a point-based score.

Among 3,357 adults, about one in nine was readmitted within 30 days of a hospital stay. The score was tested on a held-back sample for accuracy and calibration, aiming for a tool clinicians can actually use. If it holds up elsewhere, the index could help hospitals target follow-up calls, home checks, and early clinic visits to the patients most likely to return.
pmc-13372195:
Ankit Kumar and co-authors read wrist X-rays to judge age in north India in a 2026 study. Courts and clinics often need an age when birth proof is lost or in doubt. Bone growth at the wrist gives clues for teens and young adults.

The team read 174 X-rays of people aged 14 to 24 at a trauma center in Lucknow. Men made up about two in three of the group. Growth stages were scored joint by joint. Growth speed can shift by place and stock, so local norms count. The set adds India-based norms that can make age calls in court and clinic more fair.
pmc-13372695:
Jai Sidpra and co-authors mapped brain links for a grave child tumor in a 2026 study. The tumor grows in the midline of the brain and is near always fatal. In lab models it taps into brain cell links to grow and spread.

The team asked if that web shows in real children's scans and if it links to how long they live. They built a brain-wide map of the tumor's links from patient data. The map may help sort risk and pick care paths in trials. It also backs the idea that cutting the tumor's links could be a new way to slow it.
pmc-13373295:
Rukhsana Kausar and Shahir Ulazam report a rare, grave bleed in a young child in a 2026 case report. A hole had formed between the chest's main artery and the food pipe, a fault that is rare in kids and hard to spot. The child threw up a large amount of blood after a short virus ill.

Blood tests showed a sharp drop in blood strength, and the full bleed plan was swung into play. Scans showed the bad link and a fault in the artery's shape. A covered tube was placed in the artery to seal it. Tests ruled out germs and tissue ills as the cause. The child healed well.
pmc-13374195:
Qingqing Liu and co-authors joined two risk marks for sugar disease in a 2026 study of older adults in China. One mark blends blood fat, blood sugar, and body shape. One mark counts swell signs in the blood. Data came from a long study that ran from 2011 to 2020.

The group held 6,216 adults free of sugar disease at the start. High reads on each mark went with more new sugar disease on their own. Both high at once gave the top risk. The pair may help clinics spot high-risk adults years early, when food and habit plans can still turn the tide.
pmc-13375895:
Sylvia A. Newbold and co-authors traced a cut part of an epilepsy protein in a 2026 mouse study. The protein sits on a sex gene and, when half the cells lack it, fits and thought loss can come. Full lack does not bring fits, which is a deep quirk.

The team showed the protein is cut in brain cells of the top sheet too, and its tail rides to the cell core with help from port proteins. Gene reads showed the tail shifts many genes' acts. Live checks tied the tail to the count of cell spines, through a gene set. The tail may be a drug aim of its own.
pmc-13375995:
Chajira Garrote-Achou and others tune brewing medium to boost postbiotic product germ-killing power in a 2026 study. Postbiotics, non-living microbe products, focus the food industry as natural preservatives, yet yields depend heavily on growth medium. The team tuned medium for Pediococcus acidilactici CECT 9879, first screening carbon and nitrogen sources, then testing yeast parts and basal medium parts, then refining with response surface methodology.

Yeast-derived parts and sodium acetate showed strong linear, quadratic, and interaction effects, defining clear optimal ranges. Under optimised medium, the minimum inhibitory concentration against Escherichia coli fell from about 48 percent to about 32 percent by volume. The work shows that medium tuning alone can substantially raise postbiotic product potency, supporting cheaper, more strong food biopreservation.
pmc-13376795:
Suresh Phatak and co-authors set three flow views next to each in boys with a held testis in a 2026 study. To judge the gland, staff must see its small blood flow. Old flow views miss slow, fine flow in such small glands.

A total of 40 boys under age five at one large center got all three views with a fine probe. Each view had its own best pulse set. The fine view was built to catch low-speed flow the old pair can skip. Truer flow reads help teams call if the gland is sound and where it sits, which guides the fix.
pmc-13377595:
Vivek Kamat and co-authors back dual sense pads for wear health checks in a 2026 review. Such pads now ride on skin and watch body and world marks all day. Two sense ways lead: charge flow and light. Each has its own strong and weak suits.

Next pads will run both ways in one rig, the team holds. Cloth pads that watch wounds and sweat pads for stress marks show the charge path. Light paths add cross checks on skin and blood facts. A pair of views on one spot can cut false reads and stretch what a small pad can swear to.
pmc-13378495:
Hengyu Liu and co-authors wrote a 2026 review of natural materials for repairing osteochondral tissue, where cartilage meets the bone beneath it. Such damage heals poorly because the tissue is layered and has little ability to repair itself. Materials taken from living sources can resemble the original tissue closely.

The review sorts materials by origin: human, animal, plant, and microbe, and explains how each source shapes its repair method. For animal materials it pays close attention to cleaning methods that remove cells while keeping useful parts. The authors note that most approved repair products worldwide use natural materials. Readers get a guide to matching material choice to the repair task.
pmc-13379995:
Jacob K Korir and co-authors report a 2026 study of how Kenya governs nutrition work across different sectors. Poor nutrition has many causes, so health, farming, education, and other sectors must act together. How well that joint governance works over time was poorly documented.

The study assessed governance in 2023 and, looking back, in 2012, using a standard assessment tool. It gathered views from 112 people in government and non-government roles. Commitment, capacity, and working mechanisms for action were examined as drivers of progress. The findings show where governance strengthened over the decade and where it still lags, offering a basis for the next steps in scaling up nutrition action.
pmc-13380095:
Megan Quimper and colleagues report a 2026 study on a training program for women's health doctors in Guyana, and a fall in mothers dying around childbirth that followed. Many countries in the region face high maternal deaths and a shortage of specialists. Guyana had no home-grown training in obstetrics and gynaecology before this program.

The four-year program began in 2012, using curricula from universities in the United States, adapted to local needs. Visiting and local faculty trained the country's first home-grown specialists. In total 32 doctors had completed the program, and nearly all still practise in Guyana. The authors link that growing workforce to the observed decline in maternal deaths.
pmc-13380195:
Raquel García Hernáez, Alicia Padilla Galo, and Francisco-Javier González-Barcala review a 2026 topic on hard training and asthma in athletes. About a third of adults worldwide do not get the weekly aerobic activity health guidance recommends, and exercise usually helps the immune system. Very heavy training, though, may briefly lower immune defences.

Asthma and exercise-triggered narrowing of the airways are more common in athletes than in the general population, especially in endurance and winter sports. In some groups the rates are strikingly high. Causes include training load, heavy breathing, air conditions, and personal sensitivity. The review sets out how these factors combine, to help clinicians and coaches judge risk in high-level sport.
pmc-13380795: Park replies to a letter questioning validation of the authors' kidney replacement therapy risk calculator for Korean children with chronic kidney disease, in a 2026 published response. Park admits an error in the original abstract: the group 1 patient count was misreported and calibration slopes were described inaccurately, with corrected slopes of 0.894 to 0.908 for group 1 and 0.860 to 0.874 for group 2, and a formal correction promised. The authors accept that recalibration and local refinement are needed before wider use, and describe a Korea-optimized model in development.
pmc-13385795:
Bo Zhang's team tested adding anlotinib to durvalumab maintenance in extensive-stage small-cell lung cancer, in a 2026 phase II trial. First-line immune therapy plus chemo has helped, but survival gains remain limited. The DURABLE trial randomized 66 patients to durvalumab plus anlotinib or durvalumab alone after first-line durvalumab plus platinum-etoposide chemo.

Median time without progression from randomization reached 5.4 months with the pair versus 1.9 months with durvalumab alone, a clear gain at the trial's lenient threshold. Grade 3 to 4 drug-related adverse events ran 24.2 percent with the pair versus 12.5 percent alone. Marker analyses aim to refine who benefits most from added anlotinib.
pmc-13385895:
Guigui Ye's team steered high-energy triplet states with temperature-responsive twisted molecules, in a 2026 study. Controlling excited-state transitions matters for advanced optoelectronics, but high-energy triplet states are short-lived and elusive. The team used annulation to tune the size, geometry, and electronic properties of pi-conjugated systems.

Temperature acted as a trigger to control two distinct high-energy triplet pathways, one passing through singlet states and one through the lowest triplet state. The approach yielded temperature-modulated blue-to-red afterglow with an energy gap up to 0.76 electron volts between delayed fluorescence and phosphorescence. The design offers a blueprint for responsive organic semiconductors.
pmc-13386395:
Yanwu Yang and co-authors engineer a selenium-based bridge into insulin glargine, a long-acting insulin, to stop it clumping into the fibrils that ruin stored insulin. Fibril formation forces a costly global cold chain for insulin products. Their 2026 study replaces two cysteine building blocks in the molecule with selenocysteine, forming a diselenide bridge.

Computer simulations supported that interpretation. pmc-13386495:
Akel Azzi and colleagues survey French dialysis units on guarding against highly resistant bacteria in 2026 work. Dialysis patients face real risk of carrying vancomycin-resistant enterococci or carbapenemase-producing gut bacteria. A random sample of 200 units was invited, and 103 took part by email survey and phone follow-up.

Only a minority of units could reliably flag patients needing screening or track carriers by computer. Under a third assigned dedicated caregivers to carriers, and rules for lifting precautions varied widely. Staff chiefly blamed missing national dialysis-specific guidance and poor flow of carrier status information between services.
pmc-13388495:
Xu and colleagues built a body-wide computer model in 2026 for brigatinib, a pill that blocks the ALK protein and treats a form of lung cancer. Dosing advice is thin for Chinese patients and for people with liver or kidney damage. pmc-13388695:
Yunjeong So's team followed seven mother-infant pairs through weaning to learn how the infant gut microbiome matures when milk gives way to solid food. Faecal samples from before, during, and after weaning were tested for growth on human milk sugars and on dietary fibres, backed by gene reads and cultures from 137 maternal bacterial strains.

Certain Clostridia wielded both toolkits together and outgrew specialists, hinting at a process by which adult gut species take hold during weaning.
pmc-13389095:
N. Fuster-Martínez and co-authors test whether gold nanoparticles make proton radiotherapy more damaging to cancer cells, and they refine the experimental setup for such studies. Proton therapy concentrates dose at a precise depth, sparing healthy tissue, and nanoparticles might amplify its effect, but published results conflict. The team optimised irradiation conditions by adding a Mylar film to culture plates, keeping the medium volume minimal and allowing rapid coverage after exposure. DNA damage analysis was performed to support the survival results. The authors set out to quantify the radiosensitising effect with its uncertainty and to provide a more efficient, reproducible setup for future nanoparticle and beam studies.
pmc-13389195:
Yumeng Li's team quantified brain maintenance, the idea that some brains stay sharp despite ageing, by weighing brain structure with brain function in 1,280 older adults. Maintenance clustered in prefrontal, cingulate, and precuneus regions and in higher-order networks, and higher scores went with slower mental decline, lower amyloid burden, and distinct memory, focus, and speed profiles. The measure offers a grounded marker of resilience for ageing and dementia research.
pmc-13389395:

That keeping suggests ranked value judgements are a deep feature of learning, not a quirk of human choice.
pmc-13391495:

A modified rule incorporating the unit-free staying length, which captures motion-extended interaction range, merged data across active and passive markers, diverse shapes, and thrust mechanisms. The result gives a guessing system for micro-swimmer transport in tissues, holey media, and other non-balance mixed systems. The law held across active and passive markers.
pmc-13391795:

pmc-13392195:
Rida Khan and colleagues review, in 2026, traditional fermented foods worldwide as a dietary answer to folate deficiency. Folate is a key nutrient for core body tasks. Needs rise sharply in pregnancy. A lack of it is a global concern for mums and unborn children.

Examples include Nigerian ogi fermented with Lactiplantibacillus plantarum. Food and health readers gain a world list of such foods. Each entry can guide plans to prevent low folate with the foods a place has known for ages.
pmc-13393295:
Verneri Kryssi and four colleagues report a 23-month-old girl with Morquio type A syndrome. Her loose top neck joint, a known hazard of her condition, gave way in a minor fall days ahead of planned stabilising surgery. Morquio A, a storage disorder classed as mucopolysaccharidosis IVA, weakens the structures bracing the first two neck vertebrae. Imaging showed the atlas slipped forward over the axis, injuring the upper spinal cord and leaving her with four-limb paralysis symptoms.

pmc-13393695:
Yuchen Han and colleagues compare two radiation schedules for localized prostate cancer in a 2026 Chinese study. Shorter, hypofractionated radiation can save time and may suit tumor biology, but long-term data in Chinese patients were limited.

Thirty patients received 45 gray in 9 fractions in a prospective trial from 2011 to 2017, matched against 95 patients given a moderately hypofractionated schedule at the same center. Survival was tracked with Kaplan-Meier methods, and urinary and bowel side effects of grade 2 or higher were graded. Oncologists gain ten-year context for choosing between the two schedules.
pmc-13394695:
Patrizio Lancellotti, Yun Yun Go, and Magnus Bäck write, in 2026, an editorial on the cost case for early valve care. Their piece discusses a study of TAVI, a valve placed through a tube, in people with tight aortic valves but no symptoms. New European guidance backs early valve work for low-risk patients. The question is whether acting early pays off for health systems.

The study they discuss modelled nine European countries over a lifetime. It built on a trial named EARLY TAVR and used local costs and life tables. Early TAVI looked cost-saving in the models. The writers stress wise patient choice and team talks. Money proof, they say, must join health proof.
pmc-13395095:
Anqi Liu leads a 2026 review of exosomes, tiny parcels shed by cells, as weapons against drug-proof bacteria. Antibiotics keep losing ground as germs gain resistance. Exosomes from body fluids carry cargo from their parent cells. They can kill germs directly and also coach the immune system through antigen display.

The review sorts how exosomes are gathered, checked, and classed for infection work. It weighs their built-in germ fighting and the tricks used to load or aim them. Animal studies across many infection types are covered. Hurdles for clinic use include dosing, targeting, and clean production. The authors see a strong next path past standard antibiotics.
pmc-13395195:
Moshe Shegal and co-authors ask, in 2026, whether countries where people flourish also give more to charity. A world study scored flourishing across 22 countries, from more than two hundred thousand people. Scores blend happiness, health, meaning, character, and close ties. The team set those scores against a world giving index that tracks helping strangers, time given, and money given.

Higher flourishing went with more help for strangers and more time given as volunteers. The link to money gifts was weak. The authors say well-being ties more to hands-on kindness than to cash. They frame giving as a health-linked habit, for giver and receiver alike. Country policies might grow both at once.
pmc-13395295:
Parvathy Santhosh, Ale Abraham, and Sujoy Khan review, in 2026, odd triggers of food anaphylaxis, a fast and grave allergic attack. Most food attacks follow plain allergy paths, but some hide behind extra factors. The review covers three such puzzles. One needs wheat plus exercise, one follows tick bites and red meat, and one links cat allergy to pork.

Signs can swing from hives to full collapse, and delays muddy the hunt. A sharp history, skin prick tests, and blood tests for exact triggers form the core of diagnosis. The authors stress testing routes that work where labs are thin. Travel and new diets make these cases more likely to appear anywhere.
pmc-13395395:
Astrid Pedersen and others track multiple sclerosis rates in Sweden from 2001 to 2021 in a 2026 study. Year trends may hint at causes and steer care funds, yet nation-wide studies with fresh data over decades stay rare.

The team tied many Swede health files together. It used two case rules: illness codes from 2006 to 2021, and the Swede MS file from 2001 to 2021. Rates were set to a world age norm. Trend math tracked new cases and total cases over time. In all, 13,055 new cases were found. Health chiefs gain two decades of firm Swede figures for care design.
pmc-13395895:
Zhiyuan Sun and co-authors unveil, in 2026, RAFTER, a tool that tags RNAs only when they are truly being turned into protein. Ribosome scans can mistake idle ribosomes for working ones. RAFTER fuses an RNA editing enzyme to the factor that ends translation. Since that factor joins only at the true end of a protein build, its tags mark productive work.

The tags let teams count translation levels with high accuracy at scale. The method works down to single cells, the team reports. Older tools, such as footprint reads, demand heavy setup for such fine work. The authors pitch RAFTER for disease studies where protein output, not RNA count, is the real story.
pmc-13396095:
Huanhuan Wang and others tie LIMS2 loss to lung gland cancer growth and defense shifts in a 2026 study. LIMS2 frames cell bones and cell-ground grips, but its pattern and weight in lung gland cancer were half known.

Cancer gene files showed LIMS2 far lower in tumor than in sound lung, and cell tests weighed how restoring it shifts cell growth and drift. Math tools tied low LIMS2 to defense cell inflow and checkpoint gene patterns. The paper names LIMS2 both as a growth sign and as a clue to the defense scene inside lung tumors.
pmc-13396195:
Marina Ninkov and colleagues review what happens when stool transplants meet cancer immunotherapy, in a 2026 article. Fecal microbiota transplantation moves gut microbes from a donor into a patient, while checkpoint inhibitor drugs release the brakes on immune cells so they attack tumors.

Results of combining the two have been uneven. Some patients respond better, others develop harsh immune side effects, and the difference seems to lie in which microbial jobs take hold in the gut. The authors sort trial evidence by these functions, drawing lessons for choosing donors, tracking the gut over time, and designing safer trials that test the pairing with more care.
pmc-13396695:
Ying Liu and co-authors asked whether a wildly swinging blood pressure in the first day after a heart attack predicts death, using a large American intensive care database. Their 2026 study draws on MIMIC-IV records of patients admitted with acute myocardial infarction.

The swing was measured as the coefficient of variation of blood pressure over the first 24 hours, a statistic that scales variation to the average level. Patients were split into thirds by that measure and followed for death in hospital and at 30 days, one year, and three years. Earlier studies had disagreed on whether short-term variability matters beyond the average pressure, and this cohort tests the claim at four time horizons.
pmc-13396995:
Yihealem Yabebal Ayele and co-authors present an adult whose severe belly pain looked like appendicitis but came from a twisted apron of belly fat, in a 2026 case report. Primary omental torsion, where the fatty omentum twists on itself without another cause, is a rare and easily missed source of an acute abdomen.

With appendicitis excluded, careful exploration during surgery found the twisted, starved tissue. Cutting it away brought rapid recovery, the authors report, and likely prevented worse complications such as dead tissue and abscess. Their message is aimed at surgeons in settings with limited imaging: when the appendix looks innocent, keep looking.
pmc-13397095:
Hongzhen Du and co-authors review the two-way traffic between mood disorders and long-term body diseases, with the heart and metabolic system as the main crossing. Their 2026 review notes that about 36 percent of people with several chronic conditions also carry a psychiatric illness, with women, older adults, and poorer groups hit hardest.

Depression and anxiety travel with diabetes, obesity, high blood pressure, metabolic syndrome, and heart disease. Each side worsens the other's outlook and raises death rates. The authors sort the epidemiology first, then the shared mechanisms, from inflammation and stress hormones to behavior, aiming at care that treats the pair together instead of in separate clinics.
pmc-13397695:
Demuyakor Isaac and co-authors are named on a 2026 retraction notice for their 2024 study of patient safety culture in Ghanaian regional hospitals, published in BMC Psychology. The editor withdrew the qualitative study after doubts about its peer review led to a fresh review after publication. That second look found fault with how the work was done and reported.

Reviewers cited unclear recruitment, vague selection rules and unstated interview questions, plus claims in the results that lacked firm support. The authors offered an explanation, but the journal judged it insufficient and retracted the paper. Whether the authors accept the decision is not stated in the notice, which now stands at the head of the record.
pmc-13398095:
Man Sun, Dan Zang and Jun Chen write a 2026 letter raising three cautions about a study linking gum therapy to body-wide changes in patients with type 2 diabetes and gum disease. The study under discussion, by Diao and colleagues, tracked mouth microbes and metabolites after non-surgical periodontal therapy. Such multi-omics work is shaping joint care ideas, so its reading deserves care, the writers argue.

Both trial arms got surface cleaning and hygiene coaching, so some shifts may reflect shared care rather than deep cleaning alone; one key metabolite rose in both groups. Pooling fluid from set teeth may also blur signals from the worst pockets. Lasting blood-sugar gains need data on medicines, diet and activity before credit goes to gum treatment.
pmc-13398695:
Songming Ding and colleagues describe scope treatment for bile leaks that follow drain removal after liver transplant. Their 2026 case series covers six transplant patients whose leaks appeared once the T-tube came out, all with duct-to-duct joins. Biliary problems remain transplantation's Achilles heel, striking 5 to 25 percent of recipients in the ranges cited, though leaks of this type rarely kill if caught in time.

Each leak was sealed from inside using a fully covered, self-expanding metal stent placed by ERCP, the scope route now preferred for such leaks. All six cases were managed successfully in the series. Placing the series beside the published record, the authors argue the covered stent is a dependable first move.
pmc-13398895:
Fernando Yue Cesena writes a 2026 editorial, in Portuguese, on what business intelligence dashboards can do for public health, spotlighting the iCardio platform. Health data have exploded through electronic records and wearable monitors, yet the numbers sit fragmented across sources that resist comparison between countries and years. The Global Burden of Disease effort standardises over 400 outcomes across more than 200 territories, as the piece notes.

Against that backdrop, Souza and colleagues present iCardio, an online tool visualising Brazilian cardiology procedure and surgery data from the national DATASUS system. Built with national research council funding, it turns raw tables into live, visual insight for decisions. Cesena frames such tools as the bridge between data piles and policy.
pmc-13398995:
Gustavo A Santa Cruz reviews microdosimetry for boron neutron capture therapy, a cancer treatment that uses neutron capture by boron-10. One gray of boron dose corresponds to just three or four short-range reactions in a single cell, so chance variation leaves some tumor cells untouched.
