Short particle ranges, comparable to cell structures, and uneven boron distribution further undermine simple dose descriptors. Microdosimetry offers models and measurements that link these spectra to biological effect and support quality control. The work guides physicists and clinicians toward more honest dose interpretation in this complex therapy.
pmc-13399695:
Sarah Hsin Cheng and colleagues report a rare skin metastasis from esophageal squamous cell carcinoma in a 2026 case. During his fifth treatment course, examiners found a hard, reddened nodule on his left upper back. The painless lump had no discharge or ulceration, and its nature was unclear enough that the team biopsied it.

Under the microscope the skin held keratinizing squamous cell carcinoma growing through the dermis, with tumor cells invading small vessels. No abnormality showed in the surface epidermis, a pattern supporting metastasis rather than a new skin primary. The diagnosis proved an ominous turn. Soon afterward he arrived at the emergency department with severe headache, vomiting, and altered consciousness, and scans showed multiple brain metastases among other deposits. The authors note that esophageal cancer almost never seeds the skin, so they urge biopsy of new nodules in such patients rather than watchful waiting.
pmc-13399795:
Robert Śmigielski, Jan Mateńko, and Daniel Kopko describe repairing a torn lateral meniscus root by borrowing a small ligament that already lives in the knee, in a 2026 technical note. The anterior meniscofemoral ligament, also called the ligament of Humphrey, connects naturally to the back horn of the lateral meniscus. Detached roots raise joint contact pressure and threaten any cruciate graft, so a firm, living reattachment is valuable.

A tunnel is drilled in the tibia where the root remnants sit. The freed ligament is threaded through that tunnel, dragging the meniscus root back to its footprint, and fixed inside with an interference screw or a hybrid arrangement. Because the graft is the patient's own ligament with a favorable pull direction and built-in continuity with the meniscus, the authors expect stronger fixation and better biological healing than suture-only repairs. They caution that the approach is not yet widely practiced.
pmc-13399895:
Nam Jun Baek and colleagues add a barbed suture to the standard pullout repair of a torn medial meniscus root, in a 2026 technical note. When the root tears, the meniscus squeezes outward and the joint degenerates. A barbed suture locks itself as it passes, holding even tension without knots.

The construct combines three passes. Two simple vertical sutures are placed five to ten millimeters from the torn edge with a self-retrieving passer. Then the barbed suture is delivered through the posteromedial capsule, crosses the back horn, and exits at the middle of the torn root. Its barbs grip the meniscocapsular tissue so the meniscus is drawn inward and centered. All three sutures travel down one tibial tunnel and are secured on the front of the shin with knotless anchors. The authors call the method simple and reproducible with standard instruments.
pmc-13400595:
Haicheng Ma and co-authors propose, in 2026, a two-way conversation between regulatory T cells and cancer-associated fibroblasts that keeps tumors shielded from immunity. Regulatory T cells calm immune attack, while fibroblasts around tumors support that suppression. The exact molecular links sustaining their partnership were unclear.

The review centers on tiny parcels released by regulatory T cells carrying a small RNA, miR-146a, which may reprogram fibroblasts through several known signaling nodes. In return, fibroblasts release attractants and growth factors that draw in and maintain the regulatory cells. The authors stress this loop rests largely on indirect evidence from separate models, so it needs direct testing. They discuss ways to break it, from blocking parcel release to neutralizing the RNA.
pmc-13400695:
Larysse Maria Santiago de Castro leads a scoping review, published in 2026, of how dietary glutamate and related chemistry may harm the optic nerve in glaucoma. Glaucoma slowly destroys retinal nerve cells, and excess glutamate signaling is one suspected driver. The review asks what nutritional or drug strategies might protect the retina.

Searching three databases for recent English studies, the team gathered 39 papers and sorted them into six themes, from biomarkers and drug interventions to antioxidants, cell death pathways and inflammation. The evidence ties glutamate-related damage mainly to internal imbalance rather than diet alone. Studies span lab markers, natural compounds and protective drugs, but varied methods prevented pooled analysis.
pmc-13401295:
Eman Abd Elmenum Shosha and colleagues report a 2026 survey of chicken infectious anemia virus across ten Egyptian governorates, with a focus on Upper Egypt, where data had been scarce. The virus keeps threatening poultry despite heavy vaccination, largely through vaccine-escape variants.

From 400 samples collected in 2024 and 2025, a TaqMan qPCR test found the virus in 30 percent, that is 120 samples. Five representative isolates were fully sequenced and classed as Genotype II, differing notably from the Genotype I vaccine strains, with amino acid similarity around 85 to 87 percent. One isolate, PX96998, proved to be a mosaic, its genome showing recombination breakpoints between closely related Genotype II lineages. The authors link this genetic variability to the vaccine strains in use.
pmc-13401495:
Keiichiro Aoki and co-authors published a 2026 pilot study of CogEvo, a tablet-based cognitive test, in patients recovering from acute stroke. Thinking problems are common after stroke and lengthen hospital stays, while standard paper tests such as the Mini-Mental State Examination have ceiling effects and often go unfinished in the acute phase.

Seventeen consecutive stroke patients at one centre took CogEvo alongside the MMSE and the Trail Making Test during occupational therapy assessment, on average about two weeks after admission. CogEvo scores orientation, attention, memory, planning, and spatial cognition. The team correlated its composite and domain scores with MMSE results, hospital stay length, stroke severity, and age, using rank correlations and separate complete-case analyses for the trail test. The study asks whether the tablet tool is feasible and meaningful right after stroke.
pmc-13401595:
Sarah M Alhammad and co-authors wrote a 2026 study of a hybrid deep learning system for predicting house prices, aimed at real estate valuation and investment decisions. Their model marries a gated recurrent unit network with a multilayer perceptron, then tunes it with two nature-inspired search methods.

A binary whale optimization algorithm chose which property features to feed the model, while ant colony optimization tuned its settings. The test bed was a public Kaggle dataset of 500 housing records with structural, location, and amenity attributes, split 70, 20. 10 percent for training, validation, and testing, with normalization fitted only on training data to avoid leakage. The hybrid beat standalone recurrent, convolutional, and long short-term memory models, reaching an R-squared just above 99 percent with low error across several measures.
pmc-13401695:
Shahnaz Armin and colleagues examined liver involvement in children hospitalized with COVID-19 in Iran in a 2026 cross-sectional study. Children usually fare mildly with the virus, but reports of liver effects kept growing, and their significance was unsettled.

The team reviewed 301 children with confirmed COVID-19 admitted to Mofid Children's Hospital in Tehran between March 2020 and July 2021. Liver involvement was defined as an ALT enzyme level above 40 units per litre. Raised ALT appeared in 84 children, just under 28 percent of the group. Clinical features, lab results, and imaging were compared between children with and without liver involvement using single-factor and multivariable regression. The analysis aimed to describe how liver involvement presents in paediatric COVID-19 and which children it strikes.
pmc-13401995:
Gilberto M Lozano Dubernard and co-authors present a 61-year-old man whose darkening skin led doctors toward failing adrenal glands. Scans showed calcium deposits in both adrenal glands, calcified lymph nodes, and a calcified spot in the liver, a pattern pointing to granulomatous disease. Blood tests found very high ACTH, the hormone that drives the adrenals, supporting primary adrenal failure.

What makes the case hard is overlap. Gut infection with non-tuberculous mycobacteria and Crohn disease can look alike on scans, scopes, and tissue samples, and all three problems appeared together here. The authors note that no solid population data describe how often this mix occurs. Their report helps clinicians sort look-alike gut and hormone conditions when calcium deposits and bowel disease appear in the same patient.
pmc-13402095:
Kentaro Goto leads a multicenter team tracking whether working-age patients in Japan got back to work after surgery meant to cure stomach or esophageal cancer. Working status was checked before surgery and at 6, 12, and 18 months afterward. The group also recorded time to first return, quality of life scores at six months, and weight loss after surgery.

Of 158 patients, 124 were working at 18 months, close to four in five. Older age and stage III or higher disease predicted staying out of work, while desk jobs and self-employment helped people return. First return came at a median of 30 days after stomach surgery and 70 days after esophageal surgery. Poor appetite, money strain, and weight loss of 10 percent or more flagged patients who may need extra support to keep working.
pmc-13402295:
Lei Huang and co-authors report a light-driven method that rebuilds furan rings into pyridazines, a ring type valued in drug design, without any added photocatalyst. Furans and nitrogen-rich rings called N-heteroarenes resist neat, site-selective editing because several spots react at once. Their trick pairs the furan with hexafluoroisopropanol in a hydrogen-bonded donor-acceptor complex that light can excite.

Excited pairs switch on oxygen from the air, making reactive oxygen species that pry the furan open into a chain with two carbonyl ends. Adding hydrazine then closes that chain into the six-membered pyridazine ring. The route worked across many starting materials, tolerated complex drug-like pieces, and ran in continuous flow with better speed and scale. A sibling reaction on pyridine salts, giving ortho-substituted pyridines in yields up to 93 percent, shows the wider editing platform behind the method.
pmc-13402895:
Shivani Senthil Kumar and colleagues report a rare case of Cotard delusion, treated with oral and long-acting injectable antipsychotics. The delusion is the nihilistic belief that one is dead or that organs have ceased to exist. First described by Jules Cotard in 1880, the condition usually rides on severe depression, though it also appears in schizophrenia and other psychoses, sometimes without low mood at all. Sufferers may stop eating, drinking, or washing, convinced self-care is pointless.

Among psychotic inpatients, systematic reviews place Cotard features in well under 1 percent of consultations, which makes each documented course valuable. Pairing daily oral medicine with a long-term injection guards against the adherence collapse the delusion itself invites. The authors offer the case to clinicians who may meet this striking syndrome once in a career and need a treatment foothold.
pmc-13403095:
Krenar Dobroshi and colleagues evaluate unipolar radiofrequency, a single-pole energy device, for tightening aging faces without surgery. Unlike other radiofrequency designs, the unipolar field heats tissue in a controlled zone, prompting collagen remodeling. Their chart review covered 93 treated patients, scored by blinded judges on the Global Aesthetic Improvement Scale and a modified Fitzpatrick wrinkle scale from before-and-after photographs.

Improvement averaged 1.9 points on the improvement scale, and wrinkle scores fell by a mean of 0.3 points after treatment, a change the authors report as significant. More sessions tracked with better improvement scores, and patients rated themselves satisfied to much satisfied, with minimal discomfort and no serious adverse events. The authors present unipolar treatment as a low-risk option for laxity and wrinkles, within the limits of a review with no control group.
pmc-13403295:
Laura I Gil Pineda and co-authors benchmark three enhanced sampling methods for exploring the shape-shifting of a disordered protein fragment, beta-catenin residues 17 to 48. Disordered proteins dodge standard structural tools. Phosphate tagging at serines 33 and 37 can reshape this fragment behavior. The team ran Gaussian-accelerated dynamics, metadynamics, and weighted ensemble runs beside ordinary runs. They tested both tagged and plain states, guided by two different steering variables.

The methods did not converge on one shared landscape; each explored partly distinct territory. Metadynamics and weighted ensemble runs reached shapes ordinary runs never visited, while accelerated dynamics largely overlapped the plain runs. The serine angle variable captured tagging-driven shifts better than end-to-end distance. Combined pools even revealed in-between shapes bridging the two states. The lesson for modelers is that sampler and steering choice together decide what a simulation can see.
pmc-13403395:
Berliner and co-authors ask, in 2026, how heart and breathing steer cerebrospinal fluid flow when the spinal canal's fluid space is obstructed. It is a step toward understanding post-traumatic syringomyelia, the fluid buildup that can follow spinal cord injury anywhere from one month to 45 years later and strikes one-third of injured people. In rats with a tied obstruction, they varied ventilation, heart rate, and blood pressure while tracking tracer movement live.

The obstruction reduced fluid flow. With it present, rapid heart rate reduced spinal flow further. Hypertension reduced fluid entry into tissue above the blockage yet increased tracer influx in the brain, and spontaneous breathing also boosted brain influx relative to ventilation. In the unobstructed cord, the same manipulations barely mattered. The authors warn that blood pressure dysregulation after injury may shape cyst risk, and call for more work on the timing effects they observed.
pmc-13403595:
Chi Cuong Tran led a 2026 report on a metal coil that slipped after treatment of a burst brain aneurysm. A 65-year-old woman had emergency coil treatment through a vessel for bleeding around the brain. A scan right after showed the coil had moved into the parent artery.

A loose coil there could block flow and cause a stroke, so open surgery followed at once. Surgeons pulled the coil out through a small artery cut and clipped the aneurysm neck shut. Later imaging showed good brain flow and a fully closed aneurysm. She left the hospital in stable shape, though with some nerve deficits.
pmc-13404095:
Constanza Morén and team tested a puzzle-based peer-teaching activity to replace rote memorization of antibiotic classes in nursing pharmacology. Their 2026 educational work takes on absenteeism and low drive in content-heavy courses, where nurses must learn many antibiotic groups for safe prescribing. Active learning could aid recall, yet proof for the Puzzle technique in this topic was thin.

Among 330 second-year nursing students at the University of Barcelona, three groups used the Puzzle method. Each student took one antibiotic topic to teach peers, while two control groups got standard lectures only. Puzzle groups scored clearly higher on quizzes and exams. The work backs peer-teaching puzzles for antibiotic pharmacology, while noting that single-course results should be tested across programs.
pmc-13404195:
Natasa Macak Stefanovic led a 2026 study of RNA signals six months after a heart attack, hunting marks of lasting change. One long RNA, MALAT1, soaks up a small RNA that normally reins in a swelling enzyme. The team checked genes in 534 patients and 381 controls, with RNA reads in a smaller subset.

Patients carried higher MALAT1 levels than controls half a year after the attack. The swelling enzyme ran higher in patients with advanced heart failure. One gene variant in MALAT1 appeared more often in patients, and a paired variant mix raised risk. MALAT1 may serve as a long-term marker, pending bigger checks.
pmc-13404295:
Betelehem Kassa and team surveyed ethics training needs among pediatricians and residents in Ethiopia. Their 2026 conference-based work takes on morally fraught cases heightened by scarce resources, absent child protection laws, and few ethics consultants or committees. Ethics teaching stays thin in undergraduate programs and absent from most residency plans.

Among 200 conference goers, at a 92 percent response rate, 85.8 percent felt their ethics teaching was too thin for frequent dilemmas, and 58 percent reported no formal route to handle ethics concerns in their hospitals. Common dilemmas included family refusal of care, team-family clashes, and holding back or withdrawing life-prolonging measures. The work calls for structured ethics courses and consult routes in Ethiopian child care.
pmc-13404495:
Anton Barnett and a large team describe a 2026 trial protocol for PROGROUP, a group-based programme for adults with severe obesity in the United Kingdom. About five million people in the country live with severe obesity, which shortens life and limits daily living. A smaller feasibility trial of the same programme supported moving to a full study.

Clinics will recruit groups of 30 adults and assign them evenly to PROGROUP sessions or usual care. A linked study in primary care will run smaller groups of 15 and watch how the programme fits routine practice. Weight, clinical measures and patient-reported outcomes are compared at six months. Process and cost-consequence analyses run beside the trial, and the design accounts for new obesity medicines entering NHS care.
pmc-13405095:
Taras Yevusiak and colleagues set out the REST trial, a 2026 protocol on stopping the weight-loss drug semaglutide. The drug produces large weight loss and better heart risk markers, yet most people regain weight after stopping suddenly. Whether tapering the dose softens that rebound is unknown.

Adults with obesity who lost at least 10 percent of their weight on semaglutide, then held steady for 12 weeks, will join. One group reduces the dose gradually over 16 weeks before stopping, while the other stops at once. The main outcome is the difference in weight change between groups. Blood pressure over 24 hours and fasting ghrelin, a hunger hormone, are also tracked.
pmc-13405695:
Pierre Kiesewetter, Thomas L Milani and Christian Mitschke test whether running speed changes how shoes perform, in a 2026 footwear study. Most shoe research fixes one standard speed, yet runners outdoors pick their own pace. Shoe effects measured at a set speed might not carry to natural running.

Twenty-two runners completed outdoor trials in seven shoes varying in cushioning and sole stiffness, each at a fixed and a self-chosen faster speed. Four sensor-derived measures were compared across conditions. Faster running raised all measures, but no interaction between shoe and speed appeared in the reported statistics. Relative shoe rankings stayed stable across speeds, easing worries that lab-speed testing misleads.
pmc-13406095:
Quan Zhou, Qi Ouyang and Hongli Wang model how a broken body clock worsens inflammation, in a 2026 mathematical study. Jet lag, shift work and ageing all disturb daily rhythms and heighten inflammatory responses. The mechanism linking clock damage to overreaction was unclear.

Their model couples the circadian clock to the innate immune response, including hormone control and a self-amplifying inflammation loop. The clock normally gates inflammation by shaping a two-state switch in that loop. Simulated jet lag or weaker clock genes tilted the switch, trapping the system longer in its high-inflammation state. Bursts of cytokines grew larger and lasted longer, matching the pattern seen in disrupted sleep.
pmc-13407695:
Henna Ali and co-authors survey, in 2026, mutations in the FGFR4 gene across human cancers using a large shared genomic database. FGFR4 helps drive cell growth and blood-vessel formation. Yet it is far less studied than its three sibling receptors. The team catalogued its mutations in the AACR Project GENIE collection.

The analysis covered 4,565 tumour samples from 4,283 patients. Mutations appeared most often in lung cancer, colorectal cancer, and melanoma, clustering in the protein's kinase and immunoglobulin-like domains with similar patterns across cancer types. One hotspot group, at amino acid 401, carried a higher mutation burden. More companion alterations appeared too. Closer checks blamed a subset of hypermutated tumours, not the hotspot itself. Sex showed no link, while ancestry groups differed.
pmc-13407895:
Hui Li and co-authors describe, in 2026, reprogramming the lung's resident macrophages into cancer fighters inside the body. These lung macrophages normally shield tumours. They suppress T cells and adopt a pro-tumour state. The team built an inhaled liposomal nanomedicine. It homes to the lungs and seeks out the macrophages. Inside them it switches on a cancer-targeting receptor gene.

The converted cells attacked lung cancer three ways at once: engulfing tumour cells directly, presenting tumour material to other immune cells more effectively, and flipping to an inflammatory state. In female mouse models, the induced immune activation and memory strengthened checkpoint-inhibitor drugs and suppressed spread. A nanomedicine route to cell therapy without removing cells from the body is demonstrated.
pmc-13408095:
Alexandra Becker and co-authors separate, in 2026, the heaviest hydrogen isotope from its lighter siblings using a silver-loaded sponge crystal. Splitting tritium matters for recycling fusion reactor exhaust. The team passed an equal-parts mixture of ordinary, heavy, and tritium hydrogen gases over silver-exchanged zeolite Y. They read the split by thermal desorption.

The recovered mixture came out enriched to a ratio of 1 to 41 to 175, a striking sorting from the equal start. Two-isotope experiments backed numerical predictions, and selectivity for tritium over ordinary hydrogen reached 244 at liquid-nitrogen temperature. Energy-efficient isotope sorting is the selling point: cold adsorption on the tailored zeolite achieves what usually demands far costlier cryogenic distillation trains.
pmc-13409395:
Marc Scott, Fulvia Pennoni, and Ignacio Bórquez tackle a measurement problem in 2026 at the heart of life-course research: how unsure should we be about what a person's life does next? Social scientists compress lives into sequences of states, at school, at work, partnered, and entropy measures summarise the scatter. The authors customise that machinery so uncertainty is always conditional on the path a person has actually travelled.

Fitting different Markov chain models to the same sequences produces a family of uncertainty measures that can bend with individual history, alongside companion measures of each model's predictive power. Comparing models then shows exactly where added complexity buys foresight and where it merely redescribes. Splitting by demographics or clusters enriches the narrative further. The contribution is a disciplined vocabulary for saying what a life-course model knows and what it only guesses.
pmc-13410595:
Medard Djedanem and colleagues asked in 2026 whether giving seasonal malaria prevention to older children helps in Niger. The drugs, sulfadoxine-pyrimethamine with amodiaquine, are already given each month in the rainy season to children under five, and the team compared two districts in Zinder over three years.

One district widened the program to children aged five to ten while the other kept the under-five limit, using clinic records on fever, malaria cases, and deaths. Readers can see how the widened program tracked against the older rule, giving health planners local evidence for deciding who should receive the monthly courses.
pmc-13410795:
Jong Bin Kim and co-workers build in 2026 soft robots with many arched legs made from liquid crystal elastomer, a rubber that bends with heat and light cues. Real limbs give animals spring and posture control, while most soft robots crawl flat with low bodies. Arc legs lift the body and open new moves.

The fibers were shaped to twist and flex in planned ways, then set into printed bodies copied from an octopus and a rolling spider. Robots could raise, lower, tilt, and spin their bodies with wide freedom. One version rolled at over a body length per second and climbed a steep slope. High body position adds useful instability, while feet anchor each push.
pmc-13411195:
Gina Keppel and colleagues report in 2026 how a colorectal screening trial managed to enroll rural patients, a group trials often miss. The Colonoscopy Outreach for Rural Communities trial tested remote nurse guidance to raise colonoscopy completion, and this paper reviews which clinics and outreach steps actually brought rural people in.

Of 527 enrolled patients, three quarters lived in rural areas, and clinics in rural counties drew almost entirely rural patients, while city clinics still added rural ones. The paper hands trial teams a workable playbook for reaching country patients through local primary care partners.
pmc-13411295:
Wenqian Wei and co-authors compare two emergency strategies for strokes caused by tandem lesions, blockages in both a neck artery and a brain artery. Their 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis asks whether adding intravenous clot-busting drugs to catheter-based clot removal improves outcomes over catheter treatment alone.

Nine studies covering 1,756 patients were pooled, 976 receiving combined treatment and 780 catheter treatment alone. Combined treatment achieved successful reopening of the vessel more often and left more patients functionally independent at ninety days. The risk of symptomatic brain bleeding did not differ significantly between strategies. Ninety-day mortality was lower with combined treatment. The authors conclude that adding intravenous thrombolysis may improve functional results in this stroke type, while the evidence remains comparative rather than definitive.
pmc-13414995:
Mairi Ziaka reports a single patient case in 2026 that may widen the known picture of azathioprine hypersensitivity. Azathioprine suppresses the immune system and can trigger a rare reaction within the first weeks of use. The patient, a woman aged 75, became ill three weeks after starting the drug.

Alongside fever and other body-wide features typical of the syndrome, scans showed enlarged lymph nodes in both lung roots and the chest center. Such node swelling has not been reported with this reaction before. The report weighs other possible causes for the nodes. Clinicians meeting this syndrome may now add lymph node enlargement to its possible signs.
pmc-13415395:
Nobuyuki Nakajima and co-authors report a rare case of one cancer growing inside another, in 2026. A woman aged 64 with long standing hormone driven breast cancer developed a kidney mass of twenty-three millimeters. Robotic partial kidney removal revealed clear cell kidney cancer, with nests of breast cancer cells inside it.

Staining separated the two tumors cleanly: kidney cells carried PAX8 and CA9 markers, while breast cells carried CK7 and GATA3 with weak hormone receptor staining. Kidney cancers host such tumor in tumor spread more often than most cancers. A kidney mass in a breast cancer patient can hide this pattern even when scans look ordinary.
pmc-13416195:
Timothy Fullman and colleagues tracked 192 female caribou of Alaska's Teshekpuk herd by GPS from 2004 to 2021 to see how winter ranges shift. Animals must weigh loyalty to known winter ground against moving to better conditions as weather, pregnancy, and summer forage change.

The herd still used the same four winter areas as in earlier decades, with growing use of eastern areas, and reuse beat chance even though individuals often switched areas year to year. Fall warmth, low precipitation, and summer conditions shaped choices most, giving wildlife managers a weather-aware view of herd movement.
pmc-13417195:
John M Talbott and colleagues design a glowing probe that can track methylglyoxal inside living cells, in a 2026 chemistry study. Methylglyoxal is a reactive sugar byproduct tied to cell stress, brain disease, and diabetes. Older probes confuse it with common aldehydes, or need harsh light that harms cells.

Their design tunes the energy levels of a dye core so it stays dark until methylglyoxal binds, then lets go again. That reversibility allows watching levels rise and fall over time under gentle visible light. Tests in mouse brain tissue showed dose linked signals. The design rules may guide other reversible sensors for metabolic stress.
pmc-13418095:
Joanna Maria Gonçalves Souza-Fabjan and colleagues compare two embryo production routes in sheep and goats, in a 2026 review. The older route gathers embryos from live superovulated females, while the newer route makes embryos in the lab from collected eggs. Cattle breeding shifted fast to the lab route, yet small ruminants still rely mainly on the live route.

Reasons include fragile eggs and embryos in these species and the lack of easy repeat egg collection that cattle enjoy. New non surgical embryo recovery has also strengthened the live route's welfare case. Lab production will likely grow as a complement rather than a replacement, the authors argue.
pmc-13418795:
Tingting Wang and colleagues compared antipsychotic drugs paired with electroconvulsive therapy for acute schizophrenia in a 2026 real-world study of 465 patients. All received six bitemporal shock sessions over two weeks, yet which companion drug best lifts symptoms and with what side effects stayed unclear.

Every group improved, and after adjustment, clozapine and sulpiride combinations beat shock therapy alone on overall symptom reduction, while several drugs also led on positive symptoms. Clinicians gain a comparative map for pairing drugs with shock therapy, pending fuller safety comparisons across all drug pairings studied.
pmc-13419195:
Dave and colleagues present a 2026 review of the brain as a hiding place for HIV, based largely on autopsy tissue from people who had the virus. Modern drug therapy suppresses HIV in blood but cannot clear virus genomes woven into long-lived cells. The brain has limited immune access, so the team surveyed postmortem evidence.

Studies find HIV DNA, RNA, and even whole, working proviruses in brain tissue from people whose blood virus was fully suppressed. The main shelters appear to be microglia and brain macrophages, immune cells of the myeloid line, while infection of astrocytes, the brain's support cells, stays debated. These shelters stay active and pair with chronic brain inflammation, which may drive the thinking and memory problems seen in treated HIV.
pmc-13420095:
Bernardo Garcia Barroso and colleagues measure the front thigh tendon as a graft source for rebuilding torn knee ligaments, in a planned case series. The rectus femoris tendon has drawn fresh interest as graft material beside older hamstring and kneecap options. Gentler harvest methods promise grafts long enough for doubled or tripled strands with less donor-site harm.

The mean graft length reached 30.8 centimeters in the series, with an error range of 3.4 in the same units, and nearly every graft passed the 24-centimeter mark. Problems during harvest were logged as carefully as the lengths. Body measures that predict graft size before surgery form the practical heart of the paper. Surgeons planning ligament repair get numbers they can plan around.
pmc-13420295:
Hammer and colleagues reported in 2026 a single-operation treatment for a five-year-old boy with a Wilms tumour. Wilms tumour is a childhood kidney cancer, and his tumour had grown into the large vein that drains the kidney area. He also had a patent foramen ovale, a small hole between the heart's upper chambers that normally closes after birth.

In one operation the team closed the heart hole, removed the affected kidney, and cleared the tumour clot from the inferior vena cava. The combined procedure used heart-lung bypass, meaning a machine took over circulation during the delicate steps. The boy recovered without complications after surgery. At six months he remained well and free of tumour. The authors stress careful pre-surgery checks in such children and the value of heart and cancer teams working as one.
pmc-13421095:
Gavriel Brody and colleagues report an emergency-led urgent care unit built inside a community health center in Kiryas Joel, New York, serving a largely Ultra-Orthodox Hasidic population. Underserved areas lean on emergency rooms for minor problems when same-day care is missing. The unit offers long hours, holiday opening, and referral links shaped to the community it serves.

Visit volume climbed from 1,215 encounters in 2020 to 13,636 in 2025 in the reported counts, a rise the authors put at 1022.3 percent across the period. Cultural and language barriers that once suppressed care seeking were met by design rather than by posters alone. The growth itself makes the case: build urgent care that fits a community, and the community will come before crises do.
pmc-13421295:
Mašek, Buss, and colleagues reviewed in 2026 how the gas around heated biomass shapes the charcoal-like product called biochar. Biochar is made by pyrolysis, meaning heating plant matter with little oxygen. The review compares nitrogen, steam, carbon dioxide, methane, ammonia, pyrolysis gas itself, and mildly oxidative settings.

Nitrogen is the common lab choice, but other gases can build desired traits in a single step. Steam and carbon dioxide, for instance, can raise porosity, meaning the share of tiny holes that give biochar its working surface. Reactive gases can also add chemical groups that help biochar bind pollutants or feed soils. The review weighs gains against costs, safety issues, and effects on the gas and liquid products of pyrolysis. The authors close with open questions and a roadmap for smarter, cheaper biochar production.
pmc-13421695:
Jingyi Wang leads a sixteen-author team reporting, in a 2026 study, a chemical recipe that turns scar-forming astrocytes into new neurons inside a brain damaged by bleeding stroke. Adult brains replace lost neurons poorly, and converting abundant support cells in place is an attractive workaround that had rarely been shown under real injury conditions.

Their seven-compound cocktail, delivered by pumps into the brain, reprogrammed astrocytes into working, electrically active neurons, confirmed by genetic lineage tracing in mice. A form of iron-driven cell death called ferroptosis rose during conversion, and blocking it changed the efficiency of the process. The team combined staining, gene readouts, circuit tracing and behaviour tests to verify the new neurons.
pmc-13421795:
Yilma Markos Larebo leads a six-author survey, published in 2026, of what Ethiopian health workers know and feel about mpox as the virus re-emerges. No earlier study had covered the Central Ethiopia Region, where public facility staff would meet the first cases.

An online questionnaire reached 419 workers in June 2025. Fewer than half — about forty-seven percent — had good knowledge, and a similar share held positive attitudes. Advanced degrees, certain professions such as health officers and pharmacists, and positive attitudes themselves predicted better knowledge, while some income patterns surprised the authors. They argue the figures expose a training need before an outbreak tests the system.
pmc-13422795:
Stanley Goodbody, Brian W Johnston, Chloe Lord, Angela Hall and Ingeborg D Welters set out, in a 2026 protocol, a systematic review. It asks whether heart rate variability can warn that a critically ill patient is about to deteriorate. The measure — tiny beat-to-beat timing changes — reflects the autonomic, immune and breathing systems at once, and it can be monitored continuously and painlessly.

Standard prognostic scores rely on intermittent snapshots that age fast. The review will gather randomised and observational studies of hospitalised critically ill adults, judging how well variability measures predict death and other major outcomes, and appraising how the measurement itself was done. Reporting follows the PRISMA standard. The protocol promises a verdict on both predictive value and method quality.
pmc-13424095:
Isabella Gomez and co-workers tested in 2026 how early-life events link to obsessive-compulsive symptoms through self-concept in 242 non-medical adults. The feared self, the person one dreads becoming, is thought to drive obsessive-compulsive illness, yet how it forms from childhood experience was little tested.

Path analysis tied strict raising and bad puberty-timing views to worse symptoms through mixed self-concept and a twisted feared self. The non-clinical sample means results speak to symptom pathways, not to diagnosed illness alone.
pmc-13424295:

pmc-13424595:

Adjusted models weighed social background, other illness, and lifestyle, so sex gaps could be read fairly. The paper helps readers see where care for men and women parts ways as people age.
pmc-13424895:

pmc-13425095:

pmc-13425595:

pmc-13425795:
Chiara Di Gravio and colleagues examined long COVID and work in England in a 2026 population cohort study using REACT survey data. pmc-13425895:

pmc-13426195:

pmc-13426495:

Women were grouped by epidural duration, with non-recipients counted as zero, and a data-driven cutoff split longer from shorter exposure.

Delayed onset with longer epidural exposure would suggest a practical lever during labor care. Blood checks run each few hours in the ward, so a late rise in blood force can be caught and curbed in good time with drugs.
pmc-13427095:
Matthew Yau, Erin Gallagher, and Jennifer Rose-Smith write on caring for a person at the end of life in a 2026 French-language guidance article for clinicians in Canada. pmc-13427495:
Umayr R. Shaikh and coauthors examine bemotrizinol's approval as a turning point for United States sunscreen regulation in a 2026 article. pmc-13427795:
Alfarawan and colleagues tested in 2026 whether dropping a routine preventive antibiotic dose changed outcomes after robotic repair of belly wall hernias at one German center. Wound event rates at thirty and ninety days were nearly the same in both groups, and infections were rare either way. Hospital stay matched at two days, and no patient subgroup gained from the dose. The authors conclude that skipping routine prophylaxis in this setting appears safe, sparing antibiotics without added harm.
pmc-13428395:
Noor Ul Ain and co-authors follow, in a 2026 study, whether treating a storage disease can slow the birth of abnormal antibody-producing cell clones. Gaucher disease builds up a fatty substance that the immune system keeps reacting to, and patients develop monoclonal gammopathy, a precursor of myeloma, far more often than expected. One modern pill suppressed the fatty target more deeply than the older enzyme infusions. Adjusted analyses pointed the same way. The work offers rare human evidence that cutting a defined immune trigger can bend a precancer's course.
pmc-13428695:
Martínez-Tabar and colleagues ask whether the source of dietary protein, plant or animal, predicts how long people live. Their 2026 study uses the SUN cohort, a Spanish project of university graduates. Diet was measured by a validated food questionnaire at the start and again ten years on. The analysis covers 17,989 adults, followed for a median of twelve years, during which 460 deaths occurred.

Animal protein intake showed no link to total mortality. Plant protein also failed to tie to deaths from heart disease or cancer taken alone, so the benefit sits in the all cause total. In a Mediterranean population with a young average age, the protein source, not just the amount, tracked with survival.
pmc-13429695:

A convolutional memory network then learns flashover behaviour from that coupled physics. Grid engineers get a predictor that respects how arcs actually speed and stretch, rather than freezing them into a single steady state.
pmc-13431495:
Ozlem Kalaycik Sengul and co-authors reviewed hospital records in 2026 for liver strain in children admitted with chest infections after the COVID years. The grave cases stood apart: every case of sharp liver failure, and every case of very high enzyme spikes, sat in the flu group, most tied to one flu type. pmc-13433195:
Rebecca Farina, Eric Tchetgen Tchetgen, and Arun Kumar Kuchibhotla built math tools in 2026 to set honest forecast bands for survival times when some study exits hide the true end. Tests back the edge.
pmc-13433495:
Mahsa Javadian and colleagues review how tiny sacs from breast tumours, packed with long non-coding RNAs, steer macrophages and tumours as they grow side by side. That flip drives tumour growth, immune reshaping, and drug-proof traits. pmc-13433695:

A central theme is delivery: siRNA only helps if it reaches tumour cells intact and in sufficient dose. pmc-13434495:
Maike Kötzsche and colleagues survey hunger among university students in nine European countries in 2026. A web survey during the Covid years drew 3,250 students who could be scored with a shared United Nations scale. The scale asks about skipped meals and empty cupboards in a set way.

Rates of mid or high food insecurity ran from 3.1 percent at one Italian site to 32.1 percent at a Turkish site. Seven of nine sites topped ten percent, above the broad European mean. Risk rose for students born outside Europe, with less schooled parents, or on loans. Campus food aid looks like a core need, not a perk.
pmc-13434795:
Riovie D Ramos, Tanghua Li, and Kyle M Morgan mine old reefs to judge reef futures in 2026. Growth records from 288 past reefs at 92 Indo Pacific sites were placed on one scale. Past growth rates set a fair test for how fast reefs can climb as seas rise.

Sea level pace plus local shape and ecology jointly set past growth. Most sites lack the pace to match high emission sea rise, 76 percent by the count here. pmc-13435095:
Kentarou Nishimura and coauthors test a blood sugar chain ratio as a psoriasis gauge in 2026. Psoriasis lacks blood tests that track severity and drug response well. Blood came from 45 patients, plus comparison groups with eczema and healthy skin.

The ratio of two sugar chain types ran higher in psoriasis than in healthy controls. It rose and fell with skin severity scores. Accuracy matched two known blood marks of swelling. Shifts in the ratio tracked gains after body wide therapy, notably with newer biologic drugs. Age, sex, and other illness did not sway it much. A cheap blood check may aid visit by visit care.
pmc-13435195:
Martina Mana and colleagues check whether quick test recipes agree on dementia in Parkinson disease in 2026. Charts for 190 patients fed 68 screening recipes built from two short thinking tests. Daily function was scored two ways, by one hard item or by a total score.

Dementia rates swung from 2.1 percent to 16.8 percent by recipe choice. Recipes sharing a function rule agreed well, while mixed rules agreed poorly. A lean pair of items, word recall plus a counting task, matched the full battery verdict closely. A simple rule lets clinics tune the cutoff to local rates. Test choice, the work warns, can double count a ward.
pmc-13435395:
Saber Kouas's team tested salt-tolerant phosphate bacteria in 2026 to help barley cope with salty soil plus low phosphorus, two stresses that often strike together. Seed coating with different bacterial isolates was tried on seedlings under salt alone and salt with phosphorus shortage, tracking growth, water status, photosynthesis, ion balance, and antioxidant defenses. Effects varied by strain and plant part, so no single isolate won on every measure.

Farmers in dry, salty regions get a low-cost, eco-friendly lead for biostimulants. Field trials will decide which strains hold up outside the lab.
pmc-13436195:
Norris and colleagues set out in 2026 the evaluation plan for Move Together Buckinghamshire. The program serves inactive adults over fifty with long-term conditions in deprived parts of the English county. Inactivity is common in this group, and generic offers rarely stick. The program pairs each user with an activity referral specialist for a one-to-one session, three follow-up contacts, and access to an online booking platform over twelve weeks.

The protocol covers the first eighteen months of delivery. Activity, quality of life, loneliness, and confidence will be tracked to one year after the program. Focus groups will probe how users and staff experience it, and an economic study will price the setup and running.
pmc-13436595:
Alyssa Harrell-Webber and coauthors survey 1,022 United States adults on weariness with opioid messages in 2026. The poll ran in August 2024 and scores exhaustion from constant crisis coverage. Mean fatigue sat mid scale, with gaps by sex, schooling, income, and politics.

Higher fatigue tracked stronger stigma toward people with opioid use disorder. Higher fatigue also tracked weaker support for treatment policies. Personal history with the crisis shaped scores as well. Campaigns that repeat the same alerts may dull their own aims. Planners should rotate fresh angles and voices to keep support alive.
pmc-13437195:

Their 2026 study looked back at forty-eight patients treated at two centers under general anesthesia. Twenty-seven patients also got an ultrasound-guided block into the lateral pterygoid muscle, a deep jaw muscle, while twenty-one did not.

Six hours after surgery, the block group reported a median pain score of zero at rest, against three in the comparison group. Scores also ran lower at two hours and later that evening, then evened out by the next morning. Block patients waited a median of ten hours for their first rescue pain drug, against seven hours for the others, though that gap was not firm. No harm tied to the block was recorded. The authors call the results early hints, pointing to a registered trial now testing the idea.
pmc-13437295:

Scans showed a severely thickened heart wall and weak pumping, pointing first to hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, an inherited condition. A heart biopsy found those same young cells packed through the muscle. After three rounds of chemotherapy, no disease remained in his marrow, and his heart shape and function returned to normal. pmc-13438595:

It also reframes pollinator communication as an open channel third parties can hack.
pmc-13439195:

That frame may guide future drugs for related channel diseases.
pmc-13439295:

Removal showed the clearest symptom gains, while bleeding and narrowing struck only the tissue-cutting methods. Short follow-up and small groups mean durability is still an open question.
pmc-13439495:

The authors conclude both techniques are comparably safe here.
pmc-13439595:

The authors stress that drought timing, not just severity, shapes elephant behaviour.
pmc-13439895:

pmc-13440095:

pmc-13440595:

pmc-13443195:

pmc-13445695:

Fight-back genes were few, but a plasmid-borne gene plus plasmid spread signals spread risk. Twenty-eight harm leads, mostly shared with Staphylococcus aureus, suggest sideways transfer, marking the species for animal-health watch.
pmc-13446195:

pmc-13446295:

pmc-13447095:

pmc-13447295:

pmc-13448095:

Their 2026 study uses 24 mice in three groups: a normal schedule group, a schedule shifted group, and a shifted group given probiotics. pmc-13448195:

pmc-13448495:

pmc-13449495:

pmc-13473295:

pmc-13474795:

pmc-13499595:

No primary tumour existed in gut or pancreas. pmc-13500095:

pmc-13500395:
Yoshiharu Sugino and others map bovine brucellosis and its socioeconomic correlates in northern Sri Lanka. Brucellosis harms livestock productivity and can infect people through unpasteurized milk and contact.

Agricultural land use tracked positively with seropositivity, while barn cleaning tracked negatively. pmc-13500495:

pmc-13501295:

pmc-13501695:
Xiangzhen Meng, Luo Wang, and Xinlun Tian present a 2026 review of cell and vesicle therapy aimed at diffuse alveolar damage, the core lung injury pattern behind several lethal conditions. pmc-13501795:

pmc-13503695:

The team reworked a known copper-based crystal by swapping one link for a part with free nitrogen sites. Those sites grip the acid-like hydrogens of propylene and flex the frame open at low pressure. Propane does not trigger the same move. The crystal is made in water, stands up to water well, and keeps the traits that suit large-scale use.
pmc-13503995:

Silencing the gene in lab and animal tests slowed cancer growth and movement, and switched ferroptosis back on. The authors propose the gene as a target for tailored care.
pmc-13504795:
Kuo-An Wu leads a team searching fluid from infected lungs for a marker that flags dangerous worsening, in a 2026 study. Fluid that builds beside an infected lung can turn severe, forming thick pus pockets with high death rates. Early warning would help doctors act sooner.

A check group of 220 patients with varied chest fluid causes confirmed the marker sorted severe cases with high accuracy. Cell tests showed the protein drives two inflammatory signals through a known switch. The team proposes it as marker and target.
pmc-13504995:
Zexuan Lv leads a team reporting two cases where an adrenal tumor caused Cushing syndrome by making a pituitary hormone, in a 2026 paper. Both patients had stubborn high blood pressure and low potassium, and one fell ill during pregnancy with atypical signs. Hormone tests showed very high ACTH and cortisol with a lost daily rhythm. Scans found adrenal masses, and robot-assisted surgery removed them. Tissue tests confirmed the tumor type with hormone staining in spots. Hormones fell fast after surgery, pressure and potassium improved, and no tumor returned.
pmc-13505095:
Qiulong Yan leads a team asking which gut microbe patterns mark who benefits from stool transplant for irritable bowel syndrome, in a 2026 re-analysis. pmc-13507195:
Xuehao Fu leads a 2026 team that sequences the giant genome of Nigella damascena, a buttercup relative with ornate petals, to learn how jumping genes inflate genomes. Its genome spans about eleven billion letters, roughly thirty-five times that of columbine, a small-genome relative. Family history points to a much smaller ancestral genome.

Insertions stretched gene spacers, rewrote coding parts, and even created new genes, touching about a fifth of protein-coding genes. Such changes likely shaped fancy petals, fused seed cases, and special chemicals. Jumping genes act as architects, not just bulk.
pmc-13507295:
Shaojin Ma, Yan Bai, Jiajia Shao, and Xue Bai test, in 2026 work, how cooking oil thickness affects dishwasher cleaning. The heated peanut oil cleaned worse, especially in standard mode, forming a film on ceramic under microscope views while the thin oil stayed as separate particles. Wash mode mattered more for thick oil. Regional test standards should reflect local diets.
pmc-13507795:

pmc-13508195:

pmc-13508295:
Vivien Lee and six co-authors study a workshop where people with disability teach medical students how to communicate, in work published in 2026. Themes showed professional values grow through direct experience, watching role models, reflection, and honest conversation in a learning group. Tutors learned alongside students from the disabled teachers, a rare leveling. Gaps were named too, including how disability had been absent from teaching before. pmc-13509795:

pmc-13510595:

pmc-13510895:

pmc-13511095:

pmc-13511295:

pmc-13514195:

pmc-13514295:

pmc-13515995:

pmc-13516295:

pmc-13517595:

pmc-13518795:

pmc-13518895:

pmc-13519095:

pmc-13519495:

pmc-13519895:

pmc-13520095:

pmc-13520195:

pmc-13520295:

pmc-13520395:

pmc-13520695:

pmc-13520995:

pmc-13521695:

pmc-13521895:

Scattered light was measured by polarisation.

pmc-13521995:

Blood levels varied most in the six to eleven age band, with higher exposure noted. Response among severe cases rose from about 56 percent at three months to about 72 percent at six months.
pmc-13522495:

pmc-13523295:

The authors detail the clinical, imaging, tissue, and molecular features to raise awareness of this uncommon presentation.
pmc-13524095:
Xu and colleagues review new work on TaMIP1, a wheat gene that helps roots grow. Wheat gives about a quarter of the food energy people eat worldwide. Dry spells hit wheat hard, and roots are the first parts to face dry soil.

Work by Fan and others found two forms of the gene tied to root weight. Plants with the stronger form grew more roots and stood up better to drought. Mutant plants with the gene switched off grew fewer roots. Adding extra gene copies in rice also boosted root growth. Pairing the best forms of two root genes gave strong roots and good grain traits at once.
pmc-13524795:
James M. F. Morris and colleagues report a 2026 molecular electronics study on charge transport through bare linear carbon chains. Carbyne, a chain of carbon atoms in a single line, promises outstanding electrical and mechanical behavior. Yet it is hard to make, and the end groups used to stabilize models distort its electronics.

Using a scanning tunnelling microscope break junction, the team transferred carbon fragments from gold compounds directly onto gold electrodes, forming stable junctions with chains up to sixteen atoms and no end caps. Shorter chains behaved like oligoyne models, with conductance falling as length grew. Longer chains showed bonds evening out toward a cumulenic structure and remarkably stronger transport. Direct gold-carbon contact gave high conductance and near-ballistic flow, pointing toward carbon-based nanoelectronics.
pmc-13527095:
Zuo and colleagues describe a 2026 single-molecule system that hides and reveals information through timed color changes driven by light. One designed molecule undergoes a chain of light-driven reactions with no catalyst, meaning no helper chemical is needed, and its glow shifts color step by step.

The molecule starts out yellow, turns red after about five minutes of light, yellow again near twenty minutes, and blue by about eighty minutes. Each step follows a set chemical change, from splitting with water to oxidation by light. The team used the timed colors to build time-gated 3D codes and gel pads that reveal, conceal, and erase messages in stages. Such materials could strengthen anti-counterfeiting labels and data protection.
pmc-13527995:
Dennis Getange and six colleagues test mosquito-based surveillance for livestock germs in Kenya in a 2026 study. The method, called xenosurveillance, uses blood-feeding insects as living samplers. Traps were set near livestock pens in Kajiado and Naivasha counties. The team caught 4,673 mosquitoes from five genera. Only 56 had recently fed on blood.

Those fed mosquitoes were ground up and tested for their meal source and for germs. All pathogen hits came from blood-fed insects. Anaplasma bacteria turned up in two mosquito species, matching cattle and goat blood meals. A related germ, Candidatus Neoehrlichia mikurensis, appeared in Mansonia africana. That zoonotic germ had not been reported in Kenyan mosquitoes before. The authors call this first round promising but preliminary for watching germs where farms meet wildlife.
pmc-13528095:
Moore Ikechi Mike-Ogburia and five colleagues test people with suspected tuberculosis at a Nigerian teaching hospital in a 2026 study. The Port Harcourt study ran from April to August 2024. It enrolled 242 patients with TB-like symptoms. Sputum gene tests checked for TB. Rapid antigen tests checked for COVID-19. Questionnaires captured habits, housing, and health history.

TB was found in about twenty-two percent of patients. Not one patient tested positive for COVID-19. No mixed infections appeared. Background traits like age or sex did not predict TB. Close contact with a long-coughing person raised odds over fivefold. HIV infection, smoking, and crowded, poorly aired housing also raised risk. The authors urge stronger contact tracing and joined TB and HIV services. Smoking cessation support is part of their advice.
pmc-13530195:
Dominika Granda and colleagues link eating patterns to premenstrual symptom severity in a 2026 study of young women in Central Europe. Earlier work came mostly from Asian groups with mixed answers, leaving European evidence thin. Questionnaires on food habits and symptom screening covered 609 women aged 18 to 35.

Grouping by diet produced three patterns: a healthy pattern, a Western pattern, and a low-intake pattern. Women in the Western and low-intake groups faced markedly higher odds of severe symptoms than the healthy group. The low-intake group also showed higher odds of moderate symptoms. The design cannot prove cause.
pmc-13530795:
Huntley and colleagues present in 2026, as conference poster 101, outcomes of percutaneous knotless bridge repair of torn Achilles tendons in active patients. This minimally invasive technique anchors into the heel bone instead of relying on surgical knots that can fail.

The retrospective series covered 101 acute ruptures treated from 2020 to 2024, nearly all sustained during sport, basketball most often. Among the 49 patients whose return-to-sport status was documented, about eighty-five percent resumed their activity at an average of roughly thirty-three weeks. Most of those performed at their pre-injury level or better. Scores on Achilles-specific and foot function measures averaged in the mid-nineties, classified as highly functional, and pain faded across the first nine months. Nicotine users returned at a clearly lower rate than non-users.
pmc-13531495:
Samatar Osman and colleagues build a 2026 framework for what makes a referral from family doctors to hospital specialists a good one. Poor referral letters delay care and waste resources, yet no shared standard existed. Three databases supplied studies from 1999 to 2024 for a scoping review with qualitative analysis.

Fifty-four studies yielded four themes: complete patient history and tests, clear clinical reasoning, patient understanding and preference, and barriers such as time pressure. A practical checklist distilled those themes for daily use. The authors aim for letters that carry enough detail to act on without burying specialists in paperwork.
pmc-13531895:
Farzaneh Motafeghi and colleagues pair in 2026 an old antibiotic, thiostrepton, with cisplatin against ovarian cancer cells that learned to resist cisplatin. Resistant cells in dishes received each drug alone and together for a day. Tests covered survival, energy, membrane damage, DNA injury, oxidative stress, and cell death signals.

The pairing killed far more cells than either drug alone. Oxidative stress and DNA damage climbed while antioxidant defenses fell and power-station function faltered. Inflammatory signals rose, and a growth pathway output shrank with its target genes quieted. The antibiotic restored drug sensitivity through several routes at once.
pmc-13532795:
Pernille Kølbæk and colleagues checked whether new diabetes found in psychiatric care actually gets treated. Published in 2026, the chart review sampled patients in Denmark's Central Region psychiatric services whose lab tests first flagged diabetes between 2019 and 2024. People with severe mental illness die younger, partly from diabetes driven by lifestyle and psychiatric drug effects.

Among 416 patients with new diabetes, only about one third received a documented intervention within three months, most often referral to a family doctor. Diabetes drugs started in only a small share of those treated. The sole factor tied to missing care was lower body weight, with lean patients far more likely to go without action. The authors call the gap a warning for metabolic safety in psychiatric services.
pmc-13534395:
Xijia Wang and colleagues report in 2026 that USP11, an enzyme that removes ubiquitin tags, protects the heart against harmful enlargement. Enlarged heart muscle often precedes heart failure, and protein tag control helps keep cell signals stable. USP11 levels fell in stressed mouse hearts and in treated heart cells.

Raising USP11 in heart cells eased enlargement and scarring after pressure overload and improved pumping. The enzyme binds and steadies SIRT6, a protective protein, by stripping tags that mark it for disposal. Blocking the growth pathway through SIRT6 explains the benefit, pointing to a new drug target.
pmc-13534495:
Afruz Dilshad Arney and colleagues profile in 2026 leaf extracts of Urena lobata, a plant used in folk care, for antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and clot-dissolving traits. Oxidative stress fuels many chronic diseases, so plant compounds draw screening interest. Extracts were split into fractions and tested in lab assays plus computer docking.

The ethyl acetate fraction showed the strongest antioxidant action and steadied red cell membranes at levels close to a standard drug. It also dissolved clots well in lab tests. Docking suggested strong binding to a key inflammation enzyme, supporting follow-up isolation work.
pmc-13534895:
Tabea Stark and Stefan Muller discuss in 2026 work casting PML, a nuclear protein, as a guardian against toxic protein clumps in amyotrophic lateral sclerosis. Clumps are a hallmark of nerve diseases, and cells clear them through a tag-and-shred system. The reviewed study links an ALS-related NEK1 variant to this cleanup route.

The faulty protein is drawn into PML bodies, where it likely gains tags that mark it for disposal. In mice, losing PML worsened ALS-like signs, while raising PML delayed onset. Boosting PML thus emerges as a possible therapy path for related diseases.
pmc-13536595:
Seyed Saman Nemati and colleagues build in 2026 a biosensor that detects harmful Gram-negative bacteria using colistin, an antibiotic that binds their outer walls. Fast, selective detection aids diagnosis plus food and water checks. The chip uses a coated silicon platform that changes current when target bacteria bind.

The device picked out six Gram-negative species at low counts while ignoring two Gram-positive controls. Spiked bottled water and urine tests matched lab buffer results closely in recovery checks. The team sees promise for low-cost screening, pending wider real-world testing.
pmc-13536795:
Moshood Folorunsho Adeyemi and co-authors review face and mouth tumors over ten years at a Nigerian teaching hospital in a 2026 records study. Tissue reports from 2015 to 2024 supplied age, sex, site, and diagnosis for 588 patients. Lesions were grouped as benign or malignant, with statistical tests for age and sex patterns and comparison with reports from other Nigerian regions.

Benign lesions made up the large majority, led by a reactive lymph tissue overgrowth most common in childhood. A jaw tumor called ameloblastoma led benign true growths, especially in teens. Cancer odds rose steadily with age, and men faced higher cancer odds than women. A surface cancer type dominated malignancies, mostly in patients aged 50 years or older. The authors call for stronger diagnosis and screening services.
pmc-13539795:
Xia Wang leads a 2026 prospective study of a surgical fix for large holes in the macula, the small central area of the retina that gives sharp vision. The holes measured at least 400 micrometres across, a size that often resists standard repair.

Surgeons treated 31 eyes with vitrectomy, peeling of a thin inner membrane, and an injection of balanced salt solution under the retina through a fine needle. Nearly all holes had closed within a month, and sight measures kept improving through three months of checks. The five stubborn cases that had failed before also closed, with no complications reported during follow-up.
pmc-13540295:
Qingjing Xue and five colleagues run, in a 2026 randomised trial, an eight-week program pairing a gentle Chinese exercise routine called Baduanjin with computer-based cognitive training for people with schizophrenia. Medicines handle many symptoms of schizophrenia yet leave thinking, social function, and quality of life lagging.

One hundred twenty inpatients were split evenly between computer training alone and the combined program, which added forty minutes of Baduanjin to each session five times a week. Both groups improved in thinking and social scores. Only the combined group cut overall symptom scores, and its gains across every measure were larger. The authors support exercise as an add-on worth wider testing.
pmc-13542095:
Guiyan Zhao, Jiayuan Ouyang, and Jianhui Yang build, in a 2026 study, a hybrid deep learning framework for forecasting financial prices, a task plagued by noise and shifting patterns. Their design stacks three stages, each handling a different weakness of raw market series.

First, variational mode decomposition splits the price series into cleaner component waves. A convolutional self-attention block then sharpens the representation at each time step, and a bidirectional transformer reads the sequence in both directions to catch long-range dependencies. Across several financial assets and many market features, the combined model beat statistical, machine learning, and other deep learning benchmarks on error measures. Charts showed forecasts tracking actual market movements closely.
pmc-13542195:
Dessus and colleagues uncover a self-amplifying loop that jump-starts autophagy, the cell's system for engulfing and recycling worn-out material, in 2026 cell biology research. When starved, mammalian cells build autophagosomes, membrane sacs over 1,000 nanometers wide, within 30 minutes. A lipid-making enzyme complex, PtdIns3K-C1, produces a signal lipid that recruits other proteins, including the ATG8 family member GABARAP, onto the sac, called a phagophore, to drive its expansion.

Working with purified components on artificial membranes, the team showed membrane-bound GABARAP binds directly to the enzyme complex and potently switches it on. That creates a positive feedback loop: the complex's lipid signal recruits GABARAP, and GABARAP then makes the complex produce more signal right where growth is needed. The loop explains how phagophores ignite quickly rather than creeping into existence. Dessus argues this ignition circuit is a control point for tuning autophagy in disease.
pmc-13543595:
Xianzheng Jin's team asked in a 2026 study whether dabbing benzoyl peroxide on the shoulder before arthroscopy cuts contamination by Cutibacterium acnes. That skin bacterium hides in hair follicles and glands where standard antiseptic scrubbing barely reaches. Records covered 162 patients, half pretreated with the five-percent gel and half given the standard prep alone, with deep samples from joint fluid, tissue, and instrument surfaces grown for the organism.

Deep contamination struck about sixteen percent of pretreated patients against about thirty-five percent of controls, a relative risk near a half, and the pattern held across stricter definitions. Pretreated patients also carried fewer bacteria on the skin and had fewer tainted samples each. Clinical infection events in the short term did not differ. A cheap drugstore gel, the authors suggest, cleans the operative field.
pmc-13547195:
Xuan Yang and co-authors built in 2026 a prognosis model for head and neck squamous cell carcinoma from genes tied to gut microbes and the chemicals those microbes make. Gut bacteria influence many cancers, so the team assembled a risk score from 19 such genes using public tumor data and checked how well it separated patients by survival.

Patients scored high risk died sooner than low-risk patients, and the differing genes clustered in immune pathways. One immune signal, IL10, was confirmed at higher levels in tumor tissue than in neighboring normal tissue. Two common gut bacteria tracked with IL10 levels, hinting that they may shape outcomes through it. The authors propose microbe-linked genes as another route to prognosis and treatment ideas.
pmc-13547295:
Yeswanth Paluri and co-authors tested in 2026 concrete made partly from reclaimed asphalt pavement, old road material, reinforced with steel fibers for pavement use. Twenty mixes varied the share of recycled aggregate up to 30 percent and the fiber dose up to 1.25 percent. Strength, bending behavior, stress response, and resistance to repeated flexing were measured, and machine learning models were trained to predict the results.

More recycled aggregate steadily weakened the concrete, a flaw blamed on the weak bond around asphalt-coated stones. One percent steel fiber reversed much of the loss, lifting splitting and bending strength by roughly 45 percent and greatly extending fatigue life. A gradient boosting model predicted properties with high accuracy, which the authors offer as a design aid for greener pavements.
pmc-13547395:
Giorgio Angelotti and co-authors showed in 2026 that the surface shape of carbonized Herculaneum papyri carries enough signal to find ink. That is a promising detour for reading the only library surviving from the ancient world. Ink and scroll are both carbon, so X-ray methods barely separate them. Working with precision surface measurements of opened fragments, the team trained a deep learning model to separate inked from blank areas using topography alone.

The model found a usable signal even though letters are not generally raised and roughness cues are not universal. Fine side-to-side sampling proved crucial, since performance faded as resolution dropped, and transfer to a completely new papyrus varied. The authors call the work a proof of concept that can guide imaging choices for still-closed scrolls.
pmc-13547895:
Ricardo Reques and colleagues tested in 2026 whether a frog's eyes darken measurably as it dries out, offering a hands-off way to judge water stress in wild amphibians. Twenty-five adult Boana punctata tree frogs from Chaco province in Argentina were dried in stages by gentle airflow or by dry rice. They were then rehydrated for two hours while their irises were photographed and weighed-in by hydration level.

Darkened iris area grew by about one and a half percent for every one percent of hydration lost. The pattern held consistently across both drying methods, body sizes, and individuals, though larger frogs started from a paler baseline. Rehydration partly reversed the change. The authors validate iris darkening as a non-invasive stress marker for frogs facing a drying climate.
pmc-13548095:
Minako Iida and the Asia-Pacific Blood and Marrow Transplantation Group reported survey results from 2022 and 2023 on how the region chooses donors and stem cell sources for blood stem cell transplants. Half-matched family donors have reshaped practice, yet regional patterns by disease were poorly mapped. The survey sorted donors into identical siblings, half-matched or other relatives, and unrelated donors, and sources into marrow, blood, cord blood, and mixes.

Half-matched donors supplied roughly forty-five to sixty percent of transplants, ahead of unrelated donors, with identical siblings last. Peripheral blood was the dominant source at about sixty to seventy percent. Leaving China out of the count shifted the balance toward unrelated donors. Patterns otherwise held across leukemia, marrow failure, and blood disorder categories.
pmc-13548495:
Swapneel Mirani and colleagues survey what shapes public attitudes toward dementia in the United Kingdom in a 2026 study. Their online questionnaire gathered demographic details alongside three established scales covering dementia attitudes, wisdom, and views on aging. The authors wanted to know which personal traits track with warmer or colder feelings toward people living with dementia.

Working professionally in dementia care, scoring higher on wisdom, and holding positive views of aging all went with friendlier attitudes. Older respondents tended to hold more negative views, while women scored more positively than men. Two subscales stood out most strongly: psychosocial growth and the emotional side of wisdom. The authors suggest these links could guide stigma campaigns, staff education, and policy work.
pmc-13548595:
Seher Nur Sulku and colleagues examine how happiness in Türkiye shifted through the COVID-19 pandemic, in a 2026 analysis of national survey data. About ten thousand adults answered the country's Life Satisfaction Survey each year from 2019 to 2021. The team modeled who counted as happy across five grades, from very happy to very unhappy, looking for determinants that held steady or changed under pandemic pressure.

The share calling themselves happy or very happy slid from roughly fifty-four percent before the pandemic to under forty-nine percent in 2020, then recovered slightly. Health stayed the most cited source of happiness. Marriage, higher income, and satisfaction with health, income, and social life all raised happiness, and happiness traced a U-shape across age. Hope about the future stood above everything else, multiplying the odds of being very happy many times over in every year studied.
pmc-13550395:
Lili Zhang and colleagues review how enzymes that strip ubiquitin tags from proteins govern ferroptosis, an iron-fueled cell death, and thereby steer cancer drug resistance, in a 2026 article. Resistant tumors often lean hard on their defenses against ferroptosis, whose core regulators are controlled by how long the proteins survive and where they sit in the cell. Deubiquitinating enzymes edit those fates.

The review maps which enzymes stabilize or doom each ferroptosis regulator. Some act through disposal by the proteasome or lysosome. Others change activity directly. It then gathers evidence tying these ubiquitin edits to resistance against chemotherapy, targeted drugs, and immunotherapy. The authors close with strategies for attacking the ubiquitin and ferroptosis axis to wake stubborn tumors back up to drugs. Forcing this distinctive death, they argue, could crack resistance that blocks the usual routes.
pmc-13550495:
Muhammad Zohaib and colleagues write a unified mathematical description for tunnel supports that yield on purpose, in a 2026 engineering study. In squeezing soft rock, stiff linings crack because they cannot give, so engineers insert limiters, inflatable airbags or steel bellows, that compress at a set force. Until now their design rested on rules of thumb. The new model spells out three stages: stiff elastic yielding, hardening after yield, and final locking at ultimate resistance.

Eight dimensionless scores grade qualities like ductility, strain uniformity, and adaptability. Large model tests showed airbag limiters cut vertical deformation by about a third against rigid supports and adapted earliest, while bellows dissipated more energy and kept strain more even. Maps built from stiffness ratios turn the model into a selection tool for squeezing ground.
pmc-13551695:
Zezhi Fan, leading eight colleagues, published a 2026 review of how nerves and the immune system talk to each other inside tumors. Neural signals reach cancer and support cells through synapse-like contacts and chemical messengers, shaping immune behavior. The review gathers evidence that this traffic can exhaust killer T cells, expand suppressive populations, and help tumors resist immunotherapy.

The influence runs both ways: tumor signals remodel neural activity, forming a regulatory network the authors call neuro-immune-tumor crosstalk. How neural, immune, and metabolic pathways integrate remains incompletely understood, and a young field called cancer neuroscience has formed around the question. Proposed responses include nerve modulation, neuroactive drugs, and combinations with immunotherapy to sharpen precision treatment.
pmc-13551795:
Merve Armagan-Bogatekin published a 2026 study of how language shapes chats with ChatGPT. Thirty-three bilingual users talked with the bot in Turkish, their home language, and in English. Each talk was followed by an interview of about half an hour. Topics covered skill, cultural fit, feelings, and how human the bot seemed. The author coded the talks for themes.

Users with weaker English saw the bot as more human in Turkish. They also felt closer to it in their home language. English chats struck them as more efficient and smart. Culturally specific phrases sometimes landed poorly. The author calls this a trade-off between warmth and perceived skill. She warns that 33 users cannot speak for all.
pmc-13554095:
Azusa Asai leads an eight-author team using eye tracking to reveal how experts inject a single sperm into an egg in a 2026 study. The task, part of fertility care, takes years of training to master. Judging skill has rested mostly on embryo outcomes rather than on the worker's craft. The team filmed and compared the gaze of experts and beginners during the delicate work.

Experts finished faster and with far steadier timing than beginners. With practice the novices sped up, yet stayed uneven, above all while turning the egg. Their eyes also lingered longer and jumped more often between points. Experts showed tight, repeatable gaze paths. The authors see such gaze records feeding machines that grade skill or guide robotic help.
pmc-13554195:
Alexandra Manchel and colleagues used patient-specific computer models of liver metabolism to hunt for treatments for alcohol-associated hepatitis, publishing the work in 2026. This acute liver disease has almost no drug options beyond steroids, which help only some patients and raise infection risk. The team built 89 personalised metabolic models by merging a generic human cell model with liver gene-activity data from patients of varied severity and healthy controls.

Simulated knockdown of two sugar-processing genes, Hkdc1 and Pkm, pushed metabolism back toward a healthy pattern, and a new glucose-use score tracked disease severity and predicted who would respond. The score held up in an independent patient dataset. The authors propose targeting those two genes as a metabolism-based therapy worth testing for reversing the disease's warped glucose handling.
pmc-13554295:
Meltem Yağcıoğlu and Mehmet Salim Öncel apply a standard river model to the polluted Dil Stream in Kocaeli, Turkey, in a 2026 study. Farm, home, and factory waste flows into the stream's southern reaches. The team split the stream and its branches into eleven reaches and sampled twenty-eight points over twelve months. Four measures were modelled: acidity, oxygen, organic load, and nitrogen.

April data tuned the model, and November data tested it fresh. Fits ran strong for most measures, with organic load and nitrogen matching best. Error scores stayed modest in both tuning and testing rounds. As the first such model for this stream, it gives managers a base for trying cleanup scenarios before spending on works.
pmc-13554595:
Zunaira Aamir leads a seven-author team reporting chronic myeloid leukemia care in Pakistan, where newer drugs and testing remain scarce, in a 2026 study.
