Records covered seventy-three patients treated in Karachi between 2018 and 2025. The older drug imatinib served as first treatment for nearly all. Responses were judged by blood recovery and by molecular tests where available.

About a third of patients reached an optimal response, while nearly half met failure marks. Middle risk scores and unusual gene-test patterns tied to weaker blood recovery. A decision to switch therapy strongly predicted a better overall response. Only two patients advanced to the blast phase. The authors urge public-private teamwork to widen access to modern drugs and monitoring.
pmc-13555895:
Solama Akter Shanta leads a six-author team measuring how lameness changes milk in Bangladeshi dairy cows in a 2026 farm study. Sixteen lactating Holstein-Friesian cows were followed at one commercial farm over a year. Twelve lame cows were sampled before, at, and after diagnosis, while four healthy cows gave baseline values. Milk yield came from farm records and quality from a bench analyser.

At diagnosis, daily yield had dropped by about a fifth from pre-lameness levels. Cell counts signalling udder inflammation more than doubled. Conductivity, acidity measures, fat, lactose, and total solids all rose as well. Lameness scores correlated strongly with those inflammation markers and against yield. The authors stress early hoof care under tropical farm conditions.
pmc-13556095:
Domitille Palix and three colleagues pooled in 2026 what studies say about sleep in people receiving methadone treatment for opioid use disorder. Poor sleep is often mentioned in clinics, yet no one had gathered its frequency systematically. Their review covered 38 articles, and thirteen studies that used a standard sleep quality scale fed a prevalence analysis, with the rest summarised in words and tables.

About three quarters of patients counted as poor sleepers on the standard scale, and the authors estimate that future studies will find between half and nearly all patients affected. Daytime sleepiness reports ranged widely, and overnight recordings showed poor sleep efficiency plus frequent sleep apnoea. Evidence certainty was rated moderate. The team urges clinics to ask about sleep routinely and to weigh the social vulnerability that travels with it.
pmc-13559595:
Wen and colleagues published a 2026 umbrella review on diet and lung cancer risk. Umbrella reviews grade the strength of many past reviews at once. The team gathered 57 meta-analyses covering 57 diet-related factors. They rated both study quality and the strength of each claimed link.

Folate, a B vitamin, linked to lower risk with moderate-grade evidence. Most other factors rested on low or very low grade evidence overall. Healthy eating patterns tracked with lower lung cancer risk in pooled data. Western meat-heavy patterns and high sugar-load diets tracked with higher risk. The authors warn that weak methods bar strong causal claims today. Better forward-looking cohort studies top their list of needs ahead. Weak control for smoking habits clouds many of the pooled diet claims.
pmc-13560395:
Mehdi Oudrhiri Safiani and colleagues report idiopathic posterior reversible encephalopathy syndrome in a four-month-old baby, an age where this brain swelling state is almost unheard of. Their 2026 case report tells of a healthy baby brought in with repeated seizures and no fever. Blood work, spinal fluid, and CT scanning all looked normal.

MRI told the story: matching bright patches across both occipital lobes on fluid-weighted scans, with signal changes hinting at a mix of vasogenic and cytotoxic swelling. Wide testing found no high blood pressure, body-chemistry fault, infection, immune attack on the self, or toxin to blame, leaving the case idiopathic. Seizure drugs calmed the fits, and the early course stayed good with no quick return. The authors urge clinicians to consider this diagnosis in unexplained infant seizures and stress MRI early, plus long developmental follow-up given the uncertain outlook.
pmc-13560595:
Catherine Falconer and colleagues argue that chronic school absence should be treated as a public health priority rather than a purely educational problem. Their 2026 framework paper notes that missing more than a tenth of school time now affects over one in four American students after the pandemic. The authors synthesize evidence across education, public health, and child development.

Attendance, in their model, reflects layered determinants from the individual child out to family, school, community, and structural conditions. Poor health, unstable housing, and unreliable transport sit largely beyond any school's control, yet current responses lean on individual responsibility. Three principles guide their alternative: treat attendance data as a vital sign of student and system well-being, build cross-sector partnerships with aligned goals, and design strengths-based prevention. Without the reframing, they warn, efforts will stay fragmented and underpowered.
pmc-13562095:
Mustafa Yildirim and colleagues publish a correction to their registry study of type 1 and type 2 heart attacks occurring in atrial fibrillation, drawn from the HERA-FIB registry. The 2026 notice, issued in Clinical Research in Cardiology, fixes three passages of the first article version that had escaped correction before print. The underlying study weighed predictors of a composite clinical endpoint and troponin changes by trigger.

One fix lowers the hazard ratio for prior heart attack among the endpoint's predictors, from the printed value to a corrected estimate with a revised confidence range. A second corrects the log-rank p-value in a survival figure legend. The third redoes a figure caption on troponin change by trigger type in type 2 cases, shifting which triggers rank where. The notice states the original article has been corrected. Readers of the registry findings should use the amended numbers.
pmc-13562495:
Yuxuan Xu and three colleagues examine a recently described form of cell death, disulfidptosis, and what its gene signature means for stomach cancer. The death pathway triggers when cells starve for glucose, yet its link to patient outcomes was unclear. The 2026 study merged single-cell and bulk gene data from tumours to find core genes, built a survival model, and mapped how marked cells talk to immune cells. Three genes stood out: SPARC, CYR61, and TIMP1.

High signature scores went with certain mutations and with tumours emptied of immune activity. Cells carrying SPARC and CYR61 sat mostly in vessel lining and fibroblast populations, the support tissue of the tumour. Signalling from those cells appeared to quiet B cells, T cells, and other immune defenders through named receptor pathways. The authors propose the signature as a forecast tool and a guide for tailoring immune therapy.
pmc-13563695:
Davide Coraci and five colleagues audit the last, least-studied stage of newborn hearing screening in Italy's Friuli-Venezia Giulia region. Finding deafness early shapes a child's language and learning, and screening programmes promise a stepped path from first test to treatment. The 2026 study examines Level 3 of that path, where diagnosis is confirmed and care begins. Records covered 106 children enrolled from 2019 to 2023. The team mapped how babies move between birthing centres, paediatricians, hospitals, and the regional specialist centre, splitting the stage into four phases.

The weak points were organisational rather than medical. Handoffs between local and specialist facilities set off cascade effects that delayed diagnosis and the start of treatment. False positives, lost follow-ups, and patchy documentation all surfaced in the flow data. The authors argue that fixing coordination, not buying better tests, is where this programme gains most, and they sketch directions for tightening the chain.
pmc-13563795:
Ke Yang and eight colleagues use genetics to ask whether inflammation causes head and neck cancer, or the cancer stirs the inflammation, or both. Ordinary studies cannot untangle that loop. Their 2026 approach, Mendelian randomisation, treats inherited gene variants as natural experiments, since genes are fixed before disease begins. Two-sample and two-step mediation designs linked the cancer with immune cell types and inflammatory proteins, and gene and protein datasets checked whether the flagged players shift in patients.

Three factors looked protective: the chemokine CXCL11, the immune switch CD40, and part of the interleukin-10 receptor. One protein, cystatin D, raised susceptibility. The cancer itself causally reshaped immune populations, from T cells to natural killers. Single-cell data showed CXCL signalling between monocytes and T cells. The authors frame inflammation and this cancer as mutual drivers, with CXCL11 a hub worth targeting for detection and immune therapy.
pmc-13563895:
Suli Yang and four colleagues profile COVID antibodies in a Chinese cohort and then hunt for fragments that mimic human proteins, a suspected route into long COVID. Their 2026 study assayed blood from 315 healthcare workers for the markers IgM and IgG plus neutralising antibodies, sorting results by age, sex, vaccine timing, and symptom history. Screening compared spike and nucleocapsid stretches against human proteins for lookalikes, and a plate assay tested patients' blood for antibodies against those mimics.

Exposure was universal: 97 percent carried IgG and 94 percent neutralising antibodies. Ageing tilted the pattern, IgM rising while IgG and neutralisers faded, and women ran higher IgG than men. Neurological symptoms came with stronger antibody levels. The screen found 29 candidate mimics in spike and 10 in nucleocapsid. Eight peptides drew antibodies over twice as strong in infected patients as in the uninfected. The authors link cross-reactive antibodies to the autoimmune thread of long COVID.
pmc-13569595:
Amber Franich and colleagues ran workshops where emergency clinicians ranked warning signs that a patient's problem may stem from their medicines. Pharmacists in emergency departments cannot review everyone, so they need a short list to find high-risk patients early.

Fourteen clinicians from two Gold Coast hospitals, six pharmacists, five nurses, and three doctors, took part in two one-hour sessions. They cut a long list of 34 possible criteria down to twelve, then to a final six. Top ranked was a presentation the patient or team blamed on a medicine, followed by bleeding and falls. Other picks covered patients unable to give a clear history, unverified medicine lists, and drugs needing blood level checks.
pmc-13571395:
Anudeep Nakirikanti and colleagues present, in a 2026 case, a 35-year-old with vascular Ehlers-Danlos syndrome who suffered repeated acute coronary events from spontaneous coronary artery dissection. The syndrome is a fragile-vessel genetic condition. The dissection, a tearing inside a heart artery wall, was found on CT angiography. Each episode brought renewed decisions about intervention.

After every event, a full heart team chose medicine alone, and symptoms settled without stenting or surgery. Few guidelines cover recurrent events in this setting, leaving teams to judge who truly needs a procedure. The authors argue that structured heart-team judgment, not habit, should drive care when evidence runs thin and vessels are fragile.
pmc-13571495:
Gu and colleagues mapped in 2026 how Japanese encephalitis virus rewires building-block metabolism in brain cells. The virus is a mosquito-borne cause of brain inflammation in Asia and is built from RNA, which needs pyrimidine bases as raw material. Using single-cell gene data, the team charted pyrimidine metabolism cell type by cell type. They paired the maps with lab assays of viral growth.

Viral replication depended critically on cells making pyrimidines from scratch, the de novo pathway, rather than recycling them. The virus also created dependence on glutamine uptake and on aspartate production through an enzyme called GOT. Those dependencies expose possible drug targets: blocking de novo synthesis should starve the virus of building blocks. The authors frame metabolic dependence as a vulnerability for antiviral design.
pmc-13571795:
Stevens and colleagues ask who confirms a prenatal screening result with a diagnostic test, and who does not. Blood based screening can flag a sex chromosome variation, an extra or missing X or Y chromosome. Only a procedure such as amniocentesis can confirm it, and many flags prove false. Their 2026 study reviews 692 patients with positive screening results who had counseling at two centers between 2014 and 2024.

Only one patient in four took diagnostic testing. Those who did were older, lived in richer areas, came to counseling earlier, and more often held commercial insurance. Testing rates ran higher for non Hispanic Asian patients. They ran lower for non Hispanic Black and Hispanic patients, and lower when the screen suggested variations. In adjusted models, deprivation and insurance type were the drivers, while Spanish preference and interpreter use tracked with lower uptake. Access, not choice, shapes follow through.
pmc-13572495:
Soumyajit Das, with six colleagues, reports a 2026 study of sound-based welding for battery parts made of unlike metals. Ultrasonic welding joins aluminium to copper-nickel parts in lithium-ion battery packs without melting them. Joint quality sets both strength and how well current flows, which matters for energy storage systems.

The team varied press force, weld energy, and vibration size, then measured shear strength and electrical resistance. Press force and energy shaped strength more than vibration size did. Strength peaked at 942 newtons in one setup and 236 in another, then fell as extra energy overheated the joint. Resistance dropped as weld energy rose. The weld face grew harder than either base metal. Cross-section scans tracked mixing at the seam to judge weld quality.
pmc-13572895:
Sarah Moreau, with three colleagues, compares lab methods for splitting mirror-image forms of five azole drugs. Azoles serve as medicines and farm chemicals, and the two mirror forms of a drug can act quite differently in the body. Clean splits are needed to test each form on its own.

One route used a column packed with human serum albumin, a blood protein. It split one azole in part and a second weakly. The team then tried eight ring-shaped sugar helpers in a capillary method, which needs tiny amounts. Two helpers split four azoles well under set buffer mixes. The fifth, penconazole, resisted all single helpers, so a pair of helpers in a basic buffer achieved its first full split in this work. Low helper doses keep the methods cheap to run.
pmc-13573395:
Peipei Wei, with seven colleagues, reports a 2026 study of a plant enzyme that unexpectedly made drought tolerance worse. The enzyme, PpBMT, comes from a medicinal plant and builds coumarins, a family of scent and defence compounds. The team switched it on in Arabidopsis, a standard lab plant, and tested the plants under mock drought.

Under dry stress, the altered plants fared worse than normal ones, with less growth, less leaf water, and less green pigment. Their water balance and damage defence systems both faltered. Drought genes first spiked, then fell quiet in a disordered pattern. The altered plants did hold more coumarins, but not the enzyme's direct product, which hints at wider network upset. The authors warn that piling up a compound does not by itself buy stress strength.
pmc-13573595:
Zhu and colleagues built PSTN, a framework that fuses single-cell and spatial measurements across time. It follows a fungal infection of rice as it unfolds, in a 2026 computational study. Rice blast, caused by the fungus Magnaporthe oryzae, can cut yields by up to a third, and the infection rewires both host cells and tissue layout. Existing integration tools treat each time point separately and lose that continuity.

Zhu trained their network to map cells to tissue locations stage by stage while a temporal rule ties neighboring stages for consistency. On rice data at zero, twelve, and twenty-four hours, the method beat four rivals across three gene-set sizes, holding reconstruction error low with correlations. Shuffled-gene controls collapsed performance, proving the mapping uses cross-modal correspondence. An mouse cortex dataset supported the reconstruction engine, and the authors offer the tool for systems.
pmc-13575095:
Karen Blackmon and colleagues created and validated a scale that measures felt safety across a whole lifetime, in Kenyan adults. Safety supports mental wellbeing and may shape brain ageing, yet existing scales miss cumulative experiences across life stages and settings. Their 2026 study built the Lifetime Sense of Safety scale, which uses a red-to-green visual scale to rate felt safety retrospectively, and tested it for consistency and reliability.

Two related factors emerged, childhood safety and adulthood safety. Women and people experiencing poverty reported lower lifetime safety, and total scores fell as stress and anxiety rose, and rose alongside resilience and memory. The authors present the scale as a valid tool for studying how lifetime safety shapes brain health, and they call for longitudinal work linking it to hormones, inflammation, and brain imaging.
pmc-13575195:
Karthikeyan Sathasivam leads a 2026 study making biodiesel from a green microalga and adding hydrogen to clean up diesel engine running. The alga, Nannochloropsis, stores energy-rich oil. Ultrasound helped draw out about 720 millilitres of bio-oil, which was converted to biodiesel with 92 percent extraction efficiency in a single-pot process.

Fuel checks used magnetic resonance, chromatography, and infrared methods to confirm the product was fit for use. A blend called B20, mixed with hydrogen, burned more steadily than plain diesel, with slightly higher peak pressure and heat release. Smoke fell from 62 to 44.8 percent opacity, and carbon dioxide output dropped from 9.3 to 8.5 percent. Nitrogen oxide levels stayed in a similar range. The authors call the blend a cleaner option for diesel engines.
pmc-13576195:
Heli Järnefelt leads a 2026 Finnish register study asking whether short psychotherapy at primary care level leads people into long-term therapy later. Health systems must ration scarce therapy resources wisely. The data came from national registers combined with the country's largest occupational health provider.

The cohort covered more than 1.26 million working-age Finns. Taking part in primary care level therapy between 2019 and 2020 linked to a much higher chance of long-term rehabilitative therapy in the next two years, with odds ratios between 7.05 and 15.51 across models. A history of mental disorder also raised the odds. Older age, female sex, and higher social position added further likelihood. The authors suggest planners can use these patterns to forecast demand for long-term therapy.
pmc-13578295:
Ali Melih Kanca and İlker Türker built a detection system called GraphDL that turns network traffic into graphs before hunting for cyber-attacks. Flow data were cut into time windows, and a visibility graph was drawn for each traffic feature. Measures such as centrality and clustering were then pulled from those graphs and fed into a convolutional neural network classifier.

Tested on the CICIDS2018 data set, accuracy ranged from about 76 percent to about 97 percent depending on window and feature choices. A simpler model using raw flow features performed strongly at far lower computing cost. GraphDL therefore offers a structural way to capture timing and nonlinear patterns, but its extra computation must be weighed against that advantage.
pmc-13578395:
Yanling Lan and co-authors ask what makes chat with an AI feel like real mental health support for young adults, in a 2026 mixed methods study. Just over one thousand users aged 18 to 35 took a survey in mid 2025, and fifty users gave long interviews. Support here means what users felt they gained, not a clinical result.

Trust in the chatbot strongly predicted both a sense of warmth and healthy use habits. Healthy use meant steady limits, clear goals, and reflection on the habit. Only healthy use linked directly to felt support, and it carried the effect of trust. Strong attachment to the AI and a sense that it acts on its own both weakened the chain. Warmth alone read as a surface cue, not the cure.
pmc-13578695:
Ningning Che and colleagues asked whether a blood test can warn which early Parkinson's patients will develop motor complications. Levodopa, the main Parkinson's drug, often brings motor fluctuations and involuntary movements over time, eroding quality of life. Their prospective study followed 173 early-stage patients for up to seven years, measuring five blood markers at baseline, one year, and two years.

Motor fluctuations struck 41.6 percent of patients and dyskinesias 17.9 percent. Those who developed complications started with higher neurofilament light chain, GFAP, and amyloid-beta 40, but only neurofilament light chain predicted complications on its own after adjustment. Higher levodopa dose and worse anxiety and depression also predicted trouble. The authors propose the blood marker for early risk sorting.
pmc-13579395:
Fenna J de Bie and colleagues tested aclarubicin, a cancer drug, on cells taken from patients with skin T-cell lymphoma, a rare skin lymphoma. Old drugs in this class, such as doxorubicin, harm the heart and so have strict dose limits, while aclarubicin harms chromatin with no such build-up of heart harm. Tumour cells and normal CD4 T cells were both exposed to a set of these drugs in lab dishes.

With a brief two-hour dose that mimics blood levels in patients, aclarubicin killed tumour cells at far lower doses than the rest, with a half-kill dose eight to twenty times lower. It also did better when T cells were switched on. The drug merits more lab and clinic tests in this lymphoma.
pmc-13581295:
Makoto Tahara and a large trial team report five year results for gentler chemo dosing with radiation after surgery for advanced head and neck cancer, in a 2026 follow up. The Japanese trial had assigned 261 patients by chance to the standard drug plan, a high dose every three weeks, or a smaller weekly dose. An early read said the weekly plan was no worse for survival.

With a median watch near five and a half years, five year survival ran higher in the weekly arm on paper, and the formal no worse test passed with room to spare. Cancer free spans also leaned weekly. No late side effect split the arms by much. The authors lock in weekly dosing as a sound standard option for patients whose high risk tumors were cut out first.
pmc-13582695:
David Wong, Ethan Allen, Yitong Li, Terese Bird, and Jitendra Mangwani interview medical students about near peer teaching. Their 2026 study sits at the University of Leicester. The topic is bone and joint exam skills, an area where new doctors often graduate shaky, though such cases fill clinics. Twelve students who had near peer tutoring for their practical exams spoke in semi structured interviews until themes ran dry.

Four themes came out: the learning setting, exam craft, the tutor's traits, and scheduling. Students prized the safe feel and the fresh exam tips only a recent passer can give. A tutor's warmth and drive mattered as much as knowledge. Running the sessions outside class freed some students and squeezed others, so the group suggests folding near peer teaching into the timetable itself.
pmc-13584595:
Shouwen Zhang and colleagues run a school-year mini basketball program for preschoolers in urban China in this 2026 trial. Basic movement skills, such as running, throwing, and catching, build the base for later active life, yet many young children lag behind where they should be. Eighteen whole classes were assigned by chance to mini basketball or to the usual gym curriculum.

Children in the basketball classes gained more movement skill over the year than children in regular classes, beyond what growing older alone would explain. Gains in ball-handling skills depended on age, with four- and five-year-olds improving more than three-year-olds. The authors present the program as a workable way for preschools to build movement skills during the normal school day.
pmc-13584895:
Cristina V. Lopez-Gallego, Monika Timmer, Jocelyne Vreede, and Marcellus Ubbink probe a tiny bond that helps bacterial enzymes defeat antibiotics. The enzymes, class A beta-lactamases, break down penicillin-type drugs, and they are built stiff so their working parts sit in exact places. Two building blocks just behind the active site, numbered 233 and 246, share a short hydrogen bond in nearly all such enzymes.

Working with the tuberculosis bacterium's version of the enzyme, the team swapped each block for a simpler one to break the bond. The change hurt activity and stability only slightly, and swapping block 246 hurt more than swapping 233. Computer motion studies showed the working parts settling into less active poses. The picture that emerges is of a backup network that fine-tunes the active site rather than a single key support.
pmc-13585995:
Krzysztof Marek Mitura, Piotr Konrad Leszczyński, and Sławomir Dariusz Szajda introduce a journal collection on ambulance care before the hospital. Out-of-hospital emergency services start with the emergency call and end at the hospital door, and how they are organized shapes whether patients live or die. The editorial frames the collection around how such systems are built, what they do, and where they are heading.

Studies in the set cover system design in several countries and the blending of ambulance care with primary care in rural areas. Others model where to place resources, build registries for public defibrillators, or study the training and resilience of the crews themselves. Read together, they show a field moving from a race-the-clock transport model toward joined-up, data-led care centered on the patient. Gaps remain, above all in testing system-wide changes before they are rolled out.
pmc-13587495:
Nour Yazbek and colleagues chart gestational diabetes at a large Beirut hospital across five years that included the pandemic. Gestational diabetes is high blood sugar first found in pregnancy, and it endangers both mother and baby while forecasting later diabetes. Their 2026 study pulled records for 2,595 mothers who delivered at Beirut's Hôtel-Dieu de France hospital between 2018 and 2022.

Across the whole span, about four in a hundred women had the condition. The share more than doubled over the period, from under three percent to over six, with a peak landing in 2020 as COVID-19 and Lebanon's economic collapse struck together. Older age and obesity at the start of pregnancy were the clear risk marks. The authors call for stronger prevention, screening, and treatment plans matched to local needs.
pmc-13590495:
Shu-cheng Huang and colleagues showed that dietary strontium eases tibial dyschondroplasia in broilers through the gut-bone axis. This leg disorder plagues fast-growing broilers, harming welfare and production, and strontium's bone benefits were known but its gut-mediated mechanism was not. Their 2026 study fed affected broilers 200 milligrams of strontium per kilogram of feed and tracked bones, gut microbes, and metabolites.

Strontium restored tibial microstructure, corrected blood calcium and phosphorus, aligned cartilage cells, raised bone density and blood-vessel growth, and switched on bone-building pathways while suppressing bone-resorbing RANKL signals. It also reshaped gut microbes, boosting Pediococcus pentosaceus and cutting Levilactobacillus brevis, changes tied to lower levels of the bone-harming metabolite 9-cis-retinoic acid. Added retinoic acid worsened disease, while strontium co-treatment blunted that harm.
pmc-13591195:
Eiichiro Ono and colleagues traced how dodder weeds, which live off host plants, gained the knack to make sesamin, a plant chemical once tied to sesame. Dodders hold twins of the sesame gene CYP81Q1, and the gene's proteins still make sesamin in lab tests. Gene trees point to a jump from a Lamiales host into an old dodder line.

Dodder attack itself seems to drive the jump, since attack lifts host gene use and gene flow through the sucking root joint. Once in dodder, the gene gained introns step by step, many marked by jumping-gene cuts, while its work stayed intact. Gene jumps through parasites, then intron gain, thus give plants a fresh path to new chemistry.
pmc-13591795:
Renad Alhomidi Almotiri leads a 2026 review of numbing methods for injections into the eye, a treatment many retina patients must repeat for years. Pain at each shot can push patients to quit care. The team gathered 14 trials with 1,300 patients that scored pain on standard scales. Drops of lidocaine, tetracaine, and proparacaine were the main options compared, along with add ons such as cooling patches.

All three main drops gave mild pain scores, with no clear winner among them. Cooling patches, though, cut pain further, and one weaker drop paired with cooling scored best of all. Numbing shots under the eye surface caused more bleeding and swelling than drops. The team advises standard drops plus simple cooling.
pmc-13592095:
Juan Carlos Gómez de la Torre and colleagues showed that private-lab data can strengthen foodborne-disease tracking in Peru. In lower-income countries, tracking misses private-lab test data, blinding officials to germ burden and drug toughness. Their look-back study read stool-culture data spanning 47,724 samples for Campylobacter and non-typhoid Salmonella.

The bug showed up in four point one percent and Salmonella in two point two percent of samples. Infants faced over 20-fold higher odds than people aged five and older. Cipro toughness topped 95 percent in both Campylobacter species; azithromycin toughness reached eight point two and thirty-eight point nine percent. Salmonella toughness hit forty point six percent for ceftriaxone, thirty-two point six for cipro, and eleven point three for azithromycin. The bug showed age-linked seasons, peaking from July to October. The authors argue private-lab data can speed national tracking.
pmc-13592595:
Md Mamunur Rashid leads a team mapping season by season hotspots of neck blast, a fungal disease that can wipe out rice at the grain filling stage. Their study zone, Cumilla District, is among Bangladesh's most intensive rice areas. Field data from 2017 to 2025 across rainfed and irrigated seasons were sorted with clustering and spatial statistics, then interpolated into risk maps.

One subdistrict, Nangalkot, stayed a stubborn hotspot in the rainfed season, while irrigated season peaks hit several areas at sixty to seventy five percent severity. Weather trends during the crop's reproductive stage tracked the worsening pattern. The maps flagged zones with high odds of severe disease, Rashid and the team report, arguing for local resistant varieties and forecast based spraying.
pmc-13597995:
Omar Mohammed Al Hawwari and colleagues randomized three hundred patients with a major front-wall heart attack. They tested whether adding ivabradine protects the heart in the first months. Ivabradine is a pure heart-rate slowing drug. It was added to standard beta-blocker care. The open-label trial ran at Ain Shams University hospitals in patients whose resting rate stayed high.

By three months the ivabradine group's pumping fraction had improved more than the control group's, and their hearts' filling volume shrank while the controls' grew, signs of healthier remodeling after the attack. Final heart rate sat far lower in the treated group, in the low sixties against the mid-seventies. Assessors of the scans and events were blinded to allocation, strengthening the reading. The authors present early rate control beyond beta-blockade as a promising, gentle lever after this kind of infarction.
pmc-13599695:
McCrossin and colleagues test in 2026 whether online training helps parents of children with neurodisabilities, conditions affecting the developing nervous system, and whether adding a coach helps more. Family well-being was the outcome that mattered.

The randomized trial assigned 454 families to a self-directed online program, the same program with coaching, or a control group. It tracked a standard family functioning score over ten months. Among parents who completed most of the program, both versions improved family well-being compared with the control group, whose scores worsened over time. The coached version produced stronger and longer-lasting gains, especially for family communication. Between one in ten and just over one in four participants across the two programs achieved change large enough to count as clinically reliable.
pmc-13602095:
Boby Muslimin and a large team study the giant featherback in 2026, a freshwater fish once thought globally extinct. Living populations of Chitala lopis were rediscovered in Indonesia's Sundaland region in 2022, and managers need tools to tell groups apart. The team combined DNA from 39 fish across eight rivers with scale shape measurements from eight body areas.

Genetic analysis revealed two family lines: one from Central and South Borneo, and another spanning West Borneo, Riau, South Sumatra, and Jambi. Scale size varied strongly by body position, largest along the side and back, smallest near the pectoral fin. Family line shifted relative scale height slightly, and both line and sex nudged overall scale shape. Males showed larger shape change across body positions than females, though both sexes followed parallel patterns. Scale geometry is a weak quick tool for separating stocks, the authors judge, but the baseline helps protect an endangered fish.
pmc-13602295:
Yeeun Sun and colleagues mapped how dopamine loss and brain blood-flow decline unfold over time in Parkinson's disease. Pinpointing subtypes could sharpen prognosis and personal treatment, yet how the two declines sequence together was unclear. Their 2026 study applied subtype-and-stage modelling to dual-phase PET scans from 708 newly diagnosed patients and 50 healthy controls.

Three subtypes emerged: one starting with one-sided dopamine loss in the rear putamen, one with early diffuse symmetric striatal loss, and one starting with rear-brain blood-flow decline. Dementia risk within four years ran higher in subtypes two and three than in subtype one. Risk nearly doubled in subtype two and nearly tripled in subtype three, while dyskinesia and freezing risks stayed similar. Sun and colleagues propose the trajectories as markers of cognitive decline.
pmc-13609795:
Wanting Rong and five colleagues design a low-power readout chip for precision magnetic sensors. Tunnel magnetoresistance sensors are sensitive and frugal, but their tiny bridge output drowns in DC offset and low-frequency flicker noise. Their application-specific circuit centers on a chopper-stabilized programmable amplifier with eight gain settings up to 128. Extra tricks hold gain steady across the full input range, answer transients faster without burning static power, and calibrate offset digitally.

Built in a standard 0.18 micrometer CMOS process, the chip was tested inside a compact magnetometer prototype. Across a plus-or-minus 100 microtesla range, nonlinearity measured just 0.1 percent of full scale. Magnetic noise density hit 0.13 nanotesla per root hertz at one hertz. The readout chip and sensing bridge together consumed 10 milliwatts. The authors claim an excellent balance of power, linearity, and resolution, positioning the design for portable, high-precision magnetic measurement.
pmc-13612695:
Saritha Ranabothu and colleagues compared outcomes for children receiving kidneys from COVID-positive donors versus COVID-negative donors. Organ shortages delay children's transplants, and donor COVID status was an open question for safety. Their population study drew on the national transplant registry, matching 143 COVID-positive-donor recipients against 1,808 COVID-negative-donor recipients from September 2020 to February 2025.

Use of COVID-positive donors rose from about 3 percent in 2020 to about 11 percent in 2025. Survival, graft failure, delayed graft function, and hospital stay showed no significant gaps between groups over a median follow-up of about 14 months. Ranabothu and colleagues conclude COVID-positive donors are a sound option for children.
pmc-13614295:
Huang and colleagues report a 2026 materials study inspired by vine tendrils, which coil by growing unevenly on two sides. The team built shape-memory polymer composites that can be programmed cold, meaning bent into a temporary shape without heat.  Sugar beet pulp, a farm byproduct, provides the bio-based filler.

Using a magnetic process, the team patterned the composite into uneven zones: a polymer-rich region and a pulp-rich region that answer force differently, like the two sides of a tendril. The mismatch makes the material coil as it recovers, mimicking the plant's trick. Cold programming widens their use, and crop waste cuts reliance on fossil plastics.
pmc-13614895:
Nidhi Parmar comments in 2026 on a two-year trial comparing two ways of clipping a full upper denture onto four implants in the jaw. Patients with no upper teeth received implant-retained overdentures, held either by telescopic attachments or by a snap system sold under the name LOCATOR. Forty patients took part, split at random between the two systems, and also received two implants below for an opposing denture.

Grip strength was measured with a digital force gauge right after fitting, then at one, twelve, and twenty-four months. Scans tracked how much jaw bone was lost around the implants over time. The commentary helps dentists judge which clip keeps its hold longer and treats bone more kindly, a practical choice faced whenever a loose upper denture needs implant support.
pmc-13614995:
Branimir Ivanic led a 2026 review that pooled sensor data on head impacts in team sports, asking how hard the blows are when a concussion occurs. Concussions remain common and hard to predict. Two measures matter: straight-line acceleration of the head and twisting acceleration. The team searched three databases through late 2025. They kept studies that recorded peak values during concussive blows in team-sport athletes, and compared those blows with blows that caused no concussion.

Thirty studies covering 3,262 athletes entered the pool. Concussive blows averaged about 69.6 g of straight-line acceleration against 25.3 g for non-concussive blows. Twisting acceleration was also far higher in concussive blows. Values differed by sport, age, sex, and sensor type. American football was highest on straight-line force and rugby highest on twisting force. Wide overlap between concussive and non-concussive blows rules out any single cutoff.
pmc-13615495:
Willows and colleagues set out in 2026 a way to deliver genes into the nerves that thread through fat tissue in mice, a step toward studying and treating metabolic nerve disorders. Nerves in fat help govern energy balance, but viruses used for gene delivery rarely reach them cleanly. The team screened seven adeno-associated virus shells, natural and engineered, for their reach in the groin fat pad.

One shell, AAV-PHP.S, stood out for lighting up nerve fibers in that fat depot. Dose tuning then cut stray expression elsewhere while keeping nerve targeting. With that setup, the team aimed the virus at one class of sensory nerves and labeled their branches in many colors. They also delivered a designer switch that lets researchers fire those nerves on command.
pmc-13616395:
Manab Mandal leads a team measuring how heat flows unevenly through thin flakes of rhenium disulphide, a two-dimensional material whose lopsided crystal makes its two in-plane directions behave differently. Such direction sense, called anisotropy, matters for chips that must shed heat along chosen paths. Using a laser method that reads two vibration modes of the crystal at once, the team measured heat conduction and heat expansion along both axes in a single setup.

For a five-layer flake, heat ran at about 28.78 units along one axis and 22.25 along the other, while expansion also differed by axis. As flakes grew from five to eight layers, the gap between directions widened steadily. One measurement capturing both modes at once replaces error-prone paired experiments, and the numbers feed designs for electronics built from low-symmetry flakes.
pmc-13617895:
Ahmet Cavusoglu and Buket Erdem use computer simulation to study a hard clear-aligner job: sliding an upper first molar forward without tipping it excessively. Power arms, small posts that change where force applies, can help, but their best length and pairing were unclear. The team built six finite element models combining arm lengths of six, eight, and ten millimeters with two attachment layouts, then applied a standard forward force from a temporary anchorage screw.

In every model the molar moved mainly forward and toward the gum, with the crown traveling farther than the root tip, the signature of tipping. Longer arms consistently reduced tipping and lowered stress in the ligament that holds the tooth, yet they produced less crown movement and bent the aligner more. Shorter arms stressed the ligament most. The authors conclude arm length trades control against movement amount, and attachment choice fine-tunes the balance.
pmc-13618795:
Giuseppe Dal Ben and a large group of Veneto health officials publish, in Italian, proceedings documenting health care at the Milano-Cortina 2026 Winter Olympic and Paralympic Games. The local health authority ULSS 1 Dolomiti and the Veneto regional service provided top-level care to the world's best athletes while never dropping service to residents and tourists. The authors describe the challenge as unprecedented and worth archiving as an institutional duty.

The proceedings retrace the operating model through accounts. They cover rapid rescue in extreme mountain settings at the field of play, the Olympic polyclinic built at Codivilla Hospital, and the invisible shield of public health and advanced logistics. More than two thousand staff and volunteers took part, including a thousand clinicians, nurses, physiotherapists, and technicians working as one team. The authors call this human capital the legacy, and they note the operation's success was recognized by Olympic and Paralympic leadership.
pmc-13618895:
Anish Kirtane and three colleagues separate environmental DNA in alpine streams into its three physical states, membrane-bound, stuck to particles, and freely dissolved. The three decay at different rates and so tell different stories. Their state-sorting workflow was applied at two hundred twenty-one sites on fifty-eight streams across eight lake watersheds, with genetic barcoding for animals and plants.

Animal DNA appeared in all three states, each holding some unique diversity, but the membrane-bound fraction carried nearly eighty-eight percent of all sequence variants, dwarfing the adsorbed and dissolved shares. Plant DNA showed up only in the membrane-bound state. Only that state also showed clear downstream transport, its reach varying with local hydrology, while lake surface samples turned over to a different community. Water temperature aligned most strongly with community change. The authors say most earlier studies unknowingly measured mainly the membrane-bound state.
pmc-13618995:
Patience Mthunzi-Kufa and six colleagues review how light-based tests could bring lab-grade testing to clinics across South Africa and low-resource settings. There, distant labs, staff gaps, and slow sample transport delay answers. The article measures photonics devices against the World Health Organization's ASSURED and REASSURED criteria: affordable, sensitive, easy to use, rapid, robust, deliverable, connected in real time, and environmentally sustainable.

The advances include small optical biosensors using fluorescence, Raman scattering, and heat-based detection, phone-linked microscopes and spectrometers, cheap laser and LED light sources, and hybrid lateral-flow tests with optical readouts. Linked reporting, they argue, multiplies impact by enabling surveillance and letting nurses run tests under digital supervision. Gaps persist in field validation, quality checks, and training. The authors close with advice on regulation partnerships, human-centered design, shared data pipelines, and investment in local manufacturing so innovations survive outside the lab.
pmc-13619095:
Srividya Neelakantan led a 2026 phase 1 trial of PF-07261271, a bispecific antibody that blocks two inflammatory pathways at once for potential use in inflammatory bowel disease. Current drugs usually hit one pathway, so a single agent aimed at both the p40 subunit of interleukin-12/23 and the cytokine TL1A might work better. The randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled study tested single rising intravenous doses and repeated under-skin doses in healthy adults.

Thirty-five people enrolled, twenty-seven in the single-dose part and eight in the repeated-dose part. The drug was generally safe and well tolerated, with all side effects mild or moderate. Blood levels fell in several phases, with longer persistence at higher doses, and under-skin dosing reached about 48 percent bioavailability. Dose-dependent rises in both targets in blood showed the drug engaged its targets.
pmc-13619995:
Farhat Khalily and three colleagues tested edible gelatin films loaded with citrus peel extracts as a natural wrap for chicken burgers. Extracts from grapefruit, orange, and lemon peels were mixed into the films at three strengths, and wrapped burgers sat in frozen storage for 147 days. The team tracked oxidation, spoilage chemistry, acidity, and several microbe counts along the way.

Films slowed both oxidation and microbial growth compared with unwrapped burgers. The strongest grapefruit film gave the lowest rancidity and spoilage readings on the final day, and the strongest extracts of all three fruits suppressed every microbe group measured. Grapefruit peel also carried the most antioxidants and phenolic compounds, followed by orange and then lemon. The authors propose such films as active natural packaging that could extend meat shelf life without synthetic preservatives.
pmc-13620195:
Menatalla Nadim, Yasamin Mirzabeigi, and Yamac Akgun make a mechanistic case for testing plasma exchange in hantavirus pulmonary syndrome, a lung and heart illness that kills roughly four in ten patients. No drug has proven effective against it. The disease's damage runs through the blood plasma itself, where cytokines, viral proteins, and immune complexes injure vessel linings and flood the lungs.

Plasma exchange physically clears those circulating drivers and already serves many approved uses with a similar logic. The authors argue timing would matter most early in the heart-lung phase, and that replacing removed plasma with donor plasma could also help the disease's clotting problems. They set their idea honestly against the mixed record of plasma exchange in similar conditions. A recent Andes virus outbreak on a cruise ship prompted the piece, and they stress that only a systematic case series could test the idea.
pmc-13620295:
Alemayehu Abebe Guji and six colleagues report a young Ethiopian man whose rectal growths looked like cancer but came from a parasitic worm infection. The twenty-five-year-old arrived with belly pain, blood in his stool, anemia, and weight loss. A camera exam found one large stalked polyp, six centimeters across, plus several smaller flat ones in his rectum.

Tissue testing showed eggs of Schistosoma mansoni packed in the polyps with strong allergic-type inflammation and no cancerous change. He received the antiparasitic drug praziquantel plus iron for his anemia. Doctors snared the smaller polyps with a cold loop and took the big one out in pieces with a heated loop. Three months later his blood counts had improved, stool tests were clear of eggs, and a repeat camera exam showed healed lining, no polyps back. The authors warn against radical cancer surgery before tissue proof in endemic regions.
pmc-13621795:
Lilangi S Ediriwickrema leads a team testing whether a light-based imaging method can measure the skin around the eye in a steady, repeatable way. The method, called spatial frequency domain imaging, reads how tissue absorbs and scatters light, which hints at changes below the surface. No standard values existed for this region, even though eye diseases can alter it.

The researchers imaged twenty-five healthy volunteers and recorded values for areas below the eye and on the forehead, which served as a comparison site. A smaller group was imaged from two angles, and the angle made no real difference to the readings. Darker skin, scored on the Fitzpatrick scale, showed more absorption and less scattering. The team offers these normal ranges as a base for later studies of thyroid eye disease and other problems near the eye.
pmc-13623795:
Maya Honda and colleagues published a 2026 review of how breast MRI should guide local treatment choices under the updated BI-RADS system, version 2025. MRI before surgery is the most sensitive way to size up a new breast cancer, finding extra disease in the same breast in a fifth of patients. Whether that extra knowledge helps patients has long been debated.

The review turns the new reporting rules into surgical guidance. A category flags suspicious spots close to the main tumour for simpler handling. Measured distances carry weight: the gap between tumour and nipple helps judge whether the nipple can be spared, and the gap to skin helps predict clean margins in skin-sparing operations. The authors cover muscle involvement, the new lymph node section, and using MRI to pick candidates for a tumour-burning procedure instead of surgery. Their aim is a shared map for radiologists and surgeons.
pmc-13624195:
Dilara Onan and colleagues published a 2026 narrative review arguing that migraine, migraine-linked neck pain, and low back pain grow from shared wiring faults in the pain system. They are shared faults, not separate local problems. The three conditions often appear in the same patient, yet clinics usually treat each site on its own.

The review gathers clinical and brain research on central sensitization, the state in which the spinal cord and brain amplify pain signals. All three conditions show over-responsive pain circuits, weak built-in pain dampening, and pain that spreads beyond its starting point, with fear of movement keeping the system wound up. Drug treatment for the neck pain follows migraine principles, while neck muscle problems may need their own therapy. Exercise and migraine-specific drugs carry the strongest support among the options. The authors recommend judging and treating the mechanism, not just the painful spot.
pmc-13624295:
Debisa Eshatu Wendimu leads a team translating a children's skin quality-of-life questionnaire into Amharic and checking that the translation still measures what it should. Skin disease weighs heavily on children, and Ethiopia lacked a validated local version of the standard ten-question index. The work sat inside a hospital study of cutaneous leishmaniasis, a parasitic skin disease common in the region.

Translators rendered the questionnaire back and forth between languages, experts checked its content, and children confirmed the wording was clear. Testing on 188 children, about two-thirds of them with leishmaniasis, showed steady internal consistency and strong agreement between raters. Scores separated mild from severe disease, single from multiple sores, and small from large lesions, and they fell markedly after ninety days of treatment as children improved. The authors endorse the Amharic version for clinics and research across Ethiopia.
pmc-13624695:
Guanqun Zhu and co-authors engineer fat-derived stem cells to carry extra CD73, a surface protein, and test them on rats with nerve-injured bladders. Neurogenic bladder, where nerve damage leaves the bladder inflamed and weak, has no treatment that rebuilds the tissue well. The treated rats received the boosted cells after pelvic nerve injury, and cell-culture tests probed how the cells calm bladder lining cells and immune cells.

Treated rats regained better bladder pressure control, smoother muscle layout, and fewer dying cells. Fluid from the boosted cells helped lining cells grow and move while easing their death, and immune cells shifted toward a healing type. Protein surveys showed a broad turn toward repair programs, which supports tuned stem cells for bladder repair.
pmc-13625195:
Erica Bell and colleagues ask how tightly irritability is bound to mixed mood states in bipolar disorder. Mixed states blend manic and depressive signs at once, and clinicians have long noticed a short fuse riding along. The team reworked data from a therapy trial, following 82 patients across ten check-ins over eighteen months and rating both felt irritability and mixed symptoms each time.

Irritability showed up far more often when mixed symptoms were present, and that link held through the whole study, even as treatment eased both mood and irritability ratings. Strikingly, irritability lingered for nearly half the time when no mixed symptoms were present at all. The authors argue irritability sits at the core of the illness, not at its edges.
pmc-13625395:
Matilde Maddaleno, Fernando González, Erika Vivanco, and Venkatraman Chandra-Mouli, publishing in 2026, trace how Chile cut teenage childbearing faster than almost any neighbor. Births to girls aged fifteen to nineteen fell from about fifty-two per thousand in 2010 to about eleven per thousand in 2023. The team read policy files, service data, surveys, and past studies to learn which system changes traveled with the fall.

They credit steady political backing, rights-based reforms, teen-friendly primary care, and wider access to contraception, including long-acting methods. Gains were real but uneven, since poorer and remote areas still show lower contraceptive uptake. The authors warn that a case study cannot prove cause, yet Chile's mix of commitment and services offers a workable template.
pmc-13627895:
Tamer Hodrob and six colleagues compare oral cholesterol-lowering drugs that are not statins, for people whose blood fats stay too high on statins alone or who cannot tolerate them. The team searched four major databases for clinical trials in adults with dyslipidaemia, a condition of unhealthy blood fat levels.

Forty-three trials with more than seventeen thousand participants were combined in a network meta-analysis, a method that compares treatments across separate studies. Drug pairs worked best: obicetrapib with ezetimibe cut LDL cholesterol the most, followed by bempedoic acid with ezetimibe. Side effects were mostly mild, though two drugs saw more people stop treatment, and the authors note that long-term heart outcome trials are still missing.
pmc-13628195:
Wieczorek and colleagues presented three cases, with a linked review, of dormant herpesviruses waking up in ill patients whose immune systems were thought normal, in a 2026 paper. Cytomegalovirus and human herpesvirus-6 live in most adults. Severe illness itself, through sepsis, trauma, or prolonged ventilation, can disturb immune control enough to reactivate them, with growing signs linking reactivation to worse outcomes.

Wieczorek describes one patient whose rising viral DNA in blood came with gut and lung problems. A second patient's reactivation attacked the making of platelets, causing immune thrombocytopenia. A third had rapid decline in nerve function and virus DNA in spinal fluid matching brain inflammation. Symptoms are vague and DNA tests are not always on hand. The authors urge doctors to consider reactivation when an ICU patient deteriorates without a clear cause. They warn that separating harmless viral shedding from disease needs viral load trends and the picture.
pmc-13629995:
Leah Costlow and ten colleagues modelled whether large-scale food fortification also makes a healthy diet cheaper to buy. Fortification adds vitamins and minerals to staple foods. They combined shop food prices and fortification policies from 89 lands. They built thousands of least-cost diet pairs, with and without fortification. The pairs spanned age and sex groups.

The team assumed strong use of current standards. Those cover wheat flour, maize flour, rice, and oil. Median diet costs then fell modestly. The drop ran to a few percent, depending on the adequacy case. Wide gaps appeared between lands and groups. Middle levels of fortification gave the largest savings in their analysis. The authors present well-designed fortification as a useful economic partner. It can complement other policies on food access.
pmc-13630795:
Lucy Zhang and two colleagues reflect, in a 2026 author commentary, on their study of breast cancer surgery. The study covered young women with node-positive cancer. All had chemotherapy before surgery. The question grew from clinic talks. Beyond the share of removed nodes that test positive, does the sheer number removed predict return of the cancer?

Their study split patients into three tiers of lymph node ratio, the positive fraction. All women had at least one positive node among at least three removed. Within each tier, return of the cancer showed no clear link to the total removed. One positive node of three behaved like six of eighteen. The authors call for larger forward-looking work. It should guide how much underarm surgery is enough.
pmc-13631295:
Ming Sun and eight colleagues combined diet records, blood chemistry, and machine learning to sharpen metabolic syndrome risk assessment in a rural Chinese population, published in 2026. The syndrome, a cluster of abdominal obesity, blood sugar, pressure, and lipid problems, affects a third of Chinese adults, and rural diets differ sharply from the urban patterns most studies use.

Among 2,810 adults, four dietary patterns were linked to the syndrome, and blood profiling in 400 participants found seventy-one differing metabolites behind them. Dietary patterns tied to meat and traditional dishes carried risk signatures, while a rice and tuber pattern pointed the other way. Adding the metabolic markers lifted model accuracy substantially, with a support vector machine performing best. The authors pitch the fusion for precision prevention.
pmc-13632195:
Lala Joulha Ian and Lennart Dimberg asked which simple body measurement best predicts heart attack and death in men. Doctors use several measures of body fat, from the standard mass index to waist size and belly depth. In 1993, one thousand middle-aged Swedish men from the car industry took health exams that recorded six such measures. The pair then followed the men for twenty-eight years through national registers.

Useful data came from nine hundred fifty-nine men. All six measures correlated with each other and with known risk factors. Once those classic risk factors were counted, most measures lost their link to heart attack and death. Waist size relative to height held up best, though its edge over the others was small. The authors present that ratio as the more reliable choice in this group, while noting that no measure wins by much.
pmc-13634095:
Nurshad Ali reviews uric acid metabolism through a multi-omics lens in a 2026 paper on cardiometabolic disease, asking whether high uric acid actively drives illness or merely marks it. Once dismissed as a gout byproduct, uric acid is now tied to hypertension, type 2 diabetes, kidney disease, metabolic syndrome, and artery disease. The review weaves together genome studies, epigenetics, gene activity, proteins, and metabolites. It traces how uric acid is made, moved, and felt in tissues.

Key transporter genes, including SLC2A9, ABCG2, and SLC22A12, shape urate handling. Methylation, histone marks, and non-coding RNAs link genes to environment. Tissue-specific studies show how transport and inflammation are tuned in kidney, liver, fat, and vessels. Metabolite studies tie high uric acid to disrupted purine, redox, lipid, and inflammatory networks. Causality still varies by context and pathway.
pmc-13637895:
Tao Pan and twelve colleagues present a multi-omics portrait of cervical cancer in Chinese patients, a population whose molecular profile has lagged behind others. The team assembled one hundred twelve pairs of tumor and neighboring healthy tissue. Each sample passed through layers of analysis at once: gene mutations, copy number changes, RNA activity, and proteins. Linking the layers shows which mutations change cell behavior.

Mutation burden matched other populations, and three mutational signatures dominated, tied to a viral-defense enzyme family, aging, and DNA repair. Three genes stood out as drivers. Pathway activity sometimes agreed across layers and sometimes diverged, warning against single-layer conclusions. Gene and protein patterns nominated cell cycle control and tissue remodeling as targets, with one protein flagged for diagnosis and therapy. Immune profiling split patients into three types. The authors offer the dataset as a resource for precision treatment in Asian patients.
pmc-13637995:
Jona Voss and two colleagues report crystal structures for three related tetrazine compounds, a family of electron-hungry rings prized for fast, selective linking reactions in chemical biology. The starting material carries a protected alcohol arm. Treating it with boron tribromide stripped the protection to free the alcohol, while a brominated version formed alongside. All three solids went under single-crystal X-ray diffraction, with solution spectroscopy completing the characterization.

Packing told the interesting story. The starting compound and the bromide stack their flat rings in tidy antiparallel piles. The alcohol broke ranks: its hydroxyl group hydrogen-bonds to a nitrogen on a neighboring ring, bending molecules into dimers and reducing the ring stacking to a faint parallel echo. That hydrogen bond pattern is rarely documented for this ring family. The authors supply precise geometries for chemists who build marker molecules from these tetrazines.
pmc-13639095:
Xiaolu Guo, with Supriya Sen, Julian Gonzalez, and Alexander Hoffmann, published this 2026 study on how macrophages tell apart mixtures of immune signals. Macrophages are sentinel immune cells, and the work asks how they keep responses specific when several warning molecules arrive at once.

The group built a math model of single-cell responses driven by the protein NFκB, then checked its predictions with live-cell microscopy. They found that the timing of NFκB activity partly reveals which signals sit inside a mixture. Some signal pairs helped each other, while others blocked each other. Blocking arose when pathways competed for shared helpers, and that competition actually sharpened how well cells could tell one mixture from another.
pmc-13639195:
Brogan Johnston led a 2026 systematic review of posttraumatic stress disorder among paramedics, a workforce exposed to trauma yet less studied than police or firefighters. The team searched databases systematically, appraised studies with standard quality tools, and synthesized findings narratively. Forty-three studies covering 12,783 paramedics entered the review, with twenty-nine reporting prevalence.

Reported PTSD rates swung widely, from 1.0 to 82.4 percent, with fifteen studies landing between 14.6 and 40 percent. Weak social backing, poor sleep, job stress, anxiety, and depression consistently raised risk, while resilience, social backing, and a sense of coherence protected. Longitudinal studies hinted at lower rates than cross-sectional snapshots, and no study examined complex PTSD at all. Service leaders get a mandate for longitudinal research, complex PTSD assessment, and support built around sleep, social ties, and workplace stress.
pmc-13643795:
Curtis and Kern analysed in 2026 how the DNA letters around a variant shape how often it arises in people. They used whole-genome data from 500,000 UK Biobank participants. Variants seen exactly 25 times, called AC25 variants, closely mirrored true new mutations in their type mix.

Variant frequencies depended strongly on their three-letter context. Changes from C to T were far more common when the C sat in a CpG context, a C followed by a G. Counts of variant types in a three-letter frame were well explained by seven known mutational signatures from cancer studies. Wider five-letter context mostly added little, but in some cases bases two steps away more than doubled a variant's frequency. The authors say context rules could improve judgements about whether a variant causes disease.
pmc-13645695:
Issah Zabsonre Alhassan and three colleagues survey diagnostic medical imaging students at five Ghanaian universities about artificial intelligence in their field. Their questionnaire went to 296 students between June and August 2024. It asked what students knew about AI tools, whether they had used them, and how they felt about AI entering their training. The study is presented as a first step toward updating course design.

Nearly all students had heard of AI, and most had already used an AI product. Three quarters backed adding AI as a core course topic. Students who believed AI will help medical imaging were far more likely to support that teaching change. Male students also showed stronger support than female students. The authors say imaging programs in the region should build on this openness by adding structured AI content.
pmc-13645895:
Shoichiro Mizukami and nine colleagues report, in 2026, a rare case in which bowel cancer that had spread to the liver appeared to vanish on its own, beside an unusual growth. The patient was a seventy-one-year-old man treated earlier for rectal cancer. Eight months after that surgery, scans showed two liver lesions judged to be spread of the cancer. Part of the liver was removed.

Tissue from one lesion held dead cancer mixed with inflammatory changes rich in a marker called IgG4. Blood tests and lymph node samples then confirmed a body-wide inflammatory condition, IgG4-related disease. Twenty months after surgery the man stayed free of recurrence without chemotherapy or steroids. The authors present the overlap of vanishing cancer and this inflammatory disease as a clue for researchers studying how the immune system can turn on tumors.
pmc-13647095:
Jessica Ball and three colleagues pool trials of single-session, self-guided mental health exercises for young people, in a 2026 review. Such one-shot tools appeal because therapy waits are long, stigma deters many, and some youths prefer to start alone. The registered review searched four databases for randomized trials. Twenty-five trials with 5,628 participants qualified, and nineteen entered the pooled analysis.

The exercises produced a small reduction in anxiety symptoms and a smaller one in depression symptoms. Results varied a lot between studies, and the range of plausible effects in future settings included zero, which tempers confidence. Risk of bias ranged from low to high across the set. The authors judge the tools promising rather than proven, and they call for more and better trials to see whether brief self-help can narrow the treatment gap for young people.
pmc-13647995:
Ahmed Nouh and four colleagues describe a prospective surgical study of fixing broken distal radius bones, near the wrist, with a volar plate while sparing the pronator quadratus muscle. Standard surgery usually detaches that muscle, which is hard to reattach and can leave the plate rubbing on nearby tendons.

Seventy-three patients were enrolled, and the muscle was successfully preserved in sixty of them. All fractures healed, with union beginning by three months in many cases and the rest confirmed by six months. The authors report good function and X-ray results, and they note the approach can be converted to the standard route when reduction proves difficult.
pmc-13649695:
Agata Olearczyk and seven colleagues surveyed a random sample of 1,004 adults in Poland on phone visits with family doctors. Phone care can cut travel and time costs, yet proof that felt time savings drive use was thin in Central Europe. Their survey ran from late 2025 to early 2026.

In simple models, reported time savings showed no clear link to phone visit use. In the fullest model, which also held place of residence and region, the link turned strong: the more time people felt they saved, the more they used phone care. Households in weak money shape used phone care less than rich ones. The authors urge action on regional gaps in digital access and facts.
pmc-13651195:
Marijo Šimunović and three colleagues, publishing in 2026, teach a neural network to proofread genome assembly graphs. Assemblers stitch DNA reads into graphs where errors create wrong turns. Correcting them by handcrafted rules struggles most in two-copy genomes at modest coverage, exactly where sequencing thousands of species gets hard.

Their program, GnnDebugger, uses a graph neural network, a model that learns patterns across connected nodes, to classify each graph edge as genuine or erroneous. The classifier proved especially reliable for diploid genomes at coverage of thirty-five-fold or lower. Feeding its verdicts into a standard read-correction and assembly pipeline produced more accurate assemblies than the heuristics alone. The authors argue that learned correction can replace rule-based cleanup in difficult scenarios and adapt more readily to newly sequenced species, helping scale complete genome projects beyond model organisms.
pmc-13651595:
Christoph Schaefer and two colleagues present ICARION, an open-source simulation framework for following ions as they drift through electric fields and neutral gases. Such motion powers ion mobility spectrometers and mass spectrometers, and many instruments sit in awkward middle regimes where collisions must be tracked particle by particle rather than averaged.

The framework's modular design lets users mix and match field, collision, and reaction models under one structured configuration. It can chain several instrument domains with wildly different pressures and time scales into a single continuous run, as coupled mobility-mass instruments require. Validation exercises covered collisional cooling, two-body reaction rates, and transport in uniform fields checked against established tools. The authors stress that the work validates the framework rather than adding new physics, and they note a built-in field solver for user-drawn electrodes as planned work.
pmc-13658695:
Yuxin Zhang and four colleagues combine published trials to judge whether exercise therapy helps teenagers with adolescent idiopathic scoliosis. Exercise programs are widely offered for the spinal curve, but individual studies are small and disagree. The team searched Chinese and international databases, screened studies by set rules, and graded their quality with a standard risk-of-bias tool before pooling results.

Outcomes covered the Cobb angle of the curve, rotation of the trunk and of individual vertebrae, and quality of life scores from a scoliosis questionnaire. Pooling gives families and clinicians a firmer answer than any single clinic study can, including how large the average benefit is and how certain it looks. The review also shows where the trial evidence is weakest, which tells researchers exactly what the next study needs to fix.
pmc-2020495:
von Elm, Altman, Egger, and co-authors issue the STROBE Statement, guidance for reporting observational studies in epidemiology. Much biomedical research watches people rather than assigning treatments. Reports of such work were often inadequate, making strengths, flaws, and wider relevance hard to judge.

The STROBE Initiative drew up a shared checklist of what authors should report. It covers design choices, bias risks, and how results were reached. Journals and reviewers use the checklist to push for clearer papers. Better reporting lets readers decide for themselves how far a study's claims should travel.
pmc-3398395:
Price reviews and synthesises the first twenty years of PET and fMRI studies of heard speech, spoken language, and reading. Brain scanning had been used to investigate the anatomy of language for over two decades when she wrote. Hundreds of studies had accumulated, with conclusions that did not always agree.

Price groups those conclusions by activity and brain area to build an overview of the language network. Her synthesis offers a reference map for which regions support listening, speaking, and reading. Such maps guide surgery planning and research on language loss after stroke.
pmc-3546795:
Teschendorff, Marabita, Lechner, and co-authors present a fixing method for Illumina methylation beadchip data. The Infinium chip was a leading tool for genome-wide association studies of these marks, which scan methylation across many people. A flaw is that its probes come in two different designs.

The two probe types give widely different data distributions, biasing results if left uncorrected. Their beta-mixture quantile method corrects that design bias. Better correction means reported links between methylation and disease are more likely real, an essential step as such studies inform medicine.  Large consortium studies adopted the correction as part of their standard pipelines.
pmc-4489295:
Metsalu and Vilo built ClustVis, described in 2015, a web tool for viewing clustered data. Principal component analysis, or PCA, is a widely used way to shrink high-dimensional data down to a plottable form. Users often follow it with a plot of two components, yet no easy web interface existed for the method.

ClustVis pairs PCA plots with heatmaps, which show clustered values as colored grids. Scientists can upload a data table and get publication-ready views without installing software. Clustering reveals groups in data from gene studies, surveys, and many other fields. A simple, shared tool helps teams check patterns before deeper analysis.
pmc-4532895:
Agarwal, Bell, Nam, and their colleagues studied microRNA target prediction in 2015. MicroRNAs guide gene silencing by pairing with sites on messenger RNAs. Pairing often involves the microRNA's seed region, but not all such canonical sites work equally well.

The authors combined computing with in vivo crosslinking data to learn what makes a site effective. Many messenger RNAs are targeted, yet context around the site shapes the outcome. Their model predicts which sites in mammalian messages truly repress a gene. Sharper predictions save lab effort and improve maps of how microRNAs control development and disease.
pmc-6027495:
M Danaei and colleagues reviewed how particle size affects lipid nanocarriers in medicine in 2018. Fat-based carriers can hold both water-loving and fat-loving drugs. They protect drugs from breakdown and raise the share that reaches the body.

Size and size spread strongly shape where carriers go and how long they last. Small, uniform particles tend to behave in a more predictable way in blood and tissue. The review gathers evidence on making and measuring particles to hit a target size. Formulators use it to set quality limits before a carrier is tested in people.
pmc-7003895:
Iris Nagtegaal, Robert Odze, David Klimstra, and coauthors presented the 2019 WHO classification of digestive tumors in 2019. The World Health Organization tumor classifications set the shared language of cancer diagnosis. Pathologists worldwide grade and name tumors by these books.

The digestive volume updates types for the esophagus, stomach, bowel, liver, and pancreas. Molecular findings now sit beside microscope appearance in several definitions. Some tumor groups were split or merged to match new evidence. Any lab diagnosing gut cancers works from this standard, which makes the summary widely consulted. The classification is revised on a regular cycle as new tumor evidence accumulates.
pmc-8728295:
Yasset Perez-Riverol and colleagues described in 2022 the PRIDE database, the world's largest public archive of proteomics data from mass spectrometry. PRIDE stores the raw evidence behind studies that identify and measure proteins in samples. It is also a founding member of the ProteomeXchange consortium, which coordinates protein data sharing worldwide.

The article reports the archive's growth and its newer services, including better search and links to other resources. It explains how researchers deposit data and how others reuse it to check findings or ask new questions. Open archives like PRIDE underpin the credibility of proteomics, since claims about proteins can be traced back to shared raw data.
pmc-8758495:
Harald Hampel, John Hardy, Kaj Blennow, and colleagues reviewed in 2021 the amyloid-beta pathway, now placed at the center of Alzheimer's disease research. Amyloid-beta is a small protein fragment that gathers into plaques in the brains of patients. Advances in molecular medicine have tied this pathway to the chain of events that leads to failing synapses, dying neurons, and dementia.

The authors lay out what is known about how amyloid-beta is produced, how it spreads, and how it injures the brain over time. They also discuss the pathway's place beside other suspects, such as tau protein. The review frames the debate behind the newest Alzheimer's drugs, which aim squarely at this pathway.
pmc-8960395:
Marco Solmi and a large team of collaborators pooled in 2021 the world's evidence on the age at which mental disorders first appear. Prevention and early treatment work best when services know when each disorder typically begins, yet the peak ages of onset were not firmly established. The team carried out a large scale meta-analysis of nearly two hundred epidemiological studies from many countries.

Combining those studies, they estimate the ages by which set shares of cases of each disorder have begun, from phobias and anxiety in childhood to later onset conditions. Their findings underline how many disorders start in the teenage years. The results give schools, clinics, and policymakers a factual basis for aiming early help at the right ages.
reflections-and-comments-1865-1895:
Edwin Lawrence Godkin, founder of The Nation, gathered thirty years of his essays in this book, dedicated to Charles Eliot Norton. Its dates, 1865 to 1895, frame the pieces. Topics at the head of the contents include peace, culture and war, and the comparative morality of nations.

Godkin writes on Horace Greeley and John Stuart Mill, on panics, and on the church and science. The South after the war, judges and witnesses, and the role of universities in politics all draw his comment. Lighter pieces treat the morals and manners of the kitchen, summer resorts, and chromo-civilization. The set shows a sharp editor thinking in public about American life.
remote-viewing-evaluation-air-1995:
The CIA paid for a hard count of remote viewing's worth, and the count ended the program in 1995. An Evaluation of Remote Viewing, by the American Institutes for Research and dated September 29, weighs the STAR GATE work in full. Two camps of reviewers split on the lab proof, but the field word was grim.
